Torchlight II is as great as the original, the cartoonish graphics are nice for a change of pace. The game play and difficulty levels are in line with the average RPG of its type. Control on a PC is fantastic, the mouse movements are accurate and easy to control all facets of the game interface.

Torchlight II was made by a devleoper of Diablo II who also created the truly underrated FATE series. As a result this game heavily builds off of both of those other titles and feels like the true sequel that Diablo III should have been. While not everything in the game is 100% perfect, it is improved further by some excellent mods on the Steam Workshop and will certainly keep you entertained for countless hours.
Overall, if you're a fan of Action RPGs or even remotely hink this game might interest you at all, I urge you to give it a shot. I highly doubt you will be dissapointed.

If it cost more than it did, I don't think this game could get away with what it does. Fingered has simple gameplay with easy controls and a great deal of visual personality, but will be overstaying its welcome by the time you're a skilled enough detective to actually finish the game.
The frequent comparison Fingered gets is to Guess Who, and that's certainly apt, but I found that as I chased down all of the achievements it started to also feel a bit like a contemporary roguelite. Similar to how you can luck into a powerful item combination in Binding of Isaac, in Fingered, luck can determine if you have clear and useful clues and visually distinct suspects, or if you're left guessing between similar candidates and hoping for the best. In theory, every set of clues is complete enough to pick out the exact candidate, but the random element is always a factor.
Completing the game requires a thorough understanding of its visual vocabulary- for example, being able to distinguish between goths, punks, and hipsters, or knowing whether a pair of glasses is smart or just stylish, or when a beard is full enough to count as scruffy. Developing this kind of deep understanding of often arbitrary rules of categorization runs the risk of making the simple, early stages tedious to repeatedly navigate for a chance at the more difficult later stages. The single music track can also be grating on the ears. Between these two factors, the game felt kind of irritating to pursue to 100% completion. (At the same time, 100% completion is accessible enough that I still felt compelled to go for it, so I guess it wasn't SO bad...)
But Fingered still offers a fairly unique puzzle experience, and enough of a challenge to make an ultimate victory feel rewarding. And it costs less than two shiny american dollars, so it's easy to overlook the lack of bells and whistles (and volume/music options). And if you're a fan of Edmund McMillen's previous games, it's definitely worth a look, even if the gameplay is a big step away from standard fare.

Having grown up with the Harvest Moon series, this game was right up my alley. Before I mention anything else, I should say that I like that there is support for same-sex relationships (since I'm not straight.)
Getting used to PC controls was hard at first, and the default controls are a bit inconvenient, but they can be changed, so that's not an issue. But that's not the fault of the developers.
While there is still some missing content (for instance, areas of the map that are inaccessible) I expect them to open up in a later update.
Two things I noticed: After saving and exiting the game, the next time I started it up most of the NPCs had forgotten who I was! I had to reintroduce myself to them. Also, my character (a male) is referred to as a female by some of them (another issue I expect to be fixed in a coming update.)
Besides that, the nostalgia is real. It reminds me of the older HM games (before the focus seemed to shift) which I really, really like. If you're already into these types of games, get it while it's discounted.

Early Access Review, 11/4/15
Short Version:  A storycentric farming game that seems like it could be fun in the end, but is still too buggy/unpolished in the current Early Access state to really be so now.  I would give a sideways thumb if I could.
Rather than just another flash/facebook farming game, Wild Season is a farming sim with a VN hook. The filler gameplay is much of what you'd expect from a Farming Sim (clearing, planting, expanding, etc), but the storyline adds a reason to continue and grow.  Even as you strive to build up your dusty little rock of a farm into a glowing field of green, much of the focus is on exploring the mysteriously isolated town you have suddenly found yourself a part of.
All in all, Wild Season is a game with promise, but is the very definition of 'Early Access' - multiple bugs are readily apparent (as of 11/4/15) so only buy at this time if you want to support the devs, contribute to the game's progress, or try it out early while builds become more solid.
Current Bugs/Issues:  There are some graphical hitches with character text alternating speeds and animations repeating strangely (characters dashing in-and-out of closed doors several times before they enter), along with various other gameplay bugs. Additionally, the controls still need a great deal of love - it seems to want to be controller-friendly (and given the 3/4 overhead classic rpg feel, it should be), but many controls are not intuitive or simply do not work without a keyboard and mouse - the 9 hotkeys and menus for instance. However, the mouse/keyboard don't feel quite right either, with movement issues and action delays, so you seem to need 4 hands to use all three inputs at once.  Targeting plots on your farm is also a bit of a chore, and character text does not always respond to a button push, which immediately breaks immersion (and makes the many text-boxes in the long intro rather painful to get through).
In the end, Wild Season might be worth a go - but ONLY if you can tolerate early, still-glitchy builds (especially at the current $16 price point, which is high for an unpolished game).  Judging it as a released product, I have to give a thumbs down, but the devs seem to be actively fixing reported bugs and other issues every week, and listening to all feedback given. So, the game may be worth it eventually, but if you want to buy a finished, product to enjoy fully now, you should probably wait until forum topics and recent reviews can confirm a complete, relatively bug-free experience.

The story seems very nice so far. You play as an inexperienced farm owner, living in a town full of people who are polite, but strangely cold and standoffish.  Why do the townsfolk distrust and dislike you so much? Will they help you with your farm, despite their feelings and your lack of experience?  Will you be able to do this on your own if they don't help? The story is well written, and more than enough to make me want to keep playing.  But there's just so...much...dialogue....   The dialogue text appears on the screen slowly, and I read fast. With no option to speed up the dialogue or skip parts of it, getting through the game's opening can feel like a real chore.  There is however a quick start option, so you can skip the opening scenes completely and go straight to the game.

It's mostly the typical farm sim stuff:  You plant crops, raise animals, clean up your farm and do other management type chores.  Fans of the genre will feel right at home here, and newcomers will be able to get into it easily.  The tutorials can be a bit wordy, but most game tutorials have that problem, and it's not as bad as many.  I haven't run into any major glitches yet.

The graphics are very cute, colorful and 16bit-looking. They fit with the gameplay and story very well, and bring in a huge nostalgia factor, for me at least. I feel like I'm playing a Game Boy Advance or SNES again. The music fits too:  Simple, relaxing tunes that make you feel like you're living a country life.

I played using a mouse and keyboard, and the controls seem to work well enough.  I did have one pretty frustrating issue:  I started playing in windowed mode, and after going through a good 40 minutes of story, I figured out that about half of the controls weren't working.  I restarted (quickplay this time) in fullscreen, and everything worked fine.

The game has the option to raise and lower the volume for music and SFX.  You can also change between a few resolutions and play in full screen or windowed.  Some more resolution options might be nice, but I can't think of much else you'd need for a game like this. Again, I hope they add an option to speed up text for dialogue.  Slowly reading through the opening scenes can be a little painful.

Wild Season is currently an Early Access game, meaning there will be bugs and glitches, your save file may or may not get wiped at some point, and things may not always work the way they should.  This is true for ALL early access games!  Sadly, there will be people who buy the game on a whim without understanding what early access is, and give a negative review based on things the devs haven't gotten around to implementing or fixing yet.  Please don't be one of those people!  You should only buy this game if you enjoy the genre, want to support the project, are willing to put up with glitches, and are interested in providing polite feedback and helpful criticism. Early access is for patient and understanding gamers.

I won't give a rating on Wild Season yet, since it's an early access game and any rating would likely change based on how the game changes.  I will say that's it's a fun little farming sim with cute graphics, good gameplay, nice music and a entertaining story. There are glitches here and there, probably even some that I haven't seen yet. But looking around, I've found that the devs respond quickly to community posts, and there are updates on a fairly regular basis. More than that, I feel like there's a lot of love and hard work being put into this game, and in my opinion, the effort is worth supporting.

----11/3/2015: Build 0.7.0.12----
Wild Season is a very adorable surprise. I originally had mixed feelings about this game, believing it to be another run-of-the-mill RPG Maker game using a new Unity skin. However, this game sets itself apart with Harvest Moon-like gameplay elements providing a breath of fresh air in a sea of stale indie games. Be aware that this review is based off of an early access product.
The story is about a young up-and-comer who recieves a "new" farm in a colorful community. What begins as farming sim slowly introduces scents of mystery as the entire town seems to want you gone. Not if you have anything to say about it....
Although Wild Season shows great promise and interesting gameplay mechanics, it is still full of minor bugs and absent of many fairly basic game options. Below is a list of noticeable bugs (none that are game-breaking) and important suggestions.
For those that are not aware of the Early Access concept, it is perfectly acceptable for bugs to be present and game mechanics to be missing. With that in mind, I would not recommend purchasing the game at this point in time unless you are able to tolerate minor bugs and an unfinished, yet growing story. However, if you do purchase this game, you will be given a chance to help the developers shape the future of Wild Season. I can at least say that I have enjoyed what I've played so far, and hope to see more people get a jump on Wild Season!

After putting about 4 hours into Wild Season, I have to say I am pleased. It is a very easy going farming sim with a lot of depth and extra things to do to keep you busy (I have hardly scratched the surface). The gameplay is smooth and maybe a little bit repetitive but i suspect you get that with most farming sims ;) It has a large variety of crops to plant, as well as trees and animals, fishing, cooking, mining and horse racing. I'm glad it isnt time based like other flash farming sims. It also seems to have a story to it :D
The music is nice enough, though I would prefer more tracks rather than the one on loop, There are several bugs, though none are game breaking (small graphics glitches and the occasional pathing issue) and it is lacking any tutorial on the mechanics, so there is a slight learning curve. The controls were pretty clunky, though the gamepad works great. The artwork is cute and easy to look at.
I will definitely be putting more time into this one!

This is a corny 80's-style retro-future comedic FPS -- a non-serious look at a fictional neon-filled post-apocalyptic 2007.  If you've watched Commando, Predator, Robocop, TMNT, and the like -- you'll probably catch quite a few homages to those.  If you want serious business or anything not covered in massive helpings of cheese, look elsewhere.  If you want a corny power-trip with a goofball plot and a protagonist frequently cracking one-liners after killing enemies, this will entertain.
It's very much in the style of the player as cinematic-level action hero -- you start pretty strong and pretty well armed, and it escalates from there.  There's a bow for silent ranged kills, takedown melee kills that can chain to multiple targets, a sniper rifle that you can upgrade to fire rounds that cause large explosions (think back to the original Robocop), an assault rifle that can be upgraded to fire laser blasts...
It's pretty accessible.  I'm by no means an FPS fanatic, and on the default medium difficulty most things struck me as generally on the easy side -- it becomes not "can I take out this garrison", but "would I prefer to do it quietly, or do I feel like guns blazing, or maybe it's time to lure in a Blood Dragon -- basically, a giant neon-lit T-rex that can fire laser blasts from its eyes -- for some chaos".  There's one main-story mission that has a pretty severe difficulty spike in it, but difficulty can be adjusted on-the-fly.  This is definitely meant more to amuse and entertain rather than challenge and stump you.
It's not a terribly long game.  Got all collectibles (some weapon attachments are unlocked with by accumulating them, so they matter somewhat), finished all side missions (which are almost either 'rescue a hostage' or 'kill a rare instance of one enemy type' at a specific location;), finished all story missions in under 17 hours, and many players will do this significantly faster.   There isn't randomly-generated content other than spawning of friendly/enemy NPCs (with no interaction beyond non-interactive greetings or killing, respectively) and it's not that long until you've been everywhere important, acquired all the weapons, hit the level cap, and killed at least one of every enemy type.
As with most ~recent Ubisoft games, buying it on Steam will not exempt you from needing Uplay.  I experienced no trouble with this.  The game does have some crash bugs, though -- in particular, the game sometimes crashed if I inadvertently attempted to buy a health pack ("nano-meds") from the store when I already had a limit.  Watch out for that if you're on a mission; once you start one, you can't leave the area without failing it and losing progress, and you only get checkpoints -- you can't actually save until you finish or fail it.    Individual missions usually aren't terribly long, but keep this in mind if you only have short intervals in which to play.
Other notes --
Soundtrack suits the game very VERY well.   It's by Power Glove -- @

Also,  this is a standalone expansion.  I've never played any other Far Cry game, anyway, and gather that the rest of the series tends to actually be much more serious in tone.
Was originally $15 and Ubisoft is not averse to sales.   If you don't want two DRM systems for the same game, you could buy it directly via Uplay.

- Being a judge/god/person who controls life. You may have to do "mercy" killings. Or can you afford to care for the disabled while that person could make room for a youngling of strong physique and ability?
- Being a commander. Leading troops into battle. Well, not directly. You kinda tell em "you're a soldier dude" and they go be soldier dude.
- Being an economist. You need to handle scarcity from the second you start your empire.
- Being a merchant. Trade is important and often the only way to get certain items.
- Being stuff I forgot.

Despite those things, I recommend this game to fans of the genre and newcomers. I think they did a good job of streamlining the formula, but I kind of missed some of the broken tropes of it's predescessors.

More of the same from Overlord 1, with some improvements, not enough improvements. The good stuff is still here, and the bad stuff is mostly still here.
The good stuff:
- Funny and fun game! The cheerful villainy of Overlord 1 is still here, with plenty of cheeky British humour and a parody of Tolkien tropes.
- Controlling your minions is as fun as ever. They are a lively bunch, scooping over their targets in a frenzy, picking up helmets and swords and what not for their own use. Their delight in evil is hilarious and strangely endearing.
- The four types of minions have different abilities, strengths and weaknesses. Acquiring each type is a quest in itself, and then you get to utilise them in various combat puzzles during the rest of the game.
- If it's your thing (it's not my thing) you can customise your evil base, invest in different buffs and level up your gear and your minions. There's a whole metagame in there.
- The story never takes itself too seriously, and the whole thing has a light, fun feel to it.
- It's an open world, and you can switch between quests at your leisure, there's no linearity.
- I'm glad there's now a minimap - Overlord 1 didn't have one and it was pain to navigate sometimes. Much better here.
The bad stuff:
- The minions might be fast and nimble, but your player character (the Overlord) is as slow and lumbering as he was in OL1. I get that it's supposed to be this way - you're the heavy tank and they're the quick little rogues - but your slowness is really tedious when much of your play time is spent slowly tromping from point to point. Yes there are portals, but not often enough.
- Controls can be rather fiddly. You're trying to manage 4 different minion groups, setting waypoints, moving them around, while also moving yourself and fighting with your own weapons and spells.
- I haven't finished the game. At least not as of this review. Maybe because I played OL1 and started this right away, but I got rather bored at some point. And the slow movement pace really doesn't help.
----------------
Overall, this gets a big recommendation from me. I suggest you start with playing Overlord 1: Raising Hell, then take a break, then start with Overlord 2.

VERY early access game...one of the earliest. The game probably should not be on Steam's EA yet it is so early in development. And for the current asking price? Absolutely not.
First off, the player is forced to wait through about 15-20 minutes of forced dialog and linear movement exploration. To be clear, there is NOTHING to do during the first 15-20 mins of the game other than click the dialog forward or move to the next building because you are forced to meet the inhabitants. I've never played a game like that, it lost my attention and interest very quickly as a result.
When you finally do get to learning about farming (cleaning up your field), you are told to weed it using your sickle. The problem is, nowhere is it explained how to actually use it (make it work). Clicking Mouse 1 and Mouse 2 does nothing. Nor does spacebar or Enter.
Apparently there are quests to help guide the player through the tutorial, but you cannot access them!  All you see on the side is the title of the quest, most of them using the identical title btw (which prevents them from being anything meaningful). It pops up when it is new and when it is completed. But disappears in between. You have no idea what to do because clicking on them does nothing and there is no Quest Log like there is in 100% of every other game that uses quests as a mechanic.
There is no in-game help, no keyboard settings or keybindings to look at. I had to search the forum for the answer, and seemingly, it's the "K" key.
Once in game, there's no way to exit other than ALT-TAB and close window. ESC does nothing. There is no saving. Plenty of bugs, plenty of non-working gameplay elements, plenty of forced dialog...the devs forgot one of the most important things for a game: fun.  And I had none of it with this game unfortunately. Perhaps when it is further developed it may be different, but as it stands now, I certainly would not recommend this game, especially for the absolutely crazy asking price. There are so many better early access and indie games that are this price or cheaper. There is absolutely no justification whatsoever for the current asking price of this game.

As Mordor lies in ashes, LotRO rises from ashes. With a free 105 level-up included with every Mordor expansion bundle now is the perfect time to give LotRO a try. Outstanding solo content, group patch coming this winter.
Put it simple: the best MMORPG out there.
It's big. What do you think is big? WoW? Check this. If you pay attention, you'll notice that any other MMORPG uses either corridor-like locations, with view always blocked by mountains, trees, buildings etc., or dramatically low draw distance, or both. Well, LotRO draws enormously vast locations with honest draw distance - not GTA V, but nothing like you've seen in MMORPG before. (The Crew was later). When you're in the fields of Rohan, you feel exactly why it is the land of horseriders.
It's authentic. I play this game for 7 years and still I stop and gaze in awe at dwarf lords sculptures in Moria. Still I take screenshots of The Shire. Still I find dozens of new landscape details. This world is handcrafted by the indigenous inhabitants of Middle-Earth - piece by piece, tree by tree, bush by bush.
It's homely. LotRO officially has the best or one of the best communities in online games.
You know, I can go down to the basic mechanics, the classes (see in comments), the raids, the PvP, the unique mechanics like Legendary Weapons and Mounted Combat, but you know what? It's boring. Every game has mechanics, classes, balance and lots of people whine there's no balance. But this game is special. It has... it IS The Middle-Earth. If this means nothing to you, just pass by. You will like it, or dislike it, nothing I can change. But if you love Middle-Earth as I do, or if you are ready to fall in love with it, then we shall meet in White City, one day.

Probably my favorite rogue like game.    Random dungeons with random weapons and strategies for each level.  Lot of fun.  I payed full price and am pretty happy with the decision. Definitely a pick up if it goes on sale though.  Its very pretty and rather than going 5-10 tries without improving your next playthrough,  Ziggurat has close to a hundred unlocks that are added into the random pickups available in the game.

Let me say that I'm not one who oten writes reviews, but my experiences with Ziggurat make me believe it is one worth reviewing.
When it comes to first person shooters I ofen enjoy games that are fast paced and  full of unique options. These would be games like Unreal Tournament, Painkiller, and the Hexen/Heretic series. I also fully enjoy rogue-likes that have the ability to be replayed without being stale, and don't rely one hundred percent on grinding your way to the top.
Ziggurat  is a mixture of all of my favorite points above. There are various characters each with preferred playstyles, boons, and disadvantages. These characters are accompanied by a large variety of weapons that come in three flavors past your pistol-style wand. You have Spells, Staves, and Alchemical Weapons (each eith their own mana pool).  If that isn't enough, theres many different weapons in each category.
There are minions that you encounter in each room, that with familiarity become less of a challenge once you figure out what works against them. Its when you get into a room vith a myriad of enemies that the fun really begins. waiting for you at the end of each floor is a boss who will put your skills to the test.
As you make your way through each floor slaying enemies, you pick up experience that, as it always does, levels you up.  Each time you ding, you are given two options that give you various "upgrades".
Overall this game is worth purchasing for the price of 15 bucks, and also has a wonderful developer who is in touch with the community, and updates are still coming.
Ziggurat is quite possibly my favorite game in my library.
And remember to always check your walls ;)

This isn't a game as much as a cut scene viewing system. Of the hour I have played, by far most of the time has been taken up viewing either unskippable animations - for example 30 seconds for a police woman to check my ID - or long, boring cut scenes.
Some of them are skippable, but some not. Had I not been able to skip the interminable number of poorly written and averagely acted cut scenes I would still be watching about the 6th one.
I simply cannot fathom why a developer would be so poor at writing a plot that it had to be delivered by an actor talking at you. In well written games, the plot unfolds as the game progesses.
The graphics look shiny but would have been "ok" 5 years ago. Now they just look dated.
Other than that, it has none of the depth of the original Deus Ex, none of the playability of the sequels and all of the cutscenes and unskippable animations of both. Combat just isn't interesting and stealth options seem limited, but to be fair I haven't played for long enough to really get a feel for it and I won't be bothering to find out as it is just a frustrating, boring experience.
I think I bought it at a large discount, but whatever I paid - it was too much.

Hare In The Hat is your basic point and click game that takes place in one room. I played both the main game and the Abyss DLC, and I've finished both minus one puzzle in the Abyss.
Pros:
- It's cheap(ish)
- The idea is simple, solve these puzzles in this one room to free the hare
Cons:
- The music kept restarting at weird points. After the first play, it would stop for minutes then start back up randomly. I didn't like that
- This game suffers from the this-puzzle-makes-no-sense virus that several other similar games are victim of
- A select couple of puzzles in both the main and the Abyss are just too hard! The sliding like puzzle in the main game where you rotate the tiles was uncool, but I managed to solve it. The Hungarian rings puzzle in the Abyss was simply torture. I can't understand why the developer thought that was a good idea. If a puzzle is so complex that there are articles about how it relates to cryptography, then that puzzle is too hard for a video game.
I didn't feel much enjoyment or happiness playing through this game, nor did I feel enjoyment when I freed the hare twice. I got both games on a good sale, but I'm still unsure whether or not I can recommend them.

Early access games always involve a gamble with your money; even with the reduced price tag, it is with great regret that Wild Season remains unenjoyable if not completely unplayable in its current state.
While Wild Season may strike as a mere pastiche of the acclaimed Harvest Moon games at first, there is enough potential here to create the same addictive experience which made its forebears so popular. The graphical presentation is cute enough, but in a more imaginative approach to the genre the backdrop teases a more sinister backbone with its setting and characters.
Unfortunately Wild Season is bedecked with far too many bugs, glitches and control issues to sustain any length of playing time. For those reasons alone, on top of the somewhat demanding fee, Wild Season cannot be recommended.
The positive, however, is that the developers communicate often with customers: they display tireless dedication with their continuous updates, with many of the player feedback being immediately acknowledged and applied in quick fashion. The overall vision of Wild Season is assuredly fun if the developers can iron out the kinks and continue to work towards filling in the major blanks missing in this early access version.

First major concern a lot of people have about LOTRO - is it dead?
No. It still has a very healthy playerbase, big enough that the even the RP servers feel populated. So don't let your worries about population turn you away.
This is a classic MMORPG. It's going to be familiar to anyone that has played Everquest, DAoC, WoW, etc. While it means you're not getting any particularly amazing new mechanics, the perk is that LOTRO has figured out how to get the best out of those systems. Leveling feels well-progressed, classes are (mostly) balanced, and there is a lot of variety even within the classes to provide lots of replay value and ways to mitigate strengths and weaknesses.
LOTRO might have the best soundtrack I've ever heard. I recommend turning off battle music and just enjoying the compositions. Bree, as well as the various Inns and Halls located therein, have some fantastic scores attached to them.
Let's be honest though - if you play LOTRO you're probably here because it's Lord of the Rings. And in that regard, you will not be disappointed. The game is steeped in the lore - books and films - and has little nods to it scattered everywhere that are rewarding for someone that is really into their Tolkien scholarship. This is not a LotR skin thrown over a MMORPG framework - this is Middle Earth proper. Even with dated graphics (updates are coming soon, as of this writing) it's still a joy to look at. If you're rolling through some place like the Shire, you'll be able to soak in that sleepy, bucolic atmosphere that the movies portrayed so well.
This is a great MMO experience, and I usually find MMOs tedious. Moreover, it's free - so your excuses to at least try it out are non-existent.

If you are still unsure if you wanna play this game, just download it, its free.

Ziggurat is a challenging first person rogue-lite game. You roam around procedural generated dungeons with various different types of enemies, traps and bosses.
The graphics are appealing, the dark theme is done very well, often at times it is so dark it's really hard to see anything and you have to use your spells to light the way.
Each dungeon is completely randomly generated, you will never run the same dungeon more than once, each room has a chance to either be full of minions, a trap room, or a reward room. Enemies drop experience orbs, every time you level up, you get to choose a special ability/skill, such as increasing the amount of health you get from health pots, or increasing your speed when you are hit. This is a nice feature which makes it feel a little different to other rogue-lite games.
You also have to manage various different mana pools, you pick up different wands and weapons that use the different mana pools, enemies drop mana pots to keep them topped up.
This is actually a really difficult game, even on easy mode, I struggled even on level one on the normal mode, but managed to get all the way to the end level and then fail on easy mode, so even that is a struggle. I have yet to try anything higher because I would just get wrecked.
In order for me to complete a run on easy mode, I had to put three hours into Ziggurat, and this is only the tip of the ice berg of what's actually on offer. I have now unlocked a further four or five characters that I can play, and then there are additional challenges to unlock more. I'd say there is easily twelve more hours of content available here.
I didn't have any technical issues or bugs, its an extremely well put together game, that runs perfectly, running most of the time at 120+ fps.
Ziggurat is probably one of the best rogue-lite games I've played and can definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a magical dungeon crawling challenge.

Ziggurat is a tasty blend of roguelike randomization with 90s era FPS gameplay, featuring rapid movement, no accursed iron sight aiming, loads of enemies and a variety of weapons, all with alternate fire modes and no reloading required. I have heard it compared more then once to the Raven Software classics, Heretic and Hexen and this comparison is apt: Not just due to Its fantasy setting and wizarding weapons, including spellbooks, staves (with one, the Serpent Staff, borrowed from Hexen directly) and alchemical conconctions, but also in its fast, frenetic gameplay, with traps, jumping puzzles, large, projectile-spewing bosses, and for all you Unreal Tournament fans out there, mutators that mix up the battles. The game is very forgiving on its easiest difficulty, affording you a tour of the experience to prepare you for the challenges ahead. I've only just completed my first run, though there seems to be many more items, characters and weapons to find. If you're looking for a test of skill with no doubt a good amount of replayability, you could do worse then to put on your robe and wizard hat, and face the procedurally-generated halls of the Ziggurat.
EDIT: Many runs later, Ziggurat remains a fresh and invigorating experience, and now with the addition of a wave-based "Gauntlet" mode, can be enjoyed in bitesize form.

Ziggurat is a first-person, rogue-lite with a randomly generated dungeon in which you control a wizard armed with spells, staves, and alchemical armaments. With a large variety of perks to choose from with each level up and the many different weapons available to you this game has a high level of replayability.
The gameplay consists of twitch-action shoot and dodge battles that occur as you explore each floor of Ziggurat. The movement and aiming of this game are very tight. It feels good to move around both in and out of combat. There are many different weapons available, each functions in a unique way which allows you to find those which fit your playstyle. A complete run on normal takes anywhere from 40 to 60 minutes with the ability to save and drop out at any time. Easy is not too challenging, normal is a good, solid challenge, and hard mode is a case of "painful.... but in a good way."
The artstyle is in a gothic style with wrought iron, cobbled stone works, and stone statues. Each room is interesting to look at but also influence combat tactics. Having stairs, pillars, and other objects to dodge around causes you to have to adjust to best deal with the type of enemies you are battling.
The music for the game is alright but I found I turned it down after a couple playthroughs. It isn't that the music is bad but that it is repetitive with the same generic soundtrack throughout the dungeon. The sound effects are solid though, each weapons' sounds help create the feeling that makes you want to use it.
Milkstone studios has created a gem easily worth picking up and playing with the addition of Ziggurat.

As you might have guessed, this game plays a whole lot like far cry 3. It has very similar missions, world map, mechanics, upgrades, enemy behavior, collectibles, movement and things like that. If you liked far cry 3, you'll certainly love this game (though I'd recommend not playing it back to back). If you haven't played FC3, I'd reccomend that first, as it is a much larger game.
This game is obviously very different in style; it goes for a black/red/neon-styled 80's cyber-action flick. And it goes all the way: corny oneliners, (deliberately) bad voice-acting and all the tropes you could want ("you don't mow lawns...you mow down lives"). It's not wacky in the way saints row does it, but more of a hommage to the games and movies of those days. It also pokes more than a few puns at modern video games and how they are handled, especially in the loading screen tips ("hints on the loading screen will give you hints").
It's obviously shorter than FC3 (or any AAA-title), but it packs all the fun in the played hours. There's infinite running, extremely fast swimming and all the upgrades you get actually matter. So if you just want to shoot and/or sneak around the place, it has all that covered with nothing of the padding or cutscènes that keep dragging on (they're there, but are so corny they're hilarious...and skippable). All in all, I clocked in 100% in just over 7.6 hours. Money well spent, if you ask me. :-)

Grand Theft Auto V is an incredible game with hours upon hours of entertainment. It has bucketloads of care and attention to detail for just about everything; such as an informative yet simple UI, extremely satisfying and consistent hitreg, hyper-realistic ragdoll physics, semi-destructible environments, unique handling for different cars, well-designed missions, easter eggs, and the list goes on. The story is expertly put together with very few (if any) plotholes, incredibly likeable main characters, and many relateable side characters. The atmosphere is spot on, where every separate area of Los Santos makes you feel like you're really there; from meth farms in Blaine County to Superficial cars and people in the hills to graffiti and gangster-ridden slums, everything is perfect.
GTA Online is not nearly such an instant hit. While the atmosphere is largely intact, and much of the attention to detail is carried over, there are a few massive problems with GTA Online that can make or break it for you. GTA Online awards players money and RP mainly for three things: completing jobs, completing heists, and participating in freeroam activities. Even then, people rarely play any jobs besides the job that gives 2x cash and RP at the time, due to how over-saturated the jobs list is. This also makes the create-a-job feature near worthless, because nobody will ever want to play a street race after they do a rocket voltic stunt race. This narrows your money earning options significantly, as you could imagine.
Heists are incredibly fun the first time you play through them, with tons of dialouge (not yours obviously) and decently entertaining setup missions. However, there comes the problem that missions designed for heavy team coordination do not work well in an environment where you'd be lucky to find someone with a mic that isn't screaming epithets.
This leaves what is, in my opinion, the best money making method: freeroam activities. Owning a motorcycle club/business/corporation/gunrunning is very fun while simultaneously being tense because you're doing it in the company of people who can snatch it right from you. However, this isn't as well-paying as heists, and getting dominated by a 6 person MC is not fun in the slightest.
On the bright side, there are a plethora of things to buy, whether it be to expand your business or just luxury goods. However, this leads to the issue where you can't buy anything because you're not earning enough. But don't worry, shark cards and subliminal messaging come to save the day! With constant annoying calls from side characters telling you to buy things from all the separate expansions, i feel you're being pushed to buy into the shark cards.
And then, the most glaring issue of them all is modders. Modders run rampant in GTA Online. In fact, they run so rampant, that the community got fed up of calling them hackers and began to call them modders. Half the servers you get into, there will be a modder, whether they're openly killing everyone, or just constantly spawning in vehicles for themselves, they'll be there. And on nearly every server, you'll see people asking and begging modders to give them money. And the best part is that R* has employed a team of chimps to stop this from happening, considering so many people have been banned for having the modded money, levels, and weapons
.
On a brighter note, the expansions for online are free, even if you probably can't afford to participate in them; and playing with friends can be pretty satisfying.
If you want to buy GTA 5, and feel like GTA Online is a nice bonus for the pricetag, buy this game immediately. However, if you want to buy GTA Online, and feel like GTA 5 is a nice bonus for the pricetag, go buy san andreas and play with the online mod for that game, because it is, ironically, moderated much more, and has a far less toxic community.

Gnomoria is a game in which you start out with a small team of 9 Gnomes and are tasked with giving those Gnomes various jobs with the ultimate goal of turning the wilderness you start off in into a bustling kingdom. As the value of your kingdom increases, you will attract more "Gnomads", and gain the attention of other kingdoms, both friendly and hostile. If you don't want to deal with the latter, you can set the difficulty to "Peaceful", which eliminates enemy spawns. The game only ends if your kingdom is completely wiped out, or if you get bored and give up. This might sound a bit familiar to some people, as Dwarf Fortress (and Dungeon Keeper, The Settlers, and Anno) was a big inspiration for the game. The developer clearly states this in the FAQ on the game's official website. This game does not have the sheer, unbridled complexity of Dwarf Fortress. It makes up for this by being much more accessible while still having a good amount of depth, and having its own innovations and ways of doing things compared to DF.
Now, the game currently lacks a tutorial, so you will need to either spend the first few hours experimenting to get a feel for things, or consult a guide/wiki while you are playing to speed things up. If that's a dealbreaker for you, I'd suggest waiting until the tutorial is actually implemented, whenever that is. That all being said, the game is still more immediately accessible than DF in my opinion due the graphics and simple mouse-based interface. The game also does not have any actual animation for character movement, somewhat true to its inspiration, but I have personally never found this to be an obstacle to my enjoyment. All it means is that the sprites "jump around" from one tile to the next rather than spending frames actually animating their arms and legs moving, which actually speeds everything up. There's also only one biome available right now, but there are plans to add some more eventually (the two specifically mentioned in the development roadmap are "Desert" and "Jungle").
The game is under active development, with updates coming fairly regularly with a schedule of one update every 2 weeks (minus the occasional hotfix). New features are added often, and as is often the case with such things new bugs will pop up. That being said, the game is very stable and the vast majority of bugs are a mere annoyance. There's nothing truly gamebreaking to worry about.
A common question that comes up on the Steam discussion forums is "how does this game compare to Towns?". I have not actually played Towns, but I know enough to at least say that the gimmick of "attracting Heroes and having them clear out a huge dungeon for you so your citizens can bring up the loot" is not present in Gnomoria. You have to dig your own mines, and you'll have to organize your own military to deal with the problem if you find yourself encountering monsters while you're doing it.
Bottomline: If you're the type of person who is enamored by the idea of Dwarf Fortress, but really just don't want to deal with learning how to wrangle with DF's unintuitive keyboard interface, or if you find DF to be essentially unplayable without throwing a bunch of mods on top of it and just don't want to deal with that, I cannot recommend Gnomoria enough. If you have no idea what Dwarf Fortress even is, but like the concept of the game described at the top of this review, I'd also say it's worth checking out.

Frustrated. That was my initial reaction to this game when I tried it months ago. "What is going on here?!" I thought, before uninstalling it. Recently I gave it another shot and I am so glad I did. If you are considering this game, do yourself a favor and watch a tutorial video covering the basics. A good 30 minute video should do, but give it a shot, it's an amazing game. Additionally, you can watch my first experience with the game here:

Gnomoria is a bit brutal to new players. You'll almost definitely have to follow a guide to survive your first year, but there's a lot of depth and enjoyment to be had building your fortress/empire once you've figured out the basics.
How many gnomes you get and how difficult the monsters are depends on your "kingdom value", so you can manage the difficulty by simply limiting the valuables you create until you're ready. Also, the amount of gnomes you get is based on how many you're supposed to have for your kingdom value. If you lose gnomes during a season you'll get more gnomes on the next migration to make up for it, so as long you don't get wiped you can always recover. Better food and drink make your gnomes work faster, better beds and rooms make them sleep less, and you can optimize storage and production chains by specializing gnomes and carefully placing your workshops.
The early game is survival, the mid game is improving efficiency, and the late game is creative construction. This type of game is probably not for everyone, but if you're a stubborn strategic control freak creative mastermind you'll love it.

Cute game. It's basically an assortment of old and proven puzzles, many of which have existed forever, with some (barely) Hidden Object thrown in. Can be finished in 1-2 hours - or even less if you're an avid puzzle solver - and I think for that, the price is fine.
I've seen some complaints about the tile swapping puzzle specifically, but to me that honestly mostly attests to the fact that, well, this is a puzzle game. I personally was too stupid for getting the radio to work without pure trial and error and got a bit annoyed at the Hungarian Rings in the DLC - but everything is solvable with a very reasonable amount of perseverance and within a very barable time frame.
There's not much more to it than this row of puzzles, though. The artwork is pretty and gave me a very 2006-ish GameHouse/PlayFirst/etc vibe (which is nice), the plot obviously is more of a vehicle, but that's completely fine. I also actually liked the lack of tutorialization; most things are intuitive anyway and it's a break from the hour-long explanation marathons you get in many games now.
Only point of criticism: The thing with all further achievements locking for the current run after you skip a puzzle - that's pretty pedantic. I get it, it's also completely avoidable, but, come on, don't treat your players like school children. It's just not polite. Either build in a skip function and achievements or don't, but don't try to force some sort of lesson on people.
That's really the only thing I didn't care for, though, and that's also mostly from a principal standpoint. You can just reset the game, after all.
So, taking everything into account, considering price, aim, expectations, I'd give this game a 6/10.
Also a nice way to farm achievements if you don't completely hate classic puzzles.

Alright, before you criticize me, I'm giving a bad review in early access because I really really gave this game a chance. I followed up on the forums, gave a bunch of my opinions, reported tons of bugs but after so long I feel I have to give this a negative review (might change in the future).
I got this game because I loved Harvest Moon, as probably most of you interested in this game love too. But hold your horses, this is in my opinion, so far, a backward step comparing to HM and the future doesn't look so bright for Wild Season as months since this was released as an Early Access it is still completely unplayable. The developers said even the little story it has in so far will be remade and there isn't anything else to do rather than literaly plant things down.
Months in so far and the single biggest thing people have been asking nonstop on forums is the controller support as keyboard controls have gone from horrible to bad. Still no controller support...
There is nothing to do around. HM revolves around exploration of a magical and charming town/surroundings full of mystical surprises that slowly the player gets to know and unlock. Wild Season is a big emptyness with nothing to unlock or do during your days. I know this is an early access, but even as an early access you should have things to do, whats the point of releasing an early access if you're still in early alpha with no real gameplay?
So basicaly in your very first free day in the game you can explore everything, talk to everyone and still won't even be night time, meaning you will have to go to bed early and all the following days there won't be any point revisiting any of those spots because nothing changes and again, there's literally nothing to do. So you use all your stamina and go rest for the next day.
Updates are in such a slow pace, that in order to fix a major bug, it takes at least two weeks (probably more) to be fixed.
There is a number of annoying little things you can't get around. The game itself seems very unresponsive and slow, hitbox to interact with NPCs is hard to find, so when an NPC is walking around it's almost a challenge to talk to them, can't read most signs, most NPCs are uninteresting and for me it has been more of a drag than a pleasure to play.
So far, comparing to Harvest Moon, a 1999 game, the only progress I noticed were the graphics (which comes with tons of problems/bugs), in other aspects, from what I experienced, this is a step backward.
This review might seem harsh, but I feel it's my responsibility to make sure developers think twice before releasing completely unplayable games so that they make some $$ and don't really deliver what was promised. So DON'T buy this game until it's fully functional and playable because there is a huge chance you will be disappointed.

So, Ive played the first original dead space (Most of it, not all), and Ive played dead space 2 for the Xbone, and now I would like to contribute what I have learnt from this game.
First things first, Ive got a pretty out dated PC (Its a newish PC, the drivers are pretty bad, wont even attempt launching OverWatch), I can play it fullscreen with a decent 45-60 frames low quality, I could probably do high at the same rates, but I'm fine with how it is now. If you have outdated drivers, chances are you can run this pretty well, so don't fret about that.
Second thing, gameplay is the most important thing alongside the question "Can you run this game". Now this is gonna be the part that destroys this game, ONLY FOR PC.
So I started up, decided to do some hard mode for a challenge. About 20 minutes in, Isaac still doesn't have his suit yet, and I'm running around, doing pretty well. Finally get to the shop, and I open it up to buy the suit, first thing- let me rephrase that, multiple things that I see, the whole arsenal of weapons and suits are available to me, 0 CREDITS. Now, the first thing that went through my mind was- "Oh, all of this stuff has to be unlocked first, yeah." and so just to test it, I bought a Earth pulse rifle. Got the weapon, full clip.
Now, second thing that went throught my mind was- "Oh, all of this is supposed to be unlockable, why is this existing right now?" and just like that, went online, "Why are all the dead space 2 items free", and apparently the problem was there was a patch previously, and it was a attempt at fixing a bug where you would have to buy items twice to actually get what you paid for. So, naturally, I bought literally everything and equipped the most OP weapons for the up coming boss fight. About 2 minutes later, the boss was obliterated, no sweat. Special side note, this patch exists ONLY for the PC version, Xbone doesn't have this problem, I've played both Xbone and PC now.
This is actually really disapointing because it really kills the fear factor to the game when you're literally just a walking tank, you're pretty much unstoppable, especially if youre a good shot, but that could be said with any gun. When you get to the second store, things actually cost money, only default and ammunition items do though.
Anyways, third and last place, the story. Story is pretty confusing so far, however most of the time with horror games, I don't care about story, I just like the atmosphere when it isn't DESTROYED by broken patches. I've heard there is a patch online somewhere, but people say it's either really annoying to install or is broken still.
IIINNnn conclusion, if you enjoy horror games that make you fight to survive with a challenge, buy this on xbox instead of PC, but if you enjoy horror games that turn out to be Just Cause, definitely buy this.

If you're looking for an awsome single player game, Dead Space 2 is for you.  Dead Space 2 is thrid-person horror/shooter game where you play as the main protagonist Isaac Clarke.  Located on the Sprawl, a giant space station, you have to fight your way through a violent Necromorph outbreak.  The Necromorphs are a parasite that reanimates corpses, turning them into monster-like creatures who spread the infection to more. The game also has an amazing backstory consisting of secret government experiments, alien artifacts, and religoius cheeki banter.
The game also has a multiplayer mode, but is pretty much "dead space" in the game now as its player base is now non-existent. The multiplayer is a versus objective mode where the humans try to escape and nercomorphs try to stop them.
Up against the other Dead Space games, I'd have to say this one is the best because its a good mix of horror and action, where the first game focused on horror and the thrid game focused on action.
I recommend this game and give it a 8/10

Brawlhalla! It's like Smash, but in my opinion, so much more! A genius little free to play game with a constant flow of updates (Once every wednesday. Thursday if in the UK) and new Legends every 4 - 5 weeks. The Pros and Cons below:
PROS
+ Like Smash Bros, with weapons
+Can run on your grandma's old HP computer
+Neat little 2v2 Ranked mode. Bring a friend!
+ Easy to pick up
+Constant flow of updates
+ A healthy selection of Weapons and Legends.
+ LOCAL CO-OP!!!
+ Controller and Keyboard support. 2 different control schemes for kb.
CONS
- Silver and Bronze Hell. The sig (heavy) spammers are frequent.
- The community can be toxic, but more often than not they're calm.
- HATTORI. So broken its not even funny.
- Lag. Even slightly can cause you to just randomly walk off the map.
- Cosmetic prices. It doesn't 'really' matter, but it sucks if you want to buy a skin.
All in all, a great game, very fun, Smash styled game. Worth giving a shot, and who knows, you might love it!

An excellent game with good replayability. It's been on my watchlist for quite a while, mainly because it has a Hexen/Heretic artstyle in it. I found the gameplay fastpaced and inventive, with lots of combinations of perks and weapons to discover. The levels have a dark fantasy gothic feel and the rooms range from large spacious fields to confined spaces.
So far playing the game has been really fun, replayability really keeps me coming back to play more of it. There is actually quite a lot of characters to unlock through playing the game and new items to discover. However, if you're looking for a deep story, you better look elsewhere. Most of the story you get is short cutscenes and short diary entries found in levels. The rest is just fun, randomised, arcade-like shooter action with tons of enemies out to get you.
The things that I really want to see in the future is multiplayer mode and more varied environments. Maybe something like that will happen in Ziggurat 2?
Overall if you're looking for a game that plays and feels like modern era roguelike Heretic, this is a game for you. The satisfaction from unlocking more secrets and blasting through the rooms full of varied enemies is really great.

Ok, I'm giving this a thumbs up because I think it has potential and it is a decent game at least; but please read through my thoughts a bit.
So, first I want to say this game is fun, for the first few playthroughs.
This game has potential, for sure.
However, after my first few playthroughs, this game starts to feel very cheap to me.  The ground and objects have massive sized hitboxes so that you can't shoot over things without aiming a whole foot over the object you might be hiding behind; this means you have to put yourself out further into the fray in order to hit some things.
The aimbotting enemies (I know they are NPCs, so aimbotting is how they do it) have a ridiculous aim.  I can avoid almost all the smaller melee based monsters with extreme ease, but the ranged based monsters are almost too good; especially when you are in a room with a lot of them.  The spawn system compounds that further by making them appear where you don't anticipate being attacked from.  Bottom line for me, is that this makes any of my deaths feel cheap.  That so many ranged monsters can get little nicks off me without any effort.
Then I was placed into a room full of the big armored guys that like to throw bombs.  Except these guy flew and their bombs left behind a fiery residue that i couldn't walk through without taking damage.
I think this is a cool idea; but the residue takes forever to dissipate, and the enemy has already launched 2 or 3 more by the time it has.  When in a room with just 2 of them means I can barely get an opportunity to attack them without running through fire.  This actually happens most often while running backwards away from their shots.
Oh right. I almost forgot about the monster spawn system!
They literally spawn anywhere in the room, after they've spawned in the room.  So, in games like this it is very important to have awareness of everything that can hurt you right?  I thought so.
But, I don't know if i mentioned that this game feels cheap yet, but this game likes to throw newly spawned monsters after you've killed the first set. It isn't like, you killed the first wave so here is wave two; more like, you kill one monster and a new one spawns.
So I'm not against things like the hydra affect, where you kill a monster and two more take its spot.  That is visual, you can see that two monsters took the spot of the guy you just killed; more challenging, makes you have to think about the order in which you kill things so you don't overwhelm yourself.
This game does do a little bit of that, but mainly it is just random spawns at random locations.  Right behind you for all the game cares.  Just a really cheap mechanic designed to get your hurt more often than you should.
PLATFORMING!!!!  WHY OH WHY!
This game starts to feel like it would belong more comfortably in an arcade. Where the challenge is designed to be high in order to get you to pay for more continues.  The platforming in this game just compounds on that idea.  I can handle the monsters all day just about; but when I get put into a platforming room i risk losing half my health or more due to the movement mechanics and lack of true awareness for where my feet are.
Let me just quickly mention that I think the movement feels pretty good- when fighting monsters and trying to dodge attacks; but platforming?  It kind of starts to feel like I'm gambling away a third of my life savings on a slot machine for only a couple meager items.
Again, bottom line for me is that the game has potential; but it just feels cheap as it is and I really feel like it would fit better in an arcade somewhere than on my laptop.
I don't want to talk about the monster designs too much, as i'm not sure I've seen them all yet.
One of the only games I can play for 14 hours straight without shame.

OK,
Having been a fan of some of the earlier Deus Ex games but also seeing lots of bad reviews / feelings about this game i ended up delaying buying this game for quite some time until it came on sale with the DLC in about February 2017. So this review is upon the state of the game at that point.
I really liked it.
Stability
I did have quite a few initial crashes as lots of other people were having and this was getting very very frustrating and would have made me initially add another "hate it" review onto the pile - but i quickly discovered that the cause of my crashes (not necessarily everyones - but maybe worth a try) was my AVG virus checker - after disabling the AVG i found the game played through from the initial mission all the way through to the end with only a single crash (that i can live with - Fallout New Vegas is an awesome game but i have forgotten how many times that has crashed on me).
Performance
Frame rate - was acceptable for me - i was playing stealthy stealthy stunny stunny game so there was no big fire fights -just lots of jenson sneaking up on people and tapping them on the head. I cannot say how well itwould play with lots of guns blazing (that will be my next playthrough)
My Kit
Windows 10 - 64 Bit
8 Gb Ram
Intel I5 2500k CPU 3.30 Ghz
Graphics: AMD Radeon R9 200 - 1080p - but not everything maxed out. DX11
Graphics
ok - but not a significant step up on the previous Deus-Ex - i found some of the facial animations just a little too cartoonish -but still ok.
Sound / Music
pretty good - a nice audio experience.
Gameplay
I liked this. It was quite long but not too long (not Alien Isolation long - although i still loved AI). The ending was a little sudden - but at this point i was ready for the end and i think it was a good time to finish. The story i quite liked. A good story about racism in a futuristic context. Some of the side missions i really liked - I Paticularly liked the Serial Killer side mission.
In the later half of the game during curfew i found the tooing and froing between different parts of the city a little annoying but that was partly because I was going for a non-lethal playthrough.
Main Gameplay annoyance - The initial mission in Dubai
This is meant to be a trainer type mission - get you used to controls and game mechanics - but you end up having to work your way through a s**tload of enemies to get to a chopper while navigating an impenetrable sandstorm.
This took me multiple attempts and i eventually had to go searching the internet to find out how to complete this (which when i found out how was very simple but .. my god .. soooo annoying to do that end bit 10 times). A friend of mine had same trouble - and actually gave up the game at this point - i am trying to convince him (by telling him how to do this mission) to carry on and give it another go.
Summary
Really good game
Some stability issues (with antivirus)
Good story
Average Graphics.
I recommend this to any fans of deus ex

I enjoyed the first part of the series, but this one was disappointing. The first half of the game was good enough, but after that the game just becomes too repetitive. You start noticing how you are again entering another room which will soon be filled with enemies and you're forced to get rid of 5-10 necromorphs. Towards the end these rooms are more frequent and the number of enemies higher, making the game more of an action game than an atmosphere based horror game. There are also other aspects that break the immersion of a doomed space station with other people and constantly remind you that events are only triggered by your character.
This game has some memorable moments and some aspects, like zero gravity, have been refined for a smoother gameplay. Upgrading your gear is also interesting, as upgrade parts are rare and everything cannot be upgraded fully in one playthrough. The gear handling is a bit pointless though, as 90 % of ammunition drops from enemies are for the currently equipped weapons. Because of this you can pretty much choose your favorite weapons and not have to switch gear based on what's available.
The sound effects and music also do their job well. The graphics are still pretty nice to watch almost seven years after the game's release.

Having played Towns and a Game of Dwarves, I'd say Gnomoria is probably the best isomorphic town management, digging and building game around right now.
It's also still in development (the version number as of right now is 0.9.9, and the next version is expected to be 0.9.10), so I expect it to get even better.
There's a lot of charming pixel art to look at, including the gnomes themselves and different kinds of decorative blocks.
It imitates Dwarf Fortress's brutal combat with strong armor, limb severing and bleeding, but unlike DF it's actually fine tuned to be fun and balanced.
The economic and crafting system is one of the better ones I've seen. I like the additional detail needed various tools in order to build workshops brings, and find it doesn't really increase the complexity of playing the game.
It's also relatively easy to setup entirely automated production chains that automatically keep production at maximum and keep going without any further player input. There's clearly been a lot of thought into how the GUI can help the player manage their settlement.
My only complaints are the keybindings, I found them a bit counterintuitive. But you can change them, so it's no big deal.

LotRO is a fantastic game, but not always the best MMO. The game, while multiplayer and hosts a variety of features for guilds and group quests, is designed just as much for singleplayer. Many times it feels like you're all alone in this vast world. hunting monsters and finding resources. It's a fantastic game set in Middle Earth where you can enjoy yourself alone or with friends. I have many fond memories of fishing, questing, and exploring.
The game is FTP, well, as much as any successful MMO can be. You can grind to get the in game currency you need to aquire DLC (all but the most expansive ones) and odds are you will be a bit willing to buy something if you enjoy it enough. You can even travel to many of these expansion areas just to see how they are, you just won't have access to the quests. I played for hundreds of hours without so much as spending a dime, it's fantastic.
I reccomend this game to anyone who wants to live in Tolkien's epic fantasy, it doesn't get much better than this!

Alright, this is a sort of half n' half review because only one part of this game sucks. The Singleplayer mode is amazing. It's a wonderful, twisting, almost 1980's action flick of a story losing none of the charm presented in the other games before it. The characters act like normal people, but are broken people living in the ups and downs of the crime life. It's immersive, exciting, fun, over the top, and sometimes a little weird, about as free roam as you can get. The single player alone is worth the price of the game due to it being so fun and giving you hours upon hours of gameplay with the option to do anything you want.
This is where the good ends, I'm afraid. They have not and will not add anything to singleplayer because the focus is completely on the Online segment. Why, you may ask? Money. Simply money. You can start at the bottom and make it to the top, sure, but that takes an ungodly amount of time and in-game money to do. Prices are as if the currency is in Yen, but you earn as if it's in USD.  You can buy in-game currency for $2-$100 dollars, but that won't get you anywhere near enough for some of the newer items they have added. Hacking is rampant because people don't want to have to spend 1000+ hours grinding until they can own a high-end apartment, and own maybe 1 or 2 new vehicles. Or they're trolls who like to get other people banned and their 1000 hour progress reset. Thats right! No second chances! In all seriousness, online is a big money-grab for Rockstar and absolutely murders the fun in the game.
TLDR; The singleplayer is amazing, I wish they'd add more to it. The online is a broken mess with a recessing economy, and is not worth it despite all of the new "content".

If you're interested in Dwarf Fortress but intimidated with its learning curve, Gnomoria is a fantastic DF-lite game with its own style. The creator is amazingly responsive and puts out updates on a very frequent basis, so even for an Early Access game it is very full-featured! I encourage anyone who has any sort of interest in a "city building" game or anyone who wants to eventually get into Dwarf Fortress to give this game a try -- it's well worth its low price!

Gnomoria is overwhelming at first — enough so that It took me a few attempts and a few wiki lookups to actually get into it.  Once I did though, it was worth the effort.  It’s a great mix of exploration, building, and managing your population of gnomes.  The menus are sometimes difficult to use (especially trading with merchants which requires scrolling through long lists) and I’ve seen an update cause my gnomes to ignore their thirst until it kills them, but it’s also under active development so things are changing and new stuff keeps getting added.  Despite it being an early access game, I think there's enough there already to make it worth its full price.
Sadly, Gnomoria has been abandoned.  It’s still fun, but the developer decided that since he wasn’t going to work on it anymore he may as well call what he had the full release, even though it still has a lot of the sort of problems I was expecting to see addressed late in development.  The UI is still difficult (the bug I see the most often is gnome skill tooltips that get stuck open) and performance is a lot worse than you’d expect for 2D sprite graphics.  It still feels unfinished, but it’s no longer early access so doesn’t say it’s unfinished.  How disappointing this is as far as it got — I was really enjoying watching the updates roll in.

In the upper-right corner of the screen you’ll see each character’s portraits along with a number for either points or stock remaining depending on the rules for that match, as well as a colored circle.  The circle starts out white, then goes to yellow, then red.  Once it’s in the red it’s very likely that one strong attack will send you flying off into the distance.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is an atmospheric indie adventure from Starbreese Studios.
It is a rather short story about two sons and their family, but it is worth every penny.
The story itself isn't very long and sometimes hard to understand due to the made-up language (or at least a non english language). And there are points in the story where you just think "but why?" but a good story doesn't always have to make sense. The story impresses with it's unimaginable way to invoke feelings in nearly every person. Besides that the game offers a great variety in locations and story fragments. It feels like every location, every part of the story and every scene was handcrafted with a lot of love.
You control the two brothers at the same time using a controller. One brother is controlled with the right stick and the right buttons, the other brother with the left stick and left buttons. The way to control a game isn't new but it isn't something you meet on a daily basis so it's something fresh. The game also offers a lot of small riddles that are easy enough to solve. All in all the game contains a lot of variety, from riddles to jump and runs and last but not least to scenes where you just walk around and enjoy the enviroment
The game uses a comic like design to show their world. It isn't nearly a style that looks vastly realistic but it is a style that helps delivering the atmosthere and setting of the game. Starbreese Studios also realised one of the most beautiful game enviroments i've seen in the last few years. I recommend sitting on every bench in this game to enjoy the view the game has to offer. You also get the feeling like every scene is completely made up from scratch. I never had the feeling that they reused an asset in the game.
The music the developers used in this game is very impressing. I recommend playing this game with headphones. Even the small details like the sound of the wind or the quiet little sound of the birds really helps keeping the atmosphere on a high level
All in all I would recommend the game to everyone who loves story based games. Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a well crafted and designed game and is, even for a short story like this, worth every penny.

I'm confused - why are so many people slating this?  It's a
game!  My (admittedly careful, stealthy and search-everywhere/talk to everyone) playstyle brought it to 70+ hours without any DLC - even if it was half that I can't understand the reviewers saying it's too short and frankly I smell something bovine when I see claims of having completed both the main story and all the side missions within just a couple of hours.
There's tons of nods to the Deus Ex universe and to the wider story and introductions to characters that fans will recognise from the original.  The graphics are detailed and excellent, level design is believable with just the right balance of secrets/other ways in without too many obvious air vents like Invisible War had.  The devs seem to have listened to criticism and fixed most of the elements that were unpopular in Human Revolution so, for example, there is now the ability to talk/sneak your way out of boss fights, great if you're playing as stealth/pacifist.  Also, playing in parallel with a friend and discussing our relative experiences it's clear that contrary to what some reviewers are saying there
impacts on your choices - I feel for the devs who know that on a typical single playthrough you're probably missing a quarter of all the stuff they put in there.
If I had to find fault, it's occasionally a bit sluggish even on my reasonably beefy machine (my fault for turning all the options to max I guess), and the load times are on the heavy side which grates when you've got to cross to the other side of town for your next mission, but on the whole I would recommend to anyone put off by the negative reviews that they give it a chance.

Again Isaac Clarke finds himself in the middle of a Necromorph-infestation and again we have to help him murder his way through hundreds of the reanimated dead to survive. The gameplay is largely unchanged, but retains all of the great qualities of its predecessor, dismembering old and new alien-varieties feels as satisfying and brutal as ever. It starts off really well with some interesting surroundings on Titan Station and some tense moments, but towards the end devolves into a mindless shooting gallery that pits you against never ending waves of enemies. The flashback-sequences are mostly well-done and pretty interesting as it gives you more insight into Isaac's personality and history, but the rest of the story and dialogue is painfully average and rather forgettable. Isaac also has a voice now, though it turns out he's just a generic action-hero after all.
The horror elements sometimes build some tension, but more often than not the ubiquitous jumpscares and laughably animated bodies being pulled into vents are either more funny than scary or just plain annoying because they happen over and over again. Coupled with the fact that the story is performed so straight-faced the unintentionally funny scares stick out like a sore thumb. However, some of the new alien designs are very cool to look at and manage to be frightening without just being amorphous piles of decaying flesh.
Generally I found it a bit underwhelming since it doesn't feel as fresh as Dead Space 1 was yet it doesn't distance itself very much from it either, mostly sticking to the tried and true methods of the first game and polishing them up a little. The last few chapters also felt very padded with a flood of enemies and almost non-stop shooting, which I felt pushed the game a bit too far into run-and-gun-territory. But underneath it all it's still a very competent game that delivers more Dead Space, so if that's what you're after, you probably won't be disappointed.

Everything changed after Dead Space.
I've always been a sci-fi fan and when I heard back in 2008 that a sci-fi game, located in space and full of alien like monsters then I didn't care anymore about my heart....or my chair. The fear never disapeared, but the game..oh boy..was so enjoyable.
Now the sequel, Dead Space 2. I remember that I read some years ago an article stating that Dead Space 2 was to Dead Space as Aliens was to Alien, nothing better to describe it. In Dead Space you are in a spaceship, a very large one indeed but still a spaceship, in Dead Space 2 the scale is much bigger and the amount of monsters and scary moments are increased in the same proportion. Even today, being a 2011 game with somewhat outdated graphics, this like the first one are 2 of the best survival horror titles out there, real jewels.
Dead Space 3 was good, for some reasons, not incredible like the first two but either way I hope to see sooner rather than later a new Dead Space title.

[Yes and No]I recommend this game if you're a fan of the recent Deus Ex titles, and can't live without more. Everthing this game does right, however, it screws up with the ending - stupidly abrupt and anti climactic. If you can get it on sale, you've done well.
Gameplay is spot on, and better than ever with a whole host of new augments. Many of the old gameplay features have been refined, and the world design is even more incredible than before. Most of the time I'd figure out a solution, turn around, and then notice another couple of ways in which I could have completed my objective, or gotten to where I wanted to go. Breach is a fun diversion.
Graphics appear to be half decent, but optimization is sorely lacking on this title. Higher settings bring even top tier hardware to its knees, and I find it unacceptable when you consider how little is being rendered compared to other titles. Nonetheless, turn off MSAA (it's murder - really) and go to town with everything else as you can afford it.
Not particularly happy about the overabundance of DLC, after I was shafted regarding the ending to the main game. I will be purchasing those when they're heavily discounted.

I've quite enjoyed this.
The main plot is quite weak and less compelling in comparison DX:HR, which really zipped you along with a global conspiracy that kept popping drama on you. I've played HR about 3 times through and still get a tingle when I 'discover' the Tyrants outside the FEMA base. In MD, there's a lot of voice acting and dialog - and some of both is quite good - but it seemed to me that a few characters in the main plot were rather wooden and their lines were....not really driving the plot.
On the other hand, this game has vastly improved gameplay across the board in comparison to DX:HR, from the cover management system, to the Hacking, to throwing grenades to just the basics of moving Jensen around or jumping onto something (finally Jensen actually feels like he's fast and athletic). Honestly, I'd be pleased to find these controls in just about any 1st person game as it's all quite intuitive and responsive.
The world building and level design in this game is as solid as in DX:HR as well. While we don't cavort between continents and have that jet-setting feeling within the main plot, there's plenty of side missions and areas to explore (the majority of which I haven't even gotten to). It's very much a Deus Ex game here and there's all sorts of ways through every challenge.
So, overall a bit of a mixed bag, but worth recommending if you understand what you're in for and don't expect a masterpiece. I'll get more than one play through out of it for sure and will probably go for a near-completionist run.
Needless to say, get it on sale.
