Brothers - A tale of two sons is a game of two brothers on the quest for healing fruit to heal their death ill father.
Story itself can be tagged as real /drama/tragedy as you come to the end of the game which points to the fragility of life and persistence of love.
A humble story for a change, if you want a rest from "save the world" and "global conspiracy" mainstream stories of which adventure genre is highly infested.
What makes this game different compared to other is two things. You control both characters (brothers) at the same time the story and there is no talking in the game. Actually, there is some but in nonunderstandable language so all communication comes from mimics and gestures. In the same nature, there is no help or hint system which will explain to you what to do (even that is pretty much clear always), characters will do with gestures.
As you travel thru different landscapes, developers made a good job in making the world alive with nice sceneries and NPCs carrying on as you pass by.
Brothers show that games can be a powerful medium to deliver a touching story even without shiny graphics or AAA budget.

Of all of the Dwarf Fortress inspired games, Gnomoria is without question the farthest along. It manages to bring much of what I loved from DF to a sensible, usable, but still powerful user interface, along with having a unique flavor of its own. in particular, this game has the best crafting system of any builder that I've ever seen, combining flexibility and ease-of-use.
The developer is extremely professional; every bug I have reported has been fixed within a week or two, and he frequently implements awesome suggestions from the forums when they agree with his vision of the game.
If you are not coming from a DF/city builder roguelike background, expect a steep learning curve. Well worth it in my opinion, that is not to say that the game is extremely challenging, in default difficulty the world is forgiving enough that you can probably get by.
The early and mid-game are extremely interesting and fun, but unfortunately late game variety is limited to training yet more powerful soldiers to curb stomp goblins, mining ore to train your blacksmiths and then smelting it down for better quality weapons, and building giant temples or awesome structures. While this is enjoyable, I do feel like a late game should be fleshed out. Given the developer's track record however, I have every confidence this will occur. I don't know how he will do it, but I do know it will be awesome.
Easily worth $20 in current form, $7.99 is a steal.

Sad to say, this is the first negative review I have ever written. Hopefully my last.
I want to preface this by saying that I'm an absolute Harvest Moon FANatic. I own nearly all of them, and spent an obscene chunk of my life playing them.
I've always wanted to have a Harvest Moon game on PC as I have a ridiculous amount of consoles and handhelds just trying to keep up with this series of games.
I also want to say that I have very high hopes for Wild Season. I seriously, truly do. But that being said this attempt at bringing a Harvest Moon game to the PC has serious issues that forbid me from recommending this attempt to anyone.
First, the development seems very lackluster and uninspired. Even now the development cycle is going to longer and longer delays in producing any tangible work.
The developers spend most of their time touring around touting the game, but spend very little time ON the game. Their twitch feeds spend the bulk of their time also either just talking about the places they've visited or other games, such as the last one where they spent more time talking about how much they wanted to play Cities Skyline then any interest in the development of their own game.
They're a small indie group trying to charge a Triple A price for a concept in which they have little to no apparent interest in developing, prefering rather to use their current  barely functional mock-up to boastfully party down on the convention circuit. Just where is the money that the backers really going for?
I truly do hope that a good Harvest Moon game does come to the PC, and I honestly do hope that Wild Season, Stardew Valley and World's Dawn does finally break the curse of failed attempts to bring a HM game to PC.
But currently, with the slowing development, erratic developer interest, and money flowing to everything EXCEPT game development I can not, in good faith, recommend this project to any of my fellow Harvest Moon fanatics.

But from what I've noticed the game at certain milestones will give you random purple rarity cards, but some are way more practical than others. Forest mage has 7 attack 11 health gives regeneration +1 to allies when summoned and instantly heals "nature" allies by 4. This is amazing if it wasn't for the fact that you don't have very much control over whether or not you get any of the three types of Faction cards, Order, Nature, Chaos. you can fight bosses in the PvE Journey mode but only every 5 hours or so. You can request specific cards from online friends but there's no real reason for people to give away cards other than to be nice. Meaning Due to RNG you might have what happened to me and get Forest mage while getting plenty of other good cards for either Order or Chaos, making Forest mage useless compared to the other Purple cards like Blood lord who  has 4 attack and 18 health but heals by 4 every time he attacks and also buffs other vampires.
Also I believe there is a problem with the matchmaking in the League PvP mode because in order to unlock the Chaos Warlord which is your character you must be at least League 23. However I was stuck in League 24 and I was constantly fighting the Chaos Warlords meaning you can get into a fight with someone of a higher rank than you making leveling in PvP a test of patience. As much as I wanted to love Wild Season I just couldn't.
This was another Kickstarter backed game that I threw my money at the second I saw it. I've played every Harvest Moon since the first and I've been waiting a long time for someone to bring something similar to PC and when I saw it happening by fans of the original Harvest moons I was more than excited.
I first tried the game in Alpha stage when it was pretty much unplayable, but the involvement from the developers kept me interested so periodically I would drop back in and try it out over and over but that seems to be my problem. If you were to ask me how the game has advanced since Alpha I couldn't tell you. The controls are unbearable, and I mean to the point you want to pull your hair out. Figuring out which button does what will put you in the mood to rage and that's before you even get into the gameplay. (It seems on the last update they've informed us they have hired two new members of the team to sort these control issues out so hopefully this could be changing in the near future)
Once I managed to work out the controls well enough to input my name and such I was forced to watch the unskippable prologue bit before being led to my farm. Then the game crashed.
Loaded it up again, and the game crashed on the menu screen. Now I've found crashing to be a frequent problem for this game which is expected in early access, but not being able to skip the start up dialogue makes it really, really unappealing for me. Now when it crashes before I've had the chance to save it I don't even bother trying again.
Now I'm sure the actual gameplay is great, following the blogs and podcasts you can see how much effort the developers are putting into it. There are tonnes of villagers, crops, animals and what seems to be a great (and mysterious) story but I can't see myself ever loving the game.
I think what I found appealing about Harvest Moon and similar games was the simplicity. Though the tasks could be seen as repetitive for boring the game kept you playing. This game seems to lack that charm.
There are too many small bothersome things that bug me as I play. Having to constantly hold a button to run, not being able to change direction when running without first stopping, animations that seem to go on far too long, unfriendly villagers and the lack of overall polish in the game all put me off.
My biggest problem is the game feels like it's made by an amateur indie studio. I'm sure there are loads of people out there who love this game, I'm just not one of them. For me the game doesn't feel like it's in Beta which makes me a little worried for the final state BUT I will be keeping my eye on it and I don't see it as a wasted investment because I know one day when it's released I will give it another try.
I finally see why the developer of Stardew Valley has waiting so long to release his game. I think games like this need to be played in their full state or not at all and despite the fact there are a tonne of good reviews I honestly think if the game was as good as those people were saying they would have clocked in far more than 1-2 hours. I play Harvest Moon for 3-4 hours at a single time.
Maybe by release Wild Season will be worth the money but right now, I'd advise you to hold onto your money and wait until it's out of development.

Alright, this is a sort of half n' half review because only one part of this game sucks. The Singleplayer mode is amazing. It's a wonderful, twisting, almost 1980's action flick of a story losing none of the charm presented in the other games before it. The characters act like normal people, but are broken people living in the ups and downs of the crime life. It's immersive, exciting, fun, over the top, and sometimes a little weird, about as free roam as you can get. The single player alone is worth the price of the game due to it being so fun and giving you hours upon hours of gameplay with the option to do anything you want.
This is where the good ends, I'm afraid. They have not and will not add anything to singleplayer because the focus is completely on the Online segment. Why, you may ask? Money. Simply money. You can start at the bottom and make it to the top, sure, but that takes an ungodly amount of time and in-game money to do. Prices are as if the currency is in Yen, but you earn as if it's in USD.  You can buy in-game currency for $2-$100 dollars, but that won't get you anywhere near enough for some of the newer items they have added. Hacking is rampant because people don't want to have to spend 1000+ hours grinding until they can own a high-end apartment, and own maybe 1 or 2 new vehicles. Or they're trolls who like to get other people banned and their 1000 hour progress reset. Thats right! No second chances! In all seriousness, online is a big money-grab for Rockstar and absolutely murders the fun in the game.
TLDR; The singleplayer is amazing, I wish they'd add more to it. The online is a broken mess with a recessing economy, and is not worth it despite all of the new "content".

Alright, this is a sort of half n' half review because only one part of this game sucks. The Singleplayer mode is amazing. It's a wonderful, twisting, almost 1980's action flick of a story losing none of the charm presented in the other games before it. The characters act like normal people, but are broken people living in the ups and downs of the crime life. It's immersive, exciting, fun, over the top, and sometimes a little weird, about as free roam as you can get. The single player alone is worth the price of the game due to it being so fun and giving you hours upon hours of gameplay with the option to do anything you want.
This is where the good ends, I'm afraid. They have not and will not add anything to singleplayer because the focus is completely on the Online segment. Why, you may ask? Money. Simply money. You can start at the bottom and make it to the top, sure, but that takes an ungodly amount of time and in-game money to do. Prices are as if the currency is in Yen, but you earn as if it's in USD.  You can buy in-game currency for $2-$100 dollars, but that won't get you anywhere near enough for some of the newer items they have added. Hacking is rampant because people don't want to have to spend 1000+ hours grinding until they can own a high-end apartment, and own maybe 1 or 2 new vehicles. Or they're trolls who like to get other people banned and their 1000 hour progress reset. Thats right! No second chances! In all seriousness, online is a big money-grab for Rockstar and absolutely murders the fun in the game.
TLDR; The singleplayer is amazing, I wish they'd add more to it. The online is a broken mess with a recessing economy, and is not worth it despite all of the new "content".

Brothers - A tale of two sons is a game of two brothers on the quest for healing fruit to heal their death ill father.

What makes this game different compared to other is two things. You control both characters (brothers) at the same time the story and there is no talking in the game. As you travel thru different landscapes, developers made a good job in making the world alive with nice sceneries and NPCs carrying on as you pass by.
Brothers show that games can be a powerful medium to deliver a touching story even without shiny graphics or AAA budget.

I don't think I've ever had such a quick turnaround from the time I got a game, installed it, played it, completed it, and had a review written up for it, but that's the kind of game Hare in the Hat is - it shows up, does what it means to do, then leaves with a silent little bow and a tip of its cap, leaving us satisfyingly entertained before it has a chance to outstay its welcome.
We're given a few lines of story about how a wicked magician holds his performing hare captive, then we're thrown onto a single static screen of a room filled with lots of objects to interact with. Clicking on an object will zoom in and allow us to inspect the scene further, sometimes we'll be able to interact with something in a very limited way, sometimes not, until we find the right item to use on it later, but it's up to us to figure out how to gradually peel away the layers of puzzles presented to us and eventually release the poor, iddle-widdle bunny-wunny.
I really like how open this is. That we can examine everything and try to figure out for ourselves what our actions should be, rather than have a completely linear, signposted experience. Though I can also see that being a major issue for some people's progression as they'll click furiously around everything they can see, all the while being completely oblivious as to what the next step to be carried out should be. But I guess that's all part of the intended challenge. Otherwise, while there are one or two puzzles that may confuse or frustrate, and they really could have explained some of them a little better (I totally fluked my way through the coin puzzle at the end), for the most part the majority of players should be able to find their way through the game without too much hassle.
The look of the game is all pretty pleasant, maybe even "cute" in its own little way, though the music leaves a little to be desired, as it plays for a moment, stops inexplicably, then starts again a few minutes later just as suddenly as it went. But as with the visuals, it's a nice enough little piano ditty carrying us through the game that, other than its jarring abruptness, has its own little charms to it that are hard to dislike.
Aside from a few minor bumps along the road of progression, it's a pretty brief experience, maybe an hour or so for most, I'd imagine, and if anything, will take you longer to farm for trading cards than to actually complete. But it's a nice, fun, pleasant, cheap little number that just about any puzzle fan should be able to enjoy.

This game is exactly what it looks like: Heretic/Hexen meets The Binding of Isaac. The gameplay basics are those of an old school FPS, while the general game design is closer to "rogue-lites".
As an apprentice, you are to take the trial of the Ziggurat, a trial designed to let only the most promising wizards succeed. Others will die, as simple as that. Those who survive will join the ranks of a powerful order of wizards.
You enter the Ziggurat, which is basicaly a multi-layered, procedurally generated dungeon. Each level starts in a room in which you get a weapon. Almost each room is filled with thrash mobs (minions) that you have to kill to get to the portal key, which allows you to summon this level's boss (guardian). Mobs drop XP (knowledge gems), life vials and mana gems. The XP allows you to chose a new perk each time you level up.
Death is permanent, so if you fail you'll have to start all over again, but the more mobs you kill, the more new items and perks will be added to the list available in your next playthrough. By completing objectives, you'll also unlock new characters to play, all of them with strengths and weaknesses.
Gameplay is fast. Rooms are locked until you kill all the mobs inside so you have to kite and use available cover. There is really an old-school feel to it with a modern touch. Nostalgics of Doom, Quake and Hexen will definitely feel at home, while players used to modern FPSs might think it's a little too stripped down to the basics.
Ziggurat is a solid game that goes straight to the point. It is very enjoyable and offers the potential for long hours of fun and punishment while allowing for short-ish play sessions. Definitely worth its price.

If you're in the market for a first person roguelike I have to suggest eldtrich over this and here's why:
Starting at the begining the story is very straightforward without giving a single satisfying answer to anything or even having an air of mystery, the storyline is there attempting to justify the game for existing but fails miserable since there is no closure and just an endless loop. The main character studied to be a mage for 20 years and in all that time learned how to use every weapon in the game but only brings a wand that shoots "pew pews" to his biggest challenge.
Gameplay wise this game is solid but lacking, nothing new or original, just the same waves of weird looking enemies that swarm you with particle effects and themselves with every room you step into, the weapons are all very simple and straightforward. You have a wand for a fallback plan and you can pick up three other weapon types; Area of effect weapon, rapid fire weapon, and a strategic weapon. Each has a few different variants but you can hold three at the same time so in the end it's just preference between heatsink or freeze- poison or damage- etc. It gets old fairly soon and you may get dizzy from the way your character sways like a flower in a tornado.
The map is a small assortment of rooms connected by short hallways in five barely different floors, it's a short game.
On each floor you have one treasure box room, a jumping puzzle, a key room, a boss room, a secret room, and the rest are just filled with enemies that spawn once you step in and the door is locked behind you.
The graphics are decent but nothing you haven't seen before and nothing that will make you gape in awe but they are standable.
The music there does little more than set the tone with a good choice of instruments but not a single tune that stuck with me or is worth hearing again.
All in all it's a game where you spawn and grab a weapon then move fast enough to avoid enemy projectiles and throw your own until you beat the five floors, nothing really stands out, not worth $15 more like $3-$7. Eldritch has a lot more freedom and sets a tone that makes you feel and fear the world around you and forces you to think outside the box and not just shoot everything that moves.

I've currently put 52 hours into this game and sadly I cannot recommend it in its current state. For a dumb party game with friends? Yes it's fine. For a competitive 1 v 1 game? Not quite there yet. To master this game you need to know 3 things.
1.
Each character can equip 2 weapons; you can't customize which weapons you want, they're pre set. Currently the game heavily favors Swords, Katars, and to a lesser extent Guns. So choose a character who can use at least one of these things and you already have a good upper hand.
2.
Hit boxes don't work the way you think. There is no collision detection in the game so just because you see your weapon hit your opponent it does not mean it actually hit. If you go into training mode you can turn on hit detection and bear witness to the most bizarre hit boxes ever conceived.
3.
Load up YouTube and look up combo videos. Each weapon has two or three combos and that's about it. You want to get those off as often as possible and pray the RNG gods favor you for an early kill. I have seen full charged heavy attacks not kill dark red status opponents. I have seen sword combos that get you from white to dark yellow with no escape. It's very frustrating to experience.
Also, there is strangely no indicator of when you can dodge. There's a cooldown for it after being used but the time until you can use it again has no display. That's pretty frustrating too.. All in all, fun party game (ala Diet Smash) but currently a poor competitive one.
It's a well-managed game for fun, raging times with friends. Although this game should be played for about 3-5 brawl rounds, it has given my friends and I some fun times. Keep up the good work!

f your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

After buying the complete pack I can say that Overlord II is a league better than the first, but for my own reasons. Some may think this game's difficulty is pretty unfair in some cases, which it can be, but it's nowhere near as bad as the first. After playing through that one, I was practically ploughing through the sequel. Until I got to the arena.
Graphically though the game ♥♥♥♥♥ itself. Cutscenes look like garbage and that's being nice. Gameplay is nice and if you play the first game then you'll notice small changes to this one. For example, the minion's formation is still triangular but it's the reverse position this time, instead of the tip facing you it's facing the rear. I don't know why but that just feels so much better
The story is okay but it doesn't seem to follow the last game to perfection. They make it pretty clear that the last Overlord's mistress was Rose, even though he could've picked Velvet instead
Like I said before, this game feels a lot easier than the first. Minions feel like they last longer in combat, and mounts really help that. As for your overlord, you no longer have to sacrifice minions for health and mana, as there are potions that can be found. The challenge can also rely a lot on strategy too. If you keep nothing but browns on your team you might not be able to survive. Keep a fair number of each minion and learn how to place them right. Reds at a distance, greens on higher platforms, and blues a safe distance from the action but close enough to heal
All in all, great game. The story is funny, the writing is loveable, and the gameplay is solid

The Joker gives a stellar performance, with Harley Quinn, and his various clowny goons for backup, in what amounts to a fantastic piece of 'experience' gaming, allowing you to take on the role of the Batman himself, and all of his gadgets, gizmos, whatsits, and his predatory shadow stalking style. Arkham is mostly open to player exploration and includes many little secrets to unlock and discover, but many of the areas have to be unlocked through story progression or attaining a specific type of gaget. Overall, it's freely explorable once you have access, and the voice performances are 5 star. The physics also the rock the world.

First impressions were positive, with a soft but detailed art style and a lovely, if minimal, soundtrack. The game ran smoothly and the controls were simple and intuitive (controller definitely recommended).
The game is a co-op single player (yes you read that right) narrative adventure in which you simultaneously control two brothers using the joysticks and triggers. It’s a clever, unique and well-executed mechanic but it does take a bit of getting used to. I was reminded of being a child and trying to rub my tummy and pat my head at the same time.
Each brother has abilities the other does not, for example, the older brother is stronger and can swim whilst the younger can navigate small spaces, they also interact differently with people and objects. They are distinct characters with their own personalities and this is clearly portrayed despite the lack of comprehensible dialogue, which is made up of well-acted, Sims-esque gibberish.
It quickly becomes clear that the two brothers must find the tree of life in order to save their dying father and the developers, Starbreeze Studios have used some fantastic narrative techniques, along with the beautiful visuals and fitting score to tell a really emotive story (seriously, it gave me ALL the feels).
There are some really simple, but touching moments dotted throughout the game, with the bond the brothers share being instrumental to both the story and the gameplay itself. I almost wish I could say more but I don’t want to spoil anyone’s experience; I will divulge, however, that you get to ride up a mountain on a goat!
I have now played this game twice and got all 12 Steam achievements; you can expect to spend 2-4 hours on a playthrough depending on your style. I would happily recommend Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons and if you already bought it but haven’t got around to playing yet – stop lollygagging and play the pretty game already!!

This game is a wonderful one. I favor it for it's well execution of teamwork mechanics, by that, you're controlling both of the brothers simultaneously and they both accomplish tasks uniquely to themselves. It's also a nice addition that each brother has different interactions with the environment and the people who inhabit the villages and land before you. The younger brother, for example, will be good at playing the harp, entertaining the harp player sitting on the chair. The older brother, though, isn't as good so he'll just end up messing the strings which will make the harp player displeased.
The story is captivating enough where you'd want to actually help these brothers go find a treatment for their father's illness. Since, after all, the young brother experienced the traumatic effect of losing his mother to drowning. So their father is all that they have left and when venturing out together to accomplish this quest, they'll only have eachother. But I think that's where the game blends in nicely is by reflecting the mechanic and the story together this way.
The visuals are nice to look at, as the game offers you some benches you can sit down at and admire the world around you. The puzzles are simple to get by as there'll be many littered about in this game. It's casual playing at it's finest and it'll take a lot to mess up. I've only died twice and that was because of a little of my clumsiness, as well as handling the challenge of using the keyboard to control both of the brothers.
Which, this game does recommend using a controller to play. That isn't to say that using a keyboard is impossible, but I see and feel why a controller would be needed. However, if you've got good coordination skills, playing on a keyboard isn't that difficult. It just involves some forward thinking and awareness to attention.
Overall, this game is pretty good and I recommend.

Played this game for way too long and way too many hours.
Great game, fab community, superb wiki resources and game mods. The game is largely free from bots, cheats, exploits and if a spammer rears its ugly head once a year (if even that...last I saw one was 2012), it's laughed out the door.
It's the theme park of theme parks, Lord of the Rings. Up to a couple of years ago, very down-to-earth and toned down graphics. Then WB games went medieval on the rear end of the game. In particular the store end of the game.
Now you get deco pets (how about a rat the size of a horse or a shining spectral bear with a little snowstorm above it), silly character costumes and store enchants to rival many Asian micropayment grinders. Happily you can opt out of seeing any deco pets and if you see a bare-chested dwarf in purple tights running around town with a chicken nest on his head...so be it.
On the plus side, there is zero focus on lingerie. The female character game models are as sexless as plywood and the males look either goofy, mildly gay or just a little burly. It's toned down but rather outdated and promises of updates to the character game models have been made.
Typically, a micropayment game is aimed at making you pay and keep paying.
LOTRO is different. If you sub for just one month (that is USD 15), you gain permanent perks and upgrades to your account and your characters that will remain forever. This means that the paywall is nearly non-existant.
Technically you can grind and grind and utilize 99.99% of the features in the game and never whip out your wallet or add your credit card to the store. You can grind out in-game cash and you can grind out store points (example: quest area covering a certain amount of levels would cost 500 store points and you would have to spend 1-2 days dsolely grinding out store points to attain that amount).
Game cash can be used to buy certain store products from other gamers. This is the one recently added pay-to-win game store bias that rubs me the wrong way. The few and far-between botters could use botted game gold to shop regular lootable items before but the choice was limited. Now they can buy most of the useful store items.
Beef:
store stuff vs game gold as long as a gamer is willing to spend
somewhat dated character game models inside a rather lovely game
no apparent effort is made to delete botters or exploiters even if these are very few
not a game in maintenance mode but manned by a dwindling number of staff
yearly novelty features quickly abandoned
bad fishing (hey, I like good fishing in a game!)
rather boring pvp
Superb:
no gold sellers
no focus on lingerie or sexualized children
the lore is deep and to a large extent exact
great atmosphere and in-game muzak
mostly great community
superb external wiki resources for any little feature or thing in the game
great options and conveniences for everything...freely adjust game window, turn weapon glow on and off, show or hide pets, chat filter if wanted, creatable user defined chat channels and tabs, save UI settings for alts but can use entirely different ones, any keyboard command adjustable and little extras like searchable NPC stores, searchable options and so on...really well done
90% well-defined character classes not overlapping too much but not strictly trinity heal-tank-dps

Hare In The Hat is a nice and short puzzle game. You solve puzzles that unlock compartments in objects and reveal items used to solve further puzzles. I would liken it to The Room, in terms of its core gameplay. The only problem is that it is far shorter and costs more than The Room. When I say that the Hare In The Hat is short, I mean that it will only take you roughly a single hour to complete the entire game, without any walkthrough or knowledge of what you have to do. On top of that, more than half of that time will be spent on one single puzzle - the sliding puzzle.
The achievements all follow linear progression... except for one, which has a *really* strange twist. One of the achievements you *have* to obtain last if you want 100% completion. It marks your account as a cheater, and from that point on you will *never* be able to get the other achievements, even after completely reinstalling the game! I have over 1,000 games in my library, and have *never* seen this in any other game. I am *not* a fan of this strange decision!
This game was initially made for iPhone, as is evident in the screenshot which is randomly included at the end of the trailer video. Simply porting a game from iPhone to Steam and charging $2 for it is a bit much. They didn't even do a good job with the port. The only option is full-screen, which renders strangely on my laptop. It *is* possible to change the resolution by piping through a launch command, but if this functionality is available... why couldn't they add an option *in-game*?
In summary, Hare In The Hat is a fun game, but considering how short it is, it is really not worth the price. Be *vary* wary of this game if you are a completionist! I got it as part of a bundle, and if you are lucky enough to, it's well worth giving a shot. If you are looking for a standalone puzzle game however, I'd have to recommend The Room instead.
There is a post about the 'Cheater' achievement over at
. Having read it I have serious doubts as to the integrity of the intentions of the developers of Hare In The Hat. "If you cheated once and spit on my efforts on making this game, I see no reason to make anything for you. No game reset should clean it. If you don't like it - don't cheat... That's my game and if you don't like my rules - get you refund and get out" - Nomad (a developer)
*Purely* based on Nomad's comments in that thread I am not only giving Hare In The Hat a negative review, but actively recommend that no-one gives these developers any money. Treating paying customers like that is deplorable.

Yes, like many people on this foruml I've topped 1000 hours on this game (including 100's of hours before it was on Steam) for less than $10? That's 1 cent an hour. No complaints there.
But, there are some serious caveats to my thumbs up.
The game is now released.
- Is it everything Robobob (The developer) said it would be 2-3 years ago? NO
- Is it still a very good game easily worth the pocket money price? YES
- Is it disappointing that magic, better enemies (and logic for combat)  and more personalized gnomes (among other things) aren't present? YES
- Can the modding community fix all these things? MOST BUT PROBABLY NOT ALL
- Should they be expected to? PROBABLY NOT
So a good solid game that falls short of what it should have been - but still a good game
Are these unfulfilled promises good for the reputation of EA on Steam in general? OF COURSE THEY AREN'T
And that's the rub.
Robobob's own roadmap for the game that was up until sometime in 2014 had 4 of 5 killer features down to be added and a collection of smaller stuff that would have made a difference.
In the end I think it was some design decisions very early in the game that stopped it.
The single threaded nature of the programming meaning that, with 30 gnomes, dozens of animals and perhaps 100 skeletons, goblins, mants, spiders and zombies roaming the game, it crawled to a halt and lagged.
Playing the beetles turned off helped,  lighting everywhere helps a lot. Unlike most games where lighting calcs destroy the frame rate, in this game good even lighting seems to make it run a lot smoother. Get those torches going!
A good PC can play indefinately if you sell your excess, don't encourage massive goblin invasions with ever larger taunts, turn beetles (and maybe spiders) off and keep your automaton population down.
A good game that falls short of a great game but still worth every cent of the measly 10 bucks it costs. It would be great if the community took it and ran to a fuller conclusion.

Enjoyable building sim game. Guide your Gnomes and build up a prosperous community for them. Reminiscent of Dwarf Fortress, but with updated graphics and better user interface. It is by no means as deep or complicated as Dwarf Fortress, but it does capture the basics of it.
Watching your original group of Gnomes successfully build up their settlement and eventually letting it grow to a busteling town gives you a gratifying feeling. To succeed you must manage the Gnomes' workload and see to it that they are well fed and kept out of harms way. Goblins and other nasties will soon try to invade your settlement, so you'll also have to build up your own army as well.  Flexibility and freedom are core in this game. Build your town how you want it.
The graphics are basic, but I find that not a problem for this kind of game. The user interface is managable, but could be better. The artificial intelligence can sometimes be a bit quirky. And finally, for me, the gameplay could be a bit more deep.

I have rather mixed feeling about the game.
First of all, it's not a "rogue-like", nor "rogue-lite", it's and action game, plain and simple. You run around and shoot wands and spells, but they could be machine guns and shotguns.  There are no stats, no character development, no gear besides a few weapon (just like in action games). The maps are randomized each run, but the rooms are extremely bland, basically squares with a few obstacles or stairs. The monsters vary visually, but don't do much, either run at you, or float around and shoot something at you. The only special attack is waves in the ground you have to jump over.
What is extremely distracting is the fact that you must constantly pick up loot falling from the killed enemies that disappears rather fast, so you can never concentrate on the combat. Every now and then, you get a not very significant upgrade. Some rooms contain shrines you can pray at, and they either reward you or punish you, which is honestly rather dumb.
Besides constant circle straffing and shooting, there is little to do, so the game makes sure you die often and play the first two levels over and over (there is only five levels altogether). Each failure brings some "unlocks" to soften the tedium.
Your mileage may vary depending on how much you love constant circle-strafing while mowing down the same dumb mobs. For me, it got old rather fast, but if you feel you want some brainless shooting entertainment, the game is perfect.
On the positive side, the game is rather nice graphically, especially for an indie game, and emanates that "polished" feeling. No crude art, no hiccups, no embarrasing bugs. It's a well tested and carefully crafted product with obviously focused vision behind it.
I don't like it that much personally, but I can imagine it's just what some people want. So I give "no" for my personal opinion and for the rather shallow content and scope, but I would give the game 60-70 percent out of a 100. It's not original (Heretic inspiration is obvious), it's not ambitious, but it's rather well made and polished. It makes rather great first impression, but the aftertaste is not all that pleasant.
If you like serious sam and binding of isaac you really should own this game!

The good:
- Guns
- Explosions

The bad:
- Campaign is too short, ( 3-4 missions )

Warning: Skipping a puzzle results in permenantly locked achievements and I will not get into the debate over the developers' personal opinion about the fact they consider skipping a puzzle cheating.  As of April 29, 2016 with the purchase of DLC Hare in the Hat: The Abyss this permenantly locked condition is released.  Reset game and try again for the achievements.
The slider picture puzzle is Hell.  But I figured it out eventually (after several hours).  I earned the SHUFFLE achievement.  HINT: Use the center top or center bottom of the puzzle, not the sides or the middle to complete.  I used the center top, and two 'diamonds'.  It was the only place I could find to reverse those last two tiles.
On April 29 2016 the DLC Hare in the Hat: The Abyss was added.  Objective: Free the hare from the confines of his underwater containment.
Not as hard as the first game and focuses solely on the mini-games and puzzles.  Still a challenge though.  Puzzles include sliders, matching, brain teasers and basic logic.
Puzzle from HELL this time is called Hungarian Rings.  Basically put the colors in the correct place in two interlocking movable rings.  I skipped it after an hour and the beginnings of  migraine.  Did not lock the achievements for the other puzzles but no achievement for that puzzle since I skipped.  I can live with that.
Recommend this add-on.  It is just as fun and challenging as the first game.

Gnomoria is, by and large, a surprisingly deep game. Often remarked as Dwarf Fortress Lite, it is a game that puts you in charge of a community of gnomes, and gives you the task of making sure they survive and thrive. Sound easy? It's not. There are many things that need to be managed, and your first few communities are almost guaranteed to die off. The control scheme and menus are at first daunting, but once you figure out the HOW of things, it's surprisingly intuitive (Hint: Right click controls almost everything). But no matter how skilled at controlling the game you become, there will always be new things to learn. From base defense against goblins biting your hearts, to properly lighting your mines so golems don't come out of the deep, there will always be new challenges, and new ways to solve those challenges. As you attempt better structures and more elaborate designs, the enemies will react to your increased worth and start bringing armor, and bigger friends, though you will also attract more gnome migrants (Known as gnomads). So if the controls seem oppressive, don't lose hope. Look up a let's play of the game, watch for a bit, then mimic. You'll quickly figure it out, and have the time of your life.

This is a ok game, at least from the little I played. I can't in good conscious recommend it though, because the most difficult part of this game is fighting with the terrible controls. All the time I spent playing this game was entirely me thinking "What the hell are you doing? Why are you using basic attack? Why won't you ♥♥♥♥ing move?" I couldn't enjoy any story that might have been there, because I was too focused on trying to fix controls.
Unfortunately, I found that there is no way to disable any of the "features" that were pushing me to my repeated death. The game tries to assist your aim, by forcing you to attack directly at an enemy when using ranged abilities, instead of shooting at the cursor. Meaning I can't make my spread-shot actually hit multiple enemies because the cone is centered directly on one enemy instead of between the enemies I need to hit. This cannot be disabled. When you attack, you automatically walk forward until the enemy you're forced to aim at is in range of your attack, even when you're holding down the "hold position" button (default is left shift). Meaning your character will just walk into ground effects, traps, whatever, instead of doing what you are actively telling the game you want it to do with the controls. This cannot be disabled. I could go on but I already feel like I overinvested.
I get that it sounds like not a big deal, but it's essential to have tight, responsive controls in an arpg. So when the controls are this clunky, it's just not worth trying to fight it in order to enjoy a game that doesn't really bring anything new to the table. If you want to play a good arpg, play Diablo, play PoE, don't play this.

Background: Played the Original Trine on Playstation.
Combat Mechanics: Same as Trine 1 just with the addition of a few new skills to unlock. If you haven't played Trine 1. It is at it's core a 3 man team. 1 Hack and Slash Knight with Sword and Board with 2Handed Hammer.  A Rogue Archer with maglines for vertical gameplay. Lastly a Wizard who is mainly crowd control and conjuration of ramps, boxes, and cages to trap enemies.
The game is 100% soloable as you can swap between the other characters at the push of a button. (Seamless transition). You gain Skill points as you collect the blue rain drop XP items that unlock new skills and functions for your 3 characters.
Healing occurs at large blue orb Check points.
This game has some inventive bosses and tries to incorporate the background when at all possible. Try not to get lost in the full screen movement.
Side note: The Art and visuals of this game is amazing. Just like sometime during your gameplay stop and just watch the screen come to life as a moving painting. Every element looks independent but flows together to create a piece of art. And and most times, it is peaceful.
Final Thoughts: This wonderful gem of a game could have ended up as a DLC for Trine 1, but manages to stand alone by itself, though its reception would have been the same. It is a great party game (odd for only having 3 player support) and it worth every penny.

From the mixed reviews, my expectations of this instalment in the Deus Ex series weren't high at all. However, overall I found myself generally enjoying the game and having a blast. In short, it's exactly like Human Revolution, nothing more, nothing less, so if you've enjoyed that and don't mind another 30+ hour game along the same vein, then you should enjoy Mankind Divided. If you're expecting any upgrade though (aside from graphics), then you'll probably be disappointed.
Mankind Divided still stays faithful to the 'Deus Ex' vibe of the previous installments in that it lets you tackle the challenges in your own way. Going in stealthly or fighting in the open are all viable methods, though stealthier and less confrontational methods usually net higher rewards. Mechanically the game is great. It offers a wide range of augmentations (some from before and some new ones), a lot of weapons, great cover system, and so on. I did appreciate some nice little touches though which Human Revolution didn't have, such as Jensen grabbing onto the ledges or boxes during platforming or climbing moments providing they're within his arm's reach. That way you didn't have to be super precise when platforming and made it much more enjoyable.
The main storyline is passable. It's not overly bad and can keep you interested to continue playing, though it has many flaws. For one, this game happens 2 years after the ending of Human Revolution, so there are a lot of events that have happened in between which the player is clueless about, and likewise some characters which Jensen knows on first name basis now, yet the player has no idea who they are. The main villain is a bit of a cliche, though to some degree likeable. In fact, most characters felt a bit flat, and you wished for some of the more promising ones to get some more screentime or their own sidequest at least (like Arya Argento).
There were some choices with long-lasting consequences present too, though I didn't feel that there were all that many of those compared to previous Deus Ex games. The conclusion felt a bit too abrupt and underwhelming, and as many players would agree, left too many things open in the air, likely setting up for a sequel. Regardless of that, the game is still enjoyable, and the aftermath of Human Revolution is presented really well with the whole segregation of society between the augs and naturals. I also really appreciated many of the tie-ins to the first Deus Ex game, with some notable characters and factions starting to come up.
Though the main story is somewhat on the short-ish side, there are plenty of interesting sidequests in the game. In fact, I'd say the storylines of some of those sidequests were arguably better than the main story, so it's highly recommended that you try them out. Jensen visits Prague (the main city hub) 3 times throughout the game, and each time some new sidequests pop up, some of which are continuations of previous sidequests. The sidequests would probably take up more than half of your whole playtime if you do them all (they did for me surely).
All the other elements of a game are pretty great. Visuals are nice, music is fantastic as always, voice acting also great. There's nothing to complain regarding these aspects.
I know the game has microtransactions and shameful DLCs in the form of complimentary gear, but you really don't need any of that. I've played through 'Give me a Challenge' (Normal) difficulty without needing to buy anything extra. The main game can be completed without reliance on DLCs.

EDIT: now that the DLC is released, you can go ahead and skip any puzzle: only the achievement for it will need a second playthrough. In other words, you're no more banned. But my opinion about how it was handled stays.
Hare in the Hat is a short yet frustrating puzzle game where you have to free the hare owned by a magician. For that, you'll have to solve puzzles, find clues and pray that you'll not throw your computer out of the window.
Why am I insisting? In reality, the puzzles aren't hard to figure. You can go by trial and errors without problems. But there is one puzzle, with swapping pieces, where you'll end up with only two pieces to switch and not managing to do so. I suppose that I uninstalled at that point the first time I've played it. Don't try to find a walkthrough, the puzzle is random.
However, the developer added achievements and trading cards, prompting me to come back and beat finally the game. The famous puzzle was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥but I was very very happy when I managed to push through it without skipping. Because skipping a puzzle here is not at all recommended unless you have unlocked all the achievements safe for the skipping one.
The developer is perhaps doing what he wants with his game. But punishing players that are skipping puzzles because he's under the impression that they're cheating, with a puzzle known to give white hair to everyone (the swap one), where you just want to skip after 30 minutes - 1 hour passed on it, after frustration and that you just want to come back after unlocking the rest... I don't agree with that. Why am I saying that? Skip a level and you will never be able to unlock the rest of achievements unless you buy the future DLC/the DLC is out, I still didn't understand that. I'm quite scared now to skip a level to reach 100% achievements.
Anyway, it's a dangerous point of view to consider that people skipping are cheaters. I've skipped puzzles before after spending time on them. I don't fall under the category of people skipping everything. It's probably the biggest negative point for the game.
Another problem is the flickering of the screen that happened a lot, especially when in Steam overlay.
Otherwise, the graphics are quite colorful and amusing, the soundtrack is good though the main sound is kinda annoying (I speak about the clicking) - I suppose that's why I disabled the audio the first time.
For the price, you can go ahead if you love puzzles. I will not put a thumb down because I disagree with the developer's point of view for an achievement as the rest of the game is good. But be warned anyway.

So should you or should you not buy this game?
Absolutely. Grand Theft Auto V is a piece of art that you really need to experience. It will provide you with lots of hours of pure fun and enjoyment if you're gonna stick with the exploring and storyline. You will feel the game paying off in the first 5-10 hours of playing.
However, unless you have a *really* good internet, you're near to wherever the servers are, and have some real-life friends you think you can enjoy the online part with - I don't think you should feel much of the Online mode. In years time, the servers have (from what I could feel) only gotten worse, which is an indicator they probably won't do much about it any time soon (if ever, that is.) You shouldn't completely neglect it, but do have low expectations on it. You'll either have quite a fun time, or quite a frustrating one - the later mostly. Unless you have A LOT of the time in your hands, don't expect to grind much.
And grinding is not an important part of the game. There is literally so much to do, don't let the frustrating online mode occasionally stop you in it.
TLDR;
Online - not worth. If you're someone who will appreciate the online most of the time, this isn't a game for you.
Offline - must-buy. Details, the story, the message it sends etc. Enjoy it.

Background: Played the Original Trine on Playstation.
Combat Mechanics: Same as Trine 1 just with the addition of a few new skills to unlock. If you haven't played Trine 1. It is at it's core a 3 man team. 1 Hack and Slash Knight with Sword and Board with 2Handed Hammer.  A Rogue Archer with maglines for vertical gameplay. Lastly a Wizard who is mainly crowd control and conjuration of ramps, boxes, and cages to trap enemies.
The game is 100% soloable as you can swap between the other characters at the push of a button. (Seamless transition). You gain Skill points as you collect the blue rain drop XP items that unlock new skills and functions for your 3 characters.
Healing occurs at large blue orb Check points.
This game has some inventive bosses and tries to incorporate the background when at all possible. Try not to get lost in the full screen movement.
Side note: The Art and visuals of this game is amazing. Just like sometime during your gameplay stop and just watch the screen come to life as a moving painting. Every element looks independent but flows together to create a piece of art. And and most times, it is peaceful.
Final Thoughts: This wonderful gem of a game could have ended up as a DLC for Trine 1, but manages to stand alone by itself, though its reception would have been the same. It is a great party game (odd for only having 3 player support) and it worth every penny.
As always watch gameplay before purchasing!

I've played both this, and the entirety of FC3, and I can say that this is a much more satisfying experience in my opinion. The improvements over the original game:
1. Shorter - You can do most all sidequests + the main quest in about 7 hours, which allows you to experience FC3's good combat system, without the over-excessive length of the original.
2. Less annoying character - FC3 had an annoying spoiled kid as the protagonist.  The main character of this is a welcome relief from him.  He's ridiculous, but of course, that's basically the point of the entire game.
3. References - A general 80s vibe, along with references to 80s things is pretty hilarious. Obviously they traded any sort of legitimate story for the joke, but thats not a bad thing in a 7 hour game.
4. Blood dragons - Pretty awesome, overall.  Similar to the dragons of Skyrim: just something that exists in the world to break up the A-to-B of questing (and of course, provide epic experiences during the questline.
Overall, worth the play.  Wouldn't pay full retail for it, but I've a very small number of games I would, so that doesn't say much.

Game's fun, albeit some times irritating and frustrating with the sheer randomness.
Room and map layout is randomly generated, as is the inhabitants within.... Some rooms you may find filled with spike traps or slime or lava, with a chest containing possible goodies (some worth the risk, some not)...some rooms have nothing more than a scroll, giving you some tidbit of knowledge or lore in regards to your surroundings...
The mobs you face all have strengths and weaknesses, and the sheer variety of them and their attack patterns will force you to prioritize if you wish to escape the room with as much health as possible...Unfortunately, items dropped by vanquished foes (health, mana, experience, etc) only remain on the ground for a limited time, which can cause much rage if you're too busy focused on staying alive and thus lose out on leveling up your character which generally speaking, gives you an quite an edge...although....
There will be times where you are "gimped" by the choices of weapons/perks that are offered to you, and there's really nothing you can do about it but try to adapt.  This isn't always a terrible thing as it forces you to learn how to be effective (or die horribly) when facing all manners of monsters with the loadout available
Graphics are nice and cartoony, they remind me of the Orcs Must Die artstyle, which I am quite a fan of.
Sound/music works pretty well for me in this settings, no complaints there.
Control is EXCELLENT, which is absolutely key to this game being fun and challenging vs exasperating and frustrating
For an $8 game (on sale) it is a steal
My only real gripe is....  no multiplayer?  This game seems like it would benefit HUGE from a co-operative mode...
Regardless, I still recommend this game if you're into twitch style FPS with elements of roguelike and you have a good spiritual relationship with RNGesus.

Black Mist is a fun Metroidvania game with some interesting mechanics.  I quite enjoy the black mist that the game gets its name from.  It adds suspense to what would otherwise be a very bland game.
The lives system is also quite nice.  Instead of having a certain amount of lives and ammo, the two are combined.  Shooting uses Energy, which can be regained from falling enemies.  Energy also acts as a life force, so when you run out, it's game over.  You lose Energy when hit by enemies too.
It's clearly a game that was made with love, but without too much ambition.  It's a nice time killer if you want something more in-depth than cookie clicker, and brings some new ideas to the genre.

Unlike the previous negative reviews, I'm gonna explain a bit in depth why I don't feel this is up to par for Edmund's standard.
Fingered is more or less a police line sim where you pick whodunit and based on the clues you'll either be wrong or right.
While some clues initially do seem hard to recognise (he looks ugly/messy/dumb/hippy/fat/goth/gay/like a bear/etc), the visual clues actually are very similar.  That being said, I feel it's unfair for people to point this out as being impossible to notice; as once you do, you will always nail that visual clue down.  I actually find it hard not to make it to day 10+, where the game does start to become difficult.
Looking messy will always have that person having disheveled hair, or a snotty nostril; for example.  Once you get that down, the curveballs are what will usually get you.  A good example is on one of the later days, a character speaks almost in gibberish for the clues.
Unfortunately, Papers Please has done this type of game far better in terms of not only visual but textual clues; and as a game as a whole.  It's not a bad game, but considering who made it, (Binding of Isaac and Super Meat Boy!) it's quite disappointing; even despite its low price tag.

Overall, I really enjoyed this game. Yes, it was frustrating when the clues were too broad or misleading or didn't make sense at all, but I felt really accomplished after I finally figured out some of the harder hints. The art is fantastic and finding the hidden characters is great fun. I found this game to be really addictive. Sometimes I'd get frustrated and want to give up, but I really wanted to beat the game, in the end. For two bucks, I definitely recommend it. It's a nice, simple, casual game to play when you're bored.

Excellent addition to the franchise.  If you liked Human Revolution you should like this, and if you haven't played Human Revolution you should definitely play that first or you're going to be a tad lost.  Graphics are a huge step up from Human Revolution, and the gameplay style has been refined to be much less clumsy and error prone.  The level design has also been tweaked to almost perfection.  Everywhere has secrets, and if you move boxes, climb in vents, and explore your surroundings you will either find goodies worth finding, or just yet another way to complete a level using just about any combination of augmentations.  Performance was fantastic on my PC, the game ran solid throughout with no noticeable slowdowns.  In fact, the benchmark performed significantly worse than the entirety of the actual game.  Linux support is also muchly appreciated and the game runs quite well in it!

Buyer Beware:
As a fan of the Deus Ex series it really frustrates me to have to seriously not recommend Mankind Divided. So far my entire experience with the game has been plagued with performance issues, graphical glitches, artifacting, frame drops in the game's central hub of Prague, hard crashes, long and unstable load times, and more.
This is even more frustrating due to the fact I'm running on fairy high end hardware. A GTX 1080 paired with an I7, running with 16gb of RAM shouldn't have these issues and many other players seem to have reported similar issues on similar high end hardware.
I've kept finding temporary solutions to new problems but the current state that the game is in is just frankly poor. It's just barely playable but keeps breaking immersion with some new obnoxious technical problem. If you can't resist staying away from the game I would recommend turning DirectX 12, contact hardening shadows, MSAA, and some of the other more demanding features off.

Somewhat fun game, but incredibly pay to win.
Fast paced mini battles, with some basic strategy involved. Extremely fun when the matches are somewhat even.
The problems arise from the unbalanced nature of obtaining the powerful cards/units. To obtain the most powerful units you must upgrade lesser cards to the legend tier. It used to take 5000 (duplicate) commons to obtain a 5 copies of the legendary. A recent patch made it cost 2000 commons to obtain 1 copy of the legendary. Only one copy is needed to use the unit, but you need increasing numbers to upgrade the unit, making this a nerf to long term progression for free players (or players not willing to spend $50+ to RNG an upgrade).
However, another downside for free to play players is the requirement to have obtained a card to 'evolve' (the term used in game to denote chancing lesser tier cards into higher tier) into a higher tiered version. Since legendary cards realistically require a lot of money to obtain (gems for 1 guaranteed legendary costs $49.99, not including DLC), this means free to play players will never stand a chance vs anyone that pays any amount of money. There are methods to obtain these cards for free, though this will take quite some time, as you will need 1499 gems (499 if you're lucky to have the epic chest upgraded on a small chance), with about an average of 30 gems free per day, assuming you log in for the 20 free gems in the 5 minute window at 18:00 UTC.
There is the occasional giveaway of the DLC to be found, which is a nice touch. However, it's nowhere near enough to stay relevant above league 20 (you need to reach league 1 to unlock the best legendary, or pay money for the DLC).
Edit:
Prior to 12/07/17 I did not recommend playing this game. However, the delopment of the game has shifted direction. A lot of the issues I had have been addressed, particularly with regards to P2W.
The game is fun. And if you can deal with the losing due to having spent less, I'd recommend you give it a go.
Edit 2:
The game has once again shifted more towards paying = winning. Game has potential to be very good. The monetization model is what is holding it back.

I picked up the Sims 3 as I wanted to dive into the Sims universe, and it was easily the best choice of my year.
The gameplay controls and mechanics were admittedly difficult to get accustomed to and took a few hours to work out, but as soon as I picked up the basics, I understood the game and how everything worked, and so I found the game entertaining to control my own Sim and live a lifestyle.
The custom content - not to be confused with expansion/stuff packs - was a great addition to the game too. Clothing, hair, objects, and many more items could be implemented into your game through the Sims 3 website for free.
One of the most repelling things for me was the sheer amount of DLC the game offered. As EA made this, I should've known better. I refuse to purchase any additional content (minus custom content) as the base game itself is plenty enough and most of the DLC offered are nothing but money grabs which add no value to the game experience in my eyes.
In my time of playing the Sims 3, I rarely experienced any lag or frame stuttering, and kept consistent frames around the hundred mark, while rarely falling below ninety, which is fortunate for me as I play on generally high settings, in particular, the Sims detail, texture detail, and shadows/lighting detail. A note that custom content can
impact the performance of the game, but not by much unless you have a few dozen custom content added to your game.

Certain parts also have a bit of Limbo to them, visually and in tone. I don't think it's as good as either of those games, but it still decently replicates some of the strong elements from them. It can be cliched or feel emotionally manipulative at times, but it's far from overbearing. It's not particularly challenging, as it's more about immersion and the emotional experience, like Ico and Limbo. And I specify Raising Hell, because it follows that particular story arch, where your predicessor is stuck in the Infernal Abyss and all the stuff that happened in the mean time.
I really like the fact that, although a very short section at the start, you get to play as a little kid, the son of the previous Overlord.
The game mechanics are similar but there's only so little you can do with magic. But I do love Evil pressence for the mind controlling.
While in the wastelands it does show you what happened to the Halflings (which I found to be an awesome cameo) it doesn't explain what happened to the Dwarfs. A game like this, especially since it has Elves, needs Dwarfs.
If you're sinister of mind, you are going to love this game, but I do insist you play Overlord and Raising Hell first because of the references tp those in Overlord 2. You won't understand them when you're presented with them.
I give this game a 75/10!

I cannot recommend this game.  I absolutley love the Deus Ex series.  However, it looks as though this will be filed with The Invisible War.  The story is more than lacking and is a subversion of what a Deus Ex game is.  One of my largest issues is not being able to use SLI; as I get the Direct X device hang/disconnected.  After a few minutes of play, the game crashes with that error.  As with of games of late, SLI/Crossfire compatibility and function are much much less driver dependant.  This issue comes from, you guessed it, the same lazy devs that brought you another Missing Link e.g.(this game).  Why SLI/Crossfire would not be a priority for them doesn't make much sense with the graphic options the game allow you to utilize.  Great at low resloution I'm sure.  With 1440p and up, with higher refresh rates you need more compute power, a single card isn't enough.  No, G-sync and Freesynce are not the answer; it's a band-aid.  This looks like another dev house that has given up on PC.  The microtransactions are an afront to all people that can think for themselves and have experience in understanding value.  Basically it looks like those responsible for the game really didn't care about the game at all.  A good game creates fans and generates money.  Those fans then continue to buy into the brands established quality.  This doesn't work if you the point of the game is to make money and that is all.
Also?!?!?!:
"Mankind Divided is designed to track your every move if your console or PC is online. Every time you shoot, every item you pick up, your dialogue choices, your system settings, even every time you jump, it’s all sent back to Square Enix servers for analysis," says Sterling
A simple search of the quote will get you there.
You'd think they'd find the anomaly with multi-card systems with all of the tracking.  But no, people must really like to start, stop, start, stop, etc., over and over.
It really doesn't seem like Square Enix or Eidos Montreal really cared about making the game.
Don't support this joke of a game for anything more than 10$.

It's an okay game but it, like towns, is a dwarf fortress clone with less features and less responsive citizens. The only real upside to it is that building upwards is less of a chore and the graphics look nice, but at present, the free game that is dwarf fortress gives you more and it'd cost you less to donate to that absolutely free game.
Admittedly DF is clunky, but it is moddable, has mods, plenty mods, gets better with mods and while it's getting updated with sparse frequency, I wouldn't reccommend -another- DF clone that has quite a few glaring bugs and doesn't seem to be updated all that frequently for a game that's supposed to be early access.
it seems like it could be a 6 or 7 out of 10 game, which means it isn't a bad game by any means, but there's better things out there than what this currently offers you, for -zilch- out of your wallet.
It's promising enough, hence the 65%-ish which I'm allowing it with the benefit of doubt.
But there are issues. blocks that refuse to vanish, unresponsive (at times) gnomes, clunky isometric controls that aren't quite targeting the things you're trying to get at. Even for seasoned players of this particular type of games it's frustrating to learn the order in which you have to excavate a thing to avoid floating floors in the middle of your glorious construction.
And it has an aversion to giving you enough -base- materials early on to actually get you going.
This is just to name a few of the things I remember from last I played it, in december.
Maybe if they could at least, for a game that pretty much grabs dwarf fortress and removes the fortress and all the things in it, and renames dwarf as gnome, refine what they have - I might reccommend it to people that don't like the -potential- complexity of DF if they did that much. Until then, this isn't quite the game it should be. It's not an issue of something as hipster-y as being casual or any notion of that silly word, it's an issue of cloning something imperfectly.
But then.. that's just my opinion, keep that in mind.

Yes, welcome to another sandbox. I had this title for a long time and only graced it with my attention recently. Honestly I did not think much of the game but somehow I ended up sinking into it a few days straight and still play it.
The reason for that is... eluding me. So prepare for more of a rant than a well laid-out impression.
Gnomoria seems to be done well enough for an Early Access title - what's there is good enough. What's not there, well, is a huge pile of features that hopefully will be added one day. Seems fairly lackluster, right? But somehow Gnomoria plays good enough to drag me in. Building structures and designing layouts in the isometric view is enjoyable if a little limited for now due to the small variety of blocks. The camera can be a little awkward at times but the basic 4-way rotation saves the day in most cases.
The economy is reasonable in terms of the supply chains - there are only a few basic resources to keep track of - making it easy to grasp the basics. But the dozens of ways to process and utilize those resources make for a deeply-interconnected web of processing pathways and making the most of available time and resources can be a challenge, as it should be! Nevertheless, it can also be a god-forsaken nightmare to manage the economy, mostly because of the Gnomes. There is no direct control over the peons and their activities, and even though a task priority system is in place it lacks fine-tuning and control within each task group (e.g. prioritising construction of one building over another). That's made even more difficult by the fact that there are way too few Gnomes to fill all the roles much less do it efficiently. Gnomes only join the settlement at the beginning of each season, their numbers and skills random, and the total population is capped with regards to the total worth of the settlement.
Now it'd be alright if time was not your enemy and Gnomes never died - sadly, neither is true. Unless playing in the Peaceful mode which disables enemies your Gnomes WILL BE KILLED by the dozen each season. Enemies are merciless, spawn with no regards to your wishes or objections, and even on Easy combat difficulty the game is god.damn HARD. What this means is that on top of managing the basic economy with way too few Gnomes at your disposal you still need to keep up the military production (weapons, armors, bandages) and training (which takes Gnomes off other tasks, naturally). Did I mention the game was difficult? No? Well it is!
For a brief summary I'll say Gnomoria is a decent sandbox title that has a lot of potential. It is also god.damn hard. If you like sandboxes and/or difficult management sims Gnomoria is a good choice.

I heard the echo bouncing off the walls of the Steam community that one of my favourite game developers, Edmund Mcmillen, had released a new game on Steam. Of course, I had to take a gander.
I knew that Edmund had been working on several things, including The Binding of Isaac Rebirth and Mewgenics (which I can’t wait for!) so I was a little surprised to hear that something completely random (or at least to me) had come out of the woodwork.
Looking at the trailer and the price, I kind of had the impression that this would be a “mini-game” type of thing that I would likely play for five minutes and never touch again. A little, but not entirely, like the little games that were in “The Basement Collection” also by Edmund.
To my surprise this game was actually more addictive than I thought it would be.
The foundation of this game being that you’re given a line-up of suspects and a witness that will give you four hints as to who the criminal is. You have to narrow down the suspects and “point the finger” at which you think is guilty. This results in that suspect being executed and if you’re right, you move onto the next case. The aim of the game assumingly being to get as far as you can without murdering someone innocent.
Seeing as I thought I would barely spend 8 minutes on this game, so far I’m 8 hours in and 88% complete with the game. I have technically “finished” the game, but I’m going to try and 100% it. Most of the achievements being mile stones in how far you get or for executing special characters that come up in the line ups.
The mechanics of this game is quite easy to figure out after a while and you will really pick up a knack for finding what you are looking for. 8 hours in and I already feel like a pro! (How sad)
Edmund’s usual art style which I know I love is used in this game and that always makes the games he released all the better to me.
All in all I think it’s a pretty alright game. If I wasn’t such a big Edmund fan I honestly doubt if I would have bought it, but in my opinion it isn’t too bad of a game for the price. It’s something small to sink into when you can’t really be bothered for the big, engrossing and time consuming games.
UPDATE: At 10 hours in I managed to 100% the game. The last two achievements I needed were for beating the game without the automatic second chance you get when failing once, and executing one of the special characters that randomly come up in the line ups. I was expecting the achievement for beating the game without the continue to be a lot more tedious then it was. In honesty, once you learn the characteristics well enough it’s not too bad finishing without fail. However, I think most of those additional hours was spent on me trying to get the special character I needed to appear.
I also decided to read through other reviews for this game, of which a lot that I read seemed to have been negative. Most of the negativity seemed to surround the clues and how “vague” they are. I would just say that you just need to keep in mind that each clue adds or rules out a certain “look” that has been drawn onto the character. Once you figure what things are associated with, you’re fine. It’s also randomly generated, so you can get some pretty ridiculous combinations.
TL;DR : It’s more fun than it may seem, weirdly addictive, easy to get used to and a fun time killer. I’d say to try it. It’s cheap, why not?
