Contrary to what the reviews indicate, the game is actually reasonably entertaining. It's in line with other simplistic flash games in depth, but its simple approach to hint-of-Plants v Zombies-flavor tactical RPG combat, combined with unit upgrades is based within tried and true formulas and works well to the format of their implementation.
The fairly generic TRPG design isn't anything which stands out, but the simple design works well for the casual appeal of the game. Likewise, the game benefits from a wide variety of available units, and combat encounters which are made more interesting by the inclusion of randomized starting elements (though these aren't always well balanced between the players, and can sometimes be absurdly imbalanced- with an already overpowered opponent receiving far more/better bonuses than you do; The imbalance does at least go both ways, however).
Past that, the game has a few muddled parts, but it's mostly accessible and straightforward, which makes it a great lightweight game. (Also, clarification, as with many games of its sort it uses AI-controlled auto-combat for PvP, so it's essentially a straight-up casual-paced PvE game.)
Buuuuut the game has a few glaring flaws that drag it down rather notably:
* Erratic power curves. In "Journey" (campaign) mode, you'll find yourself clearing quite a few weak opponents in a series, and then getting held up by a randomly boosted opponent- and, past it, the difficulty drops again. It's a system which really seems to cater to microtransaction mentality, rather than a smooth progression curve (though simple lazy design could of course also be a possibility). In league, power imbalances are countered by the fact that if you keep loading up matches, eventually you'll get paired against weaker AIs.. which, actually, does less to mitigate power imbalances and more to emphasis their existence. This isn't the kind of game where you can load up and make a bit of steady progress- if you've little time to spare, you may end up with a few frustratingly imbalanced matches and nothing to show for them. That brings me to the next point-
* A 3-minute timeout on matches (with a 1 minute timeout per round- though sometimes the entire match will actually timeout after just the 1 minute, and I thus haven't been able to figure out why). It's a PvE game. With typical flash game design. And you drop in a 3 minute match timeout? Holy crap, and I thought 10 minute timeouts were unnecessarily short. With many online games favoring "until you close the game", 2 hours, or a low-end of 40-minutes for them to boot you, even 20 minute timeouts, while perhaps the most common cutoff length of all, seems short [for a PvE game]. 10 minutes is definitely on the low-end, but 3? 3?!
3 works for an immersive, quick-paced, PvP-centric game. Something you actually will give your full attention to. For a casual PvE game with a design best suited for background play, it (and the inclusion of a round timer) is not only uncalled for, it's clearly going to significantly reduce the game's casual gameplay appeal. Just an utterly bewildering design decision- especially given that you'll receive rank loss or loss of campaign play access (which is restricted by timer recharges) as the injury to the insult. :|
*Finally, the game has FAR too-frequent bugs and polish issues. And these tend to be pretty dramatic, as well:
Example 1: I've had the opponent randomly turn into me (duplicating my name and avatar), all my units vanish (or rather, they popped off the board, no longer participated in combat, and when I clicked on them they vanished)
Example 2: In another instance, I've had a match start with me at 5 life and my opponent with 6 units out (you can only drop 1-2 units per round, and 5 damage from a single unit is pretty low-end, so suffice it to say that was more than enough to guarantee my loss).
Example 3: Several times I've killed off an opponent, only for it to have counted it as my loss. :X
More normal bugs like interface lock-ups and crashes are very common as well, game imbalances are quite noticable at times (from widely different quality units to the usual imbalanced benefit of going first that most alternating-turn games have), and the game has many components which are awkwardly implemented (in a way which either makes them confusing or has them sabotaging the player).
So yeah. It's a frustrating, crazy imbalanced, poorly-presented mess.. but, again, contrary to the general review rating, the gameplay has a nice casual appeal, with its combat definitely placing ahead of other modern, casual TRPGs (eg, Braveland) which have been frequenting flash sites and Steam. If you're itching for a really lightweight TRPG to blow some time on, the fact that this is free and quick to download definitely makes it a valid consideration, if the issues above don't sound like they'd bother you too much.
(Though, of course, don't set your expectations too high- even putting aside everything else, the game does still cater too heavily to microtransactions and appears to have several planned features not yet implemented, so the game does have a habit of cutting you off at every corner. As I said, it compares well to other casual TRPG style games, but it lacks the depth you'd expect from even a more ambitious microstransaction game, nevermind a "proper" game.)

I wish Steam had a more fine-grained rating system than just a simple thumbs up or thumbs down.
I mostly liked this game, but I found myself disappointed after reading all the raving reviews. Yes, it is a fairly well executed game, but it's also a lot more dark and depressing than the reviews let on. The whole ending feels a bit forced and manipulative to bring out an emotional response in the player and I didn't really enjoy it. Yes, I feel sad for that poor, messed up kid and broken family, but I'm not sure what message the devs want me to take away from that. Not to mention that the game is only 3 hours long with no replay value.
The best part of the game isn't the story, it's the single player coop gameplay. I hope other games pick up on this at some point. Unfortunately the controls can be confusing at times, there's some room for improvement there.
In terms of graphics and audio, the art direction is great, but the graphics themselves aren't anything special and are definitely dated. Audio was good quality and appropriately emotionally manipulative.
There were several parts of the game that could have done with more checkpoints. Some segments are fairly long, and if you mess up and fall, you have to start from the very beginning. This is exacerbated by the often confusing controls (I'm not used to controlling two characters at once) and a distinct lack of any tutorial. Most of the time the game is intuitive, but there were still several places where I died several times before I figured out what the game expected me to do from trial and error. At least there's not that many buttons to try.
Overall, I have a hard time recommending this game at the asking price. If you got it in a bundle or picked it up in the giveaway (or have some steam wallet funds burning a hole in your pocket and see this game listed for 75% off), go ahead and give it a try, you might like it. But for $15, there's a lot better games you can spend your money on.

I'm not sure I would recommend this if it didn't have such a strong finish. It's not a must-play, but it's worth it at a sale price.
It doesn't succeed in being as potent and emotional as it tries to be, but it does try. The schtick where you control two characters with two sticks is more awkward than it is novel, most of the time. But there is at least one good payoff point.
The story, both the main story and the mini adventures along the way, aren't anything special, but they get the job done.
Minor complaint: Why are the dialog sequences so long if the characters speak simlish anyways? The "talking" scenes (of which there are few) get the point across without words, but they're paced as if it's actual dialogue.
Perhaps one of the best things the game does is stay devoid of UI or unecessary frills. There are no distractions from the story they wanted to tell or the game they wanted to make. No stupid collectibles or anything. All the achievements are little exploratory things that truly feel like rewards for taking your time, rather than completionist chores.
Overall, the game is rough around the edges, and it's doesn't deliver on everything you might hope for, but it is a nice adventure to experience.

DLC Quest is like that annoying friend who fancies himself a comedian but only has one joke to tell.
It's intended as a parody of modern video game trends (namely the exorbitant amount of downloadable content often available alongside games) but is so on the nose and repetitive that it loses its effect almost immediately. It was almost amusing to have to purchase animations and the option to walk left, but by the dozenth time this same joke was being told to me I was groaning and begging it to end.
It doesn't help that playing DLC Quest is an absolutely miserable experience, consisting of the same annoying gaming cliches that it makes fun of that are even less enjoyable in such a clumsy, unimaginative game. It wants to have its cake and eat it too, which proves neither the least bit fun or funny.
There wasn't a single moment DLC Quest managed to get even a partial grin out of me, but it succeeded entirely in providing one of the dullest and incredibly tedious hours I've spent playing a game. Perhaps if you subscribe to its extremist consumer humor you'd find it more entertaining than I, but I'd sooner pay to have it removed from my library than have to sludge through it again.

In my review of
, I took issue with the conflicted themes presented by the game. It constant insisted that I was an evil Overlord spreading evil across the land. But it was in stark contrast to the game mechanics and story that I largely felt made the Overlord more of an anti-hero than anything else. Overlord I failed at its objective of treating you like a Lord of Evil in my mind. However, Overlord II didn’t.
You are the new Overlord. The story starts with you being scouted and tested as a Overlad by Gnarl. Eventually, it leads to you being banished from the mountain village where you grew up, doing lots of damage to the town’s betrayal and going into The Netherworld. After you grow up, your job is to strike out from The Netherworld to the lands above. To set the lands in darkness and/or to conquer the minds of men. To find the one ring, to rule them all and in the darkness bind them.
Ok, so there is no one ring and the overall plot is a bit odd. You go from town to town, dominating or destroying everything. Putting down a few rebellions and finding out what happened to The Tower Heart of the past game. All the while the Glorious Empire is constantly trying to stop you and/or take over the world. It then concludes in a rather long and drawn out siege of a castle. Culminating in a fight against a great, monstrous evil. Yeah, unfortunately the game doesn’t quite stick the landing with the ending. I would have rather fought a more “good-guy” bad guy such as some Holy Knight or a Julius Caesar character (to fit the Roman-esque theme they were going for). Someone who was actually trying to defend their people or ideals rather than their own selfish desires. Ok, maybe Julius was a bad example but I think you get the point I’m trying to make. Ultimately, I feel like they missed out on what could have been a really solid ending.
That all said, it’s these little touches and more that I probably forgot to mention that give you the sense of becoming a lord of darkness. While the corny humour is still present, it feels restrained enough to compliment the dark themes at play. In this case, less is more as the times that it tries to be funny actually work, rather than backfire and become tiresome. Overall, it’s a great thematic improvement to the original title.
As a whole, the combat fluctuates from reasonably challenging to borderline-ridiculously-spammy. Some enemies are a little too quirky for my taste and can flatten armies in seconds. Which I can’t really decide if I like or not. But what I do like is the pacing of the combat. Not only does it have a diverse range of enemies and fights but it also has stealth sections. Multiple sections of the game require you to take control of a single minion and lead the army without the Overlord’s body and complete the objective with what minions you have. This stealth aspect really adds a nice change of pace to prevent the RTS-esque fights from getting too samey or overdone. It’s also pretty forgiving as there aren’t any instant failure states. I really enjoyed these sections and they were a welcome addition.
Visually, this game is much better than the previous. Lush forests, sunny beaches and cold mountain villages really spice the world up. Most of the settings for Overlord II (Video, Audio & Controls) are changeable in the game’s launcher. There’s options for pretty much every custom visual setting I can think of. Most are on/off switches with Texture Detail, Debris Detail, Shadow Detail, View Distance and Particle Detail having sliders. Separate audio sliders are included (in-game) for sound, music and speech with support for up to 8.1 surround sound. Controller and keyboard + mouse are supported with key remappings for both. Controller is, in my opinion, the most optimal. Overall, the game is well optimized with consistent framerates and good looking visuals. Outside of the one crash I experienced, (towards the end of the game), the game seems relatively stable. I didn’t get a chance to experience the multiplayer because either the servers are down or no one is playing the game.
Overlord II enhances everything about the first game. It brings a more consistent theme, new minion abilities & spells, lusher environments and a feeling of being a true Overlord. It doesn’t quite stick the landing though. The story’s last chapter is drawn out and the ultimate bad guy you get to fight is disappointing. The combat is better this time with subterfuge, new enemies and different tactics/spells that can be used. But it’s still….janky at times when I don’t think it should be. There’s a good amount of content though, you'll definitely get your fill of each place the game can take you to. The replay value is a bit weak especially with multiplayer not functioning. Ultimately, this Overlord game was actually a fun time despite my problems with the combat system. The combat is improved enough that I can recommend it. With the caveat to expect frustration while dealing with some of the more eccentric bosses and monsters. Still, evil did find a way, to be fun and enjoyable. So, kudos to Triumph for that.

So. There are numberous reviews about this game and several go into detail that seems silly to me. I can't be sure if it is an attempt to seem objective or to create a viewpoint that makes the reader feel that the reviewer knows what they are talking about. I don't know why this game has so many negative reviews...
Graphics: Stunning.
Story Line: Both the main storyline and side missions are emersive and challenging.
Game Play: The game has a few challanges. The early game can be difficult at times and even though there are various ways to get through a map your choices of Augs can force you a certain way. Also you have to find the way you can make it through. Personally, I am good with this. It makes sense and I think this is a large number of the complaints with the game. That is why it is a challenge!! The more Augs you have the "easier" it gets.
Game challenge: The challenge in the game was more a problem with managing what you can and can't do. Even with all your Augs, you can't run out into the open and expect to live long. For my play through, there was only one "boss" fight and that fight was a RUN, shoot, RUN, shoot kind of fight. I would like to see more boss fights like human revolution. It would have made the game better to have six major boss fights.
Mechanics: There are a few places where switching items or changing ammo types can be tuff. I suggest binding "Y", "B", and maybe "V" to your mouse if you have the buttons. And adjust your mouse as needed, it is crazy high when starting.
Items: There are alot of items, weapons, and consumables in the game and this leads to clutter. I would suggest picking your favorite weapons upgrading those to keep you inventory light. The battle rifle is great, but ammo for it is non existent and an AP combat rifle single shot works just as good with a 4x scope.
Game Time: My play through was with all side missions; 47 hours. Ghost play style.
Over all: 9/10

GOTY 2016 for me and just as good as Human Revolution, if not better. Spent about 57 (!!!) hours to beat the main campaign and I'm not even a completionist (in the end I was still missing three Breach software pieces and many Triangle codes). I've completed all side quests and played stealth-only without killing anyone. I wanted to see every location and wanted to uncover any hidden things (hacked almost everything, read almost all notes, etc.). There are secrets everywhere with every step you make and stealth gameplay is really satisfying. The dialogues are smart (as always), voice acting is top notch and level design is excellent.
This video from Rageaholic explains and shows with proofs the hypocrisy of those who say that the ending was abrupt:
The ending is NOT abrupt and there's also an additional video after the credits. BUT the results of the side quests you did are really shown as Picus News episode. It would be better to see them as the cutscenes (
), but it seems Square Enix cut the funding for this. Just doesn't feel the way it was supposed to be like that.
The only true big things you'd read there are:
1) "Desperate Measures" literally screams "cut content" and was removed from the main game in a most awkward fashion. I didn't play System Rift, but it looks like it was cut, too. A Criminal Past is obviously NOT a cut piece.
2) Optimization is mediocre at best. The game doesn't look "next-gen" no matter how you look at it, animations are very dated (but I like them this way), AI is poor. Loading times are reeeally long and the main hub is divided in two parts. It feels like Human Revolution with better graphics. In-game physics can be very glitchy and the game simply works much, much better in the closed locations like G.A.R.M. Facility. That being said, all locations are extremely detailed and there are lots of interactive objects.
The game also crashed for me 2 or 3 times without being Alt+Tabbed. If I Alt+Tabbed the game and opened a browser, it always led to the game crash. I have 12gb of RAM, some people say the game uses up to 11.7 GB of RAM.
Breach is actually great and there's a lot of work put into it, but it also would be so MUCH better without all these timers, challenge between players, etc. like it was in the game with the Miller mission.

Outside of performance issues and length, the game itself is actually very good. A certain reccomendation - but only if bought on sale.
It's not long enough or replayable enough (very finite variability, can be a pain in terms of chugging to play at times) to justify the cost. But while it lasts, the game is great. Now that all the DLC is out, I'd say buy it - but only buy the DLC if you can get the DLC for cheap. Much like the game itself, each DLC segment is great but short. All of the DLCs (including "Desperate Measures") have this odd taste of being cut out from the main game just to be resold as DLC. Desperate Measures fills in a good part of the investigation in Prague that is left hanging in the vanilla game. System Rift actually links the rift game into the story/universe and rift seems out of place without it. A Criminal Past is crucial bridging content as to how Jensen ended up working with the TF.  And then all the packs are just consumables, microtransaction style.
This would be a real GOAT contender if Squeenix wasn't so determined to starve it of content, but still a must-buy if you can get it on sale.

First off: be aware that this game has a select target audience.  It is essentially Dwarf Fortress Lite, and therefore a micromanagement game.  This means you will spend a lot of time in menus, messing with lots of stuff to get your dudes doing what you wnat them to.  However, where Dwarf Fortress has a learning curve about like a brick wall, This game's curve, while still steep, is not near as bad.  The UI is fairly intuitive, and once you have an idea of what you want to do, getting it done is usually fairly straightforward.  A starter quest system or some other form of tutorial for the game would be extremely useful in indicating your priorities and helping fortresses to actually survive their first year (my first didn't), but unfortunately all that is availabe at the moment are youtube videos.
All in all, I would reccomend Gnomoria to anyone willing to take the time to learn how to play, as it is quite enjoyable at that point.

I bought this game as soon as I saw that Edmund McMillen had released a new IP, something I'd been waiting for ever since he announced Mewgenics.  I really should have done a bit more research into this game, and probably shouldn't have expected anything much from a $2 game.  None the less, I was very dissapointed.
In Fingered, you play some sort of detective (as well as the judge, jury, and exocutioner in a sense) who's job it is to "Finger" the guilty party out of a lineup of suspects.  You are aided by an eyewitness, who gives you 4 descriptions of the perp.  e.g. "They were definately a lardass" or "I think they looked like me".  That's the whole game.  You choose the guy who looks most like the description.
I feel like what I dislike about this game is the very thing that would make some people like it.  The suspects all look ridiculous, and the descriptions can be hard to understand at times.  Which I suppose is the "joke." Sometimes the witness will describe them as ugly.  They're all ugly.  Sometimes the witness will describe them as cute.  None of them are cute.  I realize that the descriptions are meant to indicate one specific feature of the individual, but it can be frustrating to figure out which.  This is especially true because you lose all progress after 2 wrongful exocutions, and the gameplay isn't anywhere near deep enough to justify much replay.
Ultimately, though, if you're convinced you are a member of the niche this game is targeting, whatever.  Go for it.  It's only $2, after all.

"WILL YOU CHALLENGE THE ZIGGURAT ?"
The twisted son of Hexen and Binding of Isaac.
But let me explain your adventure apprentice...
The plot:
Your are a wizard and you must find a way through the Ziggurat, an old pyramid filled with creatures and vanquish the guardian that waits at its top. This is the only way out, if you succeed, your masters will give you access to unlimited powers but if you fail... your bones will join the pile of those who tried before you.
The layout:
Ziggurat is a "rogue-lite" first person shooter mixed with rpg elements. You can choose different wizards with their own skills. From the Apprentice, the well balanced to the Alchemist expert of explosions or the Vampire with more health but cursed by his origins... You can find the one that suits your tastes.
Ziggurat fights acts around weapons, shown as wands (the basic one cost no mana), scepters (in general fast and versatile), spell books (more specific but powerful), or alchemical devices (in general can be compared to explosives with bigger area of effect).
Your ammo are different colors of mana that you can loot in containers or on dead enemies. Green for scepters, blue for spell books, and orange for alchemy.
In fact you will find everything that made the glory of old shooters such as Quake, Doom or Hexen.
The only difficult thing is that not every weapon is easy to use or effective. Add to that the fact that many wizard have preferred mana, quite often you will have to be lucky to find the appropriate weapon.
The learning curve is slow and difficult, be prepared to face many failure in front of your enemies.
By talking about enemies, they are powerful, numerous, and ... they look like pokemons!
Frankly, it's the only game i've played where even if you rant quite often, you find monsters funny and cute.
Like the carrots that runs toward you like berserkers, the living group of mushrooms, or the slimes who seems to smile at out ...
Movements and perfect use of your weapons are necessary to beat them. Ziggurat is a hardcore game where fights are tight and requires skill. Every monster have spells that can reach you in many ways, so in general if you meet a new monster, you will have to get how to dodge his attacks and be able to land your hits without wasting your ammo/mana.
In fact this is the most difficult aspect of the game. Because dodging is already hard but keeping mana pools enough filled to fight all the way is another story.
To help you in your adventures you will be able to collect experience crystals on enemies and gain levels. Each level gives you more health and let you choose between 2 cards. Each can give you new skills to help you in your fights.
You can even choose between 3 cards instead of 2. Cards gives you more mana, more health or special skills such as telekinesis to get exp crystal from afar or reduce cost when you use a weapon. There are tons of cards to find and it's a real pleasure to discover new ones.
Each characters has a "deck” of skills that you can upgrade with the new cards you find.
It's automatic, but even if you die every runs into the Ziggurat makes you stronger, you can get new heroes as well depending of what you've done into the Ziggurat (you have to find the way to unlock them).
Add to that talismans, they give beneficial effects such as protections, manas or health.
You can find them in special rooms where you have to move across traps to reach a treasure.
Some characters can even start with a talisman or cards can give you the choice to get a talisman or change the one you already have.
This won't be too much to face the bosses of Ziggurat... in fact they remind me those of Painkiller.
With less health, you still have to run, jump, shoot like a devil. They have few attacks but in general they can spawn enemies around them. If you consider that nearly all of the bosses have attacks with area of effects... you can already guess that bosses fights are really hard. 3 different bosses per levels.
To finish all level are random generated, you can (you need to !) find secret rooms to get cards and know some funny facts about Milky stone, or you can use God altars to bet health, mana or nothing to get bonuses or afflictions.
To conclude:
Ziggurat is an excellent game. A perfect example of a rogue-lite shooter, the kind of game for real gamer. Beautiful, deep, hard as hell and with weird monsters. It will keep you busy for a while.
The only bad aspect is maybe the lack of accuracy during jumps or some rooms wich are horribly difficult to manage during tight fights. Like some rooms with stairs everywhere or when you run and get stuck in door frames!
Or some wizard who are just "cooler" than the others, such as the Novice. She is the best, in my humble point of view.
So "WILL YOU CHALLENGE THE ZIGGURAT ?"
N.B: The replay value is very high, dozen of hours to master every weapons, characters, monsters bosses. Maybe one of the most interresting shooters on steam in 2015.
Plus they've added during 2015 summer: daily challenges, new monsters, 4 new bosses (the Carrot Boss is here !!!), new characters and perks. So don't hesitate and GO FOR IT !

Pretty entertaining little game that's kind of flown under the radar. Ziggurat feels like classic FPS fun, packaged in a compact, replayable roguelite package.
The game is pretty straightforward; It assembles a map of premade rooms with random contents. One of the rooms has a key, and one has a boss you need to beat to advance to the next level. The rest are monsters, hazards, or treasure. Some monster rooms have random mods, ranging from harmless (pixelating everything) to crippling (mana drain). Each of these rooms is self-contained; you have to fight it out in that room. Every game has five floors, and a full game with all five floors should take no more than an hour to complete.
Although the maps are not truly procedurally generated since the rooms are premade, the game does a pretty good job overall mixing things up when it comes to the monster fights. The terrian is varied enough that you'll come across plenty of unique situations you'll have to skirt around. Combat feels much like the old id games. Doom, Heretic etc. If you enjoyed those old games, you will certainly enjoy Ziggurat for at least a little bit. However, when it comes to the other rooms... more should have been done. There are not many hazard rooms at all, and they have little to no variation whatsoever from game to game. By the time you've played five games you've probably seen them all already, with no real twists at all. Almost all of the items and level up perks are hidden behind unlockables too which kind of hurts the variety until you play awhile.
Overall Ziggurat is pretty good. With the way it was billed I expected a bit more in my head, but I'm generally happy with the game thanks to the excellent combat. Game's worth a buy for anyone.

I will end this by saying that this game has the most beautiful scenery I have ever seen and it is truly a superb experience to see every location in the book and movie, to fight Mordirith, Saruman, the Nazgul, Mumaks and so on. I will forever play this, even though I cannot play it for more than two months  without a break anymore.

A game with a title that speaks to modern events and its series' fandom as much as the story contained within. Mankind Divided is the second game starring Adam Jensen, and a strong followup to Human Revolution.
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided takes place two years after the "Aug Incident", the global riot caused at the end of Human Revolution. Hugh Darrow--creator of mechanical augmentation--is dead, and many think the dream of human augmentation died with him. Augs are now second-class citizens, believed to be about to go crazy at any second. Terror groups form among extremists from every side. All the while, the Illuminati and the Juggernaut Collective wage an invisible war for dominance over humanity. Now living in Prague and working for Task Force 29, Jensen tries to find the Illuminati mole in the organization while simultaneously trying to prevent the Augmented Rights Coalition from becoming a terrorist group. But in a world of conspiracy, Jensen has doubts about his own employers in the Collective as well.
Mankind Divided further expands the Deus Ex tool set from Human Revolution with a number of additional changes. These include a revised energy system to avoid augmentation spam abuse, a quick inventory, weapon mods, and the ability to clamber onto surfaces that would otherwise be just out of reach. Even more so than in Human Revolution, you can play the game your way. There is only one "boss fight" in the game, and even that can be played with a stealthy or non-lethal approach.
While an amazing game, there are two main flaws and an annoying feature. The first important flaw is that this is the first Deus Ex game with only one hub location. While the previous games have only had two or three (minus revisits), Mankind Divided only has one: Prague. While all three visits to the city give new objectives and side missions, the game feels a lot more confined than previous entries. The second flaw is that it's a shorter game than Human Revolution, at 10-20 hours (based on completion and playstyle), which means that you might not realize the ending is close unless you pay attention to the story pacing. Then there are the microtransactions, which should be avoided to discourage them in future games (as they are implemented in a cruel way), but don't affect you unless you let them.
As with Human Revolution, transhumanism is a major counterpart to the conspiracy. The Illuminati are trying to turn people against human augmentation to allow them to control who has access to augs, while the Juggernaut Collective wants people to have the freedom to do as they wish without discrimination. The story is more episodic in nature than previous games, being another chapter in Jensen's story rather than a full unraveling of the Illuminati conspiracy and the Juggernaut Collective's motives. The story focuses on Jensen investigating TF29 and ARC, with the Illuminati and Collective as important supporting factions that are relegated to the "myth arc" that will be continued in future games. While the story is smaller in scope than previous Deus Ex games, this gives it much more focus and impact: it's not about saving the entire world, but a part of it. In this sense, Mankind Divided tells a satisfying chapter in the Jensen saga while setting up a potential final confrontation between the Illuminati and the Juggernaut Collective in the next game.
Important sidenote about the story: There is some expectation that those who want to know about the story leading up to Mankind Divided read "Black Light" (novel) and "Children's Crusade" (comic). These detail a number of things taken for granted in Mankind Divided, such as the appearance of Alex Vega. While I consider this a cool idea that builds up the expanded universe of Deus Ex (which Eidos Montreal is building up as the "Deus Ex Universe" of media), I've noticed that not everyone is a fan of having information debut in side material.
As with the other Deus Ex games, those who love FPS games, RPGs, sci-fi/cyberpunk, and games that allow solving your problems in creative ways will find something enjoyable with Mankind Divided. While it's not as long as Human Revolution, there are enough alternate paths and playstyles to make playing multiple times worth it, and the DLC content (Desperate Measures, System Rift, and A Criminal Past) can add 4-8 hours of extra gameplay. For those who are interested in a quirky arcade twist, there's also Breach, which can be played for free without owning the main game (listed as Deus Ex: Breach).

On the negative side, granted it's very dialogue heavy, but it's more of the same, and if you enjoyed Human Revolution, this is basically a similar experience, albeit with a number of tweaks which improve the overall gameplay.
If you are into exploring and playing Deus Ex as it's meant to be played, the city hubs feel large and full of things to see and do. If you like games where you can sneak about, discover secrets, and get rewarded for keeping your gun in its holster, you will enjoy this as much as Human Revolution once you get going. Really enjoyed this game. It's got some great balancing and challenge mechanics that allow you to take your time and progress at a pace you can handle. Get too greedy with your digging or grow your city without proper protection and deal with the consequences. Some features I really love is having individual gnomes with names that you can assign jobs, track their lives and achievements through the seasons. See how many goblins they can slay and keep them alive when they get injured.
I had a gnome called Jazz that had an arm and both legs cut off. He had served my kingdom well since its inception so I built him his own bedroom and workshop right next to each other. He then became my kingdoms master jeweler until my entire kingdom was wiped out by ogres and goblins. I was getting worse and worse attacks because master Jazz was making the best jewlery in the lands, which raised my kingdom value enough to see hordes rushing me.
You can farm crops, tend to livestock, craft all kinds of furniture and weapons and armour all which take into account minute details about what its components are and the quality of construction.
You can also terraform the lands to suit your purposes, make a base inside a mountain or build a castle whatever tickles your fancy.
You do not control your gnomes directly, rather control is done in 2 stages. First you give gnomes tasks they are allowed to perform like chopping trees. Then when you assign a tree to be felled the most available gnome runs over and does it. This cuts the micromanagement to a level you can decide which is great. You can micromanage every task to happen straight away or just set a task and forget about it, someone will fix it later. This is the opposite to facebook/browser style village games where you have to do every little thing yourself.

GTAV has been fun and addicting for many of the same reasons previous titles in the franchise have been; it's outrageous, it's massive and intriguing. However where it falls short is that it is a very shallow and streamlined experience.
This GTA map is ridiculously big and full of fun things to do or cool places to explore. Additions like golf and tennis make for games within a game. But by 2013 standards and playing games like Skyrim, it falls a little short. The world is closed off and limited in a lot of ways. Like okay I see you golf and tennis, but why can't I go to the beach and play volleyball with some ladies, or go to the park and play basketball with some of the homeys. It's situations like this that remind you that you aren't quite in an open world environment. Most of the shops and buildings are inaccessible. So you can see a nice coffee shop and it's front door is a wall. You can't go into cool hotels or even go to a mall and then just decide you wanna try robbing as many stores as you can before having to fight off the police. It would also be nice to not see the same skins used so often. The very first fire fight in the game, every single enemy looked the same. And I can't count how many times in 2 blocks I see the same fat black lady yapping on her phone. It would have been nice to see some of these features to have a truly immersive and captivating experience. As it is, this is GTAIV with more paint, better driving, less annoying SIMS add-ons like making your friends happy and having to meet up with them or relationships deteriorate.
Customization is also very limited partly because every character has a unique story you must follow. And you can't veer off of it at all. There is no element of choice at all here in a generation that usually demands one. You can't even change your default car. If you buy a 250k Lambo, you'll still have your ugly Dodge Charger spawn at your house. If you place cars you steal or buy into your garage and take them on a mission, they may disappear when the mission makes you use another vehicle. In some cases your car appears at the end of the mission but in many cases it does not. And sure you can buy property, but you can't buy homes or condos. You can't invite a bunch of girls over for a pool party. You are often left with the feeling of, why do I need to work for money when I can't show it off or do much with it anyway. If I want to feel how a Ferrari drives, I can just steal it I don't have to save up and buy it. Then what? Where is the thrill of reaping your rewards and living out the life of one of these criminals in full detail.
The iPhone app also falls sadly short. The things to do on it are boring and don't affect the game enough.
All of that being said this is still a great GTA experience with hours and hours of fun. And GTA online will be lots of fun. But it is disappointing that in 2013, almost 2014 with the technology that is available today and the rich video game history we have, companies with great franchises like this aren't pushing the envelope a little harder to make the game innovative and inventive translating into a thoroughly immersive experience for the end-user.

Fingered is a small detective game where you play as a witness (or work with a witness it's not quite clear) to review a line-up of ludicrous suspects, fingering the correct one based on the witness' memories. The fingered suspect is sent to the electric chair so you better hope you're right.
In terms of game play, the clues and witnesses start off rather simple, but get more and more complicated as they go - giving the game a nice but challenging difficulty curve.
For it's price point this game is a nice little distraction that will definitely amuse you for a few hours.

Now that I finally 100%'d it, yeah this game is amazing! It's got so much variation, so it stays interesting every playthrough. I thoroughly enjoyed it!
Many others have expressed their dislike of the style of game, they felt the hints were too archaic, the game too repetitive. Those people all have under an hour played..... They didn't even give the game a try. They didn't try to learn how to play the game, instead wanting to be carried through everything. This is meant to be a puzzle, kind of simulation type of game. If a witness comes in and describes a suspect the exact same way as a different witness, then where does human individuality come into play? Fingered plots you in a position where you've gotta identify subjective descriptions, and differentiate between strict, disambiguous opinions and those that make you think about whose family you're about to ruin.
Fingered is a solid game! It's not Super Meat Boy, it's not Isaac, it's just Fingered. It's fun, immersive, quirky, difficult, hilarious, and well worth the money.

The indie studio Blue Mammoth makes a huge step forward with Brawlhalla after his first and only game, Dungeon Blitz, a Flash based MMO played via browser that´s available at their website. We had a bit of too-much of these games until a couple of years ago and is gladly meeting the end of the line. That’s why “Brawlhalla” is like I said before a step forward and the correct one.
Brawlhalla is a brawl game (well duh!) that borrows the mechanics of Nintendo’s glorified “Super Smash Bros” by putting small cute characters (up to thirteen in the last update but with space for much more) to beat the crap out of each other using the environment and tools and some artillery.
A common critic between the people trying Brawlhalla is the lack of speed. These kinds of games are known for its fast paced, frenetic gameplay. Brawlhalla, while not exactly a grandpa, actually acknowledge that is rather slow in comparison. However, Zeke Sparkes, the executive producer of the development explains why the game is currently that way and the explanation is pure logic: The game has been thought for network playing and fast punches and sonic moves are much influenced for the kind of connection speed you have. Translation: if you have a lazy connection you´ll be f****d up by players who have good ones. They are currently changing some protocols and ports on the code to see if that improves the experience,but in the meanwhile, this is all we have. And you know what? It´s really really good as it is.
Brawlhalla is definitely on the way to become a generally pretty good brawler for PC gamers. People will never think of it as nothing more than a Super Smash Bros, however that should not be a problem. It’s a decent role model.  Of course, it needs improvements here and there, but Brawlhalla has no major issues.

Ziggurat: The fps game where you explore up to 5 dangerous dungeons, which get more difficult as you progress.
A fun and addictive game, but very difficult as you raise the difficulty. I have yet to beat it in normal mode, but I still have so much to unlock. It has a similar feel to Hexxen (all you oldschool gamers should know it), and there is a secret in every level. The levels are never the same because they are randomly generated and can have any number of different types of enemies, items, loot, designs, traps and bosses -- so you always have something different to look forward to.
You can unlock new classes/characters with different strengths and weaknesses as you play, and you can earn levels..which allow you to choose a perk each time. Some are more helpful than others, and you may only choose 1 of 2 random perks that show up. Each level offers the 2 random perks, so it's never the same. As you can see, there are a lot of random factors to this game, which can leave things a bit difficult and hard to plan for at times.
I suppose this game has a rogue-like feel to it, as you even pick up new types of weapons, and there are up to 4 different types of weapons you can hold including your standard-issue wand that you always start with.
I believe this game is a bit off-the-radar from what I can tell (maybe I'm wrong), and it seems to be underrated just a bit.
However the game feels like it is missing something, perhaps a multiplayer function of some sort would have helped it a great deal. Yes you heard me, there is no multiplayer, just a single-player mode, but a rewarding and challenging one at that.
If you love rpg elements in fps shooters, if you miss the oldschool fps style, if you love bright and gorgeous graphics, and non-buggy fluid gameplay, then this game is for you.
If you are looking for a multiplayer fps shooter, this is not your game, as it does not offer it. I believe this was a poor decision on their part, but that's just me.
The sound is pretty good, the graphics are fairly gorgeous and bright, the game runs crisp and smooth.
The music, is almost non-existent -- in its place is more of an ambience that makes the dungeons feel a bit more dangerous.

Hare In The Hat is a short point and click adventure in which your objective is to free a bunny by solving a series of puzzles. The game consists in only one location that contains different clickable objects that trigger the mini-games. There is no story attached to it and no cut scenes. And even though the game has an ending, the fact that it is comprised of only one scene suggests that this was designed more like a demo or as a first chapter of a longer game.
The puzzles’ difficulty vary from the easy jigsaw puzzle to some really challenging ones, for example a chess variation or rotating 4 pieces puzzles. Despite the fact that some of them have a brief indication about what you're expected to do, there is no other hint option or skip button. On the other hand, having hints and skip buttons would considerably decrease the gameplay hours since 90% of the time is spent on trying to solve those difficult puzzles. I personally got stuck a couple of times and I gave up for the moment, but then I went back to the game and eventually completed it. There are no available walkthroughs at the moment online, so you can’t rely on them to save you.
I didn’t encounter any bugs while playing the game, although a lot of people are complaining about crashes.
If your idea of fun is solving challenging puzzles, then this game is definitely for you and you should buy it, especially while it is 40% discounted. But if you’d rather play it with a guide nearby, then this game might end up being quite consuming or frustrating for you.

A very fun FPS/Roguelike that is very reminiscent of hexen, doom, quake and other games like it.
Tons of unlocks await you, including dozens upon dozens of different weapons, several different characters to play as each with their own benefits and/or pitfalls and many other level up cards.
The normal game mode sees you going through 5 floors of the Ziggurat, each with randomly generated layout and randomly chosen enemies in the rooms. You have 3 weapon types beyond your basic wand that each has their own power pool. You get to carry one weapon of each type, which will come to you randomly (the start of each floor offers 1 random weapon at the beginning.)
As you kill stuff and pick up their experience drops, you will level up, which gives you a random assortment of cards (2 to start, one card offers you 3 per level up) and you get to choose 1.
After normal mode there is a hard difficulty and an endless mode as well.
All in all there is a lot of fun to be had with this game.

Singleplayer/Story:
Well, who knows Rockstars gangster epos series, knows what a great job they do on this. Who ever played any of the Grand Theft Auto games will agree that the games create a great atmosphere around the well produced story.
To the graphics: I've already played GTA V on my good old Xbox 360, and I loved it. When the next-gen console versions came out, Rockstar Games had done a beautiful job on renewing the graphics, from the first-person FOV to the overall textures of the city. When the game finally released on PC, they've made a even more fascinating work. Every detail was worked out well and even not that good computers could easily beat the console graphics with *drum roll* stunning 60fps.
To the gameplay: We all agree, Rockstar Games had always a good eye for a good story. But in the former games, there was not that much to do, well apart from doing the missions or beat up some cops until GTA San Andreas and also GTA IV brought in new activities. From casinos or barber shops in San Andreas to ordering a big number 9 with extra dip at YOUR nearest Cluckin' Bell. Grand Theft Auto V brought in even new, and I mean a whole bunch of new activities to do. From hunting over playing golf or tennis to having some fun at Del Perro's Pier or even tuning your favorite car. In total, GTA V offers a huge world with a bunch of stuff waiting for you.
To the story: Without wanting to spoiler you, I can make it a bit shorter, the story is a gangster epos of the best class. The developers spent their pocket money well (amazing $265 million). I can recommend the game for everyone, it doesn't matter if you have played the previous games or not, apart from some nice references to previous games is the story in GTA V a complete own one.

GTAV has been fun and addicting for many of the same reasons previous titles in the franchise have been; it's outrageous, it's massive and intriguing. However where it falls short is that it is a very shallow and streamlined experience.
This GTA map is ridiculously big and full of fun things to do or cool places to explore. Additions like golf and tennis make for games within a game. But by 2013 standards and playing games like Skyrim, it falls a little short. The world is closed off and limited in a lot of ways. Like okay I see you golf and tennis, but why can't I go to the beach and play volleyball with some ladies, or go to the park and play basketball with some of the homeys. It's situations like this that remind you that you aren't quite in an open world environment. Most of the shops and buildings are inaccessible. So you can see a nice coffee shop and it's front door is a wall. You can't go into cool hotels or even go to a mall and then just decide you wanna try robbing as many stores as you can before having to fight off the police. It would also be nice to not see the same skins used so often. The very first fire fight in the game, every single enemy looked the same. And I can't count how many times in 2 blocks I see the same fat black lady yapping on her phone. It would have been nice to see some of these features to have a truly immersive and captivating experience. As it is, this is GTAIV with more paint, better driving, less annoying SIMS add-ons like making your friends happy and having to meet up with them or relationships deteriorate.
Customization is also very limited partly because every character has a unique story you must follow. And you can't veer off of it at all. There is no element of choice at all here in a generation that usually demands one. You can't even change your default car. If you buy a 250k Lambo, you'll still have your ugly Dodge Charger spawn at your house. If you place cars you steal or buy into your garage and take them on a mission, they may disappear when the mission makes you use another vehicle. In some cases your car appears at the end of the mission but in many cases it does not. And sure you can buy property, but you can't buy homes or condos. You can't invite a bunch of girls over for a pool party. You are often left with the feeling of, why do I need to work for money when I can't show it off or do much with it anyway. If I want to feel how a Ferrari drives, I can just steal it I don't have to save up and buy it. Then what? Where is the thrill of reaping your rewards and living out the life of one of these criminals in full detail.
The iPhone app also falls sadly short. The things to do on it are boring and don't affect the game enough.
All of that being said this is still a great GTA experience with hours and hours of fun. And GTA online will be lots of fun. But it is disappointing that in 2013, almost 2014 with the technology that is available today and the rich video game history we have, companies with great franchises like this aren't pushing the envelope a little harder to make the game innovative and inventive translating into a thoroughly immersive experience for the end-user.

The game itself gets bored and ends not half an hour in (it should be dangerously telling when there is an achievement for finishing the game in TWELVE MINUTES.)
But perhaps the worst thing about this game is the humour. It's so infuriatingly pleased with itself that I found myself looking for a DLC that would remove all of the words from the game, and also reach through the Internet and backhand the writer for actually trying to sell the hackneyed tripe I kept being forced to read. I came to dread every new line of dialogue with the insipid NPCs, mashing the "Get Through This Stupid Conversation" button in the hopes that it would turn out to be story related and I could move forward. And then, of course, I'd hit it one too many times, and the conversation would start over again. Argh.
The game, at one point, has a character that speaks entirely in old, unfunny memes. One of the "DLC packs" you are allowed to "buy" kills this character, and doing so is supposed to be some mixture of funny and cathartic. Then, the end boss casually tosses out that tired old
"you merely adopted the whatever, I was born in it" meme.
It acknowledges that referential humour is not funny, AND THEN KEEPS DOING IT ANYWAY.
Music is alright though.

Har har, it's a jab at blatant over-consumerism. Unfortunately, DLC Quest never really moves beyond that one joke, and the gameplay is so bog-standard it might have come out of a "just add water" packet.

- Breach Mode
- Crafting/Inventory/Menus/Merchants
- DLC
Overall, it is a very well crafted game.  And while the ending of the main storyline was deeply dissatisfying and abrupt, I felt like I got my money's worth.  I would easily recommend it to anyone who has no problem taking their time with stealth and story-driven games.  I focused on a non-lethal and stealthy playthrough, taking the time to explore every corner, find every side route, exhaust every dialogue tree, and incapacitate every hostile. The new game+ mode is somewhat tempting, as I would love to explore a lethal guns-blazing playstyle. The shooting and offensive augment options in the game seem just as valid and fun a playstyle compared to the game's non-lethal options.  However, I'm not sure the gameplay alone is interesting enough without the nuance of a fresh storyline.
Lets start with the bad first:
- A significant part of the first half of the game felt like a breaking-and-entering simulator. While a fairly extensive "open world" city of Prague sounds good on paper, searching through the undewear drawers of every last inhabitant of prague for 5 hours straight wasn't much fun. There are some more interesting encounters to be found while roof-hopping... but there's just too many condemned houses to infiltrate that may as well be entirely empty.  This may have been a different case if the credits (from junk found in said houses) weren't almost meaningless in this game.
-Speaking of credits, the inventory, crafting, and economy of the game were not a fun part of the game.  I never once found myself in need of credits, and the only thing that I ever bought with them were a couple of praxis kits. Selling items that were lovingly hidden throughout the environment did not feel satisfying in any way.  I never once felt the need to craft anything.
- Breach mode is disappointing mostly because it seems like a LOT of work went into it... and is just not fun.  Breach mode is basically the core stealth/hacking gameplay of Deus Ex: MD, but with no characters, no art (just flat colored "VR" environments), and no story.  Deus Ex gameplay by itself is not bad by any means, but it is nothing without the rest of what makes it whole. Breach mode is repetitive, bland, and uninteresting.
- I was expecting an abrupt ending, and was still surprised at how much it felt like the story just stumbled into a brick wall when the credits started running.  I feel like there could have been a way to smoothly cap off the climax of the main story with a bit more drama and exposition... but the pacing of the last hour got clogged up in the priorities of player choice and time skips.  This is all the more disappointing with recent news from the developers that this may very well be the last Adam Jensen game.
- I have not played any DLC, but from reading around, it sounds like they are all entirely self-contained side-stories that have nothing to do with the main plot. You cannot find these DLC missions in your main playthrough - you have to load them in separately from the main menu, and there is no interconnect to or from your character progress in Deus Ex's story mode.  I would have glady paid for these DLCs if they were side-stories inside the main game.  I may have even paid for them if they were extensions of the game's main storyline... as sleazy of a move that might have been.  Mass Effect 3 did it with the Leviathan DLC, and I wasn't particularly happy about it... but I still bought it.  I have no interest whatsoever in buying the Mankind Divided season pass or these DLCs.  I'm not even sure I would play them if they were free.
And now the good:
+ All the stealth, traversal, and combat systems felt very competent and solid. Outsmarting enemy patrols felt good and rewarding. Hacking feels like a nice balance of risk vs reward. There is a nice variety of augments to choose from and are fun to learn to use.  The experimental aug mechanic felt like it was an idea not fully fleshed out (heh), but it didn't detract from the gameplay.
+ The game is jam-packed with art and absolutely beautiful visuals (supported by relatively good graphics engine). The characters look great, and the environments are convincing. The music is very appropriate, and just plain good. It has some subtle dynamic changes based on the character's proximity to certain locations or hostile characters, which is a nice touch. The voiceover work is all pretty convincing across the board and I only very rarely encountered repeated dialogue. The whole combined environment of Mankind Divided make it incredibly easy to get sucked into the world.  This is perhaps the strongest aspect to the game.
+ Aside from some boredom early on while clearing out innocent people's homes... the level design and exploration aspects are varied and well done.  There are some interesting off-the-beaten-path encounters and puzzles to solve, and there are usually many options at your disposal to complete them.
+ The little storylines from the sidequests were where I found myself being most interested in the game.  The conversations with the diverse characters were fun, the unique environments they were in were interesting, and they seemed to allow for the widest variety of character development for Adam Jensen.  The main plotline wasn't bad per-se, but it lacked a lot of focus and coherence that the smaller storylines had.
= The main storyline felt a little "undercooked." The turn from Deus Ex:HR's sense of wonder and intrigue revolving around the concept of augmentation... into Mankind Divided's standard cliché class warfare storyline that has been done to death a hundred thousand times was disappointing.  The uniqueness of Adam Jensen's immunity is nothing more than a sidenote, along with many other high-potential intriguing elements of the first game.  The pacing of certain plot reveals seemed sometimes a bit abrupt, as many of the most important bits of story-related info came in the form of confusingly structured e-mail chains that were found seemingly randomly on someone's misplaced laptop.  That being said, the face-to-face character and story interactions that are there are fairly well written, and it succeeded in keeping me interested in what was going to happen next from one story beat to the next.  They did a good job of making most of the star characters sympathetic, and I found it engaging to explore their psychology and moral justifications via the CASIE aug sequences.
= Concerning the micro-transaction fiasco... I never encountered a single micro-transaction in the game.  Nor did I ever feel the slightest bit like I was being persuaded into buying something.  Maybe there is some of that in Breach mode (which is not a particularly notable part of the game), but honestly I don't really see what all the stink is about.  I feel like the story's ending and the DLC situation are the biggest negative points to the game.  The microtransactions (which I never saw) do not affect it in any way whatsoever.
To cap off the review, if you are the type to want to mainline the story and find stealth and side content unappealing (which is a completely valid opinion), then give this one a pass - as you might find the core content a bit thin. if you're the type that is excited by the prospect of sidequests and not afraid to venture off the directed main story path... this is certainly worth the price (especially on sale).
Dont buy it.
GTA at it's best!

GTAV has been fun and addicting for many of the same reasons previous titles in the franchise have been; it's outrageous, it's massive and intriguing. However where it falls short is that it is a very shallow and streamlined experience.
This GTA map is ridiculously big and full of fun things to do or cool places to explore. Additions like golf and tennis make for games within a game. But by 2013 standards and playing games like Skyrim, it falls a little short. The world is closed off and limited in a lot of ways. Like okay I see you golf and tennis, but why can't I go to the beach and play volleyball with some ladies, or go to the park and play basketball with some of the homeys. It's situations like this that remind you that you aren't quite in an open world environment. Most of the shops and buildings are inaccessible. So you can see a nice coffee shop and it's front door is a wall. You can't go into cool hotels or even go to a mall and then just decide you wanna try robbing as many stores as you can before having to fight off the police. It would also be nice to not see the same skins used so often. The very first fire fight in the game, every single enemy looked the same. And I can't count how many times in 2 blocks I see the same fat black lady yapping on her phone. It would have been nice to see some of these features to have a truly immersive and captivating experience. As it is, this is GTAIV with more paint, better driving, less annoying SIMS add-ons like making your friends happy and having to meet up with them or relationships deteriorate.
Customization is also very limited partly because every character has a unique story you must follow. And you can't veer off of it at all. There is no element of choice at all here in a generation that usually demands one. You can't even change your default car. If you buy a 250k Lambo, you'll still have your ugly Dodge Charger spawn at your house. If you place cars you steal or buy into your garage and take them on a mission, they may disappear when the mission makes you use another vehicle. In some cases your car appears at the end of the mission but in many cases it does not. And sure you can buy property, but you can't buy homes or condos. You can't invite a bunch of girls over for a pool party. You are often left with the feeling of, why do I need to work for money when I can't show it off or do much with it anyway. If I want to feel how a Ferrari drives, I can just steal it I don't have to save up and buy it. Then what? Where is the thrill of reaping your rewards and living out the life of one of these criminals in full detail.
The iPhone app also falls sadly short. The things to do on it are boring and don't affect the game enough.
All of that being said this is still a great GTA experience with hours and hours of fun. And GTA online will be lots of fun. But it is disappointing that in 2013, almost 2014 with the technology that is available today and the rich video game history we have, companies with great franchises like this aren't pushing the envelope a little harder to make the game innovative and inventive translating into a thoroughly immersive experience for the end-user.

Well...
As a big fan of McMillen's work so far this 2 Euro title was a no-brainer to me and I was really happy to have it considering it offers a totally well-made humorous approach to the whodunnit genre.
Why don't I recommend it?
The reasons are quite simple: The game has a bug that doesn't allow me to play it fullscreen but crashes when I alt-tab. Still, I'm glad that I don't suffer from the loading screen crash bug that other players experience (although there's a manual workaround). You might wonder why I alt-tab anyways... because the game has NO OPTIONS to change anything. Another big downside deriving from that is the lack of a music on/off switch. This is a big minus to me, because it -being a windowed game- has to be muted in the mixer of Win if you want to listen to music, watch something or play a match of Hearthstone on the side.
The gameplay itself has the typical McMillen style we all love so much but lacks of variety. Fingering suspects gets repetitive quickly and if you know the witness characters, finding the guilty is not that hard anymore, so the game has no real challenges.
I will still fire this up from time to time to see if there will be stuff added/fixed, but I doubt it. I hope Mew-Genics won't be that disappointing. The Super Meat Boy/the Binding of Isaac fanboy in me made a mistake, for the next titles I will check let'splays first, which I strongly recommend to everyone.

Ziggurat: Created by Milkstone Studios, Ziggurat is a first person shooter with rogue-like elements in which you play an apprentice wizard in training who must face the final test in order to become one of the brothers of Daedolon. That final test is the Ziggurat, a massive magic “dungeon” you must pass or die trying.
First thing I’d like to share is that this game looks fantastic. There is so much color in this game! The style is quite different, I can’t quite put my finger on it but, it reminds me of Fable for some reason. All the environments, the lighting, spells and weapons you use have wonderful affects and the overall look of the game is amazing, I really love the graphics here in this game, it makes me wish there were more to see or an adventure to go on in this world. Usually I like to also include music with the overall style but here the music is average, it isn’t bad, just standard.
The rogue-like elements in this game are the usual random rooms, weapons, enemies, loot, bosses and so forth. In fact the different types of rooms and the way they work reminds me a lot of the Binding of Isaac, some rooms will have you take a gamble in spending life or mana for potential gain or loss. Some will have treasure chest at the end of an Indiana Jones type room filled with either traps or a jumping puzzle in a room of lava. There is good variety here so traversing the Ziggurat shouldn’t feel too derivative.
There is a lot to unlock in this game, however, you can actually beat the final boss in just an hour or two, the dungeons are pretty short so be expecting to go through multiple ziggurat runs to unlock everything. A sort of missed opportunity is having the final boss be something different or, adding more levels of the ziggurat every time you play through it so that each play through feels very different and to give more of a sense of progression.
The games story is all frontloaded at the beginning cinematic and at the end of the Ziggurat, the game is entirely based on its combat. The combat is very reminiscent of games like the Unreal Tournament series or Quake Arena. The game relies on you to be fast and dodge all incoming projectiles, the more skillful you are in this the more successful you will be at the game. Weapons also lend to reminding me of Unreal Tournament, with all the weapons in the game having a main firing mode and an alternative firing mode, all this combined makes the combat feels very fast paced and chaotic, and pure fun.
I really enjoyed myself with Ziggurat, its an amazing game for only $14.99 USD. I hope this isn’t Milkstone Studios last game, I’d like to see Ziggurat get the Diablo 2 treatment, same world, similar style but completely cranked up, keeping the combat and adding in more role-playing elements and maybe a world to explore. I don’t say this often, this game is also great for kids, it isn’t overly easy or hard, its got great challenge, not super intense or gory, it’s just a solid gaming experience for all.
TL/DR; Ziggurat is a solid first person rogue-like shooter, you play a wizard with bombs, spells, magic staffs and your trusty wand. Pass the trial of the Ziggurat or die trying. With beautiful graphics and good old fashioned, fast action combat you can’t go wrong dropping $14.99USD for this wonderful indie. I look forward to more games from Milkstone Studios.
-Thumbs up from Royial

Let me start by saying this: Ziggurat is a game even the Totalbiscuit, the "Cynical Brit", liked!!! :p
Ziggurat is a first person shooter with Roguelite elements. And a VERY GOOD one at that! Remember Heretic? Now imagine it with randomized levels and permadeath. Its what you are gonna get here, and if you are interested, don't even waste your time, and buy this game now!
The game has great graphics, with amazing colorful lightning and detailed (and varied) enemies. Sure, it doesn't look like an AAA game, but its one of the best looking Indie games I've ever played. And it deserves a bonus for having some of the best weapon designs in a game (reminds me A LOT of Heretic and Hexen, but with more variety). The sounds are also very good. Nothing is too loud or too quiet in here. The weapons sounds are good and varied, and the music is great, and uses a dynamic system (the music changes whenever you enter a room with enemies in it).
The gameplay is great. The controls are precise and very responsive. They are typical FPS controls, which means you'll feel at home here. But what makes this game shine are the Roguelike elements. The game relies heavily on the randomization. The map is randomly generated, the enemies are placed at random, the weapons you get are all random, the bosses you face are also placed at random... Even the perks you can choose when you level up are random. Speaking of perksm, the game has an enormous variety of them, and every time you play, you unlock new perks. This is a great incentive to play the game again and again. Oh, and let me repeat myself: THE GAME HAS PERMADEATH. I love games with permadeath, and this game is very unforgiving at first, but the more you play, more you'll learn how to keep yourself alive.
Anyway, this game is great. Its challenging, varied, its good looking, has an amazing replayability. There are a few issues here and there (like excessive fog on some levels, some first person platforming...), but there are so many good things here that its hard not to recommend this game.
If you are a fan of the genre, go ahead, and have fun. ^^

ENG:
Singleplayer/Story:
Well, who knows Rockstars gangster epos series, knows what a great job they do on this. Who ever played any of the Grand Theft Auto games will agree that the games create a great atmosphere around the well produced story.
To the graphics: I've already played GTA V on my good old Xbox 360, and I loved it. When the next-gen console versions came out, Rockstar Games had done a beautiful job on renewing the graphics, from the first-person FOV to the overall textures of the city. When the game finally released on PC, they've made a even more fascinating work. Every detail was worked out well and even not that good computers could easily beat the console graphics with *drum roll* stunning 60fps.
To the gameplay: We all agree, Rockstar Games had always a good eye for a good story. But in the former games, there was not that much to do, well apart from doing the missions or beat up some cops until GTA San Andreas and also GTA IV brought in new activities. From casinos or barber shops in San Andreas to ordering a big number 9 with extra dip at YOUR nearest Cluckin' Bell. Grand Theft Auto V brought in even new, and I mean a whole bunch of new activities to do. From hunting over playing golf or tennis to having some fun at Del Perro's Pier or even tuning your favorite car. In total, GTA V offers a huge world with a bunch of stuff waiting for you.
To the story: Without wanting to spoiler you, I can make it a bit shorter, the story is a gangster epos of the best class. The developers spent their pocket money well (amazing $265 million). I can recommend the game for everyone, it doesn't matter if you have played the previous games or not, apart from some nice references to previous games is the story in GTA V a complete own one.
To modding: There are amazing mods out there, that you should try. From simple graphic mods to complex additions with new story elements. But watch out: You should never use any mod in GTA Online, yeah some are really impressing but some can really take the fun from other gamers.
GTA Online:
As the story mode is a great produced story, GTA Online is bringing in a whole new perspective: you play as a, by your self created and designed character, newcomer to Los Santos, just waiting to work your way up in the gangster hierarchy. Compete or form crews with other players. There are as many activities as there are in the story mode, but you can also buy yourself a nice and tidy apartment from where you can, at the end, start heists to complete with your friends. Fill your garages with cars and motorcycles as you want to and improve them at your favorite Los Santos Customs! Then use them to let your friends eat dust in diverse races across the whole map. Later on, you can buy yourself businesses to make even more money.
The only frustrating parts of GTA Online are that there are many hackers on their way on the servers and during the last year, the game has turned a very frustrating way in where you need much more money than you can make during a fair time. This is, what we call, making money by Rockstar, by forcing the players to buy sharkcards, a way you get ingame money for purchasing with real money. Doesn't sound fair? It isn't
In total, GTA V with GTA Online is a nice package with some really good spent money and a whole bunch of game hours to enjoy.

This game is an improvement over Overlord 1, but there's a critical flaw: the puzzles in it are terrible. A good puzzle is where you have all the pieces you need to start and get an "ah ha!" moment when you put them together. In this game puzzle pieces are such that when you find how they fit together, it's more of a "really? that's the solution?" A lot of the difficulty is telling apart the parts of the terrain you're supposed to interact with from the parts that are just fluff. "Oh, so that one vine I can send minions up, despite every version of that vine up to this point just being a decorative piece."
Also, minions get stuck A LOT, and when a minion gets stuck then you're down a minion for the rest of the level. This means that by the time you get to the end, half your minions are stuck on terrain and you have to try to beat the boss with just a few minions. Note: If minions die, you can easily replace them. If they get STUCK, you're screwed.

GTAV has been fun and addicting for many of the same reasons previous titles in the franchise have been; it's outrageous, it's massive and intriguing. However where it falls short is that it is a very shallow and streamlined experience.
This GTA map is ridiculously big and full of fun things to do or cool places to explore. Additions like golf and tennis make for games within a game. But by 2013 standards and playing games like Skyrim, it falls a little short. The world is closed off and limited in a lot of ways. Like okay I see you golf and tennis, but why can't I go to the beach and play volleyball with some ladies, or go to the park and play basketball with some of the homeys. It's situations like this that remind you that you aren't quite in an open world environment. Most of the shops and buildings are inaccessible. So you can see a nice coffee shop and it's front door is a wall. You can't go into cool hotels or even go to a mall and then just decide you wanna try robbing as many stores as you can before having to fight off the police. It would also be nice to not see the same skins used so often. The very first fire fight in the game, every single enemy looked the same. And I can't count how many times in 2 blocks I see the same fat black lady yapping on her phone. It would have been nice to see some of these features to have a truly immersive and captivating experience. As it is, this is GTAIV with more paint, better driving, less annoying SIMS add-ons like making your friends happy and having to meet up with them or relationships deteriorate.
Customization is also very limited partly because every character has a unique story you must follow. And you can't veer off of it at all. There is no element of choice at all here in a generation that usually demands one. You can't even change your default car. If you buy a 250k Lambo, you'll still have your ugly Dodge Charger spawn at your house. If you place cars you steal or buy into your garage and take them on a mission, they may disappear when the mission makes you use another vehicle. In some cases your car appears at the end of the mission but in many cases it does not. And sure you can buy property, but you can't buy homes or condos. You can't invite a bunch of girls over for a pool party. You are often left with the feeling of, why do I need to work for money when I can't show it off or do much with it anyway. If I want to feel how a Ferrari drives, I can just steal it I don't have to save up and buy it. Then what? Where is the thrill of reaping your rewards and living out the life of one of these criminals in full detail.
The iPhone app also falls sadly short. The things to do on it are boring and don't affect the game enough.
All of that being said this is still a great GTA experience with hours and hours of fun. And GTA online will be lots of fun. But it is disappointing that in 2013, almost 2014 with the technology that is available today and the rich video game history we have, companies with great franchises like this aren't pushing the envelope a little harder to make the game innovative and inventive translating into a thoroughly immersive experience for the end-user.
