Combat Monsters is a turn based strategy game in which you build your deck from a bunch of cards.
You earn cards by playing campaign mode, player vs player, daily challenge and by buying / selling cards.
It's fairly reasonable to say you can get any card(s) you want if you decide to put some effort to it.
Gameplay feels smooth and graphics are ok, the only thing that really bothers with the graphics is that most units look pretty much exactly the same. Example all robot archers are pretty much the same in looks, but can have really big dif in stats and skills.
Othervise I love the idea that theres several races with their unique passive buffs and a very large pool of cards to choose from, even if you just started the game.
However, theres a few big issues with the game:
1. There clearly has never been any idea to keep cards balanced, you can have a unit that costs 3 with 1/8 stats and you can have the completely same unit, but with only 1 cost. The only dif is that the other card is legendary, the other is common. This is the basis why theres so many dif cards, theres a ton of cards that are just clearly a lot worse than another one. The only trick is that legendaries are expensive and you won't get a ton of those quickly.
Theres a few dif game modes you can play from which 1 doesn't allow any rare+ cards in deck. It's reasonable to say that it's the only gamemode you can have any chance in if you are starting this game. And even then you are facing the elite players.
2. Dead community. And I seriously mean dead. You log in, theres 2 guys online preying on newbies to smash.
Other minor issues are time to time graphics bugs and that the UI for building deck / going through your cards is just horrid. One could also argue that the whole UI is complete garbage. :)
This is one of those games that I kinda like, but I feel it's not worth playing the game since theres only 1 viable gamemode that is reasonable to play. I just don't see the point in grinding out weeks or even months to get the cards to compete in the 3 out of 4 game modes which all accept powerhouse cards.
I'v played a lot of TCGs in general and some of them on very high competive level, but I can't recall ever seeing so insanely big gap between your lowly common and most rare cards. It's like playing mtg so that you get 1 mana from each land and your opponent gets 3 and he has crafted his deck accordingly. Theres just no way you will win.
Overall I would give this game something like 5-6 out of 10 and im struggling to decide whether to up or down vote here. For now i'll drop a No, but i'll check whats happening with the game in the future and perhaps after changes to the UI i'll upvote this.

Combat Monsters is a fairly complex card game with a lot of depth. The hex based movement on the board also makes it resemble a turn based strategy game.
There's a lot of variety in the the matches, thanks to the numerous features in the game. The game includes a lot of different boards, all of which have different shapes and feature several bonus tiles. There are also many different kinds of utility cards that you can use to strengthen your team and disrupt your opponents. All the different features work together well and give the game depth.
There's a ton of different cards in the game, although the developers tend to have gone for quantity over quality. A lot of the monsters are very similar to each other, and some of the spell cards require a very specific situation to be useful. I would've preferred a somewhat smaller pool of cards, with only cards that are genuinely useful and different from each other. Some monsters are so weak that they seem pretty pointless, since there are others that have the same usage cost, yet more health and attack.
The upside of the large card pool is that you have a ton of choice on what kind of deck you'd like to make. There are many different races and classes, all with their unique abilities. With all the variety available, it's fun to build new decks. You can make lots of different kinds of viable decks.
A few of the cards are a bit overly useful and fit in almost any deck, like the runes that allows you to draw extra cards every turn. This is a major advantage in practically any deck. Still, I haven't encountered anything that's clearly overpowered. The balance isn't perfect, but it's pretty good, especially considering the large amount of cards included.
These problems are mostly mitigated by how generous the game is in giving you cards. You can buy any card directly, which makes it easy to get the exact cards you want. The most popular cards cost quite a lot, but it does allow you to remove the luck element from getting the cards you want.
You get cards in the single player at a quick pace even if you don't pay any real money. You might have to replay the quests in other formats in order to get enough good cards for the hardest missions. The game is much more generous to free players than most digital card games.
If you do enjoy the game, you should buy the tripler. It triples all the cash payouts in the game. There's no time limit or any other catch to it, which makes it a great deal.
Some other reviewers complained about the game being pay to win because of how difficult the campaign is in some spots. The campaign does get hard later on, but not in a way that requires you to pay money. I finished all the campaigns with only 75% of the money an F2P player could get, so there definitely isn't a paywall in the game. As long as you're smart with your deck composition and don't rely solely on legendary cards to win, you can make great decks without paying money.
I really enjoyed that the single player offered a good challenge. It feels like a complete game by itself. In many other digital card games, the single player is more like an extremely easy tutorial for the multiplayer.
The presentation of the game isn't as strong as the gameplay is. Representing a card game with 3D models is an interesting idea. It makes the game much more animated and lively than usual. However, the art style doesn't match the game's content very well. The game's art style gives the impression of a simple, kiddy game, despite it being fairly complex. The recent update did improve the graphics somewhat. They're not AAA quality, but they look decent enough.
It's odd that the game has so few players in it, even though it's actually very well made and free to play. The player base does seem to be very dedicated to the game, so you can still find opponents for multiplayer games.
If you enjoy card games or turn based strategy games at all, give Combat Monsters a shot. It's a lot of fun.

TWICE THE CONTENT, HALF THE STORY: THIS IS ONLY DX MD PART ONE. Let me explain. Superb lore, graphics (when not glitching), music, backstory, side missions and deep environments to explore... with gameplay that will have you scratching your head and trying lots of different tactics. Character animation and dialogue can feel a bit "previous gen" at times but there are definitely some gems in there.
Now to the crux of the matter. Unfortunately over the several years of development they went way too far and weren't able to manage a suitable ending... It looks like they had to rush to finish it, so the full story arc is cut short (feels like 65% of what it should have been, story wise, yet with 200% of the content that was actually needed). If you do play lots of the side missions the ending will be somewhat bearable. If you don't, then you'll probably feel quite upset. All in all this can only be described as Deus Ex: Mankind Divided: Part One Of Two. When will Part Two come out? Maybe never.
Get this only if you're a huge fan and want to explore this meticulously crafted but flawed game.

Short Answer: Terrible Game.
Long Answer: I've played Heroes and Generals for a very long time, and I have been frustrated almost every moment of it. The game is incredibly grindy and the grind has only been made harder over the years, for instance the price to buy a new class of soldier has doubled, Everything in the game has upkeep to pay everytime you use it and using high teir equipment can even lead to a match where equipment expenses far outweighs the earnings from the match. The game is very much pay to win as a person that pays for a membership gets 2 "badge" slots rather than 1 (the badges give powerful buffs like 15% damage reduction, 25% better hip fire, and no kill cam, among many others). Many balance issues exist in game that the devs blatantly ignore, such as Russia having the only AT gun in the entire game (and the only teir 3 submachine gun), the U.S having by far the worst aircraft for the longest time.
Development has stagnated for a very long time, while there are updates containing small features like new vehicles, many highly anticipated features have been missing for years. The last new map was added 2 years ago back in 2015 (with the exclusion of a tiny map focused around one small building). this is worsened by the fact that the game only has 5 full sized maps and 4 small ones. The player cap in a match is 18vs18 and despite years of the dev's promising higher counts nothing has changed. Recent updates THIS YEAR have brought such features as: Tutorials for beginners, Medics, and Water Physics. All features that most FPS hold as core mechanics that are now just being added. More concerningly is the multiple sound, graphics, and lighting overhauls. The game overshot its lifespan before it was even released.

Gnomoria is basically Dwarf Fortress Lite.  This is not a bad thing.  It sacrifices some of the depth of Dwarf Fortress in order to bring you a working UI and graphics, while still capturing the essence of it.  You start with a handfull of gnomes, a seasons worth of suplies, two beasts of burdon, and a full year to entrench yourself before winter rolls in and everything stops growing.  Build great big fortresses, labarynths of tunnels, great big absurd structures that server no purpose at all, or whatever the heck you feel like.  The only real down side I can say for it is that it doesn't have an Adventure mode, allowing you to take a single Gnome out into the world and forge his tale.
If you've ever wanted to play Dwarf Fortress but were intimidated by the esoteric controls, or difficult to comprehend visuals, Gnomoria's got you covered.
If you've played Dwarf Fortress but found it too intense or complicated, but still want to play something like it, Gnomoria's got you covered.
If you're a Dwarf Fortress veteran who wants a break from the sheer difficulty of Dwarf Fortress, but still wants to play Dwarf Fortress, Gnomoria's got you covered.

awesome game. this is pretty much only mmo that i've ever played for a longer period of time. it is obviously very story driven game. you follow the lord of the rings story by completing epic quest line. and this epic quest/story line really is awesome, it takes you through whole middle earth, you meet tons of characters, you participate in a lot of instances and explore every region of middle earth. it really makes you feel like you're part of the story. besides this, there are loads of regular side quests, and if you take your time like me, and read text about each quest, game becomes much more immersive.
the middle earth is huge and diverse. you have nice looking shire (green, flowers, friendly people), then you have arctic cold and frozen forochel; barren, dark and hostile angmar. 10/10 for world (middle earth) variety.
you have 5 races and 10 classes to choose from. nothing too crazy, but definitely not bad. each race has it's own starter zone and unique quests, where you learn a bit about lore, and meet some characters important for that race.

game has couple of regions where you can purchase your own house and decorate it with trophies from battles.
community is friendly and mature.
f2p model: you can play whole game without spending a cent, and i know people that have done that, but it requires a lot of grind. personally, i bought eriador quest pack, and all expansions (you can get them for free if you grind enough).

So... about Blood Dragon... I bought this game not knowing what exactly to expect. I came out of this game a fairly happy person. However, there is one not so slight fault which detracts from buying Blood dragon, and that is something I suppose should be expected when dealing with Ubisoft and their AAA ilk: Uplay.
Uplay's many, many bad internet issues have subsided over the years thanks to my area receiving better internet cables, but the service still runs look utter crap both for me and others. In truth, if you want to buy any ubisoft games, I recommend you just buy them on Uplay instead, since what you get here on steam isn't a game, it's access to the service that will give you the game, which does nothing but waste consumer time. A complete pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥to be sure, but this is the 'AAA' industry, so what the hell can we do?

After 2-3 years of not actively playing it, I gave this game another try for nostalgic purposes. These are my thoughts.
A great game for its time, but destroyed by nearly every other ARPG to follow after it. Most of my hours on this game were put before Diablo 3, Marvel Heroes, and Path of Exile made substantial improvements to their games. First couple years this was out, game was bliss. Only other viable options were Titan Quest, Diablo 2, and Torchlight 1.
The game was designed to be played in Multiplayer, apparently, but I spent most of my time solo. The multiplayer is actually very bad and scales terribly with the more players you have. Monster damage and health isn't properly tuned and everything ends up doing too much damage and being sponges, especially the bosses. It also forces you to sign up for a Runic account because apparently this is a good idea for some reason. The network code happens to be abysmal as well, and handles lag in the weirdest way I've seen in a game. For the person lagging, the game creates a seperate instance, until the lag stops. Causing confusion for everyone involved (wait you already killed those monsters?).
You can manually allocate stats, but this doesn't actually matter. The most important stat will always be strength, unless you're using a shield, then you pump vitality in until you reach a high enough block chance, then back to strength. Enemies crit in this game, which is a stupid mechanic when there's no way to properly mitigate this, so you'll die to random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, making this game a poor choice to tick the "hardcore" option on.
The protection and armor systems are probably the worst I've seen in this genre. There are no percentage reductions, only "armor" for each damage type. Which is literally a flat value. So if you've got 20 physical armor, you take 20 less physical damage. 60 poison armor, 60 less poison damage. There comes up a point pretty quickly in the game where the armor stats don't mean much at all, and it's more about dodge chance, stacking self heals, getting health boosts via gear, and popping potions constantly.
In addition, no matter what mods you try, the game is inherently designed around doing what I described above, as well as using only one active skill (many of the skills for classes are worthless) and spamming it constantly. The rest of your skill points go into the overpowered passives. In addition, there are many skills in the game which scale terribly, and it's actually discouraged to improve upon them further, because it substantially increases mana costs which low level characters can't keep up with. Alternatively, some classes such as the Vanquisher (ranged gun user) can make builds around using the normal attack. But either way, the game is designed aroun you holding down and clicking on one button and mulching everything.
Modding tools came out far too late after the game was out, and the community didn't end up doing much, and the tools are limited to begin with. So the modding scene has been dead shortly after the tools came out, outside of the most popular mod, Synergies. Which seems to be dead, when it hasn't had an update in over a year.
The engine itself is quite bad, and lags horribly when too many monsters are on screen at once. It also has atrocious loading times, which are worse depending on how large of an area you're loading. For a game which has such poor graphics and didn't even look good for its time, this has always been very annoying. Titan Quest came out many years earlier and looks far better and suffers from none of this. In addition, there's almost zero benefit for using a solid state, so load times are perpetually slow!
The good thing about this game, is this was THE game to play when there were hardly any competing ARPGs on the market. Years later, this game has proven to be an outdated relic. Which in many respects, Titan Quest, which came out years before it, is still a better game.
It's totally worth buying on a sale, but not at full price. You'll possibly get one playthrough out of it. The campaign for TL2 is actually very well designed fun, but drags on at points, particularly in act 3. It offers a decent endgame and mods expand more on it somewhat.
If you've been playing other ARPGs recently, such as Grim Dawn, Diablo 3, Marvel Heroes, and Path of Exile, you'll find yourself frustrated with this game pretty quickly, as it has no depth and customization worth a damn.

I'm only about 1,5hrs into the game at the time, but it's already a very satisfying game. The visual style is nice and cartoony without being too wonky, and there's some neat little bits of humor sprinkled about here and there. The world feels genuine and familiar for any fantasy gamer and the enemies are varied but balanced.
The soundtrack bothers me, while it's excellently done and easy on the ear, it leans far too heavily on the first two Diablo games' soundtracks and doesn't quite fit the game's atmosphere. Many of the sound effects could also just as well be pulled directly from Diablo, as is the waypoint system, and the socketed items, portal and identify scrolls. I get it, it's made to feel familiar to Diablo fans and that's what appeals to me too, but some of these things just feel like lapses of imagination when the execution is so directly analogous.
It doesn't ruin the game though and the environments have more uniqueness to them, setting the game apart for its own good, and many of the more annoying features of D2 like constantly running back to town to sell stuff to make room in your inventory (you can have your pet do that for you) and playing tetris with your inventory to fit everything (items all occupy a single slot) have been left out.
Pros:
+Nice visuals and smooth play even with lots of mobs on screen
+Very good controls
+The pet is a lifesaver
+Takes the good stuff in D2 and leaves out the bad
+Game difficulty options cater to a wide audience
+Map design is refreshing while staying true to the genre
Cons:
-Unimaginative in some parts, especially the soundtrack

Tongue-in-cheek games are a novelty that can work well with good execution. Comedy in platformers specifically aimed at the very industry they are part of are a bit more rare, or at the very least do not take center stage, and DLC Quest is a fantastic example why this is so.
DLC Quest is all about poking fun at the odd microtransactions found throughout far too many games today, and uses this as the main twist. By collecting coins you can purchase "features" such as the ability to jump, attack, and so forth. This...is really all the game does to make itself unique sadly, as the writing, like the mechanics, are hamfisted and did little to stimulate even a slight smile on my face. Most annoyingly, the main story is barely 30 minutes long even with all the backtracking, and the ending happens right when actual enjoyment was starting to settle in. Abruptness isn't always a bad thing and the game lets you run around and do whatever you want, but the world is so intensely bland that I found myself going back to the main menu to see if there was anything else to offer.
To my surprise, there is a second campaign that you can play, and I was cautiously optimistic that there might be an actual game here. In a sense, there is: Actual challenges, missions and goals are set in an "ironic" sort of way for the character, and while they are set up as jokes...you still have to do them. Needless to say, the second campaign is just as short as the first, and offers nothing worthwhile.
To give credit where its due, a joke can last only so long, and this game does not overstay its welcome any more than it should, but this game still asks for money, even though it's just a measly dollar, and even then, it still provides less content than most actual DLC offers for the same price. After all, when the title tells you the joke and the joke is the whole game, I guess having expectations in the first place was a bad idea, but regardless, save yourself the money and go buy a complete product instead of one so lacking in content. <insert DLC joke here>

TWICE THE CONTENT, HALF THE STORY: THIS IS ONLY DX MD PART ONE. Let me explain. Superb lore, graphics (when not glitching), music, backstory, side missions and deep environments to explore... with gameplay that will have you scratching your head and trying lots of different tactics. Character animation and dialogue can feel a bit "previous gen" at times but there are definitely some gems in there.
Now to the crux of the matter. Unfortunately over the several years of development they went way too far and weren't able to manage a suitable ending... It looks like they had to rush to finish it, so the full story arc is cut short (feels like 65% of what it should have been, story wise, yet with 200% of the content that was actually needed). If you do play lots of the side missions the ending will be somewhat bearable. If you don't, then you'll probably feel quite upset. All in all this can only be described as Deus Ex: Mankind Divided: Part One Of Two. When will Part Two come out? Maybe never.
Get this only if you're a huge fan and want to explore this meticulously crafted but flawed game.

I have done a review of this game previously, but that review was outdated.
After playing it recently, updates and tweaks to the game have made it more playable than before, and while still messy, it is now in the "bad" games list and no longer in the "Complete Trash" games list.
So what do I say about it now? PROS AND CONS!!
Not really, Just going over some points:
* The Guns all work!
And are (mostly) balanced! Exceptions still apply, but now one can actually pick up any weapon (including a pistol!) and you can figure out a playstyle to make it work. Reto did something right somewhere... although many weapons can sound much better than they do in the game.
(example, nearly all the LMGs sound like lots of keychains rattling, vehicle MGs sound like someone banging on a table... Machineguns should sound fierce and powerful and scary! You should want to dive for cover when one of these things starts shooting in your direction!).
* Win conditions are half fixed.
I made a big deal last time about the botched win conditions for matches in this game. Well, recent updates have simplified this. There are still games where the game logic is supposed to figure out who is closest to winning after 30 min, but it can't decide and so the game runs on for many hours until one team runs out of spawns, or one team let's the other win because they want the battle to end.
So still some work needed here, but at least better than before. Most games I play end within an hour.
* Hackers.
Still a thing, and there is pretty much nothing you can do about it.
There are, however, a lot fewer hackers recently. RETO! Keep improving whatever weak anticheat you are using and finish the job! I can see a glimmer of hope in this regard (probably false hope, but this is a chance for reto to redeem themselves)
* Once again, looking into the murky subject of Faction Balance/Bias.
And I have to say: with a few limited and easily countered exceptions, the factions are MOSTLY BALANCED!
That's right, I said it! Its ON NOW!
Joking aside, except certain vehicles or weapons that, by their being, are slightly superior to others, I have to be honest... the factions are mostly balanced right now. Whatever under-the-table tweaks reto did recently, it helped a little.
Battles are no longer pre-determined depending on the map and on what factions are present. It comes down to two major factors (among many smaller ones): How well each team works together (as the game is meant to be played), or which team has more hackers... and as I stated earlier, hackers appear to be on the wane. While NO hackers is preferable, again, the game is at least playable.
* Vehicles (thanks to Kenlek for bringing this up)
Jeeps and other fast vehicles are really weird to drive, they spin out of control way to easy and take forever to get going. Bicycles are still kind of odd for some reason, and tanks are sometimes too easy to kill, and other times way to hard.
Wheeled vehicles need to be tweaked. There is not much else to it, they are OK otherwise. Maybe give the Russians some kind of gun on their jeep? If not, maybe allow certain passengers to shoot out of it as compensation for not having an MG? Just some thoughts... what do you think?
- - - -
On the subject of tanks, this is a bit more complicated, but I will go into it a bit. Tanks should be slightly harder to kill from AT grenades and such, as these were not effective in real life, and are kind of OP. However, the whole point here is that tanks are supposed to be supporting Infantry and the infantry supporting the tanks, as in real life. IRL, tanks ARE in fact quite easy to kill by close-in infantry attacks (a single molotov, used right, can disable a tank... no need for explosives). Friendly infantry are supposed to be keeping enemy AT-infantry away from the tank while the tank does its thing. To avoid the OP AT weapons available to infantry, most tankers hide on the edges of the map (where it so happens that they can be seperated and picked off individually by tank-hunters).
The reason tankers do this is because if they move in with the infantry in a Combined Arms force like they are SUPPOSED TO, they get killed by AT grenades too fast, and by enemy tanks hiding at the edges of the map... Mines and rocket launchers work as they should, IMHO, but grenades and hostile tank fire need to be tweaked to get tankers to stop being campers and start being tankers... you are in a TANK after all.
Otherwise, our beloved tankers are in a nasty pickle... move in and get AT'ed to death while your friendly infantry stand by and watch, or camp somewhere and be hunted down with no help nearby while being little use to the team.
I started playing as a tanker (with an MG-armed starter tank) and tried to play Combined Arms like a tank should... suppressing enemy infantry, giving friendly infantry rides to the objectives, being mobile cover, all that great stuff! Unfortunately, it just does not work like this in the game right now, and so tanks can't be as awesome as they should be. I went back to being an infantryman...
- - - -
I am still marking this as Not Recommended, since this game still needs a LOT of work, but I will come out and say that the game is PLAYABLE. It has risen from the abyss, but it is still at the brink... however, it looks like it may be POSSIBLE if Reto will do the work. Aside from better anticheat, I would really like to see features like Muting/ignoring players, as there are still a lot of trolls around (you know, the players who spend the entire game hiding in a corner and insulting their team for no reason). Would be nice if you could mute.
They also fixed the issue where you couldn't leave a battle and join another once you started one. Now, while you can't mute trolls, and you can't kick hackers, you CAN leave the battle and go join another. At least you have that option now.
Again, I highly advise you NOT to spend money. The pay-2-win feel is still there (slightly less so, since all weapons are usable now), but this game is not worth your money just yet. I will be keeping an eye on this game (and playing it from time to time), because while Reto is ranked up there on the hate list along with other "evil" game developers, Reto might (a BIG might) have the capability of coming back, and I would honestly love to see this game make an epic comback from the hole it is trying to crawl out of.
=============

Also, the game gets updated pretty regularly, with fixes and new content.  Some people might complain that it is short, but they have added an Endless option to difficulty, which I assume means what it says (I have not tried it yet).  This is the best thing I have played in a very long time, and it has plenty of replay value to satify those skeptics who think it might be too short.  As of 3/8/15 it is on sale, and I highly encourage anyone to pick it up.  Even once it isn't on sale, I still think it will be worth it.  I can't wait to see what these developers do next!

Others mentioned that this plays like a modded Quake. There is a familiar speed and smoothness that I really like. I've been looking for something that reminds me of Heretic/Hexen, but with a modern twist. The graphics are good enough and it plays great with a controller, too. One round is relatively short, a few hours at most, because the idea is that you'll replay it multiple times. I quite like this approach in this game, because not too much is due to random chance and you still have a feeling that your actions matter. For example, my main gripe with FTL was that even after you get good at the game, you can still do everything right and die due to bad luck. I think that in Ziggurat this is not the case. It took me 4-5 replays to kill the final boss and since there is a lot left to unlock, I look forward to ocasionally replay it and progress to higher difficulties. Overall, nothing really stands out, but the game comes together really nicely in a neat package.

An Fps Rogue-Like Shooter at its finest. Beautifully rendered in its varied architectural level design. Monsters and baddies abound in all their viciousness behind almost every door. Your trusty wand the only surefire weapon that you have, and even that needs to recharge. Running in circles to avoid the flames coming at you is all just part of the fun of this title. The difficulty is hard at times but rewarding.
You unlock new characters as you progress such as Kraz the Novice or Algorab the alchemist. All unlocked characters have different attributes and skills than the initial Argo the Apprentice that you start with. Unlocking these different characters is simply achieved by playing the game and earning different rewards.
Overall I have rated this title an 9.5/10 although its difficulty can be rewarding it can also be overwhelming at times. Such is life in a brilliant Rogue-like title like this.

+ Not frustrating when you die (you still get rewarded)
+ Packed with contents: every game offers a surprise (new power, new weapon, different room / trap / monster / boss)
+ While some tunes are frankly epic, ...
- ... some others are pretty forgettable
- Not so amazingly written, story is bland

Ziggurat is hardcore but it's never unfair. You can indeed get unlucky, but if you're skilled enough there's always a way out - and if you die it's okay, you'll do better next time.

Not sure if all the positive reviewers actually played the game, or if they were purchased reviews from Mturk or a similar piecework system: the game is that bad.
It has no real storyline, and a single platformer map (two maps if you count the 2-platform "finale" map that does nothing but lead you to a button that starts the ending cinematic) that's extremely fiddly.
For a game that's so self-consciously "calming", you'd think they could come up with game mechanics that don't just tense you up. It's not "calming", it's just slow. A single missed jump can take 30 or 45 seconds to recover from, because of the "soothing" pace.
I really wanted to like the artwork, because parts of it
beautiful. However, it was like the artist and the creative director couldn't agree on whether it should be "8-bit" or "clean and minimal", so it's not good at being either.
There were some interesting mechanical elements, like the elevators, underwater jets, and flight statues. However, none of these were used in any way other than "this is the only way to get to the next platform".
Three of the five achievements are basically clones. You have "collect all the MacGuffins", "unlock the final cinematic with all the MacGuffins", and "watch the final cinematic". It's no wonder very nearly the same number of people have completed those three achievements. It seems little, but it's just another pointer to how little thought went into the presentation of the game itself.
Another "the designers didn't care about presenting the game" bit is the lack of customisable controls. I hope you're a right-handed QWERTY-user, who likes WASD controls, because the controls are hard-coded. Lefties, people who just prefer using their right hand for directional controls, and people with non-English keyboards need not apply. (Ironic for a game "about" an Eastern religion, isn't it?)
The concept is decent, and a little jump control and running could go a long way to making it playable. Even better, if they could give us that, they could add more levels and it wouldn't be tedious. As it is, I'm left 45 minutes later basically tense and irritated by a "soothing Buddhism" game.

I'm no fan of the Dead Space games. In fact, I detest them. Dead Space 1 was, in a word, boring. Boring to the point that I barely remember anything about it. I remember the turret segments, which should have been awesome, were ruined by the atrocious controls, and I remember the two other people with Isaac being unlikeable jackasses. I haven't played Dead Space 3, and I really don't want to. Now, Dead Space 2 takes a cue from Empire Strikes Back and attempts to be better than the first game, which it manages to both succeed and fail at. The Sprawl is a great location to play through, being far more spacious and varied than the Ishimura, and we get a few glimpses of everyday life on the Sprawl. Isaac himself actually has characterization this time, albeit fairly clichéd, and most of the characters we interact with have different and compelling personalities, especially newcomer Ellie. Ellie and Isaac play off one another in ways that are both hilarious and heartbreaking, and it overall makes for better immersion.
Unfortunately, that's all I have to say that's positive. The biggest, most glaring problem is: this game is basically Dead Space 1 with a new paint job and a camper attached. Most of the enemies are copy-pasted from the first game, including the "elite" recolors, gameplay is identical, the plot amounts to "Dead Space 1, but on a space station," the wide array of weapons is, again, completely pointless since the plasma cutter is all you really need, Isaac is lead along by a female character who betrays him in sight of the oh-so-special Marker, (two this time!), and the monsters keep jumping out of the exact same "vent" (it doesn't actually go anywhere) as the first game. Oh, but wait! Now, there's extra varieties of incredibly obvious panels the monsters could be behind! Yahoo!
Now, onto the series' bread and butter; the gore and body horror. They're there and they're certainly creative, but they start losing what edge they might have had when they're in your face (literally) from the start of the game right up to the end. Much of the game's gore allowance was lavishly slapped onto Isaac's numerous death scenes...which you'll likely never see if you play at all competently.
In conclusion, Dead Space 1 is boring, Dead Space 2 is better but still boring, and Dead Space 3 doesn't look like it's worth the money spent.

You came here for a torchlight review but heres a recipe for some bangin' ravioli:
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

An MMO Classic that still plays well today.  LOTRO brings the lore and the atmosphere of Middle Earth to life with graphics, sound, voice acting and music that are simply captivating.  Anyone who is a fan of the books, movies or just loves a good story-based RPG will enjoy Lord of the Rings Online.
Recent changes to the MMO  have made it easy for solo players to play from the start all the way to the current end game, including soloing all the Books (the game's main quest line).  The Books give players an overarching goal for the entire game, moving you forward through the regions and providing an indepth story that parallels the journeys of the main characters from the Lord of the Rings series.  Along the way you will complete hundreds of additional quests, instances, skirmishes and deeds while exploring a beautifully detailed world that brings Middle Earth to life like no other game since.
Lord of the Rings is Free To Play, though you can subscribe as well.  A subscription unlocks all the regions, quests and deeds content and provides many additional benefits.  However the game is fully playable without a subscription through the use of Turbine Points, which are earned by completing deeds and can be cashed in to unlock new regions including quests and deeds.  I would still recommend that new players purchase the Quad Pack when it's on sale though, as it unlocks a ton of content for only $10 (when 75% off).  The Steely Dawn Starter Pack is also a good deal when on sale, as it unlocks the Evendim region and gives 500 Turbine Points in addition to the account items.  There are many great guides on the web for playing LOTRO using minimal purchases and earned Turbine Points.
UPDATE : 2017 marks the 10th Anniversary of LOTRO and the release of the Mordor expansion, completing the storyline of the Fellowship.  There has never been a better time to jump into this game and experience the best version of Middle Earth you'll find in a video game.

Of all the different MMORPG.s that are out there in the world, of which I've tried a few different ones, I have always come back to LOTRO as it holds a special place in my heart. It's easy to say that since you like Tolkien's books you'll like that game or that film, however I think that very few games actually manage to capture the magic and mystery that Tolkien's books give birth to.
I have played LOTRO on and off since the time when you couldn't venture further than to Mirkwood, whilst now you're almost at the black gate and very close to finishing this epic journey.
The reason I keep coming back to this game is simple, they keep adding more and more content and I want more and more lore and just the feeling of adventuring in Middle-Earth. It's just one of those feelings which is really hard to describe, but nothing will ever compare to exiting Moria after ~1weeks worth of time (IRL) questing in the depts and then being treated to the glorious Lothlorien and their beautiful forest.
That said, the game is not without problems and is at this point really old, however, if you can look beyond the slightly blurry textures that show that the game is old, there is much to love in the game.
The combat flows smoothly, sometimes there are a few problems with pathfinding for the enemies, but these are few and far between.
The lore inside of the game is canon as far as possible, though the developers have taken some liberties in their designs, of course, though I would say that there's nothing that is terribly lore breaking and you can enjoy this game and get your geek on without risking the "Peter Jackson syndrome...", looking at you Hobbit...
Is this a game for everyone? No certainly not, no one game is for everyone, but you don't need to be a Tolkien geek like me to enjoy this game. If you take some time to read the descriptions for quests etc. you'll find yourself learning loads about the world in no time. Basically, if you've ever had an interest in running around Middle-Earth and slay orcs, I'd say this is one of the better games to do that in. It may not be as big and fancy as WOW or other MMORPG:s but it makes up for it with stories and grandious environments for you to visit.
Touching on the F2P models slightly aswell. I have ever only played the game while it's been F2P, this because I was too young to be able to uphold a subscription before then on my own. I find that the F2P model is quite fair and you're even allowed to gather Turbine Points, their currency for the in game store, though questing and doing deeds in the world.
Although I would strongly recommend that whoever enjoys this game and would like to improve their life a little, should subscribe for just 1 month and then go back to playing, this will bring your account up to premium level, compared to the F2P version, giving you a lot of quality of life improvements to the game, such as more bags, higher cap on gold etc.
You will be allowed to quest up to ~Level 20 in the game for free before being required to purchase more regions to unlock the quests that lay within. Giving you, in my oppinion, ample time to form an idea about the game and decide weather or not it's worth spending that ~5€ to unlock more stuff. I did and I've never looked back on it as "wasted".
Is it perfect? No, but good enough to warrent countless of hours of playing, weather you're a Tolkien geek or no. Give it a shot without paying money and if you like it, there's a lot of content to be enjoyed here, for not too steep a price.

This is not a finished product.  At 5 bucks, it looked cool, so I took a chance.  I have played up to 15/84 in the "Journey" and most of it is trivial tutorial stuff, but some of it is very poorly presented and it takes way too long to figure out what you are supposed to do, even though it should be easy.
Right now, I can't recommend this game.  But with some clean up, properly written tutorial, and better controls (or option to set key bindings), it could be interesting.  I just don't have the patience to play it further while it is so clunky.
The "focus" level, for example, was very confusingly presented.  Without zoom out or pan screen (which come later in the tutorial), you are bound to lose track of where the cursor is in relation to the "maze" and you will never figure out where you are.  It also wasn't explained why the draw tool did not start working until you got the cursor into the yellow box.  I just figured that out with trial and error.
One of the problems is all the poor English in the tutorial.  Whoever wrote this obviously has a very poor grasp of the English language, and the phrasing is very awkward.  He needs some help from a good English writer.
Now for a few nitpicks.  The key bindings are horrible.  The arrow keys rotate in 3D space, but the num-pad arrow keys pan the screen.  Using the num pad just sucks.  Also, the screen pan is WAY too fast.  WASD should rotate in space, right click-and-hold should pan screen, and the mouse zoom should zoom in and out (currently done with Z and X).   Also, the R key is meant to reset all transforms, but it does not reset the zoom transform.
Oh, I almost forgot.  You may wonder, what is the objective in this game?  What is the goal?  It's not that clear cut.  It's stuff like "connect these two things in space using the tools I gave."  It's usually not as simple as drawing a line because there are built in physics.  For example, a cursor will move on it's own in the screen.  You can select "draw" and when you hold down the left mouse button, that cursor will draw.  However, you don't control the cursor.  It has it's own momentum and is simply "attracted" to wherever your mouse cursor happens to be when you hold down the left click button.  If the cursor gains a lot of momentum in one direction and you move your mouse pointer in the opposite, it will take a lot of time to reverse the momentum.  So you have to deal with those physical problems.  There is more to it than that, but that gives you an idea.

As a fan who has completed both Deus Ex the original since childhood and Deux Ex Human Revolution several times, I even pushed through Deus Ex 2 even though it was really terrible game compared to the original I can't recommend Mankind Divided.
Mankind Divided has a very good Half Life 2 feeling to it in Prague but it fails to draw you in because of the bland and boring characters and lack of immersion, and where Half Life 2 had fast paced action here there is no substance to make up for the lack of it. It basically is a home invasion simulator without anyone giving a sh*t.
There are so many things to complain about that this will be a very chaotic rant. But to give the game so thumbs up at least they did not try to change Deus Ex into something that it's not. It still follows Human revolution gameplay when it comes to sneaking, hacking and combat.
I will write the cons in a list instead to prevent this from becoming a several paged essay.
(*) Immersion and the Protagonist
In Deus Ex original you could choose who JC was, from his ethnicity to this character. He could be a maniacal ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, bleeding heart good guy or a professional agent that saves the status quo. In Human Revolution you still had some choice but even though Adam Jensen is fleshed out you could still make consequential choices that felt like it mattered until the horrible ending which I will not even touch... Zombie Apocalypse?!??! That's IT?!?! WTF!! WHY THROW OUT CONSPIRACY THEORY GOODNESS THAT MADE THE ORIGINAL GREAT FOR SOME GENERIC ZOMBIE SH*T?!!....
In Mankind Divided you already start as a double agent, you don't become one throught the game forming bonds with the NPC's, here it all start fleshed out. And in so doing there is no character development, you don't develop any feelings for Miller or anyone at INTERPOL or even the Collective. In the original you get to know Hanna, Manderley and Gunther throughout several quests and you get a bond with them and feel like a part of the Agency which makes it harder go rogue and eventually have to kill them later on. In Human Revolution you form a bond with Sarif, Malik and Pritchard and you feel like part of the company. But like stated, in Mankind Divided there is no story arc progression, you already start a traitor instead of becoming one through intrigue. And even though the villians in human revolution was cookie cutter boring, at least you had a reason to hate them for killing your ex wife you still had platonic relationship with. Here in Mankind Divided, you really can't care less.
*() Lack of Conspiracy
In the original you had Majestic 12, FEMA, ILLUMINATI, population control with government controlled plague and you even had Alien Greys ffs. In Human Revolution they toned it down, but still you had FEMA prison camps, government controlling vaccinations to rationing, government using climate change to take over the world (though they really blew it as I ranted about above) and the coming natural vs augmented dichotomy to drive conflict. Even in Deus Ex 2 they had some Templar sh*t, didn't make sense but at least it was something. In Mankind Divided its just "meh", some anarchist hacker group and ghetto's which is probably a metaphor for Europe pushing refugees into camps or something, but it's not a threat, and not a conspiracy so if it was the intentions of the devs to make this game into a critical statement of Europe's handling of the refugee crisis then it failed utterly and they could have made it much more interesting from all angles and perspectives.
I will end it here, many more things to rant about but others have done a good job describing the other aspects.
Thanks for reading, and don't waste your money on this game. Wait 1-2 years and play the original or Human revolution again instead.

I'm gonna weigh in here as a female gamer who has basically followed this franchise like a cult since the very first one came out. These opinions, however, may be subject to change on my next couple of playthroughs.
DXMD was good---but it was also disappointing. The game felt like it ended in the middle so that there was almost 0 closure. It felt like DX: The Fall all over again except with better game mechanics and more difficult decisions to make.
Pros:
New challenges, like trying to play stealth in broad daylight. This is totally novel in the DX franchise. It NOT being night all the time felt weird, almost unfair at first, but I appreciated the challenge to my standard strategies.
Beautiful graphics, massive environments and amazing soundtrack. McCann and his team never disappoint with their soundtracks, it would seem. The world was massive and full of opportunities to explore, catering to a wide range of approaches. Ammo everywhere, including options to make your own for your augs. Pretty well designed.
Lots of familiar threads for those who have followed the series as I have. I loved seeing them pull together pieces from the 3.5 games and numerous novel(la)s and comics that went before, trying to weave them into the story to help bring us to Deus Ex (1)'s 2052 and the state of the world there. The name dropping, the beginning of the groups, mention of the arcologies, emails and Lazarus' podcasts about things that we knew would be realities in 2052---I loved it all.
Choices. This one is a miserable sort of concession I am giving them because I don't like having to choose between lives. It's a brilliant build though, a way to truly bring the choices to life by bringing very dire consequences into play. It makes the game feel a tad unfair but interesting.
New augs. I loved the experimental augs and the serious mindblow that part of the storyline was.
Pretty interesting side quests. Beautiful work for enhancing the opportunities to explore the world they created and learning more about the post "Incident" world of 2029. Rather fantastic subplot twists in some cases. While this is a definite pro, it left room, however for the corresponding con that I must address.
Cons:
Shockingly incomplete story. DXMD gave you a multitude of threads of story, just like DXHR. Some of the things that were positioned as sidequests seemed to me like they were relevant enough to become part of the main story, but this is simply a matter of preference. You are left with this glaring hole of suspense contributed by both main and side storylines. Literally, the only way I knew I was at the last stage was when I found the Triangle Code where the game designers mentioned it being as such. I was so confused. The game is marketed as if it is a standalone story with some DLC side stories. What it really is---a half, a third, a quarter---we don't know. We're left dangling with not enough questions answered and not enough progress made on questions with ongoing answers. HOWEVER, I will admit that perhaps I feel this way because I did not explore enough. On my second (and third and fourth and...) playthrough, I'll do more to explore the areas and see if maybe they did provide more conclusive answers. Alternatively, they could have done this deliberately because they did not want it to feel like the end because it's not, considering the DXU. There's more to come, they've assured us, and so, strictly speaking, MD could not have a definitive end. Maybe we are to feel as in the middle of things as Adam certainly does. Who knows? Honestly though, I'm not sure I like it, especially when God alone knows when we're going to see the next one (even without considering the studio's new itinerary).
GLITCHING. The visual glitching is horrendous and pops up at the worst possible times in the game. Need to get through a large space full of hostiles undetected? Glitch---can't see anything in front of you. Reloading helps sometimes but this is a fatal flaw and I'm hoping they'll address it sooner rather than later, other projects be damned.
New voice actors for some of the older characters. I'll admit that this one is my own personal peeve. The voices for Reed and Sarif (and possibly Cassan) changed and I didn't like them. It felt so out-of-character and inconsistent. Naturally, I know there must have been good reasons for the changes but just that simple thing put a crimp in the game for me.
Overall though, I recommend the game as a die-hard follower and because it is an interesting play. The storyline that they do give us has interesting twists and turns. The options for the story are plentiful enough to keep me coming back to play it over and over again. If nothing else, I still gotta figure out what that cucumber achievement is about. 6.5/10

This game is incredibly fun, and engaging enough for me to write my first review ever. I'll start with the negatives first.
Only negative I see: Toxic community. Worse than the LoL community at times.
Sometimes there is clear lag that puts you in mixed positions on screen -- really throwing off your strategy.
The game, often deemed a "Smash clone," is quite different when it comes to mechanics, in a positive way.
There are basic attacks, special attacks, a dodge, and a weapon throw -- weapon's are a must in the game, which is a plus for variety.
Personally, I play this on my free time, and often use the 2v2 ranked game mode. There are various different game modes available as well, some that are really fun to play (Brawlball/Football, Snowbrawll/Snowball) that you can access through custom games, or seasonal events.
All in all, for a FREE TO PLAY game, Brawlhalla offers you a complete experience worth a premium price. It's really that much of an enjoyable game that you can start up whereever, whenever.
It's an improvement on every single level over Human Revolution. Big recommendation from me.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is an FPS/RPG with stealth elements. The game is set two years after the events seen in Deus Ex: Human Revolution - The Missing Link, and once again, we find ourselves impersonating Adam Jensen, who has been recruited in a brand new counter-terrorism organization called Task Force 29, obviously after having been put back together from the Panachea Incident's brutal effects.
Civil unrest against the Augmented people is reaching astronomical levels, because after the Signal Incident, which in short words made all the Augmented people go crazy and kill anyone in sight, the "normal" population doesn't trust them anymore, and so trust, racism and violence issues spread all over the world. In times like these, a mysterious group of terrorists decide to fight back against all the unfair treatments the Augmented are put through, and a series of bombings starts. This is where Adam moves into play, his mission is to find and stop this terrorist group, but soon, like in any respectful Deus Ex game, things will get much deeper and complicated than they seem...
The game's Longevity ranges from 15-20 to 50+ hours depending on: play style, player skill level, level of exploration done, number of side missions done, reading all the lore-related stuff, collectible finding. If you do main story only, guns blazing, no exploration or little, and no side missions, will take you less than 20 hours to finish it, while by doing for example Stealth, non lethal, all exploring, all quests, lore reading, collectible finding play through will take as far as 50 hours to do everything.
===
The gameplay of Mankind Divided is basically the one we are accustomed to in Human Revolution. If you are not familiar with it, know that Deus Ex's gameplay can be extremely variable, depending on how the player wants to approach it. The core gameplay is the one of an FPS, with a first-person view most of the time, and third-person only when in cover. But don't be fooled, Stealth, sabotage, item collecting and exploration are all fundamental in the gameplay and will each lead to its own rewards.
The player has a great degree of freedom when it comes to choose how to behave, you can go in guns blazing, killing every enemy (and civilian if you want) on sight, or use a more subtle approach and stun each enemy from stealth, or maybe hack your way through the security terminals and sabotage the automated defenses to kill everyone for you. When it comes to freedom of action, Deus Ex is the real deal, and also in theis episode it does not disappoint.
Adam will have at its disposal a very varied set of skills, called Augments, which will enable him to do many things, from hacking devices from a distance, become invisible, dash at the speed of sound towards the enemy, throw heavy objects, enhanche time perception and much more. These Augments can be unlocked through Praxis points, which can rarely be found in the world or unlocked by completing missions, defeating enemies and exploring secret areas. The great part is that the player can choose to unlock any augment he wants from the start, allowing massive customization to suit your own play style.
The game is totally free roaming and open world, most of it will be set in the city of Prague, part of it at least, and there will be many, many places to explore and things to do and discover. Total freedom of action is rule number one. Want to go on a rampage and kill half the city? Suit yourself, if you manage. Want to crack the vault of the central bank and get the sweet loot? Can do that, but won't be easy!
About the mission system, also here is total freedom for the player, you will be able to engage any mission at any time, disengage a primary mission and go do a secondary one, without generally having to worry about something failing. Missions carried out and completed earlier in the game will carry their consequences and unlock different missions and situations later, this opens up to a good replay value, because to experience all the possible situations it will take at least two playthroughs.
The challenge level depends heavily on the player's playstyle and ability. Played at maximum difficulty, it gives a decent challenge for a Stealth / Non-Lethal playthrough, so far i only played in this way, but i can safely say that it will be easier if played non-stealth, FPS style. Overall, there is some challenge but not overly so, the game is anyway satisfying enough and doesn't get boring or too easy.
The story plays along well, some points are frankly obscure and not well explained, even if you, as i did, will read all the documents and bits of text in each level, many things will not be clear, but it probably is the intention of the developers. The ending i won't say anything, but this: many people blamed it, hated it, but i think most did not understand it, also the ending of Human Revolution is similar in some ways and it opens up to a sequel as Human Revolution did.
===
Mankind Divided, with its Umbra engine, has been capable of dishing out some of the best graphics around.
Advanced light effects, tessellation, precision shadows, very high resolution textures, a plethora of filters and additional shading options, it's all there. The environment and model quality is overall extraordinary, Prague has been recreated in a spectacular way, and aswell the other places you will get to visit.
Of course, now let's talk about Performance which is the key, and about that we are not completely satisfied, as the game runs on an average of 45-50 FPS at High settings on an high end machine, generally performance is not very good even with state of the art machines with the latest hardware, FPS drops are not uncommon and generally there is not a good optimization and polishing in the graphics engine.
Still, the game is fully enjoyable as long as you have a decent configuration, you will not need a monster rig to run this decently as my faithful 4 years old rig with a 3GB GTX780Ti can run it on High and some tweaks with dignity. I would not advise to run this game on low or medium-low end systems, even at minimum the performance loss would be consistent.
Passing to bugs and issues, i have not noticed many to be honest, game's been patched through by now, major issues are gone, crashes are very rare, loading times are respectable even on HDDs, there is not texture popping, stuttering, tearing or anything like that, performance might not be optimized but is stable and solid.
===
Mankind Divided is a solid deus ex experience. Forget the pre-order stuff, forget the DLC packs and whatnot, as a game experience, i recommend it to any Deus Ex fan because in it you WILL find all the features that make this series great like you found them in Human Revolution, this is the same gameplay but expanded and brought to new life. If you are new and interested to this series, i strongly recommend starting at least with Human Revolution, the previous chapter, or if you are old-school enough, get the first Deus Ex and see what you're made of!

A sort of wizard-themed arena-shooter within randomly generated dungeons sporting a snappy art style and responsive, tight controls.
Attempt to survive the Ziggurat, making your way through five floors, challenging the boss at each to open the way to the next.
Enemies slain yield XP gems that can be used to gain levels, but time sensitive pickups discourage meek play. Every level you gain your choice of a perk, chosen from between a random selection of two perks. These perks can radically effect play, and a choice that doesn't synergize well with your playstyle may spell your doom, or radically empower you. The incredibly disfunctional or amazing builds that emerge from this system make continued runs through the Ziggurat feel very different, giving some nice legs to a game that technically speaking, has only a moderate amount of content.
New weapons, perks, and characters are unlocked simply by playing, and even a very poor run will likely yield a few new perks and a weapon. This system rewards persistence as well as skill, even if you can't make it to the last floor your attempts may pave the way for an eventual success, making the game less hopelessly frustrating than most games with rogue-like elements.
Very fun, stylish, and competently put together, Ziggurat has a lot to love for a very reasonable price.

Started a new game and got thrown right into the fray.
No tutorial, didn't even get an explanation of any game mechanics.
Got surprised and got chased around the room by 15 or more flying skull heads while dodging a never-ending barrage of dive bombs.
Got cornered by a bunch of chicken-like creatures and faced my inevitable death in a pool of acid.
Loved every second of it. This game is truly amazing.
The default controls use the standard FPS setup, which makes it easy to pick up. If you're not used to any of the controls, you can easily remap any of the keys - always a huge plus.
The music is "epic" (I rarely use this word but I can't find another word to use) and fits the mood perfectly.
The graphics look incredible. The art style and quick weapon switching animation are very similar to Bioshock Infinite. The game manages to look both bright and dark at the same time. The colors and contrast are absolutely brilliant.
The gameplay is outstanding. The game is extremely fast-paced and you need to be moving around constantly to avoid getting killed. When you level up, you get to choose either a perk or a one-time special effect. With each choice, there are tradeoffs. Do you want a permanent passive ability that will help you progress through the ziggurat? Or do you need to instantly heal to full to not die in the next encounter?
The fact that they throw you straight into the game without an explanation even adds to the experience rather than taking away from it. Expect yourself to die. Expect yourself to learn the mechanics bit by bit. And finally, expect yourself to love every moment of it. (Unless you get motion sickness, of course!)

I have to admit that this was a surprisingly fun game for what it is.  Typically I'm rather turned off by these minimalist games because it can really come off like a lack of effort.  Just a way to slap together the bare minimum to have something the developer can sell.  However, despite putting very little into the graphics, one thing that I thought was done very well was the controls.  All you do is move left and right with the space bar serving as the jump button, and in later levels you are faced with some precise and tight movements to make.  Unlike a lot of games of this style though, the controls are fluid and tight.  There's no problems with lag or delay and how hard you push the space bar does impact the height of your jump, and since the hit boxes are true to the images it never feels like a death is unfair or cheap.  You die because you made a wrong move.  Also, retrying levels after dying takes a very short amount of time to load up, which I appreciate as other cruddy games have horrible programming that lends itself taking forever to load so little that it's completely not worth it.
The tunes and sound effects aren't especially note-worthy.  Just simple, inoffensive sounds that at the very least aren't grating.  Similarly, something I see as somewhat ambivalent is the small scope of the levels.  Even later levels wind up being very short, in all but a few cases where you have to take your time getting in sync with enemy patterns and get the keys in a specific pattern.  The difficulty makes you go slower and approach smaller sub-sections carefully, but otherwise they don't have very much room to explore.  I feel like this is overall a good thing because of the difficulty since you aren't stuck working through a really long level and have to start over at the beginning repeatedly.
The achievements show that the developers did overestimate how much people were going to take an interest in the game with the level editing feature.  All I used it for was to make a level I could quickly grind the items I needed to accumulate since beating all of the main levels didn't activate them all.  Considering I beat all of the levels and got all of the achievements in under 40 minutes I definitely can't recommend picking this up for its asking price of $3.  However as part of a bundle at a price of pocket change I would suggest giving it a try.  Even if you don't take an interest in beating all of the levels because they get too tricky to mess with, I think most people could appreciate that the game loads quickly and has responsive controls.  I may have to look into other titles the developers might have put out after enjoying this title.  Overall, I'd say this game isn't really super, but it's certainly serviceable.

Excellent game/ experience. Continued in the great foot steps laid down by Dead Space 1. I have not played a AAA series with a greater emphasis on atmosphere and genuine "build up"; there are segments in the game you will crawl through at a snails pace hoping to go no further, because you don't know whether those noises you hear are just the game spooking you, or they are heralding the arrival or some horror. Graphically this game is still immersive today (2016); you can feel the dread and terror of the "haunted" space station as though you were there. The game gave you more "badass" ways to dispatch the hoards of monsters stalking you, but I did not at any stage (in moderate or hard difficulty) feel that they were overpowered or somehow ruined the experience; If you really wanted a challange, stick to the original weapon selection. People complain about the third entry into this series: but this sequel only built on what came before it: more of what you liked.
If you like any kinds of survival horror such as "Alien vs predator" or "resident evil", you should like this game. Given such an emphasis is given to the story (which is pretty entertaining), and atmosphere in this game, I do recommend anyone wanting the best experience to play "Dead Space 1" first, and even watch the suplementary graphic novels and animes: you really should dread the necromorphs.
This is a MUST PLAY game for any fans of horror, or even a fan of shooters looking for something different to a classic run and gun experience. Conversly to most shooters, this game will make you wish that the next firefight was a while away; that you'll be left alone in the shadows. Even if you are a "Halo" fan that found yourself enjoying your introduction into the "flood" for example, this game will take that experience and blow it out of the water.
Eight years on from the release of the original, and this is still among my favourite games, and it is the only of them that I actively avoid playing due to the anxiety! 10/10 must play.

Waking up in a hospital shortly after a new Necromorph outbreak on the civilian space establishment called Titan Station, also known as The Sprawl, Isaac must now find out how he got there and escape his ordeal, as he makes some new friends, and, of course, new enemies along the way, including Nicole Brennan, his dead girlfriend hallucination fueled by The Marker.
The game itself was similar to the first one, with a few exceptions like the slightly different story, the more frequent human contact and the considerable growth in terms of Necromorphs and locations variation.
has also more weapons and suits than its predecessor, each suit having its own special bonus, alongside the increased inventory slots and damage resistance of each one. A thing to note here is that the Steam version of
comes with all the DLC suits and weapons. A good thing you would say, but the downside to this is that all of them are available in the first store, in Chapter 1, for free. These suits can carry you just fine during your first playthrough, even on Zealot, the penultimate difficulty you can chose in the game (the last one is Hardcore, which you unlock after you finish the game once on any difficulty) and the weapons have special bonuses like shortened reloading time and increased primary/secondary damage which, again, can help to make your life easier, but for the sake of experience I would recommend you to wait a few chapters, at least, before grabbing them (no need to worry of spending the Nodes on a non-DLC weapon because the spent nodes on it carry over to the others of the same type). Another thing worth mentioning is that Nercomorph bodies disappear instantly if the body count exceeds, if I remember correctly, five, which can be annoying because, most of the times, you will need to stomp their bodies to get the loot, a thing that can be hardly accomplished during a big fight.
The game was, nonetheless, as expected, very enjoying, even on the second playthrough (New Game plus). The newly introduced Necromorphs and the finely forged story portraying Isaac descent into dementia made this sequel as good as the first game.

I have to admit I have been very pleasantly surprised by how enjoyable this game turned out to be.  The game itself has a nice turn-based flow with a good range of abilities, and many potential paths to success.  There is a huge amount of single player content, with an extensive campaign that is replayable for rewards with 4 different deck style variants.  It is way deeper than you might expect at first glance, and I like it quite a bit.
There is one area of content that can't be acquired by normal free play - alternate heroes, and it does stand as a blemish on the otherwise good game.  Honestly, I'd say the whole pricing structure needs a hard rethink, since I don't think it is doing what it should be... encouraging you to pay a reasonable amount for the fairly significant amount of enjoyable time you are likely to experience playing this game.

The amount of hours I've sunk into this game... the Steam tally only tells 1/4 of the story, since it's also available on mobile. The Steam version is 100% compatible with the mobile versions: your cards and coins are stored on the server.
You can buy the tripler which triples all your winning bonuses for $5, and if you like these game even a little bit  you would be crazy not to.
The game is based around summoning monsters onto a hex grid to protect your hero and attack the opponents hero and monsters. There are various spells, runes and equipment to boost your hero and monsters.  Monsters (and heroes) come in 3 classes: warriors, mages and archers. Warriors generally have more attack power and damage based abilities, archers have lower attack power but can shoot 3 hexes, mages are somewhere in the middle and can attack within a 2 hex radius. Control-decks are possible, but generally you won't be able to win without monsters.
Prizes for completing missions in the single player campaign are generous. Prizes are also paid out for winning online games against human opponents and it's entirely possible to not spend a cent and own as many cards as the big spenders as long as you are willing to put in the time: every card can be obtained without spending money except for additional heroes. This makes suggestions that this game is "play-to-win" simply laughable. Heroes have a system where there is a "hero of the week" which you can use for free, or you can purchase them outright if you decide you want one for keeps. You start the game with one permanent hero, which you can choose from a warrior, mage or archer.
The developers of this game are passionate about it, and it shows. They are regularly gathering feedback in the forums and implementing changes based on community feedback. If you experience a bug or technical issue they always respond quickly and have a fix ready in the next version.

A very fun game that will keep you occupied for hours. The game has a steep learning curve, but is very rewarding once you learn the basics.
When starting your game you have the option to choose how large the map is, how flat it is, and how steep the terrain is.
You also have the added bonus of choosing a difficulty to start on. I say bonus because not only can you select basic difficulties but you can also go into the settings and mess around with the types of monsters (you can even remove monsters altogether), their strength, how many come at a time, and how often they come.
This is just the customization for your map, I haven't even gotten to the game itself yet!
In the interest of keeping this brief I will list just a few different things I like about the game:
- Great customization (pretty much everything you do will be unique to the way you like to play)
- Changeable music styles (It's actually the same music but you can change it between an 8-bit "classic" style and a more modern "orchestral")
- Good for casual or serious gaming (With the difficulty settings you can make the game relatively easy and peaceful or very hard and challenging)
- Lots of replayability (I play the game quite a bit and have created many different levels, I have yet to run out of things to do or new ideas to try)
- Sandbox (If you can think it, you can build it. Making a kingdom? I suggest the "Huge" map size)
I might also add that there are many guides on Steam and the internet that can explain some of the more difficult parts of the game. Aside from a few minor things I'd still hope to see in the game, this game is very entertaining and well worth the price.
