If the idea behind Dwarf Fortress ever appealed to you but the ASCII graphics were a turn-off, then this is the game for you. There are still many differences between the two games, namely that Gnomoria doesn't quite have the same level of content that Dwarf Fortress offers, but then Gnomoria is also still in early access and still recieving updates.
If you're not aware of what either of the above games are, you are essentially put in charge of a group of gnomes and must see to their survival by building a settlement.  Instead of controlling things directly, you assign tasks and the appropriate workers carry them out.  The entire thing plays out as a sort of checklist: You want this, so to get this you must make that which requires the other thing.  Because of this, the game starts out a bit slow but it definitely picks up later on once all the workshops are set up.
Now, I've mentioned Dwarf Fortress several times which may seem a bit unfair to just compare Gnomoria to another game, but the style of gameplay is exactly the same.  Aside from the difference in graphics, Gnomoria definitely improves on what Dwarf Fortress lacked in approachability.  The UI is a big improvement and makes things very easy to understand due to working off of lists and menus as opposed to exclusively hotkeys.  Gnomoria still has a bit of a ways to go to be considered "approachable", however due to the lack of a tutorial of any kind but as I said previously the basics should be easy enough to understand for a new player if they take the time to skim through the different menus.
Overall I have to say I really do like Gnomoria for giving an old favorite game of mine a bit of spit and polish.  I'd recommend it to any fans of city-builders. Especially those that love heavy resource management.

Brothers is quite short (3-3.5h), but very enjoyable with a great narrative relying entirely on gestures and tone. It does not rely on any words at all, excluding explanations on controls. The characters do talk, but you are not supposed to understand them, and you really don't need to either.
The story is simple but effective. You probably already read it in the game's description. That's about it.
The gameplay of solving puzzles and basic platforming with two characters at once is not challenging but unusual and it takes some getting used to. However, it is fun throughout the entire time and does not get boring the slightest. The game *can* be played with a keyboard, but you really shouldn't; it was made for a controller.
The soundtrack is very sweet and the scenery is quite immersive, covering a large variety of environments in such a short time. Graphics aren't top-notch but it doesn't bother me at all.
Since it is a few years old now, you can easily get it during a sale, which makes up for the short gameplay.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a game that traces the fantastic misadventure that is the mechanically interdependent lives of two siblings. It’s a sweet game that is uplifting, enchanting, but also very very short. The core game mechanics, a complementary co-dependence of two characters (one short and one tall) whom you control (either with opposing thumbsticks or WASD vs. arrow keys) is neat but slightly awkward to begin with. You will master it but when you do, it's usually about the time the credits start rolling, which is a shame because the world that you will navigate through is absorbing as it is charming – like a Bob Ross painting oozing with his warm, affable demeanour, and you wouldn’t want it to end… at least not this quickly.

Alright, alright... I guess it's time to make a review on this one. Before we begin, I have roughly another 4000 hours i've put into this game before it was released on steam. This is a tough one, when I was in the peak of my playing there wasn't a better MMO out there. Fun but challenging raids, lucrative fellowships, and unique 3-mans made end game play a world of fun. And the pvp? It was unbeliavable, both sides were always out and willing to trade some deaths for some kills. After RoI, however, things started to go down hill. Textures started being reused, quests turned mind-numbing, the landscapes weren't as pretty and the end game raiding wasn't as fun. The pvp started to decline, now if a side isn't getting kills most will just log off. After that, the next expansion came out and then another, each one succesfully killing off more and more of the loyal community that this game used to have. Is it worth getting end game now? I guess. Granted that you are ready for some grueling quests level 65-105, it's still not too awful to play. Although grindy, the community that still exists does make it worth it to continue playing at max level, if you can find them that is. But for the casual gamer that isnt looking to spend 50 hours just to reach max level, it is for you that I strongly suggest you try this out. Levels 1-65 are so much fun to do, especially if you have a friend or two! The quests for the most part are fun and inventive, and there is something almost transcendic about being a big LoTR fan and following the company along on their journey! Many of the expansions are reasonably priced; you can either buy these with real money, or deed in game to earn enough turbine points to unlock them!
TL;DR
Not as good as it used to be but early levels are still a ton of fun

I have been playing GTA V since its original release date for the Xbox 360, then transferred to PS4, then transferred again to PC. This game has taken more hours from my life than any other and I don't regret anything about it. The reason I'm writing this review and recommending against this game is purely due to the money-hungry practices that Rockstar and Take-Two show regularly.
Don't get me wrong, this game is incredibly fun. The single player is some of the best out there, and mods make this game more entertaining than games coming out today (Even though there was an attempt to take down the modding community, but I'm not gonna go into that. The overflow of negative reviews and public outcry took care of that for me). The part I question is the unavailability of content updates in single player. There have been updates in past games and all have been successful and I guarantee you that if the online content was local, people would be much happier with this game. I personally believe that the reason this has not happened is purely due to the lack of payment for single player content.
Online, the multiplayer experience that everyone I knew was excited for. At first, online was a roaring success and I personally played for countless hours attmpting to get as far as I could. Then the first signs of greed occurred... I have seen prices go so high up that the clouds are jealous, and money being made stay the same if not lower. This essentially ruined the ability of being able to buy anything enjoyable in online without shelling out hundreds of dollars on shark cards.
Overall and to keep this review from turning into a ranting wall of text, I enjoyed this game. It's worth its price, especially if it's on sale... for single player content. If I'm speaking exclusively about online, I would not touch this game with a 100 foot pole due to the online community, support system, and blatant greed being shown by this game's developer/publisher and I have to recommend my review against this game purely in an attempt to encourage others to vote with thier wallets.

===
===
This title is not worth full price, not even half of that, get it if you find it with at least a 60% discount.
===
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is an FPS/RPG with stealth elements. The game is set two years after the events seen in Deus Ex: Human Revolution - The Missing Link, and once again, we find ourselves impersonating Adam Jensen, who has been recruited in a brand new counter-terrorism organization called Task Force 29, obviously after having been put back together from the Panachea Incident's brutal effects.
Civil unrest against the Augmented people is reaching astronomical levels, because after the Signal Incident, which in short words made all the Augmented people go crazy and kill anyone in sight, the "normal" population doesn't trust them anymore, and so trust, racism and violence issues spread all over the world. In times like these, a mysterious group of terrorists decide to fight back against all the unfair treatments the Augmented are put through, and a series of bombings starts. This is where Adam moves into play, his mission is to find and stop this terrorist group, but soon, like in any respectful Deus Ex game, things will get much deeper and complicated than they seem...
The game's Longevity ranges from 15-20 to 50+ hours depending on: play style, player skill level, level of exploration done, number of side missions done, reading all the lore-related stuff, collectible finding. If you do main story only, guns blazing, no exploration or little, and no side missions, will take you less than 20 hours to finish it, while by doing for example Stealth, non lethal, all exploring, all quests, lore reading, collectible finding play through will take as far as 50 hours to do everything.
===
The gameplay of Mankind Divided is basically the one we are accustomed to in Human Revolution. If you are not familiar with it, know that Deus Ex's gameplay can be extremely variable, depending on how the player wants to approach it. The core gameplay is the one of an FPS, with a first-person view most of the time, and third-person only when in cover. But don't be fooled, Stealth, sabotage, item collecting and exploration are all fundamental in the gameplay and will each lead to its own rewards.
The player has a great degree of freedom when it comes to choose how to behave, you can go in guns blazing, killing every enemy (and civilian if you want) on sight, or use a more subtle approach and stun each enemy from stealth, or maybe hack your way through the security terminals and sabotage the automated defenses to kill everyone for you. When it comes to freedom of action, Deus Ex is the real deal, and also in theis episode it does not disappoint.
Adam will have at its disposal a very varied set of skills, called Augments, which will enable him to do many things, from hacking devices from a distance, become invisible, dash at the speed of sound towards the enemy, throw heavy objects, enhanche time perception and much more. These Augments can be unlocked through Praxis points, which can rarely be found in the world or unlocked by completing missions, defeating enemies and exploring secret areas. The great part is that the player can choose to unlock any augment he wants from the start, allowing massive customization to suit your own play style.
The game is totally free roaming and open world, most of it will be set in the city of Prague, part of it at least, and there will be many, many places to explore and things to do and discover. Total freedom of action is rule number one. Want to go on a rampage and kill half the city? Suit yourself, if you manage. Want to crack the vault of the central bank and get the sweet loot? Can do that, but won't be easy!
About the mission system, also here is total freedom for the player, you will be able to engage any mission at any time, disengage a primary mission and go do a secondary one, without generally having to worry about something failing. Missions carried out and completed earlier in the game will carry their consequences and unlock different missions and situations later, this opens up to a good replay value, because to experience all the possible situations it will take at least two playthroughs.
The challenge level depends heavily on the player's playstyle and ability. Played at maximum difficulty, it gives a decent challenge for a Stealth / Non-Lethal playthrough, so far i only played in this way, but i can safely say that it will be easier if played non-stealth, FPS style. Overall, there is some challenge but not overly so, the game is anyway satisfying enough and doesn't get boring or too easy.
The story plays along well, some points are frankly obscure and not well explained, even if you, as i did, will read all the documents and bits of text in each level, many things will not be clear, but it probably is the intention of the developers. The ending i won't say anything, but this: many people blamed it, hated it, but i think most did not understand it, also the ending of Human Revolution is similar in some ways and it opens up to a sequel as Human Revolution did.
===
Mankind Divided, with its Umbra engine, has been capable of dishing out some of the best graphics around.
Advanced light effects, tessellation, precision shadows, very high resolution textures, a plethora of filters and additional shading options, it's all there. The environment and model quality is overall extraordinary, Prague has been recreated in a spectacular way, and aswell the other places you will get to visit.
Of course, now let's talk about Performance which is the key, and about that we are not completely satisfied, as the game runs on an average of 45-50 FPS at High settings on an high end machine, generally performance is not very good even with state of the art machines with the latest hardware, FPS drops are not uncommon and generally there is not a good optimization and polishing in the graphics engine.
Still, the game is fully enjoyable as long as you have a decent configuration, you will not need a monster rig to run this decently as my faithful 4 years old rig with a 3GB GTX780Ti can run it on High and some tweaks with dignity. I would not advise to run this game on low or medium-low end systems, even at minimum the performance loss would be consistent.
Passing to bugs and issues, i have not noticed many to be honest, game's been patched through by now, major issues are gone, crashes are very rare, loading times are respectable even on HDDs, there is not texture popping, stuttering, tearing or anything like that, performance might not be optimized but is stable and solid.
===
Mankind Divided is a solid deus ex experience. Forget the pre-order stuff, forget the DLC packs and whatnot, as a game experience, i recommend it to any Deus Ex fan because in it you WILL find all the features that make this series great like you found them in Human Revolution, this is the same gameplay but expanded and brought to new life. If you are new and interested to this series, i strongly recommend starting at least with Human Revolution, the previous chapter, or if you are old-school enough, get the first Deus Ex and see what you're made of!

Having played the original Deus Ex game almost 16 years ago, I have followed the title ever since. When Human Revolution was announced I had hoped it would live up to expectations of the original game, it did.
Human revolutions had everything, even nice enough to hint the feature of an old enemy "Bob Page". It had so many on the edge moments and the narrative was excellent. So when I heard of the impending release of Mankind Divided, I could not wait.
During the date of release I was in the process of creating a new PC build, and as such was not able to get MD on preorder, but as such I still kept an eye on things and seeing people’s reactions. I am glad I did this.
I only just purchased the game during the recent sale and at this time I do feel I got value for money, but have to admit I would be very disappointed if I had paid full value. Please note as part of my review there will be spoilers for both Human Revolution(HR) as well as Mankind Divided (MD).
Where to begin?
The Story
I suppose to start; the first criticism is where the story begins. At the end HR, you are asked to make a choice of three options, siding with one of two groups or none at all. It seems to me that making either one of those choices has made no impact on the story for MD. The story begins during a mission featuring TF29, a special group that works within Interpol. Seems all too convenient. Even though there are conversations with people like David Sarif about what had happened after the finale of HR, it’s never really followed up in any great detail.
Another disappointment is also an interesting concept for the game, in which it centres focus around one city, Prague. I kind of like the idea of being able to travel around like that for missions for to access certain stores, I would like to see that evolve a bit more in the next game if possible. However with that in mind, the way it is used in this game is a bit silly, there are moments when you have to complete a very minor task in one part of the town then have to return to another, and yet while this is happening you have to go through loading screens and motions that are so repetitive it becomes a bit boring.
Come the end of the story, I never felt the rush of urgency like I got when playing HR, and once completed I felt a little unfulfilled. There was so much content that seemed missing from the game that would have been satisfying, for instance the side mission you pickup of Eliza the holographic news reporter, there was supposed to be an extra step according to the conversation with her but looks like it got left out.
The storyline of Adams new aug abilities felt incredibly rushed, I would have been more satisfied with a story of Adam getting treatment after Panchia and Sarif saying "its time to unlock your potential further" However I don't doubt that the what happened after Panchia and Dubai will feature in a DLC at some point and at cost.
Finally there was supposed to be a mole, who was it? Even the post credit reveal was not the answer to the question because the reveal would have had no knowledge of certain events.
Augs and Gameplay
The new augs imo were pointless with the exception of the wireless hacking which was extremely useful, but the standard augs from HR were enough to complete this game. This brings me onto gameplay. This game seriously lacks in enjoyable gameplay. I am not a fan of stealth in all honesty, but HR allowed me to have a good balance of both stealth and gun play. MD doesn't really offer that at least not until you reach the Switzerland mission, and even that I am told is dependent on a choice you make. On a positive note I will say that once you get involved in combat, the AI is vastly improved on HR. Enemies now work in teams and coordinate, and are more likely to use grenades of various types to their advantage, yet that being said they are not ruthless, and fail to make you pay for your lack of vision, lol. You hear them use radio chatter to confirm they are engaged with you, and even though it may bring in a few more guys, once you get past them, bad guys in another area seem to have missed the call and are not prepared. This would seem a minor gripe but the bad guys in the later missions have the same abilities as you, so you would at least expect them to have inbuilt communications. To me it fails in the continuity of the story, but then again I could be looking to much into this.
But one thing that can't be ignored, there is only one boss battle, and that comes at the end. I mean WTF!!!! There is hardly a need for weapons in this game.
Graphics
Considering HR was once of the first few games to revolve around DX11, the graphics were amazing especially when you reached China. MD has taken a step backwards for some reason. I have seem pictures on TV and online of Prague and it is a beautiful city, but for some reason, even on high graphics, Prague is nothing more than a pixelated backdrop that reminds of the low end technology of graphics in the original Deus Ex. It felt to me that in a graphical sense the developers were focusing on unimportant aspects of the graphics and missing what made HR graphically amazing.
It’s also with the graphics engine I found my bugs, for instance a bug which causes a rifle to replace all weapons and even stays with you when your weapon is hidden.
Final judgement
4/10

I picked up Ziggurat for two reasons, it was on sale and Totalbiscuit recommended it. I knew it was a first person Rouge-like and that was about it. The thing I did not expect going into the game that really hooked me was the speed of the gameplay. Imagine Quake and you have an idea of the speed I am talking about. Ziggurat is much more a FPS with Rogue-like elements thrown in. On of the tags on the Steam page is Rogue-LITE, which I didn't know was a term, but fits this perfectly. There are just enough mechanics from games like Binding of Isaac thrown in without it getting too carried away. In one sense I miss that, but with the fast twitch shooter gameplay of Ziggurat it fits quite well.
The game is not perfect, enemy variety, and overall polish could be improved. The learning curve is steep as well, and I actually had to turn the difficulty down to make any sort of progress. Overall it is a fun game that combines genres in a way that I have not seen done before and I highly recommend it.

Dead Space 2 starts as a promising survival horror, but ultimately ends up being a generic, mindless shooting gallery, where one ambush is followed by another. The game is littered with closed doors that conveniently open the moment you clear the X number of enemies that spawn on you upon triggering a swarm event.
The scariest thing in this game is probably the random noise you hear every now and then, till you realize its made by objects that are glitching in walls.
The locations are pretty generic, often consisting of the same rooms and layouts copy-pasted together.
Thoughout the story you will often be interrupted by unskippable video transmissions and hallucitations, in during which you are unable to progress due closed doors (which are open the moment everyone is done talking), so if you don't really care about the story or got killed and forced to restart a segment, then it will gets more and more irritating towards the end.
The game is roughly 10 hours, and even less if you're playing on lower difficulty or don't look every in every nook and cranny, but despite its relatively short length it overstays its welcome.
Get it on a discount or not at all.
- Visuals. The lighting in particular is quite impressive
- Sound and voice acting
- Generic, repetitive shoot-em-up
- Unskippable cutscenes and annoying, frequent video transmissions
- Predictable jump scares and ambush locations

An entertaining CCG with a lot of decent options for solo play, which sadly seems an afterthought in many of the other CCGs.
Since the latest major update not only have some 1200 cards been added but it sounds like they're even more generous with the free coins and chests.  I know every time I play, usually just a couple battles a session, I'm getting a few new packs (or chests as they're called in this game) to add to my collection either as direct rewards or bought with the cash I'd just earned (admittedly I do have the tripler in effect, which helps speed things up a lot).
Compared to other CCGs, the game is definitely on the lighter/streamlined side of things.  While it now has some 1900 cards now, and unlike Yugioh, they almost all have a point (albeit there are some really odd cards that clearly, outside of pretty elaborate combos, I can't see be included in most decks).  Another honest admission is that when it comes to the monsters themselves, the vast majority of the cards in this game, it can at times feel like they filled out the ranks by simply recombining some handful of variables in every possible configuration (12 races x 3 classes x 24 different powers x etc.) although, under closer inspection, it is clear there are some powers primarily available to certain races and definitely not seen in all 3 classes).
Another interesting aspect of this game is how simple they make it to buy or sell any of it's 1900 cards.  The basic rules that appear to govern this is that you can sell any card in your collection for roughly a fourth of its retail value which in turn is primarily based on its rarity (although there is a bit of supply and demand worked in as well, so expect to pay a little more than the straight rarity would indicate for a popular card and expect to get a bit less when selling a card there is no demand for).  If you're ever short on in-game cash just sell off those rarer cards you KNOW you'll never use.
Lastly I also like how the game structures things with its 2 most common chests, the mini and full.  Mini chests, 400 gold for 6 cards, are the cheapeast way to really add a lot of cards to your collection for minimal cash with the only downside being that the distribution of cards is totally random and 90% it will just be common cards with a couple of uncommon thrown in.  Full chests, 1200 gold for 12 cards, while a far more expensive route to go for your cards, at least GARUNTEES 3 uncommons and 1 rare (or better).  So, as it stands, I find myself going back and forth between both chest types, minis to fill out my collection variety, making sure I at least have a wide breadth of all of the game's common cards, but still throw in a few full packs to get my guaranteed rarer cards.

On release I quickly installed the game based on its cool sounding premise. Its half card game and half hex tactics game combined which sounded like a great idea. Played about half way through the first chapter and decided to pick up the Tripler and a few chests because I was enjoying it. Like many others who posted in the forums and gave negative reviews (including me), I hit a brick wall in my campaign a little later. In fact that brick wall would come down like a steel blast door at times if you didn't get any good cards. I hopped on over to the AI skirmish mode to find the AI got massive mana and starting hand bonuses that my pathetic cards just couldn't deal with. After multiple frustrating matches I simply gave up on it and left a negative review. At the time in the game's initial design, I felt that all I got for my money's worth was a frustrating experience.
Fast forward to the 3.1 update and I'd figure I would give the game another shot. I'm so happy to say that those initial bad experiences are over. Actually I've been bugging out on the game for the past couple days I'm now loving it. The single biggest change they made is that you can now obtain any cards you feel that you may need using gold coins which can be obtained for free by playing or buying with cash. You no longer have to depend on the RNG gods of getting decent cards from chests which could take a long while to obtain via skirmish on release. This changes everything because now if you got really crappy cards from your chests you got in the campaign before you hit that brick wall, you don't feel like your stuck in a catch-22. That is to say you don't have the cards needed to earn gold to obtain cards needed to progress. Now you can simply get the cards you need by going into the collection and picking them up that way. However now that you can play each chapter up to four times using the new formats as opposed to release when you could only play it once means that your chance of getting stuck in that situtaion in the first place goes down as well so that's another great addition.
The biggest challenge in the game from a SP perspective is that the levels are designed completely against the player in campaign outside the starting chapter and in skirmish the AI got huge bonuses (which have now also been reduced) to both mana income and starting hand. Add to that the AI had better cards than you on release amounted to a very frustrating experience. Now that I'm able to pick up the cards that I feel I need to overcome those challenges the game changes completely. Now that I'm able to obtain cards, primarily mass removal combos that deal with an AI that can swamp you based on its mana and card advantage, I don't feel like I'm at an impasse any longer.
Its turning out to be a really fun game given the changes. You'll also be pleasantly surprised at the amount of content packed into it given its a mobile port, certainly more depth to it than most other mobile games I've played. You have a TON of strategies at your disposal due to the huge number of spells and creature types you can mix and match. Very cool to see your card game "come to life" where you control on a map the creatures you play.
Anyhow, if you’re thinking about trying the game for the first time it's worth checking out. If you're thinking about revisiting it then go ahead and give it another shot. The game really has changed completely for the better. At least this formally frustrated player thinks so. The Tripler in my opinion is one of the best bangs for your buck in any FTP game I can recall. Once you get it for a few dollars, it’s yours forever and not time based. A+ for that!!

This game is highly underrated in my opinion, and although it's an older game it still has a lot going for it.
The pros:
- Tolkien lore, sooo much Tolkien lore.
- Ever wanted to get drunk in the Prancing Pony? Now you can.
- Great community for an MMO, trolls seem few, people are friendly, player-run events a-plenty.
- The in game music system.  You can use lore-friendly musical instruments in game to play ABC files of your favourite music, and even sync with other people in your party to form a band & play the same songs in time on different instruments.
- The free-to-play model allows for a pretty lengthy free trial period.  After that you'll want to become VIP (a subscriber) to enjoy the rest of the game, HOWEVER you only need to go VIP once to unlock everything, and it all stays unlocked if you cancel your subscription, so it's not necessary to keep paying.
- Huge list of Instances, Skirmishes & Epic Battles to participate in.
- Player owned houses, and Kinship (Guild) houses which are all customizeable.
- Wardrobe feature allows for lots of outfit customization.
- Monster play feature allows for PvP battles while sticking to Tolkien lore.
- Extensive crafting system, & auctions of course.
Cons:
- Graphics are showing their age, certainly not an ugly game, but not the stunning graphics we're getting used to seeing either.
- Standard MMORPG mechanics.  Nothing particularly new or exciting in terms of gameplay, basically just another WoW clone, but with Tolkien lore.
- Free-to-play is limited, you will need to spend some money to enjoy the rest of the game.
If you're a fan of Tolkien lore then definitely give it a try, if you're not, then there's propably much better MMO's out there for you to try instead.  This game does stock-standard MMORPG pretty well, but it's main draw point is definitely the setting & lore.

After a couple of hours, the 'Mixed' status of reviews is completely understandable. The game has potential but has major flaws in its fundamental design.
What really kills this game is lack of spawn points way from base, vehicles must be manned if you want to spawn on them and captured points are not valid spawn areas meaning if no one is in a truck/motorcycle/etc. you have to go back to your first spawn. In some maps, assualt maps in paticular, the back spawn has no vehicles for you to move up with.
The lack of transferring 'progress' from one solider to another is also irritating. Meaning if you want to have multiple loadouts, you are going to have to purchase each weapon to the specific soldier. This also entails using the first default semi-auto to earn ribbons again. This also goes for consumables and badges.
The repair mechanic also seems rather obtrusive, it is clearly made inconvienant to that point to boost the 'appeal' of premium. It goes beyond grindy and becomes a wall. Premium downgrades it to grindy instead of the usual 'slightly accellerated'. I understand that the huge (relative) repair cost is to discourage/prevent nade spam, but it takes away from what gameplay there could be in my opinion.
If you want to play this, it is enjoyable, but be prepared for the repetitive nature of the beast.

For a long time we have been able to play self styled Free To Plays (F2P) games were you are to play for free if you don't mind being encouraged to pay in micro transactions. They exist in 2 formats, recently 3 if you have a smartphone, and they are; 1. Pay to Win were some, or much, of the content is locked to free players and they must pay to unlock; 2. Pay to Speed Up, or not grind as the players of H&G call it, were you can obtain everything in the game without paying a cent if you don't mind making that game your lifes work for a few years. On smartphones the third variant is Bombard With Filthy Ads and Make My Players Pay me to Stop.
H&G follows the second format with a little of the first. It is a game set in world war II were players must do battles across a bunch of different maps all to capture the points, and thus capture sucess for their team. This game is different from many other FPS's in the fact that you are able to play in actual wars which are waged across europe to settle the winner of world war II. On the play map veteran, or rich players as this is pay to not grind, purchase supplies for each battle field in the form of Assault Teams.
One of the things that sets this game apart from a traditional F2P FPS (So many acronyms) is the fact that you can use 3 variants of infantry, tanks, and planes! For reasons as yet unkown the most expensive of these 5 is the recon,  a sniper who gets a rifle, and no scope, and some ability to conceal himself. The cheapest of the 5 is the humble infantry who essentially runs into the meat grinder that is each point, and try to secure the objective with limited support from the other 4 classes.
That's about were the fun part ends, and this game begins to act very pay to winesque, if that's a word. Many of the more powerful weapons in the game can literally kill a player in one shot. There is very little actual hp as a soldier to simulate the rapidity of death a soldier experiences on the battle field. This is all well and good, but Reto has stated time and time again that it doesn't want to bring to much realizism to the game. The germans don't even have the nazi symbol, although that might be considered a saving grace depending on the player. To top it off Reto's system of balancing weapons is to make certain weapon types on each side ridiculously more powerful in the others hoping that the other weapon variants will balance this out. It's a very strange system, and a lot of the time it doesn't work.
Did I mention the grind part? For each level a players soldier earns he receives a salary. This salary is computed based on level, time actually played in the battle (respawning doesn't count, and that timer is ridiculously long), experience earned, and wether the player is a subscriber or not. This amount can be quite good if you are in a battle for long enough, and so all of the games are massively expensive. Starting out if you play the game solid for about a day you can manage to buy yourself a storm trooper style machine gun, a grenade, and maybe a pistol. I say stormtrooper because that gun is going to shoot hate at everything but your target if you dont have it at your shoulder at all times.
To top it off the respawn timers are massively long. I've timed it at roughly 15-20 seconds. Longer if you die due to a accident, or suicide. While I get there must be some punishment for death you need to factor in the additional 30 or so seconds just to get back to an objective in some cases. Faster if you buy a vehicle, but once again that costs credits and a ton of grinding to unlock. Once you make it back you may or may not be instantly killed by a sniper in a window, and while that's no stranger to most players these rifles will instant you on a torso shot when fully upgraded, and they will be. That means you have spend almost a full minute just getting back to the action, and then you go right back to the respawn.
Tanks are a fun way to get even with those pesky snipers. They can't snipe you out of the tank if your hiding inside it, but you have a whole nother can of worms here. Infantry are able to purchase anti tank mines, and explosives, and nothing is stopping them from driving up to your tank on a motor cycle, and blowing you to bits. A lot of tankers won't even be able to see these infantry due to the limited field of view the tanker experiences, and the first sign of trouble is that terrible clunking sound of a timed explosive being placed.
Flying is probably the only part of the game I have legitimately enjoyed, and so long as I'm not against russia it's fine. I say russia because the infantry get a rifle that is essentially a tank buster. I've never fired it at a tank, but it will two hit kill on a plane. If your have especially bad luck you will be shot out of the plane, and into the air. Piloting is a simple drag the mouse system with a variety of weapons avaible. The planes are all equipped with some maching guns, and bombs to kill ground troops. Some, not USA for some reason, get cannons to help them strafe enemies, or other planes. The issue with the plane system is that all characters types have limited spawns. If the enemy is keeping track they can simply kamikaze your whole team to death so long as they stay ahead on planes. Lots of cool dogfights devolve into who can kamikaze who first.
There are some good points to the game. It's essentially a free battlefield, but at the end of the day the cons far outway the pros. The community can be slightly on the toxic side, but what FPS isn't these days. It's at least got a strong following so your wait for matches will be short. My advice is if you must play a FPS, even if you can't afford one like Battle FIeld, or CoD (shudder) then give this one a try. Don't pay any money into it without some incredible thought because you will likely regret it otherwise. If you can afford to pay to unlock a plethora of things in a FPS give this one a miss then, and just buy the actual Battle Field 1. Even though it has that war map, that isn't enough of a saving grace to devote any money towards. Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a little adventure game that manages to bend one's brain not due to fact that the puzzles are difficult, as they are not, but because it allows the player to simultaneously control two characters independently from each other at the same time. Didn't expect much when starting this after having owned it for a few years and was completely blown away. More than recommended for anyone who wants to follow a nice little story without too much stress and just revel in the cozy atmosphere of absolutely stunning art design.

NOTE: A controller is NOT required to play this game. I played both characters on keyboard.
Quite an interesting game. I am mostly right-handed, and controlling two characters using both hands simultaneously was a whole new experience. The story is decent. A must-try!

If you're interested in games for pretty graphics and casual gameplay, this will be up your alley.  If you're like me and don't care about graphics and want something with good gameplay and a decent challenge, then you won't enjoy this much.  It's not a bad game, it's just very meh, and there are much better games out there that are enjoyable.  I imagine that most of the positive reviews come from people who played this co-op, but I played it single player and couldn't stand to play it for more than 30 minutes at a time without wanting to stop.
The gameplay focuses on combat, puzzles, and platforming, none of which are particulary compelling.  Let me break down 95% of combat in the game: Select Knight or Thief, spam sword/hammer or arrow attack, combat successfully completed.  Even bosses are extremely easy.  Most of the time you'll be able to heal up in the middle of combat and should you somehow manage to die, oh well, warp back to a checkpoint 10 seconds away and come back and finish cleaning up the rest of the enemies.  Combat provides no challenge and serves no purpose other than to break up the monotony of puzzles and platforming.
Now let me break down 95% of the puzzles, which are often repetitive:  Use XP to unlock fire arrows, use fire arrows to blow up destructible walls (if any), use XP to unlock wizard blocks/platforms, spam blocks/platforms, puzzle complete.  Occasionally you'll run into something where you have to stop and think a bit, but it's pretty rare, in fact, I think the only 2 times I ran into something like that was in the Goblin Menace DLC that came with the game.
The platforming is ok but sometimes your movement while jumping gets sluggish and you'll go plummeting to your death.  Particulary annoying is the Knight's hover ability.  You'll hold in the button for him to hold his shield up to hover and sometimes he just won't do it, or he'll wait until he's fallen for a second or two before the game finally figures out what you're trying to do and then you'll have to go back and try the jump again until he gets it right.
There's not much of a plot to the game, it's mainly there to give the heroes a reason to be in that area.  The characters aren't particulary fleshed out.  You'll get a little dialouge at the beginning and end of a board usually, but for the most part it's generic Knight, Thief, and Wizard.
Not much else to say, it's an ok game but there's nothing in it that's really warrants a playthrough.  Pretty graphics, simple gameplay, little challenge.  If that sounds good, you'll enjoy, if not, you probably won't.

2ndly, game suffers from 1st player wins syndrome. Assuming equal decks and equal field setting, 1st player will always win. 1st player gets first attack and second player has to react. There is a chance to outplay, but it will not happen often. Usually, you win off of the opponent messing up if they went first.
There is an Army Power System, but it doesn't seem to affect rank pairing. One would assume the Army Power System would be the way the game pairs you with opponents near the same power level. If this how it was intended to work, it currently does not work this way.

A fast paced, FPS roguelike with some light RPG elements thrown in the mix.  Overall the game is excellent with only a few complaints to be had.
Pros:
-Excellent pacing.
-Old school feeling, mostly.  Very fast movement.  Twitch aiming.
-Each playthrough is slightly different.
-Multiple difficulty levels with an endless mode.
-Good deal of unlockables.
-Developers are still adding content to the game post release, for FREE.
Cons:
-Cannot sprint while strafing.  While this makes sense from a realistic approach to human movement, the movement model in this game is anything but realistic.  For a person that grew up on old school shooters, this is slightly annoying.
-Trap rooms are repetitive.
-Some of the specialist classes have 50% of the HP of the starting class.  While good for a challenge, the perks they get are not worth losing that much HP.
All in all this game is great fun, and well worth the price of admission.  I've played it through a few times now and I don't plan on stopping yet.

A far bigger problem is deception and unreasonable greed from the developers.  "Play the game how you want" is a lie when the enemies drop so little ammo,  what's much worse is that the "solution" to this problem if you aren't a dedicated stealth player is buying credits and DLC for real money.
Compare this to an original game with way more weapon variety, enemies dropped good amounts of ammo and if that wasn't enough.....just mod the game to your taste.    But if Eidos made Mankind Divided like this, then they wouldn't be able to sell half as many DLCs.

Was that funny to you? Then welcome to DLC Quest, a basic 2D platformer that aims to make fun of some of the industry's worst business practices.
The game consists of two parts, the original campaign that harps on game design tropes and DLC practices, and the "Live Freemium Or Die" campaign that was added later as a free upgrade which loses the focus on DLC but instead addresses day one patches, trends in art style, etc..
It's a clever deconstruction, but also works as a platformer. The controls are responsive and even though there are some cheap deaths and jumping puzzles that require a decent amount of skill it never feels insurmountable or unfair.
Each campaign will take you about an hour to complete and there's some challenges and achievements for the completionists out there which stretch each campaign by another hour or so.
All in all the game entertained me without overstaying its welcome, and I'd recommend it if you think you might appreciate the humour.

After the release of Trine 3 which is considered a mixed bag it is high time I reviewed the sequel which is better in every which way than its predecessor.
The premise remains the same in the 2nd episode of Frozenbyte's amazing franchise: the mysterious object called Trine binds 3 heroes together who all have different abilities and gameplay style. In terms of story they have switched from skeletons to goblins. Not much of a change but you know it's all about saving the kingdom once more. We have the same 3 characters from the first episode and in terms of timeline we are a couple of years after the events of Trine 1.
What shines in Trine 2 is its graphics. Not that the first one was ugly, quite the contrary! Still, they managed to make the game even more beautiful (the water effect is stunning). In fact, the first game was updated with the sequel's engine and it is now only available in Enhanced Edition version.
Overall, the gameplay remains the same but they have tweaked it a bit here and there. For instance, the wizard cannot conjure floating triangles but can pick up monsters. The heroes all received some new abilities and each now seems to be more useful. And, of course, we have some puzzles that utilise physics and have to be solved accordingly.
The longevity of the game has also increased. Levels are more complex and much bigger. There are tons of collectibles to find - poems in treasure chests and also paintings (no equipment, though). You'll probably not be able to collect them all in one go! And let us not forget about the achievements - there's now a threefold increase.
I believe Trine 2 is an example as to how a sequel should be done. For fans of the first one it is a must and for those hating the 3rd (and preferably last) a revisit has been due for some time. The game also features proper multiplayer i.e. it is not LAN anymore.

Speaking of recording... good luck given that even on my system which blows the listed requirements out of the water still struggles with overheating and the like where as on games such as Dawn of War 3 which requires parts like mine doesn't even phase it no matter how much I push the limits so to speak(mind you that's just one game in comparison, I've yet to find a game that burns my system even remotely like H&G) especially after the recent graphics update they did(can barely run for a few hours on low, used to run perfectly non-stop on highest), still no update on the game's requirements despite clearly requiring more than what any average gamer would have...
Now... as I said it's somewhat balanced... each faction has it's benefits and drawbacks... Americans are all rounders who really aren't great at anything but can still hold their own vs the other 2, with Germans being a powerhouse of strong tanks highly accurate weapons, strong assault rifle which requires expereience to be good with, etc... and Russians having things like the PTRD(Anti-light vehicle weapon that works somewhat on medium unless it's been changed since i last held it, russians are still forgetting to use different weapon in first slot but most remember), high speed and high power smgs, etc...
Don't get me wrong, despite some of the set backs it's still a really fun game and being free is a plus... just know there is a real money currency system in play that can make or break it for some people especially when they have certain things costing more per in-game currency than out-game currency or vice versa....

This game on first glance is a nice, frenetic FPS with the obvious roguelike elements that make it tough to learn initially.  But it has a certain genius to it, and at the moment stands as a masterpiece of game design, and a personal favorite of mine.
Here are some important points I have to make:
- The game requires a large number of playthroughs.  Not just to get the hang of the flow of combat, but also to learn the enemy/weapon relationships.  Because you start with a small pool of weapons initially, this makes it pretty simple to do, and cuts down the overwhelming nature of the roguelike elements.  You'll die a lot initially, but you will immediately find nourishment in your demise as slowly the game unfolds itself, like a puzzle box.
- As the game begins to develop during your playthroughs, you will notice that the strategies to combat will take on a depth.  With the limited amount of health and other manas besides the wand itself you will find a certain triumph the moment you uncover the manners in which combat can be controlled and your advantage maintained.  The second this happens to you you will immediately feel like a bada**.
- Each playthrough increases in complexity to the point that you will relish the opportunity to play to floor 5, knowing that when you die, several things will be unlocked, making the next run even more random.  Not to mention that you might get to the end.
TL;DR: The game hits its stride several playthroughs in, making a $15 price tag a bargain.  It may have near inifinite replayability, since the pool of available items and weapons when everything is unlocked is a virtual playground of roguelike greatness.

I grew up on Doom and gratefully switched to Heretic and Hexen as soon as they hit the shelves; there was something gleefully odd about wielding what was essentially a magical shotgun in a fantasy setting. Ziggurat is a great throwback to the days of the glowing green crossbow...
A mix of frentic shooter and proc-gen "rogue-lite", the game outs you into the robes of a trainee spellcaster entering the titular Ziggurat, an ever-changing structure that serves as the final test for your order- survive that thing, and you're a full mage. If you played Binding of Isaac or anything similar, the core mechanic will feel very familiar- you enter a room, the doors lock on you, and then it's shooting stuff until everything except you is dead. Rinse and repeat; occasionally you'll also come across treasure rooms, bonus-granting statues and challenge rooms that put a nice little goody into the centre of a trap.
You always start with a wand, a weak but reliable fallback weapon, and you'll randomly find additional weapons divided into three classes, each with their own unique setup. Spells, staves and alchemic "firearms" consume mana from a finite pool, while your wand constantly recharges. Level-ups grant you perks that alter the game's feel significantly, allowing you to recharge health by breaking stuff, being faster, specializing on a weapon type and more- it's always randomized so each run through the Ziggurat feels pretty different.
The game itself isn't that "long"- beating the Ziggurat once, however, is nothing, as you constantly unlock more stuff: Weapons, perks, character classes, there is a huge pool of things to unlock by wreaking havok.
And that is the most important thing: The game *feels* very great, and you *will* come back to challenge yourself again just to dish out magicks and feel like a badass wizard. Combat is precise and crisp, enemy types are aplenty,  each with their own behaviour. There could be a bit more feedback on damage; you more or less know that an enemy is dead exactly the moment he drops to the floor, but that's about it, there's good oomph to the weapons and the game generally looks pretty amazing, with a somewhat cartoonish high fantasy style and a large amount of fizzy fx. Sound is not too bad either.
This is a game one can easily play through again and again, I feel, and apparently the devs are eager on tweaking and adding to Ziggurat. Just two days after my purchase I saw new room patterns and a new enemy type added, and that *is* service. There's never too many baddies to hurl magic at.
So, deep? Thoughtful? Strategic? Nope. A fast, furious, tight proc gen shooter? Yes indeed!

The original Overlord game was essentially a cult classic and I gladly consider myself one of those that absolutely loved it. I actually prefer how the original game handled some of the aspects such as armor/weapon upgrades. The upgrade options make more sense, but I felt you had to grind for money way to often and just ended up almost skipping it entirely.
The addition of mounts for your minions was actually amazing and probably the main thing that sets this game above the original. My main complaint with the game is honestly it just doesn't feel like it is as fleshed out as it could have been when it comes to things like controling the towns. I loved putting down a revolt, but since it only happens once per town it isn't even really a spoiler. The mistresses are handled the way they should be.
The magic felt weak for some reason to me. The spells help and all, but I never really felt like an all poweful cast sacrifcing minions for personal gain. I enjoyed the idea of minion level up system and bringing back high levels from the dead, but to be honest I never used it.
The game still has the same minion types as the original which is very balanced still. The tactics of killing commanders and using catepults was very enjoyable. The ability to mind control a minion and lead an assault or stealth mission was great. The games dark humor is always enjoyable. It still seems to have choices which are essentially evil vs chaos evil.
The main thing that I wish it had more of was funny bosses like Melvin Underbelly from the original. I did als find it strange that blues never got a mount when I kept thinking they would get a frog or a slug mount. Overall the humor and variety of gameplay make it a neat nitch market title.

Overlord II could have been an enjoyable title had it not fallen for perhaps the most common pitiful of the genre: The simple tactics are better than the advanced tactics.
You're given all kinds of little imps to fight battles for you, and you're given all of these opportunities to use them in a variety of ways, but in the end, it's just easier to select all of them and point them at the nearest thing that they can kill. No strategy, no immersion, just simple tasks that make the game boring.

Where do I start with this game? After spending around 25 to 30 hours, or perhaps even more (can't tell since I played it on offline mode), searching every corner for quests, reading all bit and pieces of informations and lore about the DX universe, and finally reached the end... I can't really articulate how I feel with the latest installment of this series. Was it Fascination? Excitement? Disappointment? Disbelief? It's all of these things.
Deus Ex: Content Divided is a fine example of such an ambitious  and truly excellent project made by talented and passionate devs has to be brought down by a load of publisher's meddling, chopping the fine game into pieces to squeeze as much money as possible. I don't blame Eidos Montreal for this, that all solely lies to Square Enix.  So, keep in mind that this review is for the game at it's current (mutilated) state, not what this game could've been.
First, let's talk about the positives. Or perhaps, if you already played Human Revolution (and you definitely should), what does MD improves upon HR? And that's the gameplay and level design. It looks like Eidos Montreal really listen to user feedback and massively improves those area, especially the latter. MD is simply a bigger, bolder, and more refined game than HR, created by devs that is more confident and experienced than before. I can see they put a lot of effort to make the levels more open for possibilites to any kind of character builld. Bigger places, more vents to lurk, more "secret areas" to discover, more things to hack, and all around exploring the mission and hub area is way more fun and rewarding than HR.
Prague, is the one and only Hub in this area, yes.. One. I'll come back to it later on, since I'm going to touch the good things first. Well, Prague is way more alive than Detroit. it's bigger, and it has more content, more intricate level design, and a real treat for the eye, day and night. And that brings me to side quests, another big improvement over HR, they are more varied, interesting (both gameplay and story wise), and feels grander in scale. I found the plot and characters in some of the side quests are more interesting than the main storyline.
As for the graphic, it's simply amazing! Prague is filled with these tiny details that really improve the atmosphere and visual narrative. I'll spend two paragraphs just to describe how impressive the graphic is. So, to cut it short: It's a real neat blend of impressive graphic and amazing level design, not too empty yet never overbearing.Though the animation and lip syncing could be better.
Also, top notch sounds, soundtracks, and especially voice actings. As expected.. In exception of the weapon sounds that is.
Deus Ex is always about its world, and the story about every individual involved with it. While I think the side quests are a major step up from HR, I can't say the same with the main storyline. The pacing is quite inconsistent, it starts out great, it got boring in the middle, before it goes back on track just to be abruptly cut out in the end. I find most of the main characters in MD are uninteresting, or maybe not yet at this point. Adam Jensen in particular has a weaker characterization in MD. I know it's hard to balance out a character with RPG in mind while giving the character its own motivation. HR did it better because  Adam has his personal thrive to do what he does, and he does undergone a character development. In MD however his development stuck, and his motivation is generic.
And now, let's get back to the Hub thing. Yes, it's true. Prague is MUCH better than every hub in HR. But, it lacks variety. Major theme on Deus Ex is a "world travel", seeing different part of the world and their culture and vibes in its universe. Prague, while divided into several smaller hubs lacks diversity, understandably so. Deus Ex is about chasing the roots of conspiracy throughout the world, but in MD? The plotline may suggest a much bigger stuff going on but it feels so tiny in practice. And as for the side quests, it might be better than HR individually, but as a collective, it feels.. empty? Hollow? There are surely many side quests and main quests that is cut out from this game, quest like "Desperate Measure" come to mind. It fits right in with the story, and the fact that its seperated is beyond my comprehension.
Gameplay, while greatly refined, feels unbalanced toward the end. During the last visit to Prague, Adam is already way too OP, at least for me, I can just breeze through most of the levels, and I feel like its due to the quick "rebalancing"to fit in with the length of the game. The mediocre A.I didn't help at all, they're quite easy to exploit.
In the end, DX: Mankind Divided is a game that screams potential from beginning to end. Not that it doesn't has that, but it has been cut to the point it greatly devalue what could have been a strong story and more world building elements that will eventually lead up to the legendary first Deus Ex. Looking back, I'm impressed on how many lore they estabilished on what little content left I found the story elements that includes many names that will be a major character in the first Deus Ex to be the most interesting and intriguing part of the game.And for the content they offer, I can assure you that the majority  of it are in high quality. It's a polished game with a much refined level design and gameplay, brought down by shameless money grabbing scheme. It's clear that Eidos Montreal really respect the DX universe, and gains more confident due to the success of HR, but Square Enix in the other hand has no love for art and integrity. I get this for free from my AMD card purchase, and even then it can't mask my disappointment.And yes, I highly recommend it, ONLY at, at least 60% sale, because that's exactly what you get from this. A 1/3 of a full game.

Short review:  Very solid strategy game. Worth checking out, especially if you like tabletop wargaming/board games like Warhammer, Heroclix, etc. I am a big fan of tabletop games, and this game really scratches that itch for me.
The graphics are not revolutionary but look very nice. Some of the sound effects/voices can get a little bit repetitive but it's hardly worth mentioning. Games are pretty quick, and while in single player there's no turn timer so if you need to step away for 15 minutes it's totally fine.
There is both live and asynchronous multiplayer. Asynchronous seems to work flawlessly, and while I think it's fantastic to have it as an option, live multiplayer is more important to me. And as of this writing it's pretty hard to get a live match. The devs say hopefully this will improve with time, and with the game's full mobile launch (which features cross-play with the Steam version). Speaking of the devs, they seem friendly, helpful, and active.
Even though the multiplayer is lacking action at this point, the single player is still a fun experience. There is indeed a cash shop, but (speaking purely in single player terms), I am feeling very well rewarded by the game without spending a cent. I probably will toss them a few bucks evenutally to get triple rewards.
Recommended.

Now the first thing you're going to notice is that I've only played the game for .1 hours. Before you completely dismiss this review, let me explain why my opinion matters.
You see, I was just having a nice day when suddenly a friend of mine-let's call him Mr. D-messaged me to tell me to play Combat Monsters. Being the gullible idiot that I am, I downloaded it without question. While waiting, I watched a few episodes of Not Sword Art Online. By the time the ending rolled in, I have it in my library.
Right as it finished, Mr D messaged me to tell me to get on Combat Monsters. At the time, I felt like playing Dota, but I acquiesced to his request and launched Combat Monsters.
Now everyone say first impression is everything, and I agree. My face was concave from the impression this game gave me. The low quality 3d models, the mediocre soundtrack, the whatever UI, it all added to a feeling of nostalgia. I then said to Mr. D on skype, "What the ♥♥♥♥ is this?" He chuckled, and told me to play the tutorial. Play the tutorial I did. What I am going to say next does not fully reflect on everything I feel. It is quite impossible to put this phantasmagoric experience into words. Nevertheless, I will make do with what I can. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ it sucked balls. Okay, maybe I am being a little too harsh. I will admit the tutorial guy (I will refer to him as OldBro for convenience sake) is quite funny. OldBro got to me laugh a couple of times but the fact remains, the general mechanics didn't interest me.
Wait a second, this is actually starting to sound like a review. Let me try that again.
Take 2: I suddenly realized I am playing a mobile game but now on a computer. I moved away from the screen and sat down on my bed. I closed my eyes. I saw nothing. What am I doing? Why am I playing this? Is there still hope for humanity? Why is Log Horizon season 2's pacing so awful? Mr D's confused queries on skype brought me back to reality.
"What happened?"
"It's nothing."
"Are you sure? You sound kinda off."
"I'm sure it's from Obama's healthcare. Don't worry about it."
"If you say so."
"But... Um... I can't play this game."

I hung up on the confused Mr. D. I hurriedly closed Combat Monster with Task Manger. I stared at its icon on my desktop. It's ugly visage seemed alien when placed alongside its homely neighbors. True to my word, it still lies there untouched. The thick layer of digital dust accumulated over the desktop icon acts as a natural curtain, gracefully shielding the world from the object that lies beneath it. It will stay that way.

Like a mix between Hearthstone, Yu-Gi-Oh, and that mini card game from Final Fantasy IX, but instead of taking the best parts, they were all placed in a blender and tumbled around a bit, leaving you with this game that drags its feet instead of flying around.
Gameplay: 71/100
Combat Monsters plays on a hexagon style field, like the one Chinese Checkers is played on and like Chinese Checkers, your direction and tactical choices are all around your units/monsters/cards. It's a welcome twist to the general layout the genre, but from there, the focus of the game fades away. It can't seem to decide which aspect should be the backbone of the game, is it a #card game? A monster #fighting game? A chess game? It has a lot of nice ideas, but none of them are the core for everything to be built around. The basics are still that, place a card on the field, move it around strategically based on class: ranged, #melee, #magic, equip weapons and items, cast spells, move on. The simplicity isn't a bad thing, but there's just so much more it can be.
Audio: 77/100
The effects and voices are decent enough, but they're nothing spectacular. If anything, they're almost insulting in the stereotypical #medieval #British voices that are there, as if they were all pre made from some kind of fantasy role playing game library.
Visuals: 74/100
On the #mobile versions, the game is alright. It's not sleek like Hearthstone or high end like some others, it sits somewhere in the middle, but parts here and there makes the PC version seem horrendous. Character faces are just blocky and not even in that nostalgic retro way. The characters themselves are okay, again nothing really standing out that we haven't already seen or some kind of twist that changes the norm.
Content: 73/100
There's a fair amount of things to do, but the game relies on in-game purchases, something that plagues the mobile market and something the developers over at Rubicon seem to want in the Steam version. Granted it isn't shoved down your throat like in the mobile market, but the fact that it is there is a bit of a nuisance for me: Get this pack, buy this item, on and on. And even for little things. One of the first things I tried to do was make my own "pendant," though it's more a flag than anything, and after a few minutes of customizing it, I was greeted with a prompt that "Custom Pendants are for paying customers." Again, this is something more associated and dealt with in a mobile setting, but a full blow port should have most of these things taken away.
Multiplayer: 72/100
Yes, there is a multiplayer. Yes, I tried it out. Yes, it was only a few matches. And yes, it's just like the core game from what I can tell, but instead of an AI, you have a human opponent. It's like a reverse Hearthstone. I know I should stop comparing this small company's game to the massive Hearthstone, but it's hard not to, especially with its success, there are bound to be many imitators as time rolls on.
Design: 75/100
Like I stated at the start, the game has some nice ideas, the hexagon field is one of those simple changes that increases the possibilities of the game ten fold, kind of like Tri-Dimensional Chess from Star Trek, but everything else just falls a little flat, expected, typical, and in that regard, disappointing. I was a little excited to play this, but I couldn't get into it. Maybe it's just me.
Performance: 71/100
Ran fine for the most part. Didn't experience any severe drops in frame rates or tearing. Even the max settings aren't anything to oogle over. I would assume a game like this would look a lot better on a phone or tablet, but on a full computer screen, it just doesn't hold up.
Verdict: 73/100
I tried to like this game, I really did, it had the things I like, Hearthstone inspiration, which actually got me back into card games and that fantastic mini game in the underrated FFIX, but it just can't seem to get the ball rolling. Granted the mobile versions seem to have a much warmer reception, the Steam world, not so much and I agree. It's one of those cases where the game just didn't translate as well on a bigger platform. Can I recommend it? Maybe, but unless more fine tuning is made on the Steam version, it's not something you will keep coming back to over and over again.

It's a fairly straight forward game - you choose the suspect from a line-up. You have a couple of clues to work with. Each suspect has a few attributes that are randomly generated. There's some clicking and some music and noises and stuff. The terms "flash game" and "newgrounds" are probably apt.
Interestingly, I found that this becomes a lot easier the more you play (duh) but it starts to feel like a gut feel - the game moves a lot faster after your first few attempts, and you find yourself easily flying through rounds, looking for the special characters and appreciating the distinctive art style.
Honestly, though, the best reason I have to get this is to support guys like Ed McMillen - they're the reason we can continue to have games that aren't simply re-skins of the previous edition with a $60 price-tag. Ed's games always have a feeling of exploration - usually that comes with a "hey, what's this...ah...yuck" response. That's not a bad thing.
The price (which is part of the joke as well - apparently it's a police code for homicide) is favourably comparable to a movie ticket...hell, it's cheaper than the parking ticket to watch a movie. And I've spent far more time in Ed's games than I have in the movies in the last few years. Will it pass my "dollar an hour" rule of thumb: probably, yes. Will I probably end up looking at my play time and thinking "ah...time to idle some more Skyrim or GTA...": probably, yes.

Many, many games make me wish for a “sigh” button, for a variety of reasons. Dead Space 2 makes me wish for a “sigh of despair” button.
Thrown into a startling and thrilling opening sequence, Isaac Clarke returns from Dead Space to once again dismember and destroy necromorphs. Arming himself in a plot-driven and organic way, Isaac also finds his voice, something that was missing in the first game. Spectacularly well written and well-acted, Isaac is no longer a silent avatar for the player, but a fully formed character whose destiny is to be plagued by waking nightmares.
Like a futuristic John Mclane, Isaac finds himself in a horribly familiar situation: running and fighting for his life through an industrial space maze, guided by remote voices. Unlike the errand missions and unending jump scares of the first game, DS 2 makes ironic meat of the first game’s formula with a half-way point reveal that is delicious. Replete with actual mood and atmosphere, DS 2 does have more than its fair share of jump scares, but makes up for it by honing tension to a bright gleaming point.
A few mid-to-late game set pieces tread dangerously close to vomiting all over the concept of over-the-top bad taste, but like any great horror experience makes the viewer squirm.
Caveats are few and far between, but like the overuse of jump-scares, DS 2 does milk its formula too much. Vacillating between random encounters against one or two enemies and endless swarms, DS 2 also swings heavily in difficulty level, especially in the late game. Combat and movement have been tweaked just enough to make the action quick and responsive, unlike the tank controls of the first game. While this makes the game move faster and become slightly more of an action-shooter, it makes the difficulty spikes more egregious as the need for accuracy ramps up beyond the speed of the controls.
Following the first game, DS 2 allows for a New Game+ mode, allowing the player to carry over any upgraded equipment from the 1st playthough, lowering the difficulty and increasing replayibility.
Satisfying in its resolution, DS 2 raises the bar beyond survival horror to become a truly cinematic horror experience and I can’t wait to play it again.

While not as complex as Dwarf Fortress this game has a certain charm to it. However crippling lag prevents many people myself included from enjoying it. As well it seems as though some of the requirements and general exploration and economy is broken. Monsters spawn underground after depth -7 if it is dark styming the ever worsening quest for coal. Which is itself needed to make those torches. Wood in particular is a mystery. It takes vast amounts to make a workshop or bed. Also it can be used in lieu of coal by having a furnace.
The way workshops interact to provide resources to each other, as well as the well done but perhaps not totally tuned military system are high points.
A lot of people however are unable to play this game past 15 or so gnomes due to intense system lag on even very robust machines. As well the game, pun unintended, lacks depth. You get migrants. You build your town. You mine ever further down. No caves (there are tiny ones for monsters to spawn) or other features impress enough to enable a solid game experience.
This game would be quite the gem with its simple if a tad akward interface if a few features were improved.
1. Lag needs to be fixed the game feels like it is just oozeing memory loss on 16+gb. This is a notable problem with indie games not being properly optimized to work with multiple cores or just not having tight code.
2. More going on underground. The spawning monsters in dark sections is a alpha feature of Minecraft. A alpha feature that became the standard for his game due to Notch's laziness. Perhaps having undiscovered things underground which produce or allow monsters to come in on map edges in cave systems. Spawning increasingly higher level skeletons just because it was dark is obnoxious and easily sidestepped by torch spam. Have the underground features possibly be inactive till discovered if lag is a problem. Things like golem factories or lost temples.
3. More factions or civilizations to interact with. Traders, gnomads and fort value = higher level monsters is too basic.
4. Perhaps rudimentary physics for unsupported titles. They are especially cumbersome.
While a fun couple hours and a good visual interface. This really fails to deliver a solid city builder experience. The crippling lag is especially disheartening and problamatic.
I could see recommending this game in the future if it improves. Unfortunately I have many reservations about early access games due to experience with them putting in placeholders then calling them final features.

I love Dwarf Fortress, but it can be overwhelming, especially if you've gotten away from it for a while. This game, while not quite as complex, scratches that same itch for me. The interface is simple and easy to navigate. The graphics, despite being basic and lacking animations, are still aesthetically pleasing and effective. Even the background music (especially the orchestral version selectable from Options), is nice, although a few more tracks would be welcome. There are many little details to appreciate, like how crafted items are colored to reflect the specific materials from which they were made. It's very well-paced: the more prosperous your little civilization becomes, the greater the dangers it attracts.
The developer has been posting nearly weekly updates to the game for as long as I've been playing, which has me returning to this game more frequently than nearly any other game in my library. I'm always looking forward to what each new patch brings!
If you've never played this type of game before, you should know that rather than issue direct orders, you designate projects and jobs for your gnomes. Because it's more about indirect management, planning, and efficiency, it can be very satisfying to carve out your own little gnomish citadel and watch it run like a well-organized clockwork ant farm... at least until the mants show up!

Gnomoria is built off of an awesome concept... the concept of Dwarf Fortress. The people who made this game essentially made a dumbed down version of Dwarf Fortress and added their own twists to it. This makes for a fantastic game that provides a level of almost infinite creativity and gameplay. I highly recommend this game (it's only $8.00).
This is pretty much a graphical clone of Dwarf Fortress but they didn't do much to improve gameplay or mechanics. It suffers from the same micromanagement problems of the original.

Gnomoria obviously takes much of its inspiration from Dwarf Fortress, but with a user-friendly interface and colorful graphics, it is much more approachable.  While this may not have the complexity that Dwarf Fortress does, it offers an extremely enjoyable experience and has been well worth the small price currently being charged for the game.  Fans of Dwarf Fortress or any other village management games should definitely take a look.
I have logged over 120 hrs on this game. It started out good, and has become great. It may say early access at this point, but this is already a fantastic full game.

Despite being, essentially, a game about surviving gnomes, the graphics seem very similar to Dwarf Fortress. You know, the part that lets you understand what the heck is going on in your game. It IS basically Dwarf Fortress with, uh, gnomes. You go around, collect resources, build houses, set stockpiles, etc. Now, I would've liked this game if it weren't a bit of a Dwarf Fortress ripoff. The music was unappealing because it sounded like it should come from a Commodore 64. Though I honestly don't like the idea of making a whole game out of a visionary system for a game that happened 8 years ago, which, was suprisingly popular for a set amount of years, I don't think Gnomoria got off on the right foot in general. They didn't just copy and paste, though. They added different features, like an ingame time warp option, which features three settings: Paused, Slow, and HOLY CRAP WHAT'S GOING ON! Yes, I did just make that joke, but now that I think about it, EA deserved it more (So pretend I never made that joke. I can make an EA game review and use that.). They also added a bunch of graphs. You can take all my money and kill me when someone says "Graphs! Oh goody. Now I don't have to worry about NOT being confused!" Overall: The game had a lot of potential, but the music just really got on my nerves. But if you're deaf, this game's  perfect!
