Well...I'm not sure what to do with my man card now, because I sure as hell don't need it after this.
This is a surprisingly in-depth Tactical RPG. If you're the kind of person that likes to make insane combat builds, or min max, this is a game for you. You start with picking one of 12 character classes, and this is actually really important. You're going to want to build your team around your class. However, no matter what class you pick, you ARE a summoner first. Most of your damage is usually going to come from your summons. You get summons by capturing them in combat ala pokemon (Beat them up and then use a limited ability to trap them) or by progressing the story. They also have a gatcha feature to get a random monster if you do any grinding on the free levels, which is nice.
For reference on min-maxing, here is what I did. I picked necromancer because I thought it would be funny. When I got over my shock at how the skeletons look, (Spoiler - EVERYTHING is a female anime character in this game) I tried summoning them in combat. They sucked. Then a few battles later I captured a demon that gave all summoned undead +25% to their stats. Then I got a spell that gives undead +25 to their stats. Everything is stackable in this game, and most buffs don't run out. Then I found a demon that summons more skeletons. Then I found another. Soon I had a team of nothing but demons that either buffed or summoned skeletons. And surprise! When you have more than three demons summoned, they do cumulative damage to living creatures every turn. That wasn't explained anywhere, it just sort of happened. At this point my main necromancer was the only living or non-demon thing, so I picked up an ability that changed her type to undead. I found myself steam rolling things and was super happy with my army of skeletons.
Until I found my first enemy that summoned angels. Just one angel would wreck my skeletal/demon army. Then the game became hard again, fast. I came up with a build to handle angels, and then ran into an enemy who had a system to make their main mage permanently ghost formed by abusing the power from a sprite. My skeletons couldn't touch it, and it spammed a magic nova over my army as I cried helplessly because I didn't bring any real magic to do damage, just more skeletons.
Then I got high enough level where I could summon ghosts and weights, which could cast their own magic. The ghost mage wasn't as scary anymore as my minions could plink away at it with telekinesis. Everything was going well, until I ran into the dragon summoner, and went back to crying as everything I loved burned in the fires of a thousand suns.
The game has so many creatures with unique abilities and stats, that there are probably hundreds of viable builds and strategies—all of which play heavily on your choice of starting class. Had I gone warrior, I might have went with a team of giants. Illusionist, maybe fearies. But you're not stuck either. I'm leveling up a backup team of gremlins right now to give me more magic options when I need it. My necromancer can do her thing just fine on her own now, and the gremlins can create their own havoc. Anything will work, but some things will clearly work better than others. I would replay it over and over except...
The story is really, really bad.In true B-rated anime fashion, random characters are popping up all over and I don't know why. The fun part of the game is literally just combat and party building. There is nothing outside of one battle after another, with a short break at the party screen and maybe a few rolls with my magic gems to see if I got something cool.
Also, did I mention that every single character is an anime girl? Most of them are kids too, which is somewhere between disturbing and funny. Every skeleton summoned is a little girl who is sent off to her second death at the hands of a giant girl, who was summoned by an angry lady. I can't tell 80% of my friends about this game because of how weaboo Japanese the art is. There is one monster that I was reluctant to summon with my wife in the room because I didn' want her to get the wrong idea about this game, even though it provided serious healing for my necromancer (before I turned her into a zombie too). Some of the pictures are a little too suggestive, even bordeline creepy. Which is a shame, because the combat mechanics are awesome.
Honestly, I'd say the monster system,  and combat system could work in a triple A title just fine. They'd need to improve the interface, trash the story, and re-skin the characters, but I'd love to play a game like this with a real story and some other gameplay elements besides combat. It's very reminiscent of disgea, with a heavier emphasis on team synergy, and much less on power leveling. No single character (That I've found!) will get you through this. You need a team.
If you've played disgea and liked it for either the art or the game-play, check this out. Just don't let anyone see you playing it.
If you're looking for a story... I'd pass on this, at least so far. Honestly I wish I could just skip the story parts at this point. Oh well. I'm gonna see if I can go catch Artemis. Yes, the god with the bow. I need her for one of the teams I was thinking of building. She can hang with my captured valkyries and tiamat.

I cleared the story mode after playing for pretty much 27 hours straight, that's how good it was. The story mode is quite challenging, if you avoid playing too many free battles, hence staying at the recommended level. (Btw, I played as a Necromancer, difficulty and playtime will most likely vary depending on class and playstyle).
Choose between 10 starting classes with inherently different playstyles. After clearing the story mode you gain access to a couple of new modes and you can start unlocking more masters and classes. Add 150+ varying creatures (summonings) to the mix and you have a game with a lot of replay value.
The game has a strategic aspect to it as well; as you level up you gain acces to more skills and abilities for your master and creatures, and your army of creatures just keeps growing, you'll have to choose wisely with your limited resources before you proceed to battle. At the beginning of a battle you'll only have your master at the battlefield, and will have to summon the creatures. Hence, you will have to choose between weaker but cheaper creatures with short summoning times suited for blitzkrieg, or strong creatures with high cost and/or long summoning times. Depending on choices your entire playstyle may have to change.

Trine 2 is a sidescrolling game that includes jumping, puzzle solving and fighting, all in a pleasant and well measured mixture.
Game looks nice, style is childishly charming and fanciful, in line with it's fairytale theme.
Player takes control of one of the three characters - a knight, a thief and a wizard - and freely changes between them during the adventure, using various abilities available to each one and combining them to overcome obstacles, be they botomless pitfalls, weird contraptions or enemies.
Gameplay is smooth and fun, game is fairly easy and causes little to no frustration but there's still a hefty dose of satisfaction when you manage to reach some hard to notice collectible crammed in a niche in the ceiling or a hidden chest after using up a trick or two. Levels are fairly diverse, from bread and butter enchanted forests or dungeons, to walled towns under assault to really cool and weird stuff such as being inside a sand worm's digestion system.
I unfortunately haven't tried multiplayer as of yet.
I haven't played anything of this sort since childhood times of Prehistorik and Prince of Persia in the early 1990ies, so I don't have much modern first hand experience for comparison. However Trine 2 (as well as Trine) left me very pleasantly surprised after I got it due to a random urge to buy something on a discount. Being used to "serious" games such as aviation simulators, rpgs, Total War series, raiding mmos, Eve online etc in the recent decade(s) I remembered how it felt to play games when I was a kid and I must say the change of pace is welcome.
All in all, I can recommend Trine 2. I imagine children would love it, while some of us older warhorses used to dark fantasy, dark science fiction, serious modern warfare etc can find a welcome break in this little gem.

Ziggurat is a really enjoyable FPS that blends Quake-like speed with procedurally generated floors and perma-death. You can have up to four different "weapons": your trusty wand (you start with this), a spell book, a staff, and an alchemical weapon. As you progress, you'll level up and pick perk cards to help give you some passive buffs, find new weapons and trinkets, and face off against progressively tougher enemies. The game does have a progression system, so you steadily unlock new weapons, perks, and even characters (which have different strengths/weaknesses and start with different perks).

Ziggurat drops you right into the action. Controls are tight and responsive, action is fast and intense. (And procedurally generated.) Lots of fun, and the unlockable characters, weapons, and abilities add tons of replay value.

This is the more dour Fantasy brother to Tower of Guns - It's a roguelike first person shooter using fantasy elements and weapons, and card based upgrades that only last through your current game (although you can unlock new characters). It is also very intense - I noticed I was dodging attacks in my chair, and holding my breath at the end of some of the later level's battles. Because it's a roguelike, it'll reward returning to it again (and I will, just like Tower of Guns), but I made it through the five levels of the main game and finished off the final boss (barely). The levels are beautiful, the monsters are ugly, and it's challenging but fair. I'm really glad I picked it up; it's definitely worth a try if you liked games like Hexen and Heretic way back when and want something with a similar feel. My only negative is that it doesn't have enough secrets in it, but that's not much of a complaint.

If you liked HR, you will like this.
Took about 40 hours to complete the game stealth/pacifist while also doing all of the side quests that popped up and I immediately started a new game+ run (Which lets you keep all your points/items) and did it a second time to collect up achievements.
Really liked how very open ended a lot of the quests were and gave you many different options to complete them, and in general while exploring, most areas that had a challenge presented to get to them had many alternate ways into them depending on your resources and skills, some easier than others.
Main gripes with the game are that the two main zones are not separately big enough that they should really be split like they are.  This wouldn't have been so bad if it was possible to run or quickly move between the two, but instead you have to run down to a subway and sit on a fairly long repetitive loading screen video, which isnt bad occasionally but there are points in the game where quests and side quests are bouncing you back and forward between the zones just to fetch or talk to someone and it gets really tedious having to back and forward and wait 3-5 minutes a pop on the loading screen if you cant afford the SSD space for the game.
Game also has a fairly meaty 'Breach' mode which looks like quite a lot of effort into it and is a time trial leaderboard mode where you need to hack your way through virtual space to steal information, but I did get bored fairly fast and the mode has a lot of critique for making the game arbitralily difficult to try and push people to spend real money.
If it's on sale, definitely worth it.

I had a lot of fun playing this game. Single player games with strong story lines are generally my preference and according to Steam I logged nearly 80 hours on it. Even at full price that's great value for money, pick it up in a sale and it's an absolute bargain. The variety of options available when tackling levels make it one of the best FPS games out there even if you choose a non-shooting style of play.  There are microtransactions in the game, whether you use them or not is entirely up to you, it doesn't affect much. Whilst Human Revolution might have had multiple hubs, Prague is much larger and richer in detail. I spent many hours exploring, finding side missions and other surprises. Admittedly the ending could be more epic and it's clear the intention was to continue the story in another game. Hopefully that will still happen. Overall that doesn't detract much from what I thought was a great game.
Highly recommended and the additional missions being released are a nice bonus.

I'd like to start off by saying that I noticed a trend in the negative reviews for this game.  Mostly that nearly all of them have between 4 and 10 negative votes and I'm willing to bet it's the same 4 to 10 petty people who abhore critisism in any form of something they can see only as being unequivicably perfect.  That being said, this game still has some serious faults but considering that it is still in the development phase I think at least most of them are forgivable.
VISUAL: Retro, pseudo-3D, 16bit.  I grew up on this kind of game art style so I particularly like it.  It's cheap but effective.  This game is often compared to Terraria but if I had to choose it would be this game.  I like having a small army at my disposal over a singluar character.  The graphics and sprites are probably still being tweaked and after looking at earlier screen shots the game is only getting better in that regard.
AUDIO: I like the music, but I'm weird.  I don't like all of the tracks but it's more than one singular song that plays repeatedly so I have to give it that.  I try to keep away from where my Gnomes are working because the sound effects are a bit grating but other than that it has a nice retro feel to it that keeps with the art style.
GAMEPLAY:  And now for the meat of the review.  The part of the game that has the most issues but also the most potential.  Let's kick this part off with the elephant in the room.  There is no tutorial for this life sim strategy based game.  There is a good reason for that, the base game is not finished yet.  It's still in development and making a tutorial would take away from getting the game to a finished, balanced, and polished state.  The tutorial will--hopefully--come with the v1.0 update.  Beyond that, there are several guides on YouTube that are easy to find and easy to follow to learn how to play this game.  Even finding older tutorials is enough to give you a basic grasp of the game.
The game starts paused.  You need to clear a large area of flat land for farming and pasture.  Start with foraging, then clipping trees, then fell some trees, then replace any clay spots with dirt, and mark off your farms, pastures, and groves.  You also want to dig into the hills and start building your fort.  Designate a small stockpile for soil and stone, and larger stock piles for everything else you need.  You need to start building up your workshops once you get inside.  Start with the crude work bench then find your way through the other workshops until you get to the tailor so you can make beds to sleep on.
Here's what the game doesn't tell you and several older guides don't cover:  You need to go into the population menu, pick a Gnome, go to skills, go to Misc Craft, and turn on bone carving.  As far as I have found, this is so far the singular skill that is not immediately attached to any class and has to be manually turned on.  There is NOTHING in the game so far that indicates that this needs to be done or how to do it, but it is crucial to advancing the game.  Once it is turned on, that Gnome should eventually go to the station to make the bone needle.  You will have to wait until at least your first summer to slaughter a yak to get the bones to make the needle but this should give you time to do other things.
Once you get into the game, the strategy is fairly straightforward.  Keep enough food and drink on hand for your gnomes, enough wheat straw for your yaks, keep your groves going and your tunnels deep.  Just like Terraria and other digging games, the deeper you go the better materials you find.  There's no story that I've tripped over and the Gnomes have no individuality and don't have relationships.  They work endlessly, new Gnomes finding you over time (apparently linked to your Great Hall in some way) and join your clan.
I recommend this game if you can get it rather cheap.  I bought it for $2 and got a few copies for my friends.  I really want to see where this game goes.  The workshops seem to be overflowing and a couple seem over stretched at times but I think that it works.  The longer I played the more I noticed that the characters seem very obsessed with rearranging the dirt in my stock piles until I can find them all and turn them off.  The priorities don't seem to be as effective as they should be.  Even after turning off stock piles and fields there are a list of jobs marked as highest priority that just never get done.  Perhaps it will run more smoothly in a future update.  Until then, if you see this for cheap, add it to your inventory and let it stew.

I'm not a fighting game reviewer. While I do play and enjoy games from this genre, I don't consider myself qualified to discuss the pros and cons. Understanding fighters can require long-term commitment, and their very nature changes due to techniques discovered by the players. Some of these changes can be so dramatic that the game just isn't the same anymore. So for me to review a fighter, something must be seriously wrong.
On that note, let's talk about STEEL RIVALS!
As the story goes, 18 men, women, and beasts are fighting in a tournament. The prize? A change of clothes. Now I've played a fair amount of
,
, and
. I can say without a doubt, that most of that time was spent unlocking and purchasing clothes. Playing virtual dress-up with
will never cease to be enjoyable for me. Still, I would have liked even a semblance of a storyline. Something along the lines of "so and so hates whatever their name is, and they're going to fight to the death." Instead, if you win the tournament, your fighter says "Yay I won! Here's a new outfit for me!" Gee willickers, that's just swell...
This game is described as a 2.5D fighter, but it's more of a .5D. Just so we're clear I'm saying that STEEL RIVALS is a POINT 5D FIGHTER. You can walk forwards, backwards, attack, block, or do those
moon-jumps. Now depending on the character, you're going to cross off some of those maneuvers. For example: Morgan uses magic. Her strategy is going to consist entirely of jumping backwards and throwing projectiles. If the enemy gets close, she crouches and performs a spinning slide move to knock the opponent down. In order to combat this strategy, the opponent must...I don't know.
Typically in fighters, projectiles are jumped over, or there's some other technique to handle players that abuse them. With this game...you block and then...you keep blocking? Maybe your opponent will get bored and try another move instead. Jumping over fireballs doesn't work, because every jump sends you soaring far over everything (including the opponent). I suppose you could try moving forward, and hope to bait out the slide-attack. Playing theory fighter is the most dangerous game of all, because in STEEL RIVALS, it all hinges on your opponent doing something tremendously stupid.
There's no reason for Morgan to put herself in any danger. She can continue to jump backwards, throw her mid-air projectiles, mix in a few while standing, and tire her opponent out. At worst she might get tapped by an attack and get knocked down, but there's little the opponent can do to capitalize. This is all due to the combo system. When you land an attack, you can press combinations of the first two attack buttons to create combos, then press the third button for a special finish(this uses meter). Unless you can land hits, you'll never get meter, but if you land hits that you can't combo off of, then it's all rendered moot.
But let's forget about Morgan for now and discuss another character. This guy's name is Sardis. For whatever silly reason, his two standing moves ignore attacks. This means his opponent could be doing anything, and he'll simply power through it and go into his combos. This should be game-breaking, but his ability as a fighter is shattered by simply blocking. His attacks have a ton of recovery time, so all you have to do is block and punish. This poor jerk doesn't have any options. He doesn't have quick light moves, a grab, or anything that could force the opponent to respect him. When you face Sardis, all you have to do is block...and punish. This is what I mean by a .5D fighter. Either you perform the one move that can defeat your opponent, or you don't. That is how wins and losses are decided.
Some other characters (like Maya) get dive-kicks and/or really fast attacks. Now I won't claim that my STEEL RIVALS skills are good enough for EVO but I think my dive-kick + combo into finisher strats could at least get me to grand finals. Again, this is because there aren't any decent methods for getting out of combo traps. Some characters can perform special evasive moves or counters, but that requires meter. As I said earlier, meter comes from landing hits. Maya is going to be moon-jumping and dive-kicking all the time, even if the opponent blocks everything, she can just jump out of the way and try again. Some other characters have nothing but slow moves, or they only hit high instead of mid or low. At this point they're just plain sad. All that can be said about them is: Why even wake up? You were designed for failure.
Admittedly I haven't spent a lot of time with everyone. I won a few tournaments with some of the female fighters because uh...well I was hoping they'd win some clothes. Not different clothes...just...you know...clothes...because a couple of them are wearing practically nothing. This made the tourney victories all the more bittersweet, because their new outfits tended to be even more revealing. I can't even appreciate the titillation
everyone looks like they're made out of plastic. Maya's hair is yarn for crying out loud.
STEEL RIVALS has a loooooooooong way to go before it can be considered being worth anywhere near $15. The game looks like a low-budget
, but has all the complexity of a
prequel. Your time and money are better spent elsewhere.

However, once in game, the graphics looked extremely dated, and were hard to look at. That's fine, I've played uglier MMOs. Yet, the combat felt wonky, as every mob ran through me, and the game won't let you attack from behind, so for every single mob I had to walk backwards, then attack. Camera movement was also really bad. The whole time I felt like I had tunnel vision, since I'm use to MMOs that are more friendly with both movement and visibility.
Also, every minute or so there is a reminder of what you need to buy in the store. If you're training skills, you should buy this item. If you're collecting valor, you should buy this item. If your character looks ugly, you should buy this item (though there's no item to buy to make the game look good in general). If you want to play with others, you should buy this expansion. It just goes on and on.
This is also one of the most dated looking games, both graphically, and in gameplay mechanics. There are just a lot of things that the MMO developer community has stopped doing, and for good reason that make this game seem more dated than it actually is. For instance, you need to level a character that you care nothing about to level 10 before you can make an evil faction character. This sort of nonsensical restriction I've seen in other games, and it's always a bad idea, costing them players in the process.
Basically, I stopped playing because of a lot of annoyances heaped on top of each other. The game isn't worth the long download and patching process.

Tactics were essential. Having fortresses were almost as important as fighting enemies themselves. Again classes had diversty.  You had to use more than 5 buttons.
Those were the times as I was waiting for next expansion, Rise of the Isengard. Aka Fall of Lotro. At first it looked really fun, nice leveling. Great dungeons and challanging and original raids. All good. When I got geared, I stepped to PvP zone, since you had no PvP specific armours, you had to grind some PvE to be a decent player. Anyway when I stepped in, I saw a warg 2 wargs running at me. I was like '' Oh Isair now you are dead''. But what?! I practically 3 shot them. They couldn' even hit me properly. And it was when I realised what was going on, ever since Lotro went f2p, Turbine wanted players to pay for them. And you had to pay in order to enter pvp zone with your Free People character. So Turbine made Free Peoples (Freeps) lot stronger compared to Servants of mordor (creeps) And that was when balance in PvP simply dissapeared.
Now if you were a PvE player, you might have enjoyed RoI. I do not know becouse I stopped playing on mid RoI due to unbalanced PvP.
Then Turbine went full greedy, giving new expansions once in a year with no new decent group content or a decent look on PvP.
Riders of rohan was lotro's last times with decent population. They somehow managed to bring slight tbalance to PvP. Freeps were still stronger but it was bareble. But even though I was not a main PvE guy, I compleatedevery single PvE content on RoR, why becouse all of them were easy as hell. So soem say (including me) that RoI was end of PvP and RoR was end of PvE.
Aaaand we have Helm's Deep, highly hyped expansion. A hope for Lotro's epic comeback. But NOOOOPEEE. HD was the expansion that made Lotro fall to a position where it is now. A dying game where developers try to grab your money before it dies compleatly. Terrible PvP and even more terrible PvE where all you had to do was use you 3 slots of quickslot bard to compleate a PvE session.
Rest of the expansions are fallowups of HD, really bad PvE and PvP. Although they brough some new PvE content (after 3 years) they are boring, simple and not worth it.
Now I still play the game, like an hour a week. Why? Becouse of community. Community was what made Lotro great and still lets Lotro to live these hard times.
Since you do not have any cross server stuff going on and low population, people know each other. Not by name maybe but by heart. You can start a random conversation in world chat and watch people you may know or not join it and have fun other than playing the game itself. Community of lotro is the best one you can find in any game. Friendship, love and trust just like in original Lotr.
Final conclusion should you play this game?
That really depends, if you play a game for PvE content, no. Go play WoW, rift or newerwinter.
If you play a game for PvP, play swtor, gw2 etc.
But if you want to play the game solely for relaxing chatting with other people and doing some events. Give lotro a try, you do not need to spend a lot of money since paying for either PvE or PvP just does not worth it atm.

A fun moe strategy game from what I've seen so far.
When you start the game, you'll be allowed to pick which class to start as. You won't be able to name your character.
The game also keeps track of all your records, from how many deaths your party has, your max damage, to which class you've cleared the game with.
The encyclopedia in game allows you to view the summoned unit's artwork, along with sampling their voices.
Battles are sorted by Story Mode and Free Battle.
When you start the battle, you'll only have your main character on the field, you have to summon your units to get them into the fight (similar to confine in Phantom Brave, but doesn't disappear after set turns).
There's friendly fire in this game, you can even have your character get killed by their own AOE.
Free mode allows you to grind and level up your main character, summons, and allows you to capture "wild creatures".
From what I've seen so far, you can only capture one "wild creature" per battle.
Completing free battles will also grant you contract gems to summon units. You can set the conditions of the unit, such as their element, level, etc, provided you have the gems to pay for it.
However... there are a few issues I have with the camera...
Camera angles can be rotated, at fixed 45* angles (similar to Disgaea). The true problem I have with the game is the targetting issue. When there are many units close together, AOE targetting becomes quite a chore.
All in all, it's a fun title, and definitely worth the price.

It's a rogue-like with a similar formula to Binding of Isaac- go into a room, kill everything in sight, find the boss and blow it to pieces. Except you're doing it with magic/alchemical devices from a first person perspective.
It doesn't really do a whole lot new- you do level up and are allowed to choose perks to help you out in various ways. There's four different weapon types- your wand, a spell book, a staff, and an alchemical device. Each have their own mana pool, which is quite unique- only problem is all of these weapons perform basically the same- shoot some number of bolts in some pattern, with an alternate fire that just fires more bolts. Bosses are okay- mostly they just shoot stuff at you and summon monsters, nothing really ingenious. No two playthroughs are the same, but multiple playthoughs aren't really substantially different, either.
This game could've been great, but it's not. Don't get me wrong- it's still fun. It's something to play if you don't know what else to play. I love the Hexen/Heretic vibe it has going on, and it's certainly worth getting if it's on a Steam sale, but the $15 asking price is a bit too steep for what you get out of it.

Some mad scientist at Ubisoft took a solid, respectable game engine, chained it in the basement, and injected it with the liquified essence of 1988.  What the tortured, convulsing wreckage of Far Cry 3 vomited up before expiring, they called "Blood Dragon."  And it's a blast.
The worst excesses and most overdone tropes of over-the-top '80s action movies become a to-do list here.  Training montage?
there's a training montage!   Lovers silhouetted against the sunset over the ocean?  Check, and with an inexplicable mid-dialogue transition, too!  Melodramatic voice-over?  Buckets of it.  Villain as father figure?  Sure!  And SO. MUCH. NEON!
The Far Cry 3 engine is adequate for the purpose.  It doesn't shine, it just gets the job done without calling much attention to itself.  And that's fine, because this game is all about style over substance; adequacy is all the engine is really asked to provide.
The game is somewhat short, the open world is a bit small, and there's limited replay value, but that's all okay, too.  The purpose of the experience is a phantasmagorical trip into cultural nostalgia, and that has a limited value.  Just about the time that the whole 80's-flashback experience is starting to wear thin, BAM, the game wraps itself up in a very flashy way, without overstaying its welcome.
The one major complaint I had with this game was the need to install Uplay and make a Uplay account.   Steam is already DRM.  Steam already offers achievements and meaningless metagame accolades.  Adding Uplay is inconvenience with any additional value.  But, since Blood Dragon is a short game, at least I don't have to keep it long.
This isn't a game that you'll play for years to come; it's a brief thrill and made to be that way.  But if you have happy memories of "Commando," "Cyborg," "Krull," or "Captain Power and the Soldiers of the Future," this is a purchase you won't regret.

Dead Space 2 is one of my all-time favorites. It does storytelling in a way that a lot more games need to learn to do. Dead Space 2 foregoes most of the first game's insistence that it is a horror game in favor of another type of story that is more focused on atmosphere and storytelling.
You're Isaac. Isaac isn't a silent protagonist anymore, and Isaac isn't an everyman. You don't feel scared for you own life, you worry for Isaac's. This is Isaac's story, and the over-the-shoulder camera serves to emphasize that. You're a passenger in Isaac's story. There's no choices, there's no alternate paths. You're a witness to his story and it is your job to keep him alive.
Even if the story itself isn't amazing, the way it is told is something I have yet to see matched in any game.

If you're seeing this game for the first time IT'S NOT A COPY OF SMASH. I REPEAT NOT A COPY
Brawlhalla (Salthalla) is quite a fun game to play. It's easy to learn but hard to master is what most people say and I agree with that.
Each legend has different stats that affect the legend's play style. Each legend also has 2 different weapons (Ex. Orion has a  spear and a rocket lance) The game is very solid for being in beta, heck I'd even call it a full game if it weren't for a few things that needed to be added into the game. First thing right off the bat IT'S NOT PAY TO WIN. The only thing real money can achieve you in this game is pure cosmetic items which support BMG when you buy them. I repeat, COSMETIC ITEMS DO NOT HAVE ANY AFFECT ON STATS OR GAMEPLAY WHATSOEVER. While adding to the legend stats, the stats that each legend has is Attack, Defense, Dexterity, and Speed. Each legend has a stance for each one of these attributes which allows you to mix up your play style a bit. Some might argue but right now (for me at least) all the legends are balanced. The fighting, the meat of the game. When starting, all players start off unarmed and weapon and items spawn throughout the game. Every legend has the same moves for unarmed but when it comes to weapons, it's kind of a different story. Light attacks are the same for all legends (Ex. Hattori NLight with sword is identical to Val Nlight with sword) This is where each legend becomes unique. Each legend has a set of signatures that are (obviously) special attacks that deal heavy damage and are unique to each legend and weapon. Legends can also dodge during a match allowing you to become invincible for a second. Dodging in the air and performing an attack is called a gravity cancel, which allows you to use certain moves that you normally can't use when in the air. The fighting is very solid basically. Obviously some features are missing as Brawlhalla is only in Beta. (Ex. You can only do 2v2 ranked with a friend or guildmate)
This is one of my biggest reasons of hate for this game. The community. I'd say at least 70% of the community is full of non toxic people that will help other players and actually say GG after a match. The other 30% is pure toxic. It is most likely that you will end up playing against a toxic player and will trash talk you if you end up losing to them. If you end up beating a toxic player, they will 100% of the time be salty and call you a noob (even though they are admiting a noob beat them) It's best to just ignore them. (If you say EZ after beating anyone and it was a close match, just kill your self) Another really bad thing about Brawlhalla (Salthalla) is that the servers and netcode are kind of bad and I usually end up lagging even though I have good internet connection. If you end up playing someone with bad internet, good luck.
In conclusion Brawlhalla is a great game, the pros outweigh the cons in my opinion. Wait did I say brawlhalla? I meant SALTHALLA

Edit (elaboration):
The game engine (i.e. driving, shooting, AI, etc.) is decent. The single player story is alright, but is much shorter than any of the previous GTA installments, and is over as soon as you do a mission that pays well. It is sorely lacking in many of the features that added depth to their older games, like NPC interaction and side missions. If you want to pick up this game and play it casually for 20-30 hours, you'll probably have a great time, but I would find it hard to justify paying the full $60 for this - especially after its been out for over four years.
If you want to keep playing, you will eventually end up doing GTA:Online. It is by far the greater portion of the game's content, but rather than being a rewarding and diverse experience it is a repetitive grind with minute payoffs designed to wear you down until you break and pay them more money for Shark Cards, the in game money system. They will not even allow private servers for players to tailor their own experience. The whole thing is a disgusting abuse of power on their part, and I will not be buying a Rockstar game ever again.

Z --> Dash
X --> Heavy att
C --> Light att/Pickup weapons
V --> Throw ur weapon
Arrows --> Movement
1-4 --> Taunt (Yes, not only TF2 has taunts)
Tab --> Scoreboard

Okay, I think I have a lot to say about this.
First things first, this game is wonderful. I beat the game a couple times on the original xbox 360 version, and I'd rate the story mode 4/5. Lots of things to do in this game and the map is pretty big. I really enjoy riding a bike up the mountains and then parachuting off, or surviving with a 5 star wanted level while on the tallest building in the game. Singleplayer in this game is fun already, and adding mods ontop just makes it 10x better.
Would I reccomend getting this for the singleplayer? Yes.
Oh, hey! There's also a nifty 'online' mode. I had lots of fun doing multiplayer in GTA4, so surely GTA5 has an even better online mode, seeing as there are millions of things to do in singleplayer, right?
Well, sure I guess. GTA Online has lots and lots and lots of activities to do. You can rob stores, play golf, murder people, have an arm wrestle (RIP fingers), rob banks, race, etc. There is just so much to do.
However, I wouldnt do multiplayer unless you have friends to play it with. 9/10 times there is a modder in an online server that likes to bomb everybody thats in the server or just spawn random stuff to annoy players.
Even if you play in passive mode (Essentially disables PvP) they will still often do stuff like blow up nearby vehicles, teleport, control you and your vehicles, etc.
Now, if you either play in a closed session by yourself (limits the available activities) or play with your friends, the game is pretty great. Money is NOT as hard to get as people make it sound. I got the game a few weeks ago and already managed to get a nice apartment and some vehicles. It just takes time. Even if you play for an hour a day, you can easily rob a few stores and get at least 10k a day.
If you are looking for fast money, whenever you get invited to an organization, accept it. As long as you are within a radius of your CEO, you will get paid around 5000 every 30 minutes and if you do missions with your ceo you can easily make 20k or so in an hour.
Anyways, thats my review.
TL;DR - Singleplayer is great, Multiplayer is not always great unless you have friends.

One of the most addictive games ever!!! Dungeon-Crawling First Person Shooting at its finest! Fast-paced combat! Dozens of perks, spells and enemies! Level ups! Random Dungeons! Traps! Badass bosses! Carrots! Ziggurat is the best combination of First Person Shooter and Rogue-LITE you have ever seen. THIS GAME IS AWESOME!!! (yep carrots...)
If you ever enjoyed awesome games like Heretic or Hexen, you will enjoy this game.

Overall the game is very fun, and with really nice colourful graphics. The production values are significantly higher than any other indie roguelight fps such as tower of guns, Paranautical activity and RogueShooter (which are all great games in their own right).
The magical setting, with fantasy enemies and wands and spells in place of guns makes for a nice change and works surprisingly well with the quakelike gameplay.
The aforementioned 'quakelike' gameplay is fast paced and feels good, shooting (or casting spells more like) and jumping all feel smoothe and accurate.
What I will say is it's a little dissapointingly easy, at least on the 'normal' setting, This is the first roguelight I beat on my very first try. But with more difficulty settings and MANY unlocks to go, there's plenty of replay value and reasons to come back. Unlocks include new perks, weapons, useable items and even characters.
The roguelike/roguelight FPS genre is very varied and so far, every game has enough originality to justify it's existance, Ziggurat is no exception. Hard to say if it's the best in the Genre so far, but for any fan, it needs to be in their collection.

I got this on sale after all the bugs were likely removed. There are still a few in the game, but not enough to ruin it now.
I don't know what everyone else is complaining about. The game was great. The story was complex and quite clever.... and a bit of an allegory to the troubling aspects of terrorism that we see today, in my opinion - so ten out of ten for that.
The gameplay is even more finely tuned than Human Revolution - in particular the hacking mini-game which is more complex and challenging now. The length of the game - including doing all the sidequests - took me about 40 hours or so on a pacifist playthrough. That is about as much as the Human Revolution director's cut took for me to play through.... so length wasn't really a problem for me. I found that the single player pay-to-play wasn't offputting (because the game isn't that hard to begin with really, even on "Give me Deus Ex"), and the other collectables that tie into Square Enix membership didn't bother me either. I don't know what people are complaining about here - as the existance of some of these online features didn't spoil the single player experience one bit. They may as well have not been there.
Additionally I don't believe the game ended on a cliffhanger or unresolved plot threads, but it *might* have if you left a lot of the quests undone, or failed in too many of your missions. In any case, Mankind Divided is a prequel to the original "Deus Ex" game - so those of you who have played that classic will know how everything ends up anyhow.
Fans of the Deus Ex series will feel right at home in this game. All the tropes of the series are in here that make it a real Deus Ex game - including the basketball ring - and there are many references made to all the other Deus Ex games if you dig deep enough and hack A LOT of computers (did I say A LOT of terminals). The best thing about the series is that you can approach your objectives any way you see fit. If you opt for stealth, you'll find yourself hacking terminals hundreds of times, and looking for those cliched air vents to sneak in. You could however go in guns blazing with a whole array of firepower. In addition, you have your augmented abilities to rely on. You are spoilt for choices really.
The developers have managed to pack a lot of the game around the Prague city hub - and it shows. The location get used over and over again for many of the sidequests, but as you revisit it after main story quests, it keeps changing. On a technical level it's quite brilliant what they have done here, but I found myself getting a bit bored with my lack of travel to new locales, and the lack of scope for the story. Fortunately there are no fetch quests - except for one (that breaks the fourth wall!)
Being a Deus Ex game, you're going to miss a lot of things the first time around, and it's only with repeated playthroughs that you are going to find everything. There are a pile of secrets to uncover, and little things you do can have a big impact on the story later on.... which is a standard for the series.
To top it all off, there's this "Breach" game mode which lets you play the core game in limited bursts. There's also some more DLC which will probably appear in a director's cut sometime in the future anyway... so there's even more to do.
Graphically the game pushed my GTX670 card to about 30FPS, but I didn't mind it that much. There was a bit of stuttering but it didn't get in the way of playing the game. A more modern card would get you better results clearly, but it still looked fantastic to me.
All in all, it's an amazing game. A big thumbs up from me.

I like this game. I truly do. However, right now I wouldn't recommend it simply for one reason: the grind. Money was, is, and will be one of the fundamental parts of any GTA or open world game to this day, and R* understands it. And lately, they've been exploiting it like never before - right about after the Ill Gotten Gains II came out, they realized they can suck the extra cash out of people via Shark Cards (microstransactions), and be a big earner for Take-Two and themselves, which they are, by the way. This has gone from integrating overpriced clothes and cars to messing up the game's logic itself. It's especially notable in the three major updates - the CEO update, the Biker update, and the I/E update. The three of them are the most profitable businesses in the game, netting you only about 240.000$ an hour, 380.000$ at best, which might seem good, but the amount of grinding, and the prices (300.000 for a muscle car) make you want more and more, and those who don't have enough time to grind are forced into paying for Shark Cards, which at most will net you 8.000.00 GTA$ at a price of 100 USD. And as if that wasn't bad enough, the multiple ways to earn big money like CEO/MC/I/E are cut tremendously short. For instance, apparently 500g of coke, which in the USA is worth on average 30.000$ (60$ a gram), is now worth just 30$, considering the ridiculous pricing in the Bikers DLC. Or stealing 2.000.000$ cars, and then selling them on the blackmarket for a measly 80.000$. Or even in the CEO update, where you traffick contraband, you can only buy as much as 3 crates at a time, and something always goes wrong or you have to do some task to get the damn things. So much pain, but it can be resolved with Shark Cards. Besides, the community is trash, and the game is halfway dead by now. A few words about the singleplayer - it's a great experience, the story is great (albeit with a lot of ridiculous stuff), the freedom is there, and everything is in place. Except for stuff from GTAO that's not even added, and the fact that R* treats SP like the first kid who's worse than the other.

Amazing game. I never expected to put as much time in to it as I have, and I still want to play more. The game is a simplified and more user friendly version of Dwarf Fortress. Starting with just a few gnomads, you assign jobs and tasks for the gnomes to perform in order to build a kingdom and dig up riches. Fans of god games, city builders, or other management games will find lots to like. The game is mostly feature complete as it stands.
My only real complaint is that there isn't much of an end game. Population is value based, and kind of peters out after a certain point so you can't expand endlessly. After a few game years there isn't much to do besides build interesting structures. However, the game worlds are random so each new game differs slightly.
The graphics are rather simple, there is very little animation, and the sound effects are kind of annoying so the presentation isn't the greatest. So if those things are important you may want to pass.

I like this game. I truly do. However, right now I wouldn't recommend it simply for one reason: the grind. Money was, is, and will be one of the fundamental parts of any GTA or open world game to this day, and R* understands it. And lately, they've been exploiting it like never before - right about after the Ill Gotten Gains II came out, they realized they can suck the extra cash out of people via Shark Cards (microstransactions), and be a big earner for Take-Two and themselves, which they are, by the way. This has gone from integrating overpriced clothes and cars to messing up the game's logic itself. It's especially notable in the three major updates - the CEO update, the Biker update, and the I/E update. The three of them are the most profitable businesses in the game, netting you only about 240.000$ an hour, 380.000$ at best, which might seem good, but the amount of grinding, and the prices (300.000 for a muscle car) make you want more and more, and those who don't have enough time to grind are forced into paying for Shark Cards, which at most will net you 8.000.00 GTA$ at a price of 100 USD. And as if that wasn't bad enough, the multiple ways to earn big money like CEO/MC/I/E are cut tremendously short. For instance, apparently 500g of coke, which in the USA is worth on average 30.000$ (60$ a gram), is now worth just 30$, considering the ridiculous pricing in the Bikers DLC. Or stealing 2.000.000$ cars, and then selling them on the blackmarket for a measly 80.000$. Or even in the CEO update, where you traffick contraband, you can only buy as much as 3 crates at a time, and something always goes wrong or you have to do some task to get the damn things. So much pain, but it can be resolved with Shark Cards. Besides, the community is trash, and the game is halfway dead by now. A few words about the singleplayer - it's a great experience, the story is great (albeit with a lot of ridiculous stuff), the freedom is there, and everything is in place. Except for stuff from GTAO that's not even added, and the fact that R* treats SP like the first kid who's worse than the other.

Bem, vai ser um pouco dificil falar sobre Torchlight 2, já que é um jogo no estilo RPG, o meu estilo favorito de jogos. Então, sempre tenho muito a falar, mas dessa vez, irei dar uma breve resumida do que se trata o game.
Não tem como falar de quaisquer jogos no estilo de RPG, sem mencionar o grande e poderoso Diablo. Pois bem, esse jogo aqui, em alguns quesitos, bate de forma relevante o Diablo 3, jogo mais atual da franquia. Como por exemplo o preço, Torchlight 2 é muito, mas muito parecido com Diablo 3 e o preço é bem mais baixo. Também ganha do Diablo no quesito de que não necessita de internet 24hrs para jogar, já que o jogo dispõe do modo offline que pode ser totalmente divertido, embora também tenha o modo online, bom para jogar com amigos, porque se você não tiver amigos para jogar numa party, dificilmente vai achar alguem sozinho nos servidores, porque o jogo está praticamente sem ninguém jogando os modos onlines. Se tiver interesse no jogo, pode comprar que não irá se arrepender, mas não tenha a intenção de jogar online, a menos que já tenha amigos para isso.
Torchlight 2 tem um mundo gigantesco para ser explorado, com milhares de missões primárias e outras toneladas de missões secundárias. A ação é muito frenética com MUITOS inimigos dentro do mapa, não só nas INSTANCES. Dificilmente irá achar apenas um monstro numa area do mapa, você irá achar muitos e a matança, nesse caso, é frenética.
Por fim, o que se espera de um verdadeiro jogo de RPG? Muito conteúdo de personalização? Torchlight 2 tem! Classes de personagens criativas? Confere também! Milhares de itens e sets? Torchlight 2 também tem!
Cara, esse jogo é perfeito. Tá esperando o que pra fazer a melhor aquisição de um jogo RPG da sua vida? Você vai ficar extremamente viciado. Embora eu tenha poucas horas aqui no jogo da steam, acho que já tenho mais de 200 horas no pirata, (fora da steam, quando jogava a uns aninhos atrás).
Esse jogo, é o jogo que de todos os outros que ja joguei, é o que mais recomendo. Garanto pra você que se comprar, não vai querer sair desse mundo nunca mais. Vale comprar em toda época do ano, com promoção, sem promoção, dar de presente pros amigos, não importa, o que vale é expandir esse jogo pra todo mundo. Garanto que o investimento gasto nesse game, tanto para si mesmo como para presentear alguém, será muito bem feito.

Whoa. I know it's cliched to start a review like that, but... whoa. I grabbed the game about a day ago, after hearing high recommendations from the likes of certain youtube celebrities in the gaming circle (TB, primarily, among others), and wow...
I've just cleared the game for the first time, on Normal. It was my third attempt, and I almost died multiple times.. however, I know why I cleared it. If you've played any of the Souls games or any game that seems incredibly simplistic but has a lot of depth behind it, you know what I'm talking about--I went into the zone. This game has the tightest FPS controls that I've seen since the original Doom, and I do not say that lightly.
So, if you ever wanted to play a modern-day randomized version of a game like Doom, with elements of Hexen or Heretic (magic, alchemical weapons, magic staves, multiple characters.. you get the gist), give it a go. Very, very few games can completely shut off my mind and allow me to just zone out and focus to where there's only me, and the game, and Ziggurat has accomplished this feat.
Highly recommended, at full price; a MUST BUY at discount price, and a WHY DON'T YOU HAVE THIS YET! at a massive discount price (70% and higher)
Give it a go if you like tight FPS gameplay, and if Lichdom: Battlemage didn't really do it for you. I understand the randomization of a rogue-lite game is not everyone's cup of tea, but I advise giving it a go, if only for the great weapons, controls, and the fact that weapons actually have some punch to them. The game's significantly shorter than the aforementioned Lichdom: Battlemage, but if you play this in one or two hour bursts, it's sure to create many hours of enjoyment.. and frustration as you die on the final boss. Mwa-ha-ha.

Now this here is a fun one.
Taking a few hints from good old Rogue, Ziggurat is, at its core, a first person shooter with roguelike elements like random map generation, permadeath and such.
It is a good looker, colourful, vibrant, often with dozens of enemies and fancy particle effects at the same time. The gameplay is where it shines, though.
Avoiding the trappings of many other 'roguelites', Ziggurat gives you satisfying combat with absolutely massive weapon variety. You start with a modest pool of arcane implements which only grows larger with each completed dungeon run, no matter the outcome. All of these weapons behave in different ways, feature two firing modes and draw on one of three pools of 'mana' for their ammo, save for your starting Magic Wand, the ammo of which regenrates.
The bestiary is just as varied, with several dozens of enemies and bosses of all sizes. Basilisks, orc-like brutes, living armours throwing grenades, banshees, floating skulls, slimes, killer mushrooms... if you can think of it, Ziggurat probably has a variation of it.
You delve in, you collect your weapons, gain experience to unlock perks and then, you probably die. A vicious, endlessly entertaining cycle that is sure to keep you saying 'Just one more run' for many hours. Definitely pick this one up!

I like this game. I truly do. However, right now I wouldn't recommend it simply for one reason: the grind. Money was, is, and will be one of the fundamental parts of any GTA or open world game to this day, and R* understands it. And lately, they've been exploiting it like never before - right about after the Ill Gotten Gains II came out, they realized they can suck the extra cash out of people via Shark Cards (microstransactions), and be a big earner for Take-Two and themselves, which they are, by the way. This has gone from integrating overpriced clothes and cars to messing up the game's logic itself. It's especially notable in the three major updates - the CEO update, the Biker update, and the I/E update. The three of them are the most profitable businesses in the game, netting you only about 240.000$ an hour, 380.000$ at best, which might seem good, but the amount of grinding, and the prices (300.000 for a muscle car) make you want more and more, and those who don't have enough time to grind are forced into paying for Shark Cards, which at most will net you 8.000.00 GTA$ at a price of 100 USD. And as if that wasn't bad enough, the multiple ways to earn big money like CEO/MC/I/E are cut tremendously short. For instance, apparently 500g of coke, which in the USA is worth on average 30.000$ (60$ a gram), is now worth just 30$, considering the ridiculous pricing in the Bikers DLC. Or stealing 2.000.000$ cars, and then selling them on the blackmarket for a measly 80.000$. Or even in the CEO update, where you traffick contraband, you can only buy as much as 3 crates at a time, and something always goes wrong or you have to do some task to get the damn things. So much pain, but it can be resolved with Shark Cards. Besides, the community is trash, and the game is halfway dead by now. A few words about the singleplayer - it's a great experience, the story is great (albeit with a lot of ridiculous stuff), the freedom is there, and everything is in place. Except for stuff from GTAO that's not even added, and the fact that R* treats SP like the first kid who's worse than the other.

I've been wanting to write a review for LotRO for a long time, but every time I attempt it, I find that I cannot do the game justice. Nonetheless, I love it enough that I owe it one.
I have played LotRO since 2007, and save a few hiatuses, I still play to this day. With that much history, I am sorely tempted to go into a long-winded tirade about all of my experiences with this game, how I feel about all of the changes it has endured, and share my thoughts about how it ended up where it is today. It is difficult at times to get across your point and enthuisasm without including the aforementioned. However, as this is meant to be a review and not a novel, I will attempt to refrain from that and keep my focus on the point.
LotRO is a very story-based and driven game, as you might expect from an MMO derived from Tolkien's works. While it does have the common fetch-and-kill quests and sometimes redundant feeling tasks that you'll find in every MMO, by and large the quests are compelling and fulfilling. This is especially true of the Epic quests, which deal with the members of the Fellowship of the Ring and their actions. The world is expansive and highly immersive, and there is adventure to be had everywhere, in many different forms. With a few exceptions, the development team is incredibly loyal to and respective of Tolkien's writings and based the landscape and heart of Middle Earth off of the books, not the Peter Jackson movies. You will not find another game, anywhere, that has as much love for Tolkien’s works as the Lord of the Rings Online. It felt warm and grand when I first started, and it still does today.
That being said, LotRO has been around for a very long time. It has numerous bugs and suffers from issues you might expect from a game of its age. Speaking strictly in terms of MMOs, it does not have the end game content or high numbers of raids that you might be looking for or expect. It is limited in what it can implement for mechanics and flashy gameplay; It runs on an engine built in 2002, originally used on Asheron's Call 2. It has numerous bugs and flaws that continue to harry it despite attempted fixes and updates. Those who feel so inclined can purchase many perks and advantages through the in-game store, which is obnoxious in its attempts to get you to notice and use it. Its population has waned in recent years, as have the resources devoted to it. Likewise, its focus on group play has lessened. Essentially, if you are looking for the more common focuses of MMOs these days, meaning lots of raiding, end game and group content, PvP, top of the line graphics, flashy gameplay, etc, you will not find that here in levels that will satisfy you.
Nonetheless, the game looks impressive - running it on high graphics, it hides its age extremely well. The community remains one of the friendliest and most helpful to be found in MMOs, and whether you enjoy RP or not, there are plenty of tools and resources available to cater to both casual and extreme role-players. There exists plenty of humor and easter eggs hidden around for casual players or huge Tolkien nerds to find.
To steal a quote from a blog I read recently, "It has a heart and soul that very few games can boast of having, and those looking only at the graphics, technicalities and the gameplay to judge an MMO won’t be able to appreciate its true worth, ever. LotRO is not a trendy game, possibly never will be, and it’s most likely better for it. .... we fans get to have a game that is worthy of Tolkien’s work, despite any and all flaws."
And there you have it. If you're looking for story and exploration, love Tolkien's works, or want a friendly and reasonably casual MMO to tinker around with, LotRO is an amazing choice. Despite all of its flaws, it is a gem amongst games, and is the most faithful and successful attempt at visualizing Tolkien's world. I have, would, and will strongly recommend it to anyone who is a fan of Tolkien in any way.

At face value, Ziggurat seemed poised to itch every gaming screath I had at the moment, so I took the 15 dollar plunge.  What can be said of this game?  It is VERY polished in it's visuals, art direction, and scoring.  The landscapes can be alittle overwhelming at time and setting your FOV to at least 95 is a must or you will likely be overcome in the swarm of ravenous, power A.I.-driven creatures in the Ziguarat.  Some would call Ziggurat UNFORGIVING, and they would be correct: death is, for the most part, permanent and you will lose all previous spoils after failing no matter how many levels you have descended.  The frequency of death, I find can be attributed to an abbundance of enemies that must be defeated in a circle strafe fashion with little to no cover to be seen.  What may come across as poor design to some will be a worthwile experience to any dungeon crawler, rogue-like fan (like myself).  I recommend but only if that sounds like something you're in to.

Bulls#$%. Fake. Difficulty.
I hate it in games. It makes things harder, not by being challenging or clever, but by pulling every cheap, irritating trick possible. Dead space 2 is loaded with the stuff, and it angers me more because I enjoyed the first game so much. Once in a great while, Dead Space 1 would pull something like a monster attacking me just as I left a save point. I'd be startled and think, 'Oh, you goofy guys! Ya got me!'
But when something like that happens SO OFTEN in Dead Space 2, I began to EXPECT to be attacked pretty much any time I was asked to concentrate on moving an item, hacking a lock, or repairing a macguffin. It's not scary. It's not even startling anymore. There's just the cringe of anticipation, the monster pops up, you kill it, then get back to the stupid puzzle you gotta solve so you can move onto the next room with another stupid puzzle and another jack-in-the-box monster.
Worst of all? The enemies are magic and scouting is useless. Meaning, you can visually verify that a room is empty, and enemies will still spawn in. You can back yourself in a corner, and enemies will somehow spawn behind you. You can come from a room that was completely sealed, and enemies will STILL spawn behind you. To the best of my memory, the first game did not do this. Enemies would jump out at you from hiding spots, but once you killed them off, they didn't keep on reappearing just because the room wasn't finished being difficult.
Perfect example: I fought my way through two red rooms that had no less than six enemies spawn in as soon as I turned a corner. Then, at the end of this, there was a LARGE, OPEN, COMPLETELY EMPTY room with a hacking minigame in it. I knew exactly what would happen. Soon as I started the minigame, I was bashed out of it by a gigantic monster that had somehow entered the completely empty room behind me without making a sound.
BULLS#$%. FAKE. DIFFICULTY.
Maybe if I'd just played DS2 by itself I wouldn't be as disgusted with it. But I just finished DS1 a few days ago and wrote a glowing review. Specifically, I mentioned DS1's immersion. The ship felt like a real ship that existed in physically-possible dimensions. DS2 is simply a long line from start to end. I thought the linearity would just be for the opening chapters until the familiar gameplay kicked in. Nope! Whereas in the first game, each chapter felt like you were accomplishing something, in DS2, all you're doing is scampering around trying to find someone who'll tell you what the hell is going on. It felt for half the game like I was just waiting to get to the part that mattered. And the blatantly-impossible monster spawns further broke any illusion that I was playing in a real world that existed. I wasn't seeing a space station orbiting Saturn: I was seeing a bunch of game devs setting up the next prank-like 'screw you' for the player. I stopped caring about anything that happened and finished the game only to be able to say I didn't quit.
Though to be fair, let me list some positives: Graphics are better. The suits look great. The mall and daycare were visually-interesting designs. I loved the part with the drill machine. All of the zero-G sections were great and much-improved from the first game. And, to my pleasant surprise, there is a character who I grew to truly hate over time, and the game eventually let me murder the living daylights out of them. A small moment of catharsis. Nice.
Overall though, Dead Space 2 is like any number of bad movie sequels. It tries to be better by throwing more action and danger at the story, but utterly fails to spend time appreciating the subtle things that made the first one work.
If one of the best parts of your game is when you basically just replay the original for a few levels, you've screwed up.

Dead Space 2 is a gigantic, flying leap over Dead Space 1 in many ways.

Too much action: The unfortunate side of things is that DSII is rarely scary. While DSI wasn't too scary either, it at least tried. DSII is full on action from start to finish, like Alien to Aliens. However, the truly spooky parts, like the first encounter with the stalkers in the church or the appearance of an old pal from DSI towards the end of the game are very memorable. It's a shame that the relentless action kinda ruins the atmosphere, because the creepy atmosphere in many locations can make your skin crawl.
Overall: An excellent action horror experience- by cutting off the fluff and refining the core of Dead Space combat, a truly great game was made. A classic everyone should try.

Generally I really like this game!
It combines the good aspects of Hearthstone with new, refreshing elements. And hopefully will never harm itself with the implementation of a "Wild" format. It also has a co-op mode, which is a great idea.
BUT. There is a big problem about the current balancing in this game. I look at 2 classes here. One of which is underpowered and the other one WAY too overpowered.
In a game that is inspired by Hearthstone and that has similar cards with similar stats, you should assume that the dev team knows about Hearthstone and its meta. So should they know that Hearthstones "Face Hunter" nearly always was amongst Top Tier, especially on the ladder. The Face Hunter often was on the boarder to "game breaking" and during some meta took away a lot of the fun. Because he easily outpaces slower decks with no thinking.
The Shapeshifter is Fable Fortunes version of the Face Hunter. BUT it is even vastly more powerful. Why?
I do not know why the Game Designer decided to take a Hunter as a base and then add some powerful spells from the Mage and Warlock.
What I am talking about?
Mage
Fireball, cost 4, deal 6 damage - Ambush, cost 3, deal 4 damage
Frost Nova, cost 3, Freeze all enemy units - Howl of Despair, cost 3, stun all enemy units
Warlock
Hellfire, cost 4, deal 3 damage to all characters - Surge of Fangs, cost 6, deal 4 damage to all units
Drain Life, cost 3, deal 2 damage. Restore 2 health to your hero - Snarling Lunge, cost 3, deal 4 damage to your opponent and heal your hero for 4.
Warrior
Battle Rage, cost 2, draw a card for each damaged friendly character - Blood Frenzy, cost 3, draw a card for each damaged enemy
Generally I like the idea to copy a good system and refresh it with new ideas. But the Shapeshifter should be rebalanced. Its cards are too perfectly synergistic for an aggressive playstile and do not require to make deeper decisions. Or at least the other classes should have more options to protect themselves. More units with guard that have more than 4 health.
The general "strategy" of this deck is to first rush your opponent down with good value minions. Very rarely go for trades and mostly do not care about your opponents units. If you have dealt enough damage with your low cost units your opponent will usually start placing expensive but strong units. But guess what? You have strong removal spells. Dish out that 8 damage for just 5 gold that will kill nearly every unit. Or stall out the game with cards like Howl of Despair, Stunning Slash, or Brown Bear. It doesn't matter how strong the enemy units will be. You will stun or kill them and then just go for the face. Kill or silence the single enemy unit that will have guard every turn and hit that face. If your opponent manages to kill your units then just wait and draw cards with Blood Frenzy until you draw your 4-damage spells and just kill your opponent from your hand. And do not forget to dish out 2 damage every turn from your heroes ability.
How the class was designed:
- We want a wild and aggressive class that has some good value early game units. We want them to soak up every unit below 3 attack, without consequences. Because Balverines are very evil and just like to eat other units.
- We want that units to survive and go for the face. So we pack in some strong removal spells to kill that strong enemy guards.
- In case that the enemy has too many or too strong units the Shapeshifter will need some defensive abilities. Stun is a good idea. So unit trades can be avoided what makes the units survive even longer so they can focus on that ugly face.
- Did we tell yet, that we really worry about the Shapeshifter not having units? If they somehow die we want the class to be able to draw new units or to finish the game with drawing enough damage dealing spells. Or to just kill the enemy units. We intend to let the Shapeshifter be the only class with units on the board. So the Shapeshifter will be blessed with card draw.
- Speaking of damage dealing spells, the class should have enough of them. In case that there will be a miracle of stopping its units from going to the face.
- And just to make absolutely sure that the class will be viable we should also add some selfheal. Just in case if some of the other slow classes manage to rush the Shapeshifter down he should be able to sustain until he draws enough spells to win.
Wow! We created our new favourite class! Maybe we will see the need to buff some of its weak cards, or add in some unit heals. We really worry about that units.
In the next patch we will rename the Hero League into "Shapeshifter League". That sounds cool.
Okay I will stop being sarcastic and instead try to make some suggestions. I understand and like the idea of the Shapeshifter being a dark natured thing with evil creatures.
Balverines
I like the idea that the Balverines regain health for destroying enemy units. But 2 seems just too high. The basic 4/3 Balverine will survive ANY attack below 3. That means he is the ultimative early game guard, with an attack of 4 and a low cost of 3. The same thing with the 5/5 one.
Suggestion: Reduce the heal to 1.
Howl of Despair
Please just return this card to one of the classes to whose it belongs. Alchemist or Prophet. The Shapeshifter does not need this defense.
Mortal Wound
8 unit damage for 5 gold seems a bit generous. That is 1,6 damage for each point of gold spent, where units mostly have 1 point of health per gold.
Suggestion: Either reduce the damage dealt to 7, make it 6 damage with cost of 4, or add a little negative side effect. Something like an additional damage to the own hero. Or 1 damage to all friendly units. That would highlight the sheer beasty nature of the class and of the card. And it would add decisions to the class. Not just pure damage.
Blood Frenzy
The class desperately needing this card is the Knight. It is designed around summoning cheap but weak units to make them stronger later on. The problem with this is that the Knight will run out of hand cards soon and it is draw-luck dependend. The 1/1 of its class ability will help to damage enemy units to make Blood Frenzy efficient.
Speaking of the Knight. For me it is the weakest of the classes.
The main problem is that some of its cards do not synergise well and the whole playstile with the current classes card set makes him draw-luck depending. Summoning cheap units and buffing them either by entering the field or later on is the goal. The problem is that the cards need to be drawn in the right order. For example, when focusing on 1 strength units, having the Veteran battler early on is a must. But he just has 3 health, which makes him leave the board soon. And if that happens many of the 1 strenght units in the deck will.. well, just have 1 strenght.
Veteran Battler
The main problem of this card is that it is too slow and too risky. It can be summoned on turn 2, but its ability has no use yet. With its low 3 health it has low chances to survive until turn 3. If the Veteran Battler survives until turn 3 the Knight will be able to buff about 1 or 2 units. But there is high risk and low reward for this. High risk because for 4 gold 3/3 is weak. Low reward because the added +2/+1 is what a 4 cost card would have for free (5/4), without waiting 1 turn and hoping for it to survive. Yes there is a chance to have an army of 3/X from this card, but it is not going to happen on many matches.
Suggestion: Increase its health to 5 and/or reduce its cost. It should buff units with a BASE strenght of 1. Otherwise it has a conflict with Muster.
Selfe Defence Training
As it is now, it is highly anti-synergistic with the Veteran Battler and many buffs in general. Selfe Defence Training will be a dead card after buffing 1 strenght units.
Suggestion: It should give deflect to all friendly units with a BASE strenght of 1.
I will adapt my review to future patches. For now I reached the wordlimit

I grew up with Fable: TLC, thus I adore the Fable universe. That being said, I can't recommend this game at its current state.
PROS:
- Unique-ish good cartoony visual style (even though I am not a big fan of it)
- A few good game concepts (morality and team-mode).
CONS:
- Majority of the game seems to be a Hearthstone cash-grab copy. Fable Fortunes has very few unique selling points compared to Hearthstone. Should have more unique aspects.
- The Morality system seems rather bland, although it is a super cool concept. Playing with the Shapeshifter class, I can choose the same Morality rewards 3 times, meaning I can switch my hero power on 3 different occasions, but always have to choose between the same hero powers. Why? There is no incentive to switch the hero powers. I am just completing the Morality quest three times, while the quests are also exactly the same. Feels like I am repeating the same action for three times for no other reason than to activate some (Morality:3) card abilities. I just wish there was some more depth to the morality system. Maybe I could upgrade my hero power, so for example my Shapeshifter with 3 Evil Moralities has some ultimate vampire-like hero power ors.
- A lot of the cards are straight ripped from Hearthstone (Banshee vs Doomsayer; Hobbes vs Murlocs; Caravan Leader vs Say-Hello-To-My-Little-Friend-card, etc.). I know that those cards and themes are so good that I would like to have them in every game, but since Fable Fortunes and Hearthstone are the most direct competitors among digital CCGs (gameplay and art-style in mind), the cards in Fable feel really uncreative. Changing the mana cost is not enough...The cards in Fable could host the same effects as their counterparts in Hearthstone but also include Fable-exclusive twists, which they currently lack.
- The UX/UI is horrible. Aside from every animations taking far too long, in the game I have no idea about: cards and the amount of cards in the graveyard, the amount of cards in my deck. In addition to that, almost at all times the visual clutter is just overwhelming. I tried showing this game to my friend and he instantly became cross-eyed and had a seizure. Jokes aside, this game also favours flavour-over-functionality (similar to HS), but the UI functionality is even lower.
- New Player experience. I have played HS over 2 years, I have no issue getting to rank 5 - I don't consider myself a rookie. In Fable Fortunes, I have trouble finishing the Shapeshifters last Solo match because: 1) AI is spamming 2-3 cards per turn (out of a pool of 5 different cards. wow), 2) I have 1 board clear spell in my collection. 1 board clear. 1.... I can't find any PVP matches in the span of 5 or sometimes even 10 minutes. Understandable. But to compensate that, the game should somehow boost the Single Player experience. More common cards, a larger variety on SP opponents.
TL;DR
3,5/10 - I want to love this game, however it has given me few reasons to do so.
If you like Hearthstone I'd recommend this it same and so much nicer to you if you don't buy money! Also has some fun unique mechanics such as morality and cards that change based on good and evil.

As most I started playing the game when it went free to play. I was very interested in playing an mmo in the universe created by Tolkien. At first the game may not seem attractive due to the outdated graphics, the clunky combat and the somewhat repetitive questing.
However, if you invest a good amount of time to understand it the game starts showing its jewels. As you progress through the areas you will feel your character getting stronger, becoming a seasoned warrior whose path is tied with that of the Fellowship. The main story line not only lets you experience the Lord of the Rings trilogy to its depth but also gives you an insight on secondary plotlines that were in the background of both the books and the movies.
A major advantage of the game is that it literally lets you get every part of the premium content by grinding. You can get every expansion, dungeon, skirmish e.t.c. by doing the abundant deeds spread out through all the areas. I have never seen something similar in other similar MMOs. Another great aspect of the game which adds to its immersion is the community. Everyone is very helpful to each other, bad game practices are non-existant making you feel like a member of a large fellowship.
Overall, I believe people who like me are fans of the universe Tolkien created would adore this game as its huge content lets you experience the history of the books as if you were there.

All in all, a very light-hearted, entertaining, casual game, for when you have to blast stuff away and have a good time with a moderate challenge.
