Plays like a reimagined version of Heretic or Hexen, and pays homageto that particular genre and era of gaming. Every playthrough is different, with the powerups, weapons, enemies, and rooms being randomized every time you start a new game. It can be frustrating and difficult, but not so much so that one quits playing. Definitely give it a try if you're a fan of first-person dungeon crawlers or some of the old DOS shooters.

Ziggurat is a magic themed first person shooter with roguelike elements. You are a wizard and your goal is to fight through a dungeon one floor at a time, find each floor's portal key, summon and defeat the boss, and progress to the next floor. Each floor has a random layout, and there is permadeath, so every time you die, you're back to the start of the first floor.
The FPS mechanics are great - fast movement, responsive aiming. There's no regenerating health, instead you need to find potions or make use of some other magical abilities. There are four different weapon classes - wand, spell, staff and arcane. Each class contains multiple weapons but you can only carry one of each at a time. Most weapons are direct fire projectiles, but some have special functions such as grenades, spread shots, and poison damage over time.
There is a wide variety of enemy types, from skeletons and mages to killer carrots, weird plant things and those annoying floating skulls from Doom. They have a mixture of melee and ranged attacks, and some have special abilities such as summoning minions, invisibility or firing homing projectiles.
The environment itself can be a danger too. You'll encounter various trap rooms - fireballs, spinning blades, lava pits, floor spikes. Some fight rooms have special rules such as increased or decreased damage or movement speed, enemies spawn in pairs or enemies release a poisonous cloud on death. And you can gamble health or mana at shrines - hopefully you'll get an ability upgrade, but you might suffer a downgrade.
Every time you level up you can choose one of two randomly selected upgrades, and every completed playthrough - success or failure - unlocks more that are available to choose in future playthroughs. There are the usual increased health/mana/weapon damage but also more creative ones such as do more damage when below 25% health or regain health by breaking crates.
Its a short game - there are only 5 floors and my successful playthrough took just over an hour - but there are 12 unlockable characters to play as with different strengths and weaknesses, and 3 difficulty levels plus an endless mode, so there is some replayability.
Much of the game is based on random luck - which weapons you find, which upgrades you get at level up, will you receive a positive or negative if you choose to gamble at a shrine - but I don't feel like the game is actively trying to screw me over. It feels fair, and I feel like my FPS skills can help me survive most bad situations, which in turn makes the game fun to play.
I haven't noticed any bugs. Controls are mostly rebindable, however you can't bind anything to middle mouse which is my standard jump key in pretty much every FPS, so the trap rooms that require navigating platforms feel a bit unnatural.
Overall Ziggurat is a pretty good game, and I'd definitely recommend it if you're a fan of either FPSes or roguelikes. I think there's enough content here to justify a full price purchase, which is already quite cheap.

For fans of stereoscopic 3D gaming, this game is a must-buy.  There are many games which look fantastic in Nvidia 3d Vision, but the Trine games (especially 2 and 3) are so good as to be useful for modeling the technology, in my opinion.  Furthermore, unlike many games that work well in 3D Vision and nothing else, the Trine games have additional 3D modes to make the game compatible with pretty much any stereoscopic setup you have.  If you have a modern 3D TV and choose to play this game in 2D, you are doing yourself a serious disservice.  Get an extra-long hdmi cable, if you have to, and attach your computer to your TV!  (Or invest in a 3D Vision setup, if you are a fan of stereoscopic 3D movies and games.)
The game is oodles of fun with a friend, in both local and internet co-op, with the difference being that the two characters must share a screen for local co-op; netplay has no such limitation, and you can get separated if you are not careful.  That said, I recommend the latter for those who have both options available to then.
Sadly, the game has its share of internet MP bugginess, worse than the first game did (but not as bad as the third).  It was so bad that my friend and I (with him in America and me in Japan, both of us with excellent internet connections) were not able to complete the DLC's final boss, which is arguably broken for multiplayer (possibly local MP as well, given the way the boss spazzes out and gets confused when more than one target is available).  So while I must shake my finger at Frozenbyte for not play-testing and bug-proofing the multiplayer more, I cannot in good conscious give this anything other than a thumbs-up, for its combination of appealing platforming, charming characters and voice acting, and jaw-droppingly gorgeous visuals, which really must be viewed in stereoscopic 3D to be fully appreciated.
Artistic Value: 9.5
Fun Factor: 8 (probably lower while playing solo and/or in 2D)
My Score: 8.5

Very tough to offer something that's going to stand up to Hearthstone or even Magic, but there's a huge amount to recommend Fortune.
The heroes have a real sense of personality to them, and being able to evolve them down the good/evil path as you play to unlock different abilities that allow you to adapt to how your opponent is playing is just a really strong and well implemented feature. It's genuinely lovely and done with a sense of charm and humour. It IS cool to take your Red Riding Hood style hero and turn her into a werewolf partway through the game to life-steal your way to victory.
You don't have to love Fable to enjoy the game - but if you are a fan then it's sincerely gratifying to see how respectfully and well done the application of the Fable universe is to the look, feel and good/evil aspects of the game.
It's a quality game and feels like it's been made with real care - early days now, but there's everything going for it.

Absolutely love the Fable series and was extremely excited when I found out about this game. I am not a super hardcore card game player, but so far I love this, it is unique, fun and challeging, and it is designed super well, plus, it's a new Fable game!

Recieved a closed beta key a while ago and i've been around long enough to see the game start to take shape. I haven't played a whole lot yet but from what I have played I've come up with a little pros/cons list. Ultimately I would recommend the game if you enjoy TCG type of games but wanted something a little more in depth than Hearthstone but a little easier than Magic the Gathering. Also I never did try PVP, I wanted to focus more on the co-op aspect of the game.
Pros:
-The game feels like something fresh. It may not be paving the way for a brand new genre, but being able to put guard on one of your creatures each turn is actually pretty neat. I can put guard on a 1/1 so I can protect my higher damaging cards like a 2/2 or a 3/5 or something from being attacked by the enemies creature. Or I can put it on my higher damaging card to ensure that if my opponant wants to attack me with all of their 1/1s they will all die at the cost of my 3/3 creature.
-Two player Co-op is in the game. I'm a HUGE fan of being able to play card games cooperatively, especially in games where you can buy extra cards/packs so if you go into PVP you're almost guaranteed to find a lot of the same deck types with the same ultra-powerful cards.
-Nostalgia is pretty prominant in this game if you played the Fable series. The Balverine howl is one I was tickled to hear.
Neutral:
-The card animations aren't amazing, but they aren't terrible. This is something that is currently being worked on.
-Voice Overs are basically the same. Not amazing, not bad.
Cons:
-playing Co-op with a stranger can be difficult. Not only to find a match, but because there isn't a lot of ways to communicate (That I found). You can right click to put a "!" mark over cards to sort of point someone in the direction of what you are thinking. But the game lacks any sort of "Sorry, Good job, Attack creatures, Attack heroes," type of chat. I think it would work well if similar to hearthstone I could press a button to have my hero say "My bad" or something.
-The game does have quite a few loading times.
-The game lacks any kind of in depth tutorial or even reference guide to what card abilities do.  It took me forever to understand what "morality" meant. Again it could be there somewhere, but I didn't find it.
Ultimately I would recommend trying out this game. If you'ree a die-hard TCG fan see what you think of it now. Otherwise maybe wait for it to come out of early access.

Seriously, I don't quite understand all the hate this game has received. It may not  be perfect (which game is?), but I find it at least as enjoyable as DX:HR. The plot is alright, building on the prequel and depicting the road from the Golden Age of humanity to the crapsack anti-utopia of the original game - though your choices have little impact on how it progresses this time. Adam is still as badass as ever and a nice player character overall; the new characters may be underdeveloped a bit, but fit nicely into the narration. Both the visuals and music are impressive (though the original Deus Ex remains my favorite in the music department), the gameplay is immersive and challenging enough if you opt to play on the highest difficulty and stick to the stealth style.  I do agree the game has its fair share of drawbacks: it's short, the plot ends in a rather abrupt manner (and we're not even sure we'll be getting a sequel to see the story end), the AI feel really stupid at times. But I still recommend the game, especially if you can grab it for a discounted price. 8/10.

9/10: Adam Jensen is a invisible sneaking, Illuminati fighting, computer hacking machine! Load up on Biocells and they'll never know what hit them.
Since this is the sequel to Human Revolution, it's no surprise that the game starts off by going over how the last game ended: everyone with sweet cyborg parts went crazy one day and people without sweet cyborg parts are angry at them as a whole for the lives lost that day. So augmented people like Adam are treated pretty poorly in Prague, what with the segregated subway cars and some shops being "naturals only," and it just so happens that this is also where Adam's been working with TF29 for the last few months.
Things quickly get worse, and as per tradition, Adam Jensen is just the clandestine extra-government operative to turn invisible, hack into peoples computers, steal their passwords, information, weapons, money, and ammo before drinking every container of alcohol in the place on his path to uncover the Illuminati. The game feels a bit shorter than Human Revolution, probably because there's only one boss fight that itself is only okay. There's a set of newer abilities like my favorite, the Tesla Fist, but you still have to relearn most of the original ones. You can always count on turning invisible and keeping a supply of Biocells ready, but if you'd rather gun down the opposition there's plenty of weapons.
Admittedly, I'm not a fan of these inventory grids at this point, having been spoiled by Bethesda games and their infinite containers. You can sell the guns for a decent price, especially shotguns, but the stores are only available while in Prague. You can be break the game up into 6 parts, alternating between Prague and one-shot areas, so it plays like a linear narrative that returns to a hub often. There's a good number of choices you can make throughout the game that affect different people and even some of the news reports at the end, but don't expect anything like the quartet of choices posed right at the end of Human Revolution.
Breach mode takes most of the controls and some of the abilities from the game but gives it that Tron-style neon techno look to justify the premise of this being how hackers acquire data from corporate data havens. It's got style, but it's a pretty apparent adaptation of the core game to create a free-to-play online mode.
Also, don't worry about the Triangle codes unless you feel like paying for an app in order to redeem them. Otherwise, have fun taking oblivious people out while contemplating the ethical and moral quandaries surrounding human augmentation.

The gameplay, dialogue, graphics, weapons and augmentations are all better than ever and while many seem disappointed by how abrupt the ending is, just know that it's not. The fact that (no spoilers btw) the ending isn't structured in the same way as the other games in the series are (4 obvious and starkly different endings to choose from) every main and side mission you do affects the ending, giving you more possible endings than before. And although the worldwide conspiracy continues you do spend more time in Prague than in other locations so the game feels smaller and appears to end more quickly but trust me, it doesn't. Torchlight 2, where to begin? If you played the Diablo franchise, or just a hardcore fan of ARPG's with insane loot/oldschool then this is for you. Torchlight 2 is an ARPG that you really can't go wrong with. No matter the reason you play or the experience you hope to obtain from it, Torchlight 2 caters to every type of RPG genre gamer to a varying degree.  Open world, Insane loot, 4 distinct classes, basic classic typical ARPG features that every ARPG player is comfortable with, etc, etc... The list could go on and on, however it's not for everyone. Take into consideration the kind of gamer you are and past experience with ARPG's or the lack thereof. Depending on your response to that last statement it will determine how much time is ideally required to be invested to ascertain if Torchlight 2 is really for you or not. Torchlight 2 is a VERY time consuming game, lots of grinding and farming and so forth as any other traditional ARPG of the genre entails. If you are a fan of RPG's or ARPG's, a casual gamer, or whatever the reason behind playing it might be it's certainly worth giving a chance. Also the price tag and steam sales where it often can be purchased for next to nothing definitely justify if nothing less giving it a try.

Ziggurat....Awesome game!
Graphics (9/10):
Although the graphics are a bit out dated and a little cartoony, it really gives the game a fantastic atmosphere.
Sound/Music (8/10):
While the music does seem to be one or two tracks the play through out the entire game, it doesn't really get to annoying or bothersome. Adds a little bit of character to the feel of the tower as your traverse through its dangerous halls and rooms.
Gameplay/Challenge (9.5/10):
Ziggurat deffinitely does not pull any punches when it comes to challenge. The random layouts to each floor gives a unique gameplay each time you start a new game along with the randomness of the weapons you find through out the game. Each battle room gives a unique challenge as well with some rooms giving you a random modifier during the fights. Some rooms become even more challenging from reducing the amount of damage you do with specific weapons to increasing the amount of damage the mobs do.
Boss fights for each floor can be quite a challenge, especially when you don't have the right weapons or skills fromt he random perk you pick when you level up.
Replay Value (10/10):
As I said before, each time you start a new game, it is a different experience. As you lay through the game you unlock more perks, weapons and can unlock more characters with different skill weaknesses and strenghs. You will play through the game several times before you have the right perks and weapons to complete the game. But the challenge doesn't end there, once you complete the game with one character you unlock the ability to challenge the endless dungeon mode with that character.
Overall Score (9.5/10):
Overall, if you make one purchase for a random dungeon FPS, this game is well worth the money with the endless replay value and challenge through out. I recommend this game for anyone looking for a cheap game with a high challenge and replay value.

I was "gifted" this game ... Saying that Zombie Zoeds is a bad game is an understatement. The game starts in a horribly low resolution (something close to 800x600 (EDIT: It's actually 640x480)) but this is not a problem since the game is ugly anyway.
The game itself is a twin-stick shooter where you must kill zombies and try to reach the highest score.  Well, "twin stick shooter" ... sort of. You can only aim in the direction where you're moving, meaning that you'll need to stop and rotate if you want to shoot anything in this game, making the game extremely difficult.
Almost everything is bugged: When you start a game, if you go down you'll reach an area where your framerate will decrease to 1 FPS. If you then try to go left, you'll be able to go out of bounds and you'll be stuck there forever. There is no notion of height or depth in this game, meaning that you cannot go under the trees (you'll collide with the leafs). Speaking of the trees, the zombies will often get stuck into them,
You'll also notice if you go up starting from the spawn that the menu of the game is actually a part of the map: You can see the "New Game, Loading and EXIT" writings on the ground. An absolute joke
There is an "Evacuation Zone" but it doesn't do anything. (EDIT: You can actually bring civilians to the evacuation zone for points)
You have 3 basics weapons, the first one having 3 different fire modes: Don't get fooled, there is no point swapping between each as it changes only the fire rate and you'll only use the third one (fastest firing rate) anyway. I was unable to test the 2 other weapons, and I'm not even sure they can be used at all. I tried to fiddle with Cheat Engine to see if I could add ammo to them, and I managed to shoot once with each weapon, but it didn't do anything except play a laser sound.
The sound design is horrible: You'll hear a sound of crickets which is looped during the entire game. Fortuantely there is a button to mute it, which is probably the best feature of the game.
I could go on but I really don't want to waste more time on this game. I've seen student projects being much better than Zombie Zoeds. It's not even a bad game, it's a scam and should be removed from Steam.

With Laid back feel with easy to grasp mechanics, Fable Fortune truly embodies the spirit of previous Fable games. The cards are fun with tie ins from previous games (seeing Fabled cards like Reaver and Logan :D). Unlike most card games I've played, FF incentivises you to keep playing, to not get discouraged when you lose, by still awarding you nice rewards after a PVP loss. The rewards are even nicer if you win, of course :)
It's fun to play with friends, whether against each other or cooperatively and it's a lovely revitalization of the Fable community.

I reccomend this game to Fable and card games passionates. Fable Fortune adds to the classic card games mechanics a guard system that allows to select every turn wich one of yours units in play will taunt; there's a morality system that allows to upgrade your hero power once you complete a quest of your choice. The FTP aspect is well balanced and the grind is well rewarded.
The other big element  of the game is the coop mode. Personally this is the part I like more. Two players vs AI boss and 3 difficulty levels. This mode allows to test and develope deck building skills. I didn't find no others card games with this game mode.
If you like a mix of magic and witty atmosphere, experiment with mechanics and synergy and a game that gives you more than only the PVP as end game, you gonna enjoy Fable Fortune.

It captures the feel of Fable perfectly. I was very young when I played the first fable, I loved it a lot especially how your character changed appearance based on alignment, and some of the nifty rewards you got out of them. I never played fable 2 I did play the third. And I actually enjoyed it despite some other people not feeling the sameway. Anyway onto Fable Fortune.
As I said Fable Fortune captures fable perfectly. The music really sets the tone of fable right of the bat, a very mystical tune that goes between high and low settings. When I first played when the beta started there were only a few voices in the game, those that were there were very enjoyable to hear however. They fit the characters well and often had humour to them. They have added quite a lot of new ones since then.
Now for the gameplay. I think the gameplay has a positive spin on the card game genre. You start with 3 gold pieces from the start, second player starting with a trophy card that he has picked for his deck. The characters have very distinctive themes. Alchemist is very much a buffing character having a lot of potions to throw around for many situations. Whilst my personal favourite barter, the merchant character can build up wealth and play multiple high cost card in a turn.
Maps are different as well, to choose a alignment for your character which will change the effects of their hero power, and certain cards when played. You have to complete quests which differ per map. So its always good to tailor a deck towards the map you will be playing for a edge over your opponent.
Yes there are some bugs and issues to iron out. But I am sure they will be adressed in due time. I am glad they released it as a early access so more people get to partake in this generally fun card game.

The major issue of Balrum is that it's not designed to be fun.
I would say, only the crafting/farming might do that trick for some people; but the thing with farming is that it can become very much a boulder and force you to constanty take care of your plants/animals.
That's why I personnally stoped caring about those and just crafted the only needed items: Bread and Bow to get infinite resources and focus on the main reason I play the game: the rpg side.
But before jumping to storyline/quests design, I was also quite bored with the combat mechanics and archetypes.
There are 3 archetypes: Bowman, Magic caster and Warrior.
All of them utter boring. All you want is to use your 3 dps skills, and then use your stuns to refresh dps skills cooldown and sometimes heal yourself with what you got.
It is very static and quite not tactic, it's simply time consuming.
That's probably the game biggest flaw imo, there is no fun in creating your character when you understand the ropes, character evolution is utter boring and combat mechanics utter boring.
Then comes the quests, which are not bad, nothing particulary superb, but quite decent.
With the good idea that some of them can be solved in hidden ways.
Story line is also pretty enchanting, but very linear as you have only one way to progress in the story: the way you are told.
All in all, although its charms (which are there), the game is b.o.r.i.n.g.

I like comics, I like DC comics, and I like scribblenauts.   So this should be a natural fit.
It's not.  In fact out of four Scribblenauts games, played on PC, and DS, this is with out a doubt the worst one.  In fact I'd say this is the only one I'd call "bad."
The problem is this doesn't really isn't a different game than the original games.   There's challenges (that don't work well, such as only "female characters and adjectives" what ever that means.  So you can't create a shovel. because it's not a female character.)
The thing is a majority of the game is just random "missions" but unlike Scribblenauts Unlimited, the missions are actually random.  You just get 5 on the map, maybe a few more.  If you don't like them reset and you get new ones.  You aren't actually forced to do any quests.
Each quest will give you points once you have enough points you can unlock a new map, that comes with ONE major challenge, and just a new space for random missions.
The real issue I take with this game is the random missions.  The major challenge is the real story of the game and that's mostly about the DC characters.  The random missions though range.  I really don't have anything good to say about them.  A lot of them are fetch quests.  A few are fight quests, and a few are just "I need to dig a hole"  you attack the hole with a shovel and it's dug.   There's really no link to the DC universe for these missions, even the fight or fetch quest, might refer to a DC character, but most of the time, it's random person asking for random object.
It's a real shame, because the DC universe is really vast and this game shows it with it's wealth of possible characters you can name.  The down side, is the game rarely uses that universe, and seems to have under 20 really DC inspired quests, the rest of them are just ... side quests, and because you have to grind on them to get further in the story that's a really big bummer.  It's a shame, because Marvel or DC + Scribblenauts should be an easy marriage.  Lego marvel Superheroes is one of my favorite Lego games, and Lego Batman 2 is  just behind it and almost as good.
Scribblenauts Unmasked though doesn't take enough use of the license.  Hell if they just did the level of content and number of missions as Scribblenauts unlimited, I'd probably give this game a thumbs up (Even though that game bored me, I always felt like I was making meaningful progress).  This game doesn't feel like that, instead I feel like I'm just running on a bike to get a little more of what I want, while I slog through very boring gameplay.
A shame, but personally, I can't recommend this game.  Go check out Scribblenauts Unlimited if you want to play scribblenauts.  If you want to play with DC characters, both Injustice, and Lego Batman treat them right.  But Scribblenauts Unmasked is not the right game for anyone.  Even as a fan of both franchises, I can't enjoy this game except very superficially.  A shame, because this could have been the best yet.

Truly a powerhouse sequel to one of my favorite IPs. Dead Space (the original) was a great game, blending unique mechanics with a cool art style and aspects from Alien and Event Horizon. The Sims 3 is the Sims 4's older, and better cousin. Not only does it have years and years of extra content, it also has better features in the base game. If you plan to purcdhase the game, I'd recommend waiting for a steam sale, (I brought my copy for £6.25) as otherwise you are wasting your money. Another thing to mention, is the DLC. I have nothing wrong with the game's DLC, but some of it is just so, so bad. If you plan to purchase DLC, make sure you have made sure its what you want and its worht the money, as it can be hard to uninstall them and have the game keep working. Overall, I'd recommend it, as the positives and fun factor entirely outweighs the negatives, but then again, be warned, you may need some mods to make it run on your PC.

Positive:
-Good mechanics for what content there is.
-Mostly smooth functioning.
-Good use of colored lighting, which is often neglected nowadays.
-Very good sound / music for whats there.
-Mostly interesting room layouts that make for good fast paced FPS action.
Negative:
-I cant get past the art direction. Every enemy and pretty much every environment texture looks like it was pulled straight out of WoW, or that it would fit perfectly in it. It gives an otherwise potentially atmospheric and gruesome game a childish, out-of-character cartoony vibe.
-Essentially no environmental interaction. No "use" button, for instance, because there is nothing to use. No switches, no mechanisms, etc.
-Essentially puzzleless. "Puzzles" consist of jumping onto moving platforms, which there is nothing inherently wrong with, but its not enough all by itself.
-Weaponry is not differentiated enough. In addition, almost all secondary attack modes for weapons just launch a volley of the base attack projectile, or if not a volley, a bigger single projectile. Not very creative.
-Lack of core level content.
-The game is compared to Hexen and Heretic at times. Only superficially is it like Hexen, and while closer to Heretic, it does not capture its essence.
-Randomized map layouts selecting from pre-made rooms do not qualify a game as a Rogue-anything.
-Some clipping issues and strange and/or lacking collision boxes.
Neutral:
-Perk system needs creative elements injected into it. Its not bad, but its nothing special either. Its kinda "standard", and does not stand out.
-The different characters need to be more differentiated at their core levels.
-I feel the AI needs to be more complex; more advanced in its functioning.
-I feel there needs to be a crouch button for some reason.... probably because of the FPS nature of the game. While they are at it, they mind as well throw in leaning as well (it would come in handy frequently).
-Item decay is very annoying. Im not sure what that mechanic adds to the game.
Coments:
I had very high hopes for Ziggurat, seeing it being compared to Hexen and Heretic, and touted as a "rogue-lite", but after a couple hours, I became quite disappointed with the game.
I remember Hexen vividly, and comparing Ziggurat to Hexen is not really appropriate except in the most superficial of ways, such as the mana system used for weapons. In that regard, yes, Ziggurat fully borrowed from Hexen. But thats pretty much it. It is much closer to Heretic, which was basically an overhauled Doom with a mystical bent added. But for some reason, battles just fall short of being interesting in Ziggurat. Maybe its the total lack of blood and gore... or believable art.
Honestly I got a Serious Sam sense from the game several times, which I felt was very out of place.
And I have not found many distinguishing Rogue-anything elements in Ziggurat. For anyone whose played Nethack, ADOM, or similar, expect virtually no significant resemblence whatsoever, either in actual gameplay, or in spirit. I do not think Ziggurat falls into any rogue subgenre.
I am mostly bummed about the lack of rogue-anything qualities in the game. I was under the impression that it was going to be much deeper and more indepth than it turned out to be. I was also fooled by the reviews saying this game had atmosphere and great art direction. Ziggurat definitely does have atmospheric potential... but one thing that hinders that potential is the "great art", which doesnt particularly make me feel very immersed in the game because it breaks my suspension of disbelief that what Im seeing could actually be real. It never feels like it COULD be real... it always feels... like a cliched and trite childrens cartoon at this point.
Final Thoughts:
I unfortunately cannot recommend this game as its being sold, at the price it is being sold at.
There is potential in this style of game... in this dungeon crawler shoot-em-up... but Ziggurat falls short of hitting the mark of a defining game for the sub-sub-genre, and instead becomes a mash-up of many different disparate genres that doesnt do any particular one of them very well.
---
Jan 22nd 2015 Update: Replaying Ziggurat for some hours today, I still feel the above accurately describes my thoughts on the game. I amended the positive section to say that the sound/music was very good, instead of just good. The sound team/person did a very good job.
I still wish the art direction had taken a darker, more sinister route. If it had, I probably would have been able to forgive the lack of content and lack of environmental interaction if a suitably dark atmosphere was produced, and give a positive recommendation. But as it stands, I still do not recommend the game the way it is marketed (its not a rogue-anything), nor as it is touted (its neither a literal nor spiritual successor to Hexen or Heretic).

Right, so. Fable Fortunes is an interesting game for what it represents as a whole, that is not to say that it is by any means a bad or unenjoyable game; because it isn't. While it may on the surface seem to be a Hearthstone reskin, that doesn't make it bad. In fact, it has several original features that i rather liked, for example the morality system. This is a solid game, similar to Hearthstone but with its own quirks and original content. However, it is not lost on me that the core of this game is a clone of the basic mechanics of other similar CCGs. But. The important thing about Fable Fortunes, is that it is a Fable game, it bleeds Fable, in fact it practically throws Fable in your face every time you lay a card. The comedic one liners when you play a card, the descriptions of the playable characters, the very nature of the cards themselves and how a lot of them seem simply to tie into jokes about the characters (for example the pig farmer turned Knight class' units seem to consist largely of pigs and angry peasants) it all just screams that the world of Fable is still alive, burried deep inside a simply yet enjoyable card game. The world is in there, the dry wit, ambigious sarcasm, and sheer, beautiful silliness of Fable is as raw in this as it ever has been. I know a lot of fans of the series are sad and in some cases angry that they got a card game and not a full fledged RPG, but with so little funding, so small a team, and so much disregard from Microsoft executives, i'm just glad that we have something with the name Fable fresh and new, and while this game is a bit basic and brings little of anything 'new' to the table, if it is even the smallest step in the direction of reviving the Fable franchise, then i'll be happy to throw my money at it until i have none left or my arms drop off.

I love this game, it has fast become my favourite CCG there is, and it's still early days.  I can't wait to see all the new planned features come to light and see this game fully realised.   Here are my top 3 reasons that make Fable Fortune great:
- The artwork and voices on the cards is so very 'Fable'. The cosmetics are really wonderful and the game looks great.
- I'm always changing decks for new arenas. This is great because each new arena, whether it be for coop or pvp, gets me thinking about cards differently. What is strong in one arena is weak in another and as they add more arenas and quest rewards different cards will see play in different ways and this keeps things interesting.
- Even though I've stared at this card set for ages, I keep finding new an interesting synergies. There is so much depth to the design that even after many weeks of playing I'm still surprised sometimes by new interactions that I uncover. Deck building is such an important part of any CCG and I've spent hours in Fortunes deck builder looking over the cards and working out cool interactions.
The game is definitely still in early development, so don't expect a full and complete game. If that's what you want, hang on and wait until later in the year when it gets released in full and will be free to play.  But if you want to jump in now and help the devs out, then I highly recommend getting the early access bundle.  You get a bunch of packs at a cheaper price, a unique artwork trophy card and a guaranteed fable card.  It's a great deal if you want to get in early, but as I said, if you aren't down with dealing with bugs or waiting for features that are still in the process of being developed, then better to hang on and grab the game later when it's done.

I have been a fan of Hearthstone since it was released. This game is that plus its own unique game mechanics which pushes this further than its competition.
Fable Fortune is currently still in the works, however it is already on the same level as Hearthstone.
The addition of the character building is a great mechanic as it enables your hero to get different perks that will benefit you at the current situation. Each hero class has its own strengths in certain areas and are played different from each other, you can create hybrid builds however which further adds to the depth of the game.
During the PVP or COOP quests you are given quest which will change your morality, changing your hero power and altering certain cards in your deck making each match unique with a different playstyle so the game doesn't become tedious and boring.
The current only negatives I could say is to do with the sound. I presume it is due to the game still in early development however I feel like there are certain sounds missing such as when you are in the menus and click on a button you do not hear any feed back for clicking. It is not game breaking but I felt that this made the game feel a little empty sounding and made me feel blue balled for clicking.
The pay part of the game is not at all Pay to Win formula. Just like in Hearthstone or a real physical game you use real money to get more packs of cards. This is not cheating though as in the card park it is random and you may purchase thousands of packs and only get basic cards or you can spend in game currency (which you get for taking part in matches) and only purchase one pack at a time and get nothing but Rares and Lengendaries.
Apart from that the game is a great addition to the Fable franchise and a brilliant first attempt from Flaming Fowl.

Balrum was developed and published by Balcony Team on the 1st March, the game itself is a old school RPG with a lot of survivalist mechanics, the game itself that just hits the nail on the head with most of the content that is produced in the game.
When you first start off playing this game you are given a lot of options about the way that your character will play out later in the game. These traits, will determine what kind of class shall we say that you will specialize in. Whether you prefer to be a archer, wizard or a knight you will be able to choose. The traits that you pick for your chracter will also determine what kind of skills you will aquire through your gameplay of the game.
There is a nice touch that there are almost always choices that you will have to make throughout the course of the game. This might buff your character in a good, neutral or bad way to help you out with fighting. Some of the choices might be better and more obvious than others to some people, but none of the choices make you feel like you have wasted your time on that conversation.
Acting like a true and honorable old school RPG there is hardly, if at, no help throughout this game. But that I mean there are no checkpoints, no questmarkers or anything. You mainly have to read and figure it out from that point on whare you go to gather the materials that you need. This could possibly annoy and anger some plays that don't really know what to do, but for some players it's really nice to have a challenge like this.
Although the game really does seem to be decent, the combat system is rather being and can sometimes be a bit tedious. Taking it in turns to move to chase some animals can take a rather long time and therefor you sometimes can't get to them. When you are attacking enemies it's boring just standing there just clicking the attack button until the enemies falls and dies.
The graphics in this game represent the old school graphics that really do look like a old school RPG game. Although the graphics don't look polished, and neatly represented throughout the game these are what the graphics were like at that time of creating games.
+ Old school classic RPG game
+ Has a lot of survival elements to it as well as RPG elements
+ Intriguing and interesting story
+ Sticks to the old school graphics
- No help throughout the game may anger and annoy some players
- The combat system is boring and tedious at times
- No trading carrds or achievements
If you are a true old school RPG fan then I would defiantly recommened picking up this game. For what it's worth you are definatly getting a lot of content out of this game, with the old school graphics and a large world to explore it is definatly work picking up.

I've made it to Chapter 2 so far and finally decided that I should say something about the game.
As a true old school RPG Balrum is a nostalgic reminder of the Ultima series. I keep finding myself wanting to break out DOSBox and playing Savage Empire whenever I turn this game on, but the interesting twist to this one that keeps me coming back is the survival aspect. Hunger and thirst are something that you actually have to keep your attention on while you're out exploring, or even collecting materials to craft supplies or even your own house.
Quests have been interesting and the only real downside I've found to the game is trying to find where to go right away in the beginning - sure, it's mostly explained to you, but because the map is lacking details and you have to add your own markers, that first play-time is a bit of a monster to take hold of.  I haven't really experienced anything that would make me not want to recommend this game to anyone that remembers the old days of RPG games.
The real-time/turn based combat makes for interesting times when it comes to exploration.  You get used to right-clicking to auto-move and then find yourself having to switch to either the keyboard or left-click holding to get around because there's  a damned deer somewhere nearby that initiates combat and then takes off on you.  I suppose that is the only thing I've found myself disliking about anything I've encountered so far - but because of the way the game plays, I couldn't really see a better option when it comes to combat, because real-time would become overwhelming really early in the game.
I will probably complete the game with my first character and then reroll to try something different (mostly because of all the mistakes I've made creating this one), which leads me to the last part...the replayability is there, but I could see how it would become boring once you have an idea of where you're going.  After I started moving around the map a lot more, I started noticing how there wasn't any interest once you'd discovered something and maybe that's just me (I have game ADD quite often and switch around from console to PC and through a plethora of games on both), but in the end, this is a very solid game.

I'm surprised and encouraged but what I've seen in the first few hours. There's a lot more going on here than I expected. The crafting/farming/homesteading stuff is well integrated with the more typical RPG survival/combat/progression stuff.
The only thing I'm not super pleased with so far is the blurring between turn based and realtime mechanics. I'm happy with either, but it's unclear to me in many cases how to manage the passing of turns/time, especially in combat. I imagine I'll figure it out as I get further.

The game and the gameplay itself is legit.  Isaac Clarke became a dancer in this game if how often I make him stomp the yard (or enemies if we're splitting hairs here) is any indicator.  The environment and the overall survival-adventure genre gives your heart a steady workout as you play the game, but nothing too drastic to keep you from copping out.
Despite all this however, I would have to give this game review a solid no.  And it's because the programmer for this game thought he was really funny and proceeded to ♥♥♥♥ up the programming or something for Dead Space 2.  More often than not, when you try to reload or respawn, there will be times where you will respawn empty-handed.  As in no weapons, which means not even the chance to perform melee haymakers.  You are straight up walking around empty-handed like a dumbass badass straight into a necromorph thinking you hot♥♥♥♥♥♥and all that only for you to expectedly get torn a new one.  Yes i've checked my inventory, yes i've tried to reequip my handy-dandy plasma cutter.  Nothing.  You're only option left is to reload the game again (if your dumbass saved while knowing this happened, you might very well have permanently lost that item forever unless you start a new game completely, fully-upgraded or not).  If you have really bad luck when you reload a last save, you might be caught in the loading screen forever until you decide to just quit the program itself and reload the last save (goodbye hours of progress).
But my biggest issue with this game is that for whatever the ♥♥♥♥ reason, EA thought it was a good idea to give the player every DLC weapon/armor at the start of the game, doesn't matter if you started fresh or beated the game.  From the moment you reach the first shop in the game, it's decked with weapons that can fill your inventory and armor that gives some pretty decent buffs.  Whats worse is that all of these DLC are free, no credits are needed.  If you're like me and you like the challenge of grinding through a game and actually earning your upgrades, then this is a serious turn off.  One can suggest to just ignore these free stuff and play the game as is, but the fact that these items exist at all without our say leaves a bad taste to the mouth.  There is a way to manually turn the DLC off through coding, but honestly the fact that you have to go through all that at all just to play a vanilla version of a game is jsut disgusting.
So to sum it all off, ignoring all the flaws that i've listed out, the gameplay overall is still similar to the first Dead Space we all played and enjoyed (or hated, i don't know how you roll).  It's still fun to literally curb stomp the♥♥♥♥♥♥on not just your enemies, but also dead civilians into delicious chunks.  My recommendation is that you take these complaints into serious consideration (check Google, it's not just me having these problems) and to get this game ONLY if it's on a serious sale or is given to you free.

An unlikely candidate for the most underrated game of 2016.
A lot has been made of the abrupt ending and (virtually unnoticable) microtransactions in the game, which unfortunately cast a shadow over the many things MD gets right. Mankind Divided is a significant improvement over Human Revolution in most respects. The action is better, interactions are more nuanced, and game mechanics are generally tighter, even if they follow largely the same template as before. The side quests are consistently brilliant. Prague, the game's only real mission hub, is a visual masterpiece with an effectively gritty sci-fi atmosphere. I much prefer it to Detroit and Hengsha (from Human Revolution).
Unfortunately, given lackluster sales, SquareEnix has decided to put the franchise on hold for the forseeable future. This means that the story arc presented here might never be finished. I certainly hope they change their minds.
Mankind Divided isn't without flaws (as the mixed reviews indicate), but I strongly recommend you give the game a try if you enjoy RPGs. It's now my favorite game in the Deus Ex series.
It's a shame that poor decisions by the publisher prevented MD from being the huge critical and financial success it could have easily been.

To start: I do enjoy the GTA Online aspect of the game vastly, I come back to it every few months, it can be really fun with friends, and if you find a friendly lobby you can have a great time! But IF is the key word here.
To continue, GTA Online has one of the most toxic communities I've ever seen. For every friendly person in a lobby, there's four others in black combat gear cruising around in an armored vehicle killing everyone, someone blasting people off the face of the map with a jet, or someone just straight up hacking and ruining the entire session. And yes, as of late, the developers have taken a step to cut down on the sheer number of hackers, while also punishing normal, legitimate players in the same way, many of whom have spent insane amounts of money on their obscenely priced Shark Cards.
But there's plenty of other reviews here to explain just why that's so terrible. I'm here to accent that. As I said before, the community for GTA Online is cripplingly toxic, with groups of people regularly pushing through sessions as griefers whose express goal is to make everyone in the session rage quit and move to another session. Rinse, repeat.
With recent updates the game has gotten a fairly large number of increasingly more powerful weapons and vehicles, which is awesome until you realize the average cost for one of those is insane, and the grind to get to those vehicles, properties, and weapons is equally as insane. The grind is also compounded by that griefer problem, most of the grind hinges on you gathering up various sellable goods to get a payoff. Sounds easy! Right? Not really, you could spend a good four hours of your day dedicated to gathering up your goods and such, have a full gang of five friends who are interacting and talking in a separate voice chat, and all that work you did just got deleted by a guy in black combat gear with a jet. Oh well! Maybe you should've bought shark cards instead!
So why don't you just play in a friends only session? You can! Buuut you won't be able to do the main grind things, no owning a biker club, no owning a business, no secret bunkers full of guns and firepower. So why don't you just play the game in passive mode? The mode that makes it so players can't just fly over and nuke you? Well you can do that too! But you can't own a biker club, business, etc, etc. So good luck gaining that 25 million dollars you need. Because it'll either cost you a good chunk of your life, or a good chunk of your wallet.
Don't get me wrong, the game is fun and it's great if you manage to get up with that grind through either a chunk of your life or a chunk of your wallet. It's a great playground for weird and funny stuff to happen, you could have a car show and have that one guy show up with a truck covered in bombs, then have to fend off the police for an hour among the burning husks of your car, while goofing around with the other guys. That's actually fun! It's a great game if you have the money and mental strength to play it.
So, if you can put up with having your hard earned money deleted (be it just in game or actual money you spent on cards), deal with vast amounts of grief, withstand the grind, get to the top, and push through that painfully toxic community, you'll have fun! Personally, I can only play for a few hours for maybe a week every few months before the community wears me down, and the shine of the latest update fades away under that blanket of grinding that might not even pay off in the end. So good luck! Don't get too rich, and don't expect a friendly community.

Positive:
-Good mechanics for what content there is.
-Mostly smooth functioning.
-Good use of colored lighting, which is often neglected nowadays.
-Very good sound / music for whats there.
-Mostly interesting room layouts that make for good fast paced FPS action.
Negative:
-I cant get past the art direction. Every enemy and pretty much every environment texture looks like it was pulled straight out of WoW, or that it would fit perfectly in it. It gives an otherwise potentially atmospheric and gruesome game a childish, out-of-character cartoony vibe.
-Essentially no environmental interaction. No "use" button, for instance, because there is nothing to use. No switches, no mechanisms, etc.
-Essentially puzzleless. "Puzzles" consist of jumping onto moving platforms, which there is nothing inherently wrong with, but its not enough all by itself.
-Weaponry is not differentiated enough. In addition, almost all secondary attack modes for weapons just launch a volley of the base attack projectile, or if not a volley, a bigger single projectile. Not very creative.
-Lack of core level content.
-The game is compared to Hexen and Heretic at times. Only superficially is it like Hexen, and while closer to Heretic, it does not capture its essence.
-Randomized map layouts selecting from pre-made rooms do not qualify a game as a Rogue-anything.
-Some clipping issues and strange and/or lacking collision boxes.
Neutral:
-Perk system needs creative elements injected into it. Its not bad, but its nothing special either. Its kinda "standard", and does not stand out.
-The different characters need to be more differentiated at their core levels.
-I feel the AI needs to be more complex; more advanced in its functioning.
-I feel there needs to be a crouch button for some reason.... probably because of the FPS nature of the game. While they are at it, they mind as well throw in leaning as well (it would come in handy frequently).
-Item decay is very annoying. Im not sure what that mechanic adds to the game.
Coments:
I had very high hopes for Ziggurat, seeing it being compared to Hexen and Heretic, and touted as a "rogue-lite", but after a couple hours, I became quite disappointed with the game.
I remember Hexen vividly, and comparing Ziggurat to Hexen is not really appropriate except in the most superficial of ways, such as the mana system used for weapons. In that regard, yes, Ziggurat fully borrowed from Hexen. But thats pretty much it. It is much closer to Heretic, which was basically an overhauled Doom with a mystical bent added. But for some reason, battles just fall short of being interesting in Ziggurat. Maybe its the total lack of blood and gore... or believable art.
Honestly I got a Serious Sam sense from the game several times, which I felt was very out of place.
And I have not found many distinguishing Rogue-anything elements in Ziggurat. For anyone whose played Nethack, ADOM, or similar, expect virtually no significant resemblence whatsoever, either in actual gameplay, or in spirit. I do not think Ziggurat falls into any rogue subgenre.
I am mostly bummed about the lack of rogue-anything qualities in the game. I was under the impression that it was going to be much deeper and more indepth than it turned out to be. I was also fooled by the reviews saying this game had atmosphere and great art direction. Ziggurat definitely does have atmospheric potential... but one thing that hinders that potential is the "great art", which doesnt particularly make me feel very immersed in the game because it breaks my suspension of disbelief that what Im seeing could actually be real. It never feels like it COULD be real... it always feels... like a cliched and trite childrens cartoon at this point.
Final Thoughts:
I unfortunately cannot recommend this game as its being sold, at the price it is being sold at.
There is potential in this style of game... in this dungeon crawler shoot-em-up... but Ziggurat falls short of hitting the mark of a defining game for the sub-sub-genre, and instead becomes a mash-up of many different disparate genres that doesnt do any particular one of them very well.
---
Jan 22nd 2015 Update: Replaying Ziggurat for some hours today, I still feel the above accurately describes my thoughts on the game. I amended the positive section to say that the sound/music was very good, instead of just good. The sound team/person did a very good job.
I still wish the art direction had taken a darker, more sinister route. If it had, I probably would have been able to forgive the lack of content and lack of environmental interaction if a suitably dark atmosphere was produced, and give a positive recommendation. But as it stands, I still do not recommend the game the way it is marketed (its not a rogue-anything), nor as it is touted (its neither a literal nor spiritual successor to Hexen or Heretic).

It really is one of the better fps roguelikes out there. Ziggurat is fast paced, looks and feels very good and keeps itself interesting. I feel like there could be more variety, not because there isn't a good assortment of items, but because most of them feel similar to similar items in their category. I could go on further, but its honestly worth the $15 to anyone into the genre and I would suggest it to basically anyone looking for a lunchtime roguelike. 8/10 carrots

While I initially had some issues with aiming (I'm still getting used to FPS games where I don't have the option to 'aim down the sights') the simple, yet deep system that the developers created for Ziggurat makes for a very challenging and fun game that I strongly urge people to play.
Based on the 'rogue-like' genre of games where each level is generated at random, I've never had a session play in the exact same way at all. The weapons you acquire are randomized, the boss fights at the end of a level are random, and your character perks are offered to you as (usually) the choice between two new perks. Sometimes, this does translate into a game wherein you get your enchanted backside handed to you because the random number generator gods decided that they just don't like you anymore' but the game is short enough on a playthrough that you don't feel like you've invested so much time and effort into being thwarted by bad luck. Furthermore, unlocks ranging from new abilities, perks, characters, and weapons serve to keep you charging at the Ziggurat screaming "Thank you, may I have another?!?!"
A well-developed RPG levelling system helps you build your character, unique classes of weapons even further diversified by differences between individual weapons, and a diverse range of enemies (that in later levels are enhanced by various environmental conditions) all blend together to make a very fun, challenging, and rewarding experience.

To start: I do enjoy the GTA Online aspect of the game vastly, I come back to it every few months, it can be really fun with friends, and if you find a friendly lobby you can have a great time! But IF is the key word here.
To continue, GTA Online has one of the most toxic communities I've ever seen. For every friendly person in a lobby, there's four others in black combat gear cruising around in an armored vehicle killing everyone, someone blasting people off the face of the map with a jet, or someone just straight up hacking and ruining the entire session. And yes, as of late, the developers have taken a step to cut down on the sheer number of hackers, while also punishing normal, legitimate players in the same way, many of whom have spent insane amounts of money on their obscenely priced Shark Cards.
But there's plenty of other reviews here to explain just why that's so terrible. I'm here to accent that. As I said before, the community for GTA Online is cripplingly toxic, with groups of people regularly pushing through sessions as griefers whose express goal is to make everyone in the session rage quit and move to another session. Rinse, repeat.
With recent updates the game has gotten a fairly large number of increasingly more powerful weapons and vehicles, which is awesome until you realize the average cost for one of those is insane, and the grind to get to those vehicles, properties, and weapons is equally as insane. The grind is also compounded by that griefer problem, most of the grind hinges on you gathering up various sellable goods to get a payoff. Sounds easy! Right? Not really, you could spend a good four hours of your day dedicated to gathering up your goods and such, have a full gang of five friends who are interacting and talking in a separate voice chat, and all that work you did just got deleted by a guy in black combat gear with a jet. Oh well! Maybe you should've bought shark cards instead!
So why don't you just play in a friends only session? You can! Buuut you won't be able to do the main grind things, no owning a biker club, no owning a business, no secret bunkers full of guns and firepower. So why don't you just play the game in passive mode? The mode that makes it so players can't just fly over and nuke you? Well you can do that too! But you can't own a biker club, business, etc, etc. So good luck gaining that 25 million dollars you need. Because it'll either cost you a good chunk of your life, or a good chunk of your wallet.
Don't get me wrong, the game is fun and it's great if you manage to get up with that grind through either a chunk of your life or a chunk of your wallet. It's a great playground for weird and funny stuff to happen, you could have a car show and have that one guy show up with a truck covered in bombs, then have to fend off the police for an hour among the burning husks of your car, while goofing around with the other guys. That's actually fun! It's a great game if you have the money and mental strength to play it.
So, if you can put up with having your hard earned money deleted (be it just in game or actual money you spent on cards), deal with vast amounts of grief, withstand the grind, get to the top, and push through that painfully toxic community, you'll have fun! Personally, I can only play for a few hours for maybe a week every few months before the community wears me down, and the shine of the latest update fades away under that blanket of grinding that might not even pay off in the end. So good luck! Don't get too rich, and don't expect a friendly community.

I am now 30+ hours in, and i found this fantasy cRPG very interesting. As a veteran hardcore RPG player, the following are my opinions about this game:
+ Pros:
+ Great variety of things to do and discover
+ Deep crafting mechanics
+ Challenging and varied enemies that require strategy and planning to defeat (except cerain situations, see below)
+ Massive open world that will take you a lot to fully explore
+ Good lore
+ Intesesting and rewarding side quests with many different goals
+ Gameplay greatly varies with different classes, improving replay value
+ Overall good artistic direction and visuals
- Cons:
- Traps are way overpowered if used in certain ways through combat
- Inventory sorting generally is messy and lacks in-depth categorization / customization
- Stealing from people is way too easy with any class, there even is a forget crime spell if you are caught which is fairly common (!)
- Fixed projectile traps of dungeons and certain areas can be abused to defeat any enemy without effort, as they still work in real-time while turn-based combat is ongoing (!). As a result, you can lure any enemy near say, a fireball trap, and this trap will keep spamming on it until he is dead, and since it will be your turn the enemy will just stand still until he is dead. This is a major combat mechanics flaw.
- Certain specializations are not worth being learned because the overall loot one can find greatly overcomes the one that can be crafted with said specializations.
That is all. I rate this title 8 out of 10, it is a good cRPG which is well worth its price, and if some flaws are fixed and some mechanics improved it could become a great hidden gem of the genre.

I like this game a lot.  It is definitely a hard core RPG, so not for the casual fan.  But for those people who are really into RPGs it is fantastic, with tons of content, skills, quests, etc.
One very big con is that the game kind of just throws you in and expects you to learn on your own.  The entire first town is sort of a tutorial, but that's not really advertised and it is very easy to get yourself killed or♥♥♥♥♥♥off an important NPC by accident.  One eggregious example is that looting peoples' homes will cause them to become hostile instantly.  This makes some sense (I'd prefer a warning before they draw their sword), but most casual RPG fans wouldn't expect it.  Another example is that you have to eat and drink or you die.  When I started I was constantly on the brink of starving and it took me a while to figure out that you can fill your belly and not have to eat again for a long time (also you get a bonus when you're at full food/drink).  Once you figure that out it removes almost all of the nuisance, but a new player has to find it by trial and error.  Also combat is tough and most fights require a combination of skills and strategy that you might not expect to need so early in the game.  It is a steep learning curve.  For hard core fans that's NBD, but it will definitely turn some players off.
If it were up to me, I'd put a few more obvious tutorial elements in the game to help ease the learning curve.  Once you know how to play, it's very addicting and very fun.  I'm 30 hours in and still feel like I'm just scratching the surface.

Ok, this is the new review:
Balrum is like seeing a roleplaying game through the eyes of a child.  It is a simple, yet, lush and deep role playing game.  If you have the time to enjoy it, like a good book, you will love it.
I have gotten past the easy-to-make bread situation, because if you want to be a farmer you will, literally, spend all your game time farming.  Then, head to the market and sell stuff.  I can imagine some people play like that.  Or, you can adventure and harvest crops in the world.  Either way, the days tick by.  It is pretty easy to feed yourself and make hundreds and hundreds of loaves of bread and 10s of 20s of buckets of water to never run out of food/drink, because there is no weight allotment I can find, but the game is still rugged.  I haven't adventured out past the early dungeons, so maybe there are places where food and drink become an issue.  The game also has great music.
The devs have made some serious upgrades to the UI.  Alt+left click will put an item from your inventory into an open container for you.  Also, you can store inventory items on your hotkey bar and they won't take up inventory space.  You have 48 hotbar slots, so, that's awesome.
Love it.  It's simple.  I still love Underrail, but give this game a chance too. It's awesome.

This is probably the most interesting and in depth CCG I have played, combining the wonderful world of Fable with some brilliant tactical depth to the game.
Deckbuilding in particular is the biggest positive of the game, with so many interesting and powerful combos available to explore.
This is a great game and will kickstart your love of CCGs  if you have grown bored with the current leaders in the genre.

On the surface it might look like any other CCG out there, but it has so much more to offer than any other Card Game I have played.
The in-game mechanics and very limited RNG elements gives Fable Fortune a tactical and strategical depth that other card games lack. This is also reflected in the deckkbuilding process. Good game sense and creative deckbuilding has a much bigger impact on the outcome of games than having high rarity cards and big RNG swings.
While having a familiar and accessible combat system Fable Fortune provides a fun and very unique gameplay experience.
Changing Arenas each season keeps the game from going stale. Each Arena brings a completely different meta and promotes very different playstyles. A deck that is prominent in one Arena will usually struggle a lot in another. You need to adjust your decks and strategies to the different Arenas to be successful.
The COOP mode brings a fund and interesting PVE aspect to the game which will hopefully be expanded upon in the future.
Keep in mind this is still very much in the testing stages of the development. The UI and animations is still lacking in a lot of aspects and you might experience game crashes from time to time. Some core features is still missing from th UI. Especially in-game.
The dev team does a great job and actually interacts and listens to the community.
Far and away the best CCG I have played and I highly recommend it, but keep in mind that this game is still very mucg in development and far from a finished product right now.

While the story isn't as immersive as it could be, and as has been said in nearly every review - the ending is of the cliffhanger variety, leaving much to be desired - this is an outstanding, fairly open-world game.
You are confined to certain areas for certain groups of missions, but the areas are sizable and very detailed. The graphics are gorgeous and the game is stable on a high-end rig (using i7-4790K, GTX 1070, 16GB RAM). Not one crash, no framerate hitches.
The gameplay is fluid, controls easy to use, and as in previous titles, the game is fully playable in either a total stealth or guns-blazing approach, though the latter is somewhat more difficult due to AI improvements over Human Revolution.
Overall, it's an entertaining game, well worth the sale price, arguably worth the full price as well. Just don't purchase any DLC. It's completely unnecessary and eliminates any complaints you may have heard about microtransactions. These items serve merely to give you a boost to the start of the game, but frankly, get too strong too quick and the game loses its flavor or any sense of challenge.

I would recommend people to get it on a discount and play it with a brother (or sister) of your own, personally I was disappointed.
I was gifted this game when it was on my wishlist. I wanted to get this game because I expected an emotional or inspiring or a great story, did I get any of those? No, not really.
==Spoilers Ahead==
I feel this game is a cliche and predictable story that knows that it is just that, which is why they used a made up language because it is so easily replacable with lines that even the player can think of. I respect that decision and it's a good design choice.
At the beginning of the game, you see the little brother mourning over the death of his mother which I suppose he feels quite responsible for but that death was so meaningless and the only other time besides the intro that we see the mother's spirit was at the end of the game which "inspired" him to push on and in time, save his father.
The protagonists of the games are the two brothers, one older, one younger. There is an unspoken bond between the brothers and that bond isn't always a good one, mainly because there were so little interactions between them, perhaps if I did the side activities I would've seen more but I was already bored of the game that I couldn't find myself to do those.
Towards the end, the older brother had a sudden shift of character that was out of place that led to his death, was it an emotional death? No, not to me at least. I expected him to die the moment he acted strangely and when he did, I felt nothing. What about when the little brother had to bury him? Sure it was sad for the little brother but not me. I might've felt more emotion if the brother were to let's say, step in and saved his younger brother from something instead. Throughout their journey to get some sort of liquid from a specific magical tree, the brothers were at times laughing and having fun which I can understand if it's something fun and cool but never once in my memory have I seen any of them crying and feeling depressed about their dying father which was the reason they started this journey in the first place.
Puzzles were mindlessly boring and simple, there wasn't ever once that I had to actually think about anything. They were so obvious that the moment you see it you'll go "Yeah I know what to do"
So, is there anything at all that I liked about this game? Yes, there are but they cannot by any means overwhelm the negatives of the game.
These are the things that I can think of that I liked about the game but overall it was disappointing. Look, I have an older brother of my own and I didn't play it with him but if I did, maybe I would've been more positive about the game but honestly, I don't think I will. I hate to say this but this game is too overrated but no hate on the developers.

While I initially had some issues with aiming (I'm still getting used to FPS games where I don't have the option to 'aim down the sights') the simple, yet deep system that the developers created for Ziggurat makes for a very challenging and fun game that I strongly urge people to play.
Based on the 'rogue-like' genre of games where each level is generated at random, I've never had a session play in the exact same way at all. The weapons you acquire are randomized, the boss fights at the end of a level are random, and your character perks are offered to you as (usually) the choice between two new perks. Sometimes, this does translate into a game wherein you get your enchanted backside handed to you because the random number generator gods decided that they just don't like you anymore' but the game is short enough on a playthrough that you don't feel like you've invested so much time and effort into being thwarted by bad luck. Furthermore, unlocks ranging from new abilities, perks, characters, and weapons serve to keep you charging at the Ziggurat screaming "Thank you, may I have another?!?!"
A well-developed RPG levelling system helps you build your character, unique classes of weapons even further diversified by differences between individual weapons, and a diverse range of enemies (that in later levels are enhanced by various environmental conditions) all blend together to make a very fun, challenging, and rewarding experience.

Two of the things I hate most about FPS games are bulletsponges and kiting. Unfortunately this game has both in spades. I enter a room and I'm greeted by a horde of guys with swords mindlessly running after me, so I sprint away, fire a few shots and repeat this tens of times until they're all dead. This isn't my idea of fun, it's a chore. The big, flying guys are a chore because they also take ages to kill. The stone golems that break into smaller ones are a chore. The carrots are a chose because they're about as fast as the player and will chase you down until you turn around a land a few shots.
So with all this running around, you tend to forget the other enemies with ranged attacks that can attack safely, knowing that the player has their hands full sprinting from one end to the other, trying to avoid a ball of melee death. This way you tend to forget about the ranged enemies and then you run into their projectiles. I could use a different weapon, but eventually the ammunition runs out and I'm back where I started. I really want to like Ziggurat but playing it isn't exciting, tense or fun. Sure, it's difficult but for all the wrong reasons.
In the end, it boils down to how well you can kite the enemies and how well you can keep your health up. This is really not a fun game for me so there's no way I can recommend it.

DLC Quest is a short, satirical take on the state of the gaming industry (read: DLC).
There's not a lot of gameplay going on, just jump, collect coins, buy DLC with said coins - but there's some nice jokes tucked in there and the general subject matter it's making fun of is entertaining.
That said, there's not a lot here.  The gameplay is pretty non-existant and not very fun, it's more just an interactive commic or something of the sort.
Don't go in expecting a game, but if you're the type of person that thinks manufacturer's reliance on DLC (especially for unfinished products) is a bunch of crap then picking up DLC Quest for a few chuckles is probably worth the ticket price.
DLC Quest narrowly squeaks by with a "Recommended" from me; only because I thought a few of the jokes were funny, it's short, and I got it for less than a buck.  I did get stuck trying to find the pickaxe in the second "game" included, but at that point the joke had run its course for me and I decided to hang it up.

For a buck, you'll get a few laughs, finish it quickly, and leave mildly satisfied. The whole thing pokes fun at the state of Downloadable Content in the industry and how companies nickle and dime their users by holding back already finished content from our games. I suppose it still holds true today.

I have never encountered such poignant satire in my life.  This game provides such an insightful commentary on how everyone goes to work every day solely in order to go home and purchase DLC for their video games.  DLC doesn't provide meaningful content, therefore, working is useless.  I'm not ever going to seek gainful employment thanks to this game.  In fact, since all DLC is a shallow husk of fufillment, I'm going to put a bullet in my brain presently.  That is the primary emotion DLC Quest provides, the desire to put a bullet in your brain.  I forget what that emotion is called.  Love?  It's got to be love.

This is quite possibly one of the worst games on Steam at the moment. While Steam Greenlight can occasionally let players get access to a gem of an indie game that they might have otherwise missed, Zombie Zoeds is the sort of game that makes it abundantly clear that Greenlight is more often an over-abused program that lets scamware slip through the cracks.
First off, Zombie Zoeds feels like the sort of game that you should be able to play for free on a dodgy flash website. You know the sort, right? The kind that clutters up the browser window with malicious ads that attempt to install spyware onto your computer.
Don't let the trailer video fool you, because the music in this game is non-existant, and the sound effects and animations are minimal. There's some ambient sound in the early part of the game, in the form of chirping crickets, but it seems to cut out randomly. The controls are extraordinarily awkward, instructions on keybindings are completely absent, and when you die the game simply cuts back to the title screen without any sort of "Game Over" screen. There's a basic scoring mechanic, but it's entirely meaningless and your score only resets when you exit and restart the program, rather than when you die and start a new game.
The game is missing very basic functions, such as an options screen, a volume slider, and the ability to run the game in windowed mode. On top of that, it quickly becomes obvious that the developers are native to Europe, and that they couldn't even be bothered to do some very basic translation work ("Patrons" instead of "Ammo", "Lazer" instead of "Laser").
Even ignoring that, the developers in this case have been dodgy since day one. They originally offered the game as part of a bundle, under the title "Zombie Zoids". In an apparent attempt to avoid this obligation, they changed the title by one letter to "Zombie Zoeds". When they finally owned up and distributed the game to everyone who had payed for it, the game was missing it's primary executable file and could not be played - and when they actually DID include one, it registered on some virus scanners as a potential backdoor virus.
Even now the Steam page is rife with lies, promising Steam Achievements (absent), Steam Cloud Support (absent), and Steam Workshop (absent). The only saving grace is that the game DOES have Steam Cards enabled, so if you got the game at a deep enough discount you may be able to make your money back by farming the cards.
But honestly, if you're after cards, then you'd probably be better off just buying booster packs on the Steam Market rather than cluttering up your playlist with this mess.
