Trine 2 is perhaps one of the most visually stunning 2D platforming games. Either playing co-op or on your own this really is a fantasy-themed 2D platformer with a difference. The game sets a new standard for puzzle driven adventures and the relatively short-length campaign has a wealth of overlaying puzzles and secrets and is an overall entertaining experience and a joy to play.
Instead of the usual jump and grind gameplay of the generic platformers, Trine 2 offers a more intricate puzzles with the freedom to find various solutions. Even more interesting is when you’re playing with two or more players the game becomes a colourful array of opportunities to help each other along in an almost sandbox like environment.
Switching from character to character is the only way to make any progress when playing alone in single player but invite some friends along and Trine 2 really shines through. Trine 2 features three heroes – a knight, wizard, and a thief – whom you can switch between at any point through the levels. All have their own individual strengths that they can bring to the table at any given time; this keeps the entertainment of gameplay going so you don't end up rage-quitting when getting stuck on one bit for far too long.
- Clever platform/puzzle gameplay
- Wonderful graphics with physics effects.
- Brilliant sounds and speech
- Excellent online co-operative play
- Sometimes the puzzles are a bit repetitive.
- No combat mode for the Wizard

So...a review for
, eh?
Essentially, it's a roguelike title about destroying zombie mutants by manually targeting the enemies' heads with your mouse and firing by clicking, sounds simple enough, right?  Well, during the whole game you're given only 1 hitpoint.  Get touched, it's over.
There are 3 weapons and 2 kinds of mines in the game.  You also have money that expires (there's a counter that tells you when you're about to lose one unit of currency), so you need to puchase a little strategically.
As the game progresses, newer enemies will be introduced, which makes the game even more tricky.  In the end, you can manage to finish the game in 10 minutes if you know what you're doing.  If not, then it should take an hour or two.  If you're feeling too frustrated, the developer himself recorded a playthrough on YouTube to give you a general idea of what to do.
The visuals look decent, though the intro, gameover, and ending screens look great.  The blood splatters on the wall (where the game gets its namesake) also adds some charm to the game.  The music ranges from creepy (when there are no monsters) to epic (when there are monsters).
The main disappointment with this title is that it's short and a new player won't have the faintest idea what's going on on the first floor.
also suffers by being short and with a relatively low replay value.  For a precursor to a potential sequel project, it's not too shabby.
6/10  A short, strategic shooting experience and an easy 100% that looks good, sounds great, but suffers from being short and predictable.

A rare gem among many others like itself. Gnomoria is still under development but that doesn't stop it from being fun. Updates are frequent and the developer is ingratiated with the community, often seen discussing game mechanics on the forums with other users. As for the game itself, it's virtually Dwarf Fortress with a mouse GUI. Features an 8-bit or midi-orchestral custom soundtrack which will graft itself into your grey matter.
For all the building you will be doing, the meat of the game lies within the combat, and squads. Uniforms are made(you designate the material and quality of each piece of armor and weapon that uniform will use), soldiers use these uniforms and perks, formations use soldiers and their own perks as well, and finally squads are made designating formation, and what gnomes will be in what position.
Now to clear up my earlier statement, this game doesn't try to become Dwarf Fortress with mouse support, but it is obviously heavily inspired. Do not come looking for the complexity that DF contains, though for finished releases and beyond, I can't say. Enemies are unique in their own way. Golems spawn underground in the dark, with their strength determined by the depth. Goblins and the like will spawn ground level at the edge of the map. Animals as well, but you typically see goblins during night or morning whereas animals are more popular during the day. Mants will raid you with strength and numbers based on your food stockpile.
I've followed the development of this game for over half a year and I can honestly say it's been one of the few early access games(had it before it was on steam) that I've never had one regret purchasing.

Everybody who i know who has got this game(mind you, we all have varying locations and interent speeds) has found online to be virtually unplayable. Incredible amounts of lag, disconnects, input delays, and a lack of variety in characters due to the weekly challenges making everyone play the same two. and because online play is how you get gold, forget about buying the legends without real world money. Every other game i've ever gotten and played(excluding Nintendo's awful online) runs quite well, so this relatively small and simple game should not struggle so much with a stable connection. And i'm not even going to mention toxic players. That one's a given.
Once online runs better, i will switch to a recommend. Until then, if you don't have people to play locally with you and don't want only bot matches, don't bother getting this game and certainly don't put any money into it.

7/10 Single Player, 3/10 Online - Don't beleive the diehard fans rating it 10/10. Let me first say that if you can pick this game up for under $50 with the 8mil cash online, it's worth it for a few days fun, but for the price that I paid, I'm really disappointed. I feel I was scammed into beleiving it was the best thing since sliced bread by the idiots that rated it 100% on metacritic among ohers. Unfortunately you can't beleive the reviews on this one. No, it's not worth the asking price. Single player is worth some fun but Online is frustrating at best. I've played every GTA, but this one is different with a completely different feel (and content) to Single Player and Online. Sure they're both open world, with a few things to do, but both are lacking in a lot of areas. Like others I feel Single Player is pretty good overall, but Online is terrible, so I'll deal with both differently.
Single player took me about 70hrs to get 70% complete (full story done, and most side missions). It's quite fun but there are bugs and for me the storyline was standard GTA fare; linear, predictable and annoying. You are along for a ride, with some free time during the stops. The real standout was the 3 main characters who were totally different but so much fun in their own right. The depth and feel - amazing.
Online is a exercise in multitasking and patience. I bought this game with the 8mil cash card for online and only 3 days later I'm wondering why people would pay $100 for that normally, but also wondering if I can bother playing any more. There are so many issues with online, but the main ones are:
- load times (which is about 30% of your play time) - you need to be able to tab out of play another game while you wait for people to join, wait for various places like your apartment to load etc. Load times are around 1min at best to over an hour for some missions - there's no scale down or bots to speed this up.
- It's a cash grab. Everything is overpriced and they are spamming ads in game to make you buy more, over promising and under delivering. I bought a hangar for 3mil to "start a trafficking empire" so I could earn cash, but you can't. It's completely false. The lack of real information and help in game leads to a lot of money being wasted.
- Modders / Hackers are everywhere. They pop up every few hours and do loads of random things such as respawn everyone together on the same spot then grenade everyone, or spawn around 30 random vehicles, or even spawn money. You have no control over any of this.
All said and done, a lot of other games are far more advanced and/or polished in many different aspects to this game. It's not bad, but it's not good either. R* really need to work on their online stuff though. It's truely horrendous.

It's nice enough to see the more "arcade frantic" old-school single player FPS genre (Doom, Quake, or for this game, think Heretic, Hexen) revived. This game goes even further and also gives it the roguelike treatment and unlockable abilities, items and characters, adding loads of replay value.

Boy those Roguelike games sure are a dime a dozen these days. Wouldn't it be nice if they built one around fun gameplay rather than mediocrity or super extreme fiddly RPG mechanics.
Then suddenly Ziggurat appears. Not the first roguelike FPS but this one nails the Doom feel. Lots of stafing, dodging bullets, a decent variety of guns. All wrapped up in a lovely fantasy motif that no game seems to want to truck with these days outside of a mindless clickfest RPG or Skyrim, but I repeat myself.
Fight enemies, collect weapons, level up and get random perks. Unfortunately, the game is hugely swingy on randomness, par for the genre. If you get awful perks or weak weaponry you likely won't see the end of the game so it's not something I would call a "serious" game right yet. If I lose, I think part of that is the game's fault because of all this randomness. Plus, the late game monsters have so much health that the game loses the joy of the early levels and just becomes tedious "hold mouse button against health bars."
That said, it reminds me of Doom and any game that can do that is on the right track. Easily the best roguelite I've played but that isn't saying much. I still cannot recommend it. It's fun for a while but it just doesn't hold up in the long run.

Think of it like Binding of Isaac, only 3d and very fun.
While Binding of Isaac seems more open on their storyline, Ziggurat focuses on randomly generated levels, jumping puzzles, random weapons, and your luck. The key goal to Ziggurat is to level your character up, kill enemies in each room, find a portal key to the next floor, and kill the portal guardian on each floor. You won't die as many times as you think like in Dark Souls, this is more casual to people who do desire a challenge, but not -that- challenging.
You might not get a tutorial, that's for sure, but your weapons will clear that up for you. Dodge projectiles, murder carrots, and retrieve amulets from treasure that you so desire to have. You might not finish the game in one shot, but you will have the potential to learn it's strategy. You might be unlucky, but that doesn't matter on your strategy. I managed to finish the game in seven attempts (yeah, i suck), but after those 7 attempts I got a healing amulet on the first floor, which made me pretty beefy. The first 6 attempts I was just completely unlucky with a lot of harsh rooms, a lot of champions, and a lot of obelisks.
Fortunally, I didn't recieve that much on my 7th attempt. It was like a sign of god saying "Hey, we're done messing around with you, we need our sleep." (that would be kinda funny if it was based off of that).
I may not be a hardcore Hexen fan, or a hardcore rpg fan, but this game really got me into playing it. And that's something! At it's price (not sale-wise), 15 bucks is what it offers.

I wasn't really expecting something big from
, but I was really surprised by the moment I started playing it.
The game is a explicit parody of the DLC excess shown in videogames market nowadays. Although no real money is used in-game (thank God), the player must use all the coins he gets through the game to literally buy extremelly basic features of platform games in general, such as the game's sound, animations, jumping or even walking the opposite direction. There are also NPCs that don't have any idea what they're making on the game as they're just DLCs the player buy for no reason.
With all that, you can expect no less than a very fun game that will make you laugh with inumerous puns spreaded through the scenarios - much of them related to videogame companies which exaggerate on the number of DLCs of their games.
Have a nice time playing it and laughing.

Ok so this is a first impression of the game review. I read some positive reviews and some bad ones, here's what I think from my first hour into the game:
I don't die as quick as the bad reviewers said. On normal setting, thirst and hunger aren't a problem since I did open my eyes and notices there's like a 100 times more food than I need lying around in the village. There are wells to replenish my waterskin ...
I do like the depth, in fact at times it can get overwhelming. But that is part of what we like with games with deep/complicated rules systems. You just have to expect that is what you are getting into.
I did get into a couple encounters. My first one were very careful attempts to use the best of my options (playing a spell slinging guy at first) to slaughter my chosen ennemy: a bear. I kill it, it was a close fight. Luckily I have a wolf to help me.
Then I notice another bear, after eating up and sleeping a bit ... but it has a friend I hadn't noticed before shooting my first fire blast at it ... I retreat and get help from some NPCs, we prevail. After that I got cocky with another fight, died ... and restarted.
I expect to be spending a lot of time into a character at some point, but don't mind dying while learning the game. So to me, this game is perfect. I will do a more detailed review if I play more than 40 hours !

As a 7 year veteran of this game that has purchased every expansion/class/zone I cannot in good faith recommend this game anymore, Turbine have no idea what they are doing at this point and are obviously suffering from lack of staff and have been since Riders of Rohan launched.
Turbine apparently decided a game wide nerf was in order because content was too easy, huge sweeping changes like this couldn't possibly affect anything right? NPC's in escort missions were hit by this nerf and in turn had their HP lowered to an absolutely rediculous amount causing some
to be almost impossible until completely outleveling them (96 to do a level 87 required mission) requiring you to completely bypass doing the games main story (the key reason I enjoy it and play it) and do sidequests until you are able to go back and play catch up. If you managed to complete this story before the game wide nerf you were fine. This is insanely unacceptable to require the player to be almost a full 10+ levels higher to complete in order to finish the quest.
Also of note is the absolutely abysmal or almost complete lack of optimization in the recent expansions. To put this in perspective I have trouble maintaining 15 FPS on ultra in areas with a fairly decent rig (R9 390X, i7 4790k, 32g DDR3). This game was released in 2007. I have no trouble maintaining 100+ FPS in Final Fantasy XIV on max settings. The game functions atrociously on anything above a dual core cpu and it shows. Mounted combat has been laggy and suffers from rubber banding regardless of connection since it was implemented in 2012 with no improvements, something that was touted as a main mechanic and the entire expansion was centered around. The game also suffers from extreme hitching regardless of settings/zone in every expansion past Riders of Rohan due to the way the engine is structured and reads files from an HDD, this is not fixed using an SSD or flash drive as the devs suggest in the forums.
This is completely depressing as this is easily in my top 3 MMO's I've played. I love the community and the setting for this game; I have genuinely never met nicer people in an MMO than I have in this. I enjoyed being able to create my own character and explore an absolutely gorgeous world and I really enjoyed seeing an expanded form of the LOTR universe and being a part of new stories told in it.
Maybe by some amazing stroke of luck the game can magically obtain a development team that is substantial enough and experienced enough to fix the problems with the game and restore it to the game I once enjoyed spending my time in, but until then the game is on life support and future updates will likely not fix the issues the game currently has.

I'm torn on writing this review. On one hand, it's Lord of the Rings and seeing a hobbit trying to play a guitar solo on a harp using the in-game ability to play music is hilarious. On the other hand, it's excessively pay-to-do anything unless you're willing to fork over $15/month, has very little player-player interaction for a mmorpg, and only continues to be engaging because of the large number of areas to explore while leveling up.
LOTRO, in my opinion, has more existing features to promote player-player interaction than maybe even WoW. However, it doesn't really have the player base that would use such features. Skirmishing (a.k.a. raiding) is almost impossible to find a group for outside of a kinsmanship (clan).
If you like LOTR alot and enjoy the individual explorer feel that modern mmorpg's have become, you'll probably enjoy this game. If you want a mmorpg with an endgame, I just don't see it here.

In Trine 2, you play as three alternating characters: a thief (grappling and arrows), a knight (hammer, sword and shield), and a wizard (conjuring boxes and planks for hopping onto). There's lots of platforming and puzzles of various difficulties, from “trivial” to “obvious but hard to execute” to “I hate you so much.”
You don’t need to play the original Trine to play Trine 2, since the mechanics are re-explained and the story was just "find the magical Macguffin." Trine 2 is definitely longer than the original but part of that was repetitively redoing a puzzle or hard platform jumping because the checkpoints are spaced unfairly.
Trine 2's story, involving (without spoilers) a mysterious queen with a secret, was MUCH better than the original. You get bits of the story in cutscenes and dialogue, but you get even more backstory from collectible poems that you have to go hunting in strange places to find.
Pros:
+Good play time. (14 hours for me versus 6 for the original)
+Collectibles add interesting (but optional) puzzles, plus artwork
+Fabulous art (variety of scenic vistas: lava levels, ice levels, sand/temple levels, gross inside-a-stomach levels, beautiful forest levels, etc)
+Good music. Jaunty, fun.
+Wide variety of puzzles of varying difficulty.
+DLC was good. Extra little story, nothing too special, but tons of new areas and puzzles to explore.
+Interesting skill trees
Cons:
-Checkpoints are quite unfair at times, as mentioned before. Often gives you a checkpoint right before and right after an easy puzzle, then you'll have to do 3 major platforming and/or puzzles and then hit a combat situation before you see a checkpoint again. I don't mind having a difficult puzzle with lots of difficult platforming over stuff that will kill you, but for the love of all that is good and holy, you put a checkpoint after it to reward the player for making it through. You DON'T put a battle immediately after it. That's just cruel, and unfortunately, Trine 2 is guilty of this A LOT. Frustrating.
Overall: 8/10.

Quick Summary: 2 dimensional side scrolling platformer with some combat and puzzle solving. There’s more danger than in the first Trine game, both from traps and from enemies. Co-op campaign play is available.
Once again you take on the role of 3 heroes bound by the mystical Trine artifact. Instead of skeletons as enemies, this time most of the baddies are goblins, and the enemies are actually tougher in this game. Not only because they seem to have more life, but they also seem to attack unpredictably at times. Your quest for Trine 2 is defeating the Goblin Menace (and a witch) and restoring peace to the kingdom.
Amadeus the wizard can conjure up boxes and planks for solving puzzles, Pontius the knight can kick goblin♥♥♥♥♥with his weapons, and Zoya the thief can shoot arrows or grapple onto wooden objects for platforming. Just like in the first Trine you only control one of the characters at any time, but you are free to instantly switch to one of the other two as the situation requires.  For example you enter a room and grapple up a ledge as the thief, then switch to the knight to kill all the critters, and finally switch to the wizard to telekinetically stack boxes on switches to exit the room. The game is pretty fast paced so this whole scenario could happen in 30 seconds.
Pros:
+Like the first Trine, the game as amazing graphics and art design, from the monsters to the background and particle effects. Even though the game is 2 dimensional, the incredible detail makes it feel like the background is part of the experience.
+Most of the puzzles are easy enough that casual players won’t be put off. I know I get frustrated playing puzzle games, but in Trine 2 you can run past most of the game if you don’t want to be bothered collecting experience bonuses.
+Unlike Trine 1, you can now reset your skill loadout at any time for free. This means you can easily change your character builds to confront specific challenges or complete specific Steam achievements.
Cons: No real drawbacks.
Trine 2, like the first game is something that every gamer should enjoy. If you’re looking for something to play with a casual gamer or family member, the Trine series is great for this. You’ll probably have the Complete Story edition too that includes the Goblin Menace DLC (with more difficult missions than the base game). Multiplayer coop gameplay is available and you can play with friends or strangers on Steam.

Well bloody done.
i started this game when it was in early Beta and it was already more pollished than a fully released game. (For example the failures of Citadels and Stronghold 3).   It was perfectly stable, clean and best of all, fun.  This gnome management game has only improved since then.  Gnomoria is a top down, micro management game all about the balance between defence and your economy.  To help describe this game, it may be easier to think of it as a simplified dwarf fortress.  So far Gnomoria has recieved numerous and frequent updates throughout the entiety of its developement.  (As you may have noticed, this fact is quite rare.)
Graphics:
The graphics in this game are nothing special.  That being said, its simple, 2d and nice to look at for quite some time.  It fits the gameplay and overall feel of the game.  It doesn't become an eyesore after a few hours like a bad minecraft texture pack.  The only real complaint a perfectionist could have with the graphics is the animation of gnomes moving through tiles, But trust me when i say it irrelavent for this type of game.
The Gameplay:
This is why you play this game.  All the way from the growth rate of trees, to the construction pathways for needed tools and weapons.  The only item that needs work is the settable priority for starage zones and work benches (which the developer has been and continues to work on.)
The core gameplay is all about setting tasks and then the allocation of gnomes to that type of task.  More like running a business than a typical rts.
I must advise all new players build a terrain wall around thier settlement and get the basics before managing combat.
Strengths.
As addictive as minecraft.
Once you set up your economy and defences, its quite easy to play whilst watching a movie or anime.
Weaknesses:
For those who are not patient, do not bother. Completing a task can take days ingame and real time hours.
Can be annoying to debug why a specific task is not being completed.
Summary:
One of the most unique games that i have played in the genre.  Once you get the hang of it, its an excellent game. (just do not expect your first try to do anything other than fail miserably.)
I have easily put over 50 hours into this game.  Its amazing to see a game in beta that is already near the top of its genre.

Pros - Fun casually
Cons - pay2play (lotta grinding if you want everything for free)
- terrible servers (lotta lag and missed inputs)
- characters all play very similiar; there are universal unarmed moves and each weapon has a universal basic attack, only difference is the 3 special moves for each character; a side special, a down special, and a nuetral special, which boiled down are meant for knockouts, ground control and air control respectively
- stats other than attack and defence dont matter due to dodges
- no stagger after missing an attack - most games would have you stagger or linger for a moment after missing an attack, in this game there seems to be either no or minimal stagger allowing oponents to miss an attack and immediately hit you if you try to punish, though it seems random sometimes
- power creep - many new characters that have been released completely outclass older characters due to having straight upgrades to the other characters signature moves
- hitboxes - the hitboxes in this game are terrible,
-  dodge "mechanic" - this makes the hate the game by itself, forget everything else this move kills the game. Generally speaking in fighting games you have to fight the other player by either being aggressive and dishing out punches or being defensive and punishing if the opponent overextends. In this game you have a dodge, which makes you completely invulnerable for a short period of time, not even acknowledging the other players attack allowing you to instantly execute and attack of your own. This makes most ranked games a passive aggressive-fest where 1 person will just wait for the other to finally throw out a move, dodge it and then attack the other. In most other fighting games the game timer will never reach zero, i myself have only ever had it happen once in tekken and never in any other game. In this game ive had many matches reach the 0 mark, and the game timer is 5 minutes compared to street fighter and tekkens 99 seconds. This dodge problem is amplified by there being 2 other dodge types in the game ( i wont go into those).
Overall this game is fun to play casually, and the only good online mode are either the event ones or 4 player FFA, i cant reccommend 1v1 or ranked due to the fundamentally stupid game mechanics. I myself will definately play this game with my friends on ps4 when it (eventually) comes out (also i was plat before i stopped playing so dont call me a noob).

Here we have the
:
After unearthing a strange artifact known as the Marker, Isaac finds himself on the Sprawl, a giant space station in orbit around Saturn. Unable to remember how he got here and plagued with demented visions of his dead girlfriend Nicole, he must survive another nightmarish outbreak of Necromorphs as he fights his way towards an answer he hopes will end all the chaos.
I like this Setting hmmm.Its set on a Space Station! thats orbits Saturn..interesting!
So This Game Has many new and improved features from its predeseccor such as many new suits, new wepaons, new suit abilities and new enemies to name a few. In my honest opinion, his Game takes some steps away from the Bare Horror Genre and mixes it with a bit of mass effect's Special effects. (Both made by EA, hmmmm.) its quite an action packed ride albeit a very short one! There are moments in this game where it gets very fast paced, there are other moments where its very Gory and Shocklingly Tense (In true Dead Space Style). After all, Improvements are the Main things you want to hear after you hear the Word-Sequel. So without Further ado, heres the Good and Bad, simplified..
+the Story is Short, for casual gamers this is Good News! (Approx 10-12 hours on Normal)
+Simplified Mechanics means that Tutorials take less time! yay.
Graphics feel smoother than DS1 and much more mellow colours/themes in levels.
+The Battle isnt just on the sprawl, it also spans a unique conflict in Isaac's Mind, His Mental Health is Greatly affected from the events of the previous game (No Spoilers here) and any chance of "recovery" is......Absolutely Obliterated.
+Plot (although short) is interesting and keeps you interested in the developments and futures for many of the characters.
+So many Upgrades to Choose from (Suits, health, air, armour, ammo and the tough but rewarding "pearl" that is the Work-Bench.
+So many Weapon Variations too! There are 11 Main guns in the Game but each have about 3 different variations for elemental effects or special features that belong with a special suit. Lots of work clearly done here.
+So many New Enemies! yay, there are specific enemies for dark areas, zero-G, Open Halls and even Plastered on Walls! (Euurgh.)
+Voice Acting is Slightly above average, giving Isaac a voice was a risky decision but EA pulled it off alright in the end i think.
+The Atmosphere and Environments! of Course, many new areas are seen in the Story that were only mentioned in the first game. Obviosly the biggest one being a massive Church of Unitology! this really gives a deep insight into the Culture of the Cult members and even some instances of segregation because of it! This kind of detail is rare for a game, especially for a Horror!
+Speaking of Environments, you can now fly/jet around in space in some parts. the controls took me a while to learn however.
+While this might not be a true down to the roots-horror game, its definietely a Gory Ride. Once again Dead Space lives up to its R18 Rating. One Scene Worth Mentioning is the MANUAL Laser eye surgery segment...DONT Screw up!, 'Nuff Said
+Im a Sucker for Hard Difficulties in Horror games, and luckily Dead Space 2 didnt dissappoint: The Impossible Mode from Dead Space 1 has grown into a real man now! Hard-core Gamers can now experience the (Wisely named) Hard-Core mode! The Main feature of this mode is that you now only have 3 Saves to use throughout th whole story, this combined with regular things like OP enemies, low Health and Little to NO Supplies make it a very challenging experience, almost...a Horror Game.
-Its Too Bloody Short! its a breeze on easy and normal. only on hard or above do you really see the kind of experience it intended! Gathering Supplies Really makes the Game a lot more challenging and takes away from the Constant action
-Cutscenes are very Linear and suddenly turn int QTE's when you least expect! (Timing is everything!)
-Some Lag/Frame Rate drops that i experienced. (around 2 per playthrough, not too bad)
-Theres hardly any Boss Battles in the game! and when there is, they are nowhere close to the unique battles that DS1 had!
-Because its a very short game, the time to understand Isaac's "persona" and motivations is drastically reduced. Action>"Mind Battle" with Nicole>Action>Plot>Cutscene>Boss>Action>Repeat. Thats basically a cycle of events really.
-An Abundance of Ammo is great! but DS2 has the opposite.. (in the harder modes this is changed obviously.) This doesnt help the Horror Name of DS2 and really changes it into an Action-Packed one instead. Which is True! For Some people this is good, for others its bad. But the Atmosphere overall doesnt Compare with the Confines of the Ishimura or Tight Spaces in Zero-G from the First Game. Instead, it seems like a Rushed Plot which has good directions for the story but is cut short after the Final Boss (Great Boss though) and isnt explained Clearly. Which is exactly what the Third game is for, wow!! Bloody EA...
I think this game makes many improvments in common areas, but NOT Atmosphere and the Mysteriousness and Scariness that it held deep inside the Ishimura! Story is standard really, which sets itself up for a third game very well. Not as much Backstory as the First game. Which is strange because there is a 3 Year Gap inbetween 1 and 2! BUT Since im such a fan, here is the Order of the DS Series! (To Read, Play and watch!):
Martyr (Book)
Dead Space (Graphic Novel)
Downfall (Animated Film)
Extraction (Wii Game)
First Game
Salvage (Graphic Novel)
Aftermath (Graphic Novel)
Dead Space (Mobile Game)
Ignition (Xbox Minigame)
Second Game
Third/Final Game + the DLC

This game is short, waaay too short for the story that's being told. The grand conspiracy that's set up should have more time to play out, it should all be there, but it isn't. It cuts you off right when you really get sucked in. You're ready to move up the chain of supervillains and take them out, you're ready to unravel the web of lies and maipulation, you're ready to change the world. But hell no, that can be milked for DLC and a sequel, so you don't get that. You get a dissapointing boss that goes down like a ♥♥♥♥♥ once you figure out the pattern, and an ending that leaves you will blue balls.
The mechanics are identical to Human Revolution, if you've played that game you know what you're in for. But the new experimental augmentations are different enough to add a new spice to the game. The addition of overheating and permanently tuning off old augmentations to make room for your new super augs is just poorly done. The idea is that the super augs put strain on your robot parts, and so you have to turn off a locked aug so you don't overheat. They make it seem like you'll explode if you get too overheated, but the only penalty is an occasional screen glitch. That's it. That does not justify PERMINANTLY REMOVING A POTENTIAL UNLOCKABLE SUPER POWER. It just doesn't, but the only way you'd ever know about that is if you ran overheated, which most people won't because they try to scare you out of doing that. It just feels too shady and manupilative.
Your selection of guns and gear is basically the same too, with the addition of one or two tools and a battle rifle.
The side missions are fine, some are pretty good, some aren't. The first boss you encounter is at the end of an optional quest line, and I would consider it more of a miniboss, considering how easy it is to deal with. The best I can say about it is that the story line is prety good and the arena, while small, is decent.
Most of the main story beats hit just where they were meant to. It's simple enough to follow, but intaresting enough to keep you playing. There was never a point where I wanted to shout ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t... Except the ending. You can probably guess who the main bad guy is, beacuse it it exactly who you think. The hardest part about killing the boss is dealing with the flying machineguns that he has following him. Other than that, he is stupidly easy to kill once you figure out how to do it.
Level design is good. Level design is really good, apart from a few peices. Prauge feels like a real city with real people in it. You can explore it at your leasure and the only thing preventing you from reaching a destination is imagination (and sometimes an aug you need to unlock, but there's usually another way around).  The biggest complaint I have is the subway system. I don't know if there are technical limitations that forced them to add a subway, but it feel like it was put in just to pad out the play time. Why else would so many missions REQUIRE YOU TO TAKE A 5 MINUTE SUBWAY RIDE TO AND FROM AND THEN BACK TO THE SAME PLACE. It's insanely frustrating to be forced to take the train back and forth and back and forth and back and forth when each ride takes soo long. Honestly, I think a good hour of my playtime was just subway rides.
And now I'm taking a second to ask what the ♥♥♥♥ is the deal with the hoodie guy? You know the guy, the guy in the trailers with the distinctive orange hoodie, the distinctive face, and who's featured reapeatedly in the trailers. The guy who appears for a grand total of about 3 seconds in game. The only time you see this guy is for three seconds when you pass him on the street. He was created to stand out from the crowd and to be easily identifyable. It seems shady that he's only in it for such a short time. I'd bet there's DLC coming that includes him somewhere. There's no way a throwaway character would be so distinctive.
Guess what, I just looked it up, he's in the DLC. Yay money.
And lastly progression. Oh my sweet glazy baby back jesus, the progression. Because the game is so short compaired to Human Revolution, the time between leveling up is reduced dramatically. In the begining, I thought it was weird that I was powered up to late game level so early, but then I realized the game is 11 hours long without side content and exploring. They HAD to shove praxis points down your throat or else you'd be ridiculously underpowered. I had 12 points waiting to be assigned to unlock augs at one point. I remember when praxis point really meant something, when you had to carefully construct your Adam Jensen to fit your playstyle, now you get face♥♥♥♥ed with them to the point that it might as well not even matter. Oh yeah, and you can buy them with real money. This is a singleplayer game with microtransactions that shorten the game. It makes me upset that they'd do this. It realy makes me upset.
If you're going to buy this game for the story and characters, wait until the entire game is released and bundled into a discounted package. As of now, you're probably going to pay upwards of 100$ to see the full game with periodic DLC releases and geting the rest of the story in bite sized chunks.
If you're going to buy this game to feel like a badass and murder people in the face, then go ahead. It delivers on that front at least.

Anywho, you again play as Isaac Clarke (he's an engineer) and this time Visceral (developer) gave him a voice and that adds another dimension to the game compared to DS1. As with DS1 he finds himself in the same type of living nightmare but this time its three years later and he's on Titan and as per usual things go bad pretty quickly.
Dead Space 2 isn't better or worse than DS1, its just different and there are many aspects that make the game as enjoyable as DS1. There is the same psychosis as previously encountered but things have got a little worse for Isaac. As usual there are many scary moments and while the story has moved on in some ways you start to better understand whats happening. There are many new features in DS2 that add to the depth of the game and I would say some improve on DS1 (get it if you haven't). It certainly adds another dimesion to the series and IMHO is equally enjoyable. Basically its equal to DS1 in many ways and just gives you a different feel to the series but positively so.
The game adds a new feature to the kinesis module and is a great addition which will come in very handy on harder level playthroughs. Its easy to immerse yourself and certainly the sound events will still be making you jump after many many playthroughs. As with DS1 the game is extremely well paced, getting more difficult as you progress and there are a few new 2nd playthrough modes that keep the game fresh. There are also a few benefits for second playthroughs such as acquiring new suit types. The game stays true to the survival horror genre and this time your arrival begins with Isaac in a straight jacket and no weapons to defend himself (not really a spoiler I assure you). Lets face it you will die in this game, how often will depend on your instincts and skills.
As with Dead Space 1, to get the most from this game search areas thoroughly and read, watch and listen to everything you find, your efforts will be rewarded. Play late in the evening with the lights off and headphones on but players of a nervous disposition should be prepared to sweat buckets. Dead Space 2 is yet another classic and you'll soon discover that this game crushes anything you've previously encountered. Well apart from Dead Space 1 that is LOL.

7/10 Single Player, 3/10 Online - Don't beleive the diehard fans rating it 10/10. Let me first say that if you can pick this game up for under $50 with the 8mil cash online, it's worth it for a few days fun, but for the price that I paid, I'm really disappointed. I feel I was scammed into beleiving it was the best thing since sliced bread by the idiots that rated it 100% on metacritic among ohers. Unfortunately you can't beleive the reviews on this one. No, it's not worth the asking price. Single player is worth some fun but Online is frustrating at best. I've played every GTA, but this one is different with a completely different feel (and content) to Single Player and Online. Sure they're both open world, with a few things to do, but both are lacking in a lot of areas. Like others I feel Single Player is pretty good overall, but Online is terrible, so I'll deal with both differently.
Single player took me about 70hrs to get 70% complete (full story done, and most side missions). It's quite fun but there are bugs and for me the storyline was standard GTA fare; linear, predictable and annoying. You are along for a ride, with some free time during the stops. The real standout was the 3 main characters who were totally different but so much fun in their own right. The depth and feel - amazing.
Online is a exercise in multitasking and patience. I bought this game with the 8mil cash card for online and only 3 days later I'm wondering why people would pay $100 for that normally, but also wondering if I can bother playing any more. There are so many issues with online, but the main ones are:
- load times (which is about 30% of your play time) - you need to be able to tab out of play another game while you wait for people to join, wait for various places like your apartment to load etc. Load times are around 1min at best to over an hour for some missions - there's no scale down or bots to speed this up.
- It's a cash grab. Everything is overpriced and they are spamming ads in game to make you buy more, over promising and under delivering. I bought a hangar for 3mil to "start a trafficking empire" so I could earn cash, but you can't. It's completely false. The lack of real information and help in game leads to a lot of money being wasted.
- Modders / Hackers are everywhere. They pop up every few hours and do loads of random things such as respawn everyone together on the same spot then grenade everyone, or spawn around 30 random vehicles, or even spawn money. You have no control over any of this.
All said and done, a lot of other games are far more advanced and/or polished in many different aspects to this game. It's not bad, but it's not good either. R* really need to work on their online stuff though. It's truely horrendous.

Pros - Fun casually
Cons - pay2play (lotta grinding if you want everything for free)
- terrible servers (lotta lag and missed inputs)
- characters all play very similiar; there are universal unarmed moves and each weapon has a universal basic attack, only difference is the 3 special moves for each character; a side special, a down special, and a nuetral special, which boiled down are meant for knockouts, ground control and air control respectively
- stats other than attack and defence dont matter due to dodges
- no stagger after missing an attack - most games would have you stagger or linger for a moment after missing an attack, in this game there seems to be either no or minimal stagger allowing oponents to miss an attack and immediately hit you if you try to punish, though it seems random sometimes
- power creep - many new characters that have been released completely outclass older characters due to having straight upgrades to the other characters signature moves
- hitboxes - the hitboxes in this game are terrible,
-  dodge "mechanic" - this makes the hate the game by itself, forget everything else this move kills the game. Generally speaking in fighting games you have to fight the other player by either being aggressive and dishing out punches or being defensive and punishing if the opponent overextends. In this game you have a dodge, which makes you completely invulnerable for a short period of time, not even acknowledging the other players attack allowing you to instantly execute and attack of your own. This makes most ranked games a passive aggressive-fest where 1 person will just wait for the other to finally throw out a move, dodge it and then attack the other. In most other fighting games the game timer will never reach zero, i myself have only ever had it happen once in tekken and never in any other game. In this game ive had many matches reach the 0 mark, and the game timer is 5 minutes compared to street fighter and tekkens 99 seconds. This dodge problem is amplified by there being 2 other dodge types in the game ( i wont go into those).
Overall this game is fun to play casually, and the only good online mode are either the event ones or 4 player FFA, i cant reccommend 1v1 or ranked due to the fundamentally stupid game mechanics. I myself will definately play this game with my friends on ps4 when it (eventually) comes out (also i was plat before i stopped playing so dont call me a noob).

Eurgava:- Fight for Haaria by Ibrahim Indra Baskara, is a very unique take on the RPG/Strategy genre. It feels like your playing the original Diablo or Diablo II but in a story book mode, with a distinct Middle Eastern feel. This is not a bad thing, I did actually like the movie Sahara! The 1943 version, no the rubbish they made in 2005.
The story is told from the prospective of Heizi a man coming to the end of his Pilgrimage of Knowledge, when an unexpected letter reaches him.  Heizi’s oldest brother and chieftain, gets the seven year itch, packs his bags and buggers off on a journey, leaving no schmuck in charge.  In the absence of a leader, the village is attacked and taken over by raiders.
Heizi is too late to stop the raiders but instead plans to go all Freedom Fighter like and retake his village with the help of friends. At the start you get to chose whom of Heizi’s three friends, Kin, a Labourer, Lashala, a Botanist (has some funky ears) or Patash, a Scribe (and a smurf), gets freed first (looks like you unlock additional friends later in game) and you get to use them as fighters against waves of enemy (Also first fight is your tutorial as to how the game works).
These companions are weak to start with and need to gain kills to then shed as points towards training (that’ll be fifty ears for a pint sir). Fighting is reaction based, you click LMB or double LMB to block or counter attack an enemy (when a green half moon bar shows) and repeated RMB is to attack the enemy (when a circle button appears). Clicks MUST be on the bar or circle or it’s a dirt nap for you. You can stay on and fight each wave and use Heizi or another person called Nisle (looks like Poison Ivy has joined the fight, Suicide Squad II) as Battle Aids but be warned, they take up resource points each time. Or you can opt out at any time between waves and retreat to you camp (Run Forest, Run!) with any goods you have required. Die and you loose everything you have picked up.
Back at your camp you use your plundered loot as resources to start rebuilding your village (Hey look, found this cool ring, I’ll see if it fits…….My Precious!), train or heal your friends, or go through logs (quest & item information when found). The three resources are bronze, food and other is a spice/herb called Shem (make it hash and I’m in!).
It is also here at camp you get to listen to your companions and villages talk about the village and their life and what other evils are happening in the region. The story is nicely carried along in this form but it gets a little repetitive when you are continually retreating from battle, trying to build your resources. At these lower levels you are mostly Guerilla fighting with Guerilla Fighters, it all boils down to monkey business. Until you get your fighters strong enough to make it through several waves.
There is little in the way of options in-game or at menu, just sound and music volume. Music is a nice Middle Eastern style that even though is looped, is very subtle and pleasing.
The reaction base fighting works with this game, but I do find that double LMB is a bit flawed unless you are right on the sweet spot, very annoying when in a four or more fight. A bigger click zone would be appreciated or even clicking on the actual enemy would suffice.  Another bug in the game is your item belt, won’t work by pressing any of your number keys as it states in tutorial but will work by mouse.
The hand drawn environment and characters are also well done and pleasant to the eye and the story is solid and being well told by the characters but it is repetitive at first till you Bling your team to advance the story.
A little frustrating at times, Ibrahim Indra Baskara has made a gem that needs a few tweaks. Eurgava:- Fight for Haaria is one that is good to have in your RPG library. Now that I am done, I am going to do some Dervish Dancing to that rocking Middle East beat.

Rating 9.5/10
Overview: 2d Platformer
The Good:
+ An absolutely gorgeous game both artistically and technically. Every level feels alive yet without being overly distracting towards the player.
+ Every level has its own unique environment. In addition the level design is equally impressive, the game does a great job of slowly introducing harder and harder platforming/puzzle sections. The physics based platforming means you can find solutions that were not intended by the developers.
+ Good blend between puzzles, platforming and combat
+ The gameplay has remained relatively the same since Trine 1. You have 3 characters that you can change at any time to utilize their skills to progress through the level.
+ Killing enemies or finding experience allows you to upgrade any of the three characters.
+ A lot of options to customize the game
+ Soundtrack
+ The DLC is fantastic and in some regards does an even better job of changing the environments every level than the main game.
The Average:
Hard to find an online game, not that big of a deal since the game is probably more enjoyable single player.
Some of the experience in the levels are hard to see given the lighting and backdrop of the levels.
The combat is a bit dull and not as fun. Most combat can be avoided however.
Conclusion:
This is one of my favorite 2d platformers on Steam and should be played by anybody who is a fan of the genre.

//============ Edit as of 3/5/16 ==============//
Updating this review to positive, since the devs (very quickly) addressed the complaints from others and myself about the hunger/thirst mechanic. With the new option to slow the rate of hunger/thirst and logic that pauses them during NPC dialogs, I've enjoyed a couple hours of playing. Changing the hunger mechanic was not a patch in my opinion – it's behavior was not a bug – but an improvement (based on player critique) to a game that had been officially released, and I have great respect for the developers for doing that (and doing it very fast).
I still have concerns about the hunger/thirst mechanic (shouldn't hunger also pause when I'm reading descriptions in my inventory? I just don’t think it’s fun to have hunger constantly increasing when I’m not actively controlling my character), and other real-time mechanics still continue during dialogs (finite-period status effects still count down and disappear while NPC dialog windows are open), but I've enjoyed playing the game a bit now and intend to keep playing. When I feel I've gotten farther into the game I'll try to write a well-considered review of the larger experience.
//==========Original Review===========//
Died of hunger/thirst while reading the dialog with Grandpa that kicks off the game (yes, I read slowly).
The writing is also
weak.
I'm saddened because I find the story intriguing, the graphics great, and most of the game systems fine (from what I saw of them). This game was the first time I've bought something on release day in ages, and I won't be doing it again.
-----------------
Devs: I like the looks of this game - you've clearly put a lot of hard work and heart into it, but forcing users to read-as-quickly-as-possible to avoid death (in a game that makes heavy use of the written word), effectively removes my ability to enjoy the game or feel any significant sense of immersion. Pause the hunger/thirst while dialogs are open and I will revise my review. Less critically, I personally recommend that you find an experienced editor to take a pass through the game's text: the constant use of over-short sentences and lack of adequate punctuation make the reading a slog (e.g., there are many missing commas, and you should use quotation marks to differentiate characters' spoken dialog from other text). The writing issues are mostly stylistic, but the end result is that I feel like I'm reading a paper written by a college freshman.

UPDATED REVIEW 3/3/16
Switched my review from negative to positive thanks to developers quick and responsive tweaking of game mechanics.
Having died several times within the first hour of playing due to starvation/dehydration simply by trying to read Grandpa's initial wall of text and choices and having to step away from the game for a few minutes to make a pot of coffee, I am pleased to see that enjoying the game's storyline or personal needs is no longer a death sentence for my character.
The game still doesn't pause needs while sorting through the many tabs of inventory, and your nourishment levels are still heavily drained by sleeping, which is also a need, so has to be done, but at least with new games you can also choose to diminish food/drink needs when you choose what difficulty you wish to play at.
By clicking that your needs decay at about half the rate they would if left unchecked.
Now to the game....excellent.
It's an open world exploration/crafting/semi-turn based style mirroring the Eschalon and early Divinity games.
Right at the beginning you're given a rune that teleports you to a secret, peaceful glen that you can call home, literally. There you can build a house, fill it with furniture and crafting tables, build farming plots and livestock stables, and as much storage that an OCD pack rat needs. And you can port there at any time you wish.
So far the game seems to have a massive world to explore, full of quests, harvestables, secrets, NPC's, villages, dungeons and lairs. A cornocopia of RPG adventure giddyness.
Mobs are varied, from roaming hostiles to resource meat and leather animals. They can even pop out at you from digging things up, chopping down tree's or other little gotcha moments.
Many NPC's have back stories, some freely given, most wishing to hide some secret, be it personal or main story-wise. The world itself is fleshed out with its own history and lore, intrigue and mystery enough for lore junkies.
It's definitely a worthy game for RPG fans who like big open worlds, crafting, exploration, open-ended character development, a home to call their own in, and an epic mystery to solve.
For the price and the content within it, this game is definitely worthy of any adventure gamer.

A nice little game well worth the small price. Beware though as it's not just an rpg, it's a SURVIVAL/CRAFTING rpg, which means that survival ( finding food, water, etc ) and crafting can take a huge part of your time.
It's the kind of game that you can probably play for dozens of hours, I already played several hours ( offline ) and I'm still at the beginning, trying to make a few bucks to buy skills, looking for recipes, food and stuff. Understanding game mechanics can take a bit of time too.
So, you play a little retared boy who couldn't find his way around a bush if his life depended on it, and your grandpa asked you to investigate the disapearence of your neighbors, whose house burned down for an unknown reason, but it was definitely not aliens. Probably Satan or something. A woman abused by his drunk husband found a strange tablet in the burned house, and you try to figure out what's written on it while running errands for everybody like a true hero ( feeding pigs, collecting bees, picking up mushrooms, etc. ) Even the village idiot thinks you're his b*tch.
Anyway, you'll quickly discover that the people of this peaceful village all seem to have their little secret, which makes things interesting. And I'm pretty sure I'm gonna save the world or something.
There are secrets to discover, dungeons to explore, loot to loot and mobs to fight. Sometimes the danger comes from your own backpack, as a worm can spawn in it and eat all your food.
The game has some minor design flaws, annoyances or elements that could easily be patched, but that could be a no-go for some people :
- you can't run
- you have to drink/eat/rest quite often ( but not quite that often if you over-eat and over-drink until you're full, it lasts much longer )
- you have to pay for every skill, and it's expensive
- the game is kinda slow ( slow movement, slow progression )
- you have to figure out almost everything by yourself
- you can't walk through grass and bushes, or crops, collisions everywhere
- giant spiders
- giant INVISIBLE spiders
- giant TELEPORTING spiders
- no comparison window between items
- the south is to the left ( what ? )
- you can't auto-reorder your inventory

DLC Quest is a satire of recent trends in the video game industry (based on the game's release) where companies are forcing more and more DLC and microtransactions on the players. Thus, this game is based more on its message and theme rather than giving a solid gameplay experience with story and impresssive design.
This game takes a somewhat retro graphical style mixed with a typical fantasy theme. The music is made up of chiptune tracks to fit in with the retro visuals. The story is as simple as saving a princess or saving a village from a bad guy, which are commonly seen in other games that aren't parodic in nature. These things though are the not very important parts to be looking for in this game. They get the job done by looking good enough from a technical standpoint to drive the game, since these three things are parodies of commonly seen styles and tropes in other games.
Even though this game is a parody and satire of video games, there is some actual gameplay to be had. The player runs and jumps to collect coins and somethimes kill things in this platformer game. To unlock new "features", the player needs to spend their coins on DLC and microtransactions, somewhat mirroring the real world with exaggerations. The gameplay ranges from easy in the first episode to a sightly more difficult, but not hard difficulty in the second episode.
Does the game satirize the video game industry well? It does do so in a blunt, exaggerated manner which ends up being silly game expansions the player has to buy. If the game isn't poking fun at video game companies, it then has parodies of games, ranging from making fun of certain game genre conventions to referencing specific video games. Not all the humor will leave people laughing out loud, but it should give a small laugh or chuckle for the things DLC Quest parodies.
DLC Quest should be taken as a game with a message, and it does bring some silliness when it comes to parodying the games industry. This game is definitely short, easy, and low priced, which should give a decent amount of time for the money. With a satirical and comical approach to DLC and microtransactions, this game is great for the humor along with decent platforming collectathon gameplay on the side.

Even though this game is getting a bit "old" I would still like to review this game.
The story is around 15 hours long and follows isaac clark, he woke up in a space ship after 3 years of being a "patient".
You will quickly realize that there is something wrong on the ship, its filled with necromorphs (aliens) like in the first game.
You are being guided by someone called daina, on your way through you will come across more people for example Stross also known "Patient 5" who keeps contacting you troughout the game, about the "marker" which attractes/creates necromorph's.
You will also meet someone called "Ellie" she will be helping you troughout the game and you will be helping her as well.
The gameplay is solid, the controlls are good and everything works more then well no cringy controls altough I felt like isaac's movement was a bit slow at times, especialy on parts where you where forced to sprint.
The aiming system works really solid as well, there where no annoying issue's which the first game had (where the aiming would be really slow even when you are playing on the highest sensitivity, thankfully this game has no mouse issue's at least not for me.
The game also manages to suprise me everytime, and I sat on the tip of my chair to my whole playtrough waiting for a jumpscare to come.
The environment is really well designed as well, its dark and scary most of the times and the power will often cut out and fill the area with necromorphs lurking from the darkness.
The puzzels in this game are quite intresting as well, they are not really hard to do but they managed to make me think of how to solve them for a little bit.
The game also allows you to use a store, where you can buy weapons, ammo, medkits, and even suits, the credit system works well and doesnt give you too much, but enough to make you reconsider what you buy at times.
You can also find or buy "power nodes" which allow you to upgrade your, suit, weapons or unlock storage rooms which are mostly filled with loot, you have to spend your power nodes really carefull as well, even though i felt like the damage upgrade barely did anything.
The enemy design is really great and creepy as well, i often found myself aiming for the legs to kill to slow them down, or cut of one arm and shoot it back at them, shooting at the head wont often result in a kill since they will continue to walk towards you.
The audio is really well designed as well, the voice acting was more then great and i often felt like the characters where really in pain, especialy isaac's voice, Thanks alot Gunner Wright for this awesome voice performance.
Well comming to a verdict now I would say the game never dissapointed me, has a great story and audio design
the story was really great as well and the ending was really amazing as well.
This game deserves a solid 9/10.
Thanks alot for reading everyone!

This game can be fun, but it's too random to be consistently fun.
The game features random rooms with random enemies with random buffs that you fight with an assortment of random weapons and random perks.  The inconsistency of the weapons and perks you get from run to run pose the problem; with a good build you should be able to handle any room the game throws at you.
When you level up you choose between two perks.  However, some perks are temporary, and the perks are all over the place in terms of usefulness, so you can end up halfway through the game with a very bad character.
You gain a weapon at the start of each floor.  The weapons are all fairly solid, but as they're randomly obtained there's no guarantee that you will ever get a complete arsenal, and you might get several weapons that serve the same purpose.
As an example I frequently obtained perks that increased the mana pool for weapons I didn't have and never got, because the other perk choice was temporary or was an overall penalty.  As another example I have beaten the game without finding a Staff.
An additional poor design choice unrelated to randomness is that experience is a drop the player must pick up and will despawn after some time.  This in and of itself isn't that bad, but when combined with the number of area denial attacks present, the player is often forced to choose between taking damage and missing out on XP; both options are bad.
While the gameplay is polished, how well you do in any particular run is largely up to chance.  If you have the inclination for that style of game then go for it.  It's just not my thing.

Sure I haven't played Diablo 3 and it's been around 6 years since I last touched Diablo 2 (and I doubt it works too well on Win7 anyway) but Jesus #nal ♥♥♥♥, there's really not many differences to it.
Second is that the game itself is a bit lacking on content. It does have a VERY dedicated modding community to fix it's issues, and even the ex-friend who gifted me the game told me to play it with mods, however some mods might even make the whole thing worse. In my case I've been trying to play it with the Synergies mod which adds an insane amount of content, classes and such to the game... But at the same time pretty much multiplies the amount of enemies on every area up to 2 or even 3, making the whole damn thing becoming repetitive and way too slow. Think of Half-Life, but changing every Head-crab encounter for instead being 5 each time one was supposed to appear. It's not fun, and there's a bunch of mods like these out there that instead of fixing it, make it even worse.
Something I also don't like is the draw distance of enemies. You enter a new dungeon and after taking 3 or 4 steps ALL of the enemies in the next room and maybe the other one too come all rushing at you at the same time. How f#cking fun it is to enter a new area and suddenly have a ton of enemies throwing projectiles at you before you have even noticed which way you gotta go. I seriously would have made it more wide, making enemies target you once you get more close.
Then come pets. I'm not really sure why they're here, it feels like a developer's aftertought. Ranged characters will get instantly crushed and need something to tank the damage. OH I KNOW, PETS. If instead of getting a random animal from the start of the game which servers no story-related purpose the game had a story character tagging along with you, serving the same combat purpose, I would've gotten way more interested in playing this. They're just there to tank damage and make the narrator constantly repeat YOUR PET IS GREATLY WOUNDED, YOUR PET IS FREEING, YOUR PET HAS FLED, almost made me mute the sound for a while.
Lastly, the story. I did like the intro animated cinematic, it looked great! I was really expecting the game to have an interesting story after it! ...Sadly I've played... What, 10 hours of the game? And all I can tell about the game is that a guy with tons of armor goes around beating people to heal some weird sickness by killing other stuff. That's it. Sacred had a mediocre storytelling and even that looks like f#cking Shakespeare when put aside to this game.
However, does the game do something good? Yeah. Don't get the wrong idea, I do think the game has flaws. I won't put a Recommended on it mainly because there are better alternatives on my opinion, but the game does have some solid points going on for itself.
The gameplay, taking away some weak points it's like a Diablo game made in the modern days. I would say Diablo 3, but I haven't played that one (and I probably never will anyway). Lots of weapons, lots of loot, a bunch of different classes that have their weakness and strong points, the only real problem I could find on that is the game not really explaining much of each class before choosing one.
The graphics are also appealing to the eye, I like them! Instead of something very detailed, its cartoony and fresh. I sure as hell wouldn't have used an HUD that looks so damn close to Diablo, but that's a personal opinion.
The sound department is also okay. Voices don't sound annoying or are used too much, without counting the damn narrator and his pointless comments. Seriously, why they felt the need to show you in text that you leveled up AND also have the narrator tell you about it? I GET IT, STOP. The music is also okay, and goes along nicely with the action.
Coop is also a strong element here, and I would totally recommend anyone who buys the game to play it with at least one friend. Makes the experience way more enjoyable.
I will repeat myself again, I don't think this game is bad. It's okay, but on my opinion there are better alternatives. If you want to play Diablo, go play f#cking Diablo. They're not in Steam, but you can find them in a lot of DRM-Free pages, at stupidly cheap prices. Maybe also on Blizzard's services, but I don't touch those too often. If you want something for Steam, try Sacred 1. Bigger world, better atmosphere, it's downsides being an old, dead multiplayer option and some compability issues with modern computers. Besides, Sacred 1's base price is half of Torchlight 2's.
TL;DR Edition: A decent clone of Diablo with some somewhat fresh aditions, however I don't feel like it's worth paying 20€ for a light version of the original when you could just buy Diablo 1 or 2 for way less money. If you want something similar on Steam, and also cheaper, try Sacred 1. Way more fun.

There are some genuinely great improvements to what Human Revolution established, but in a number of other ways it feels like there were some elements of the design that seemed rushed or overlooked. Sometimes I'll be able to take out an enemy over a  desk from cover, sometimes I'll be standing right behind them and no takedown context triggers.
Another annoying issue is that some game elements were really only optimised for consoles and no changes were made for the PC. The hacking minigame especially seems to be filled with giant information tabs that stop you from getting an overview, it seems clear that it was designed to be read on TV screen while sitting on a couch and not sitting in front of your monitor. Similarly, the inventory screen seems to be built for consoles and the drag and drop system doesn't work in a lot of cases.
These things shouldn't be considered gamebreaking issues but they are enough to make it feel like a less enjoyable experience overall.

Ok, so I pre-ordered DXMD and completed it on "Give Me Deus Ex" level along with all side missions within just 2 days of release. After I completed it I uninstalled it and didn't bother writing a review as they were already negative and explaned the issues fully. I really wanted to enjoy this game, as I have had great fun in Human Revoulution and for most of my playthrough I was having fun. However this game ended up being a great let down to me and I'll tell you why...
+ Beautiful Visuals & effects
+ Smooth/fluid gameplay & controls
+ Great ambient theme & soundtrack
+ Immersive environment
+ Good sound design (apart from gun sounds)
From the above you are probably wondering why this is getting a bad review, but the thing is this game lacks severly in major areas. I want to get this one off my chest quickly. Deus Ex games have always had multiple "hubs", where you can roam around environments freely, exploring, recieving quests and buying items. However DXMD only has 1 hub, which ruins the global travel theme shown in the games before it.... and ooohhhh boy the worst part about this game is the embarrasing lack of content.
I don't blame the developers at all, it seems like Square Enix had just cut large amounts out of the game to pump out later as dlc. This games story was great for the first 5 hours of gameplay, however it turned to litteral♥♥♥♥♥♥afterwards. I have seen Call Of Duty pull off better stories than this, honestly it is less than half the length of the story in DXHR and it certainly wasn't quality over quantity. One thing they advertised and hyped up, was the supposedly "important" decision making, but it ended up being almost non-existent. Instead of your choices being reflected in gameplay, it only changes what is shown on Picus News near the end of the game.
, no joke it has to be the worst ending they could have possibly come up with lmao.
I cannot recommend this game at full price, maybe if it's under £10 you should buy, infact I would wait for a directors cut version where they give you the content they took in the first place. A massive let down to DX fans, everyone would prefer Human Revolution, buy that instead if you get the chance.
I'm also worried people will be fooled into buying this game as they keep dropping prices for the main game & DLCs.
. These price drops, and the introduction of Breach being free-to-play show that Square-Enix is bent on trying to squeeze as much money out of this game as they possibly can.

Bloody Walls is very weird in a good way. I like the unique gameplay mehanics this game features
You are placed in a room and zombies will attack you from left and right side, and as soon as they touch you once, you are dead...and you will have to start game from beginning. You can't jump, so you are forced to clean one side first so you can move backwardswhile shooting zombies on other side. There isnt health, however there are "antidotes", each antidote lasts for 60 seconds, and if you run out of them you are dead. Antidotes are also used as currency
There are 10 different floors, first one has npcs which will give you small quests to collect certain items and there is also small shop which sells you 2 more guns and some landmines. Other floors are filled with mobs and you need to clean them to beat the game. Every floor has same design, however there are alot of different and interesting mobs in them.
Very weird thing in this game is shooting, i didnt like it at first, but as i played more it made me realise there are many different mob designs which work only with this shooting system. You need to click on enemies in order to shoot, you can't just shoot randomly, you have to click on correct spot like mob's head in order to shoot.
Game is pretty short, but since its completly restarted every time you you die, it can take you fair amount of time to beat it.
One more really weird thing i've noticed is that low settings gave me 40 fps and highest 60fps.

Trine 2 is everything the gorgeous, satisfying, and creative original Trine was, just a little greater. Each character has a greater selection of abilities which means a greater range of solutions to every problem. The greater number of levels each feel themselves greater: more entrancing, more extravagant, more epic. The storyline... hasn't changed much, which is to say that it still barely exists and that still suits the overall experience. There's no need to play this series in order as there's so little to miss. Even mixing levels from the later Goblin Menace expansion into the main campaign of the original wouldn't lead to much confusion, save for the loss of all those new abilities. The new highest difficulty, however, is noticeably more punishing than the original's, and sadly this isn't a good thing. Trine 2's Hard plus Hardcore setting has more of an effect on combat than any other aspect, which is by far the game's weakest feature. Trine is, after all, a puzzle game at its core and once established, it's difficult to make a puzzle harder without mucking it up with added complexity. And complexity isn't what Trine's about. It's about relatively simple people on a relatively simple quest acting creatively.
Not a bad time if you've got two friends to play it with you.

Been watching this game progress for about a year. Booted it up, started a character on Master difficulty. Died so many times that I... insert Dark Souls meme joke here.
YMMV, but Master difficulty t'aint fer thee faint o' haart, laddy!
I've only played ~10 hours, but I feel like that's enough time to get a good impression of the game and leave a review for those of you who are still on the fence. If you like CRPGs...
BUY IT NOW!!! It's more than worth the price. It's a bit like Eschalon, for those of you who've played that game, but Balrum is expanded and improved in just about every way. It's a touch o' the old Ultima Online about it, too. Just a touch. And it's a good touch. Not a bad touch.
I'm rather eager to get back to playing, so LET'S DO THIS THING:
Brutal, rewarding difficulty? Check. See inserted Dark Souls meme above. (My last death was to a giant praying mantis that prayed away my mana, poisoned me with its horrifying pincers, and healed itself when I finally had it down to a sliver of health. I died to poison as I ran for shelter, sobbing.)
Varied, multidimensional crafting? Check. I can't even. The crafting is strong with this one.
Free-form base building? Check. Build a house, build a fortress, build an orchard, build a farm, build a pigpen, build a spiderpen. DON'T LEAVE THE GATE OPEN ON THE SPIDERPEN FOR THE LOVE OF web web web venom venom death
Customizable pet? Check. I'm currently running with a giant shadow-magic-wielding rat named Boggles. And that praying mantis monstrosity I was telling you about? Also tameable. The world shall fear my giant green bug... as soon as my skill-level is high enough to tame giant green bugs.
Stats? Check. I almost came to tears over stat distribution. The game is neither kind nor generous, but I must have Stockholm syndrome, because I don't even car.
Care.
Skills? Check. More in-depth than the stats, I felt. Most skills have at least two significant effects, and sometimes three or four. And again, the game does not hand out "learning points" often, so they really matter. Ranks in the Survival skill don't just let you heal more HP at the tents you build, they also let you cure ailments like broken bones, increase the light radius of your torch, slow Fatigue/Hunger/Thirst growth rates, and give you a double digit % chance to avoid death whenever you hit 0 hp.
THAT'S A SKILL, BETHESDA.
Varied spells, combat and utility? I think so! (I just came across a teleportation spell that I hope to use mischievously. Combat spells are most certainly varied. I've been using one that creates crystalline walls to great effect.)
Factions? Check, the system is there and the character sheet has a faction affiliation section, but I'm not far enough to have actually... affiliated.
Giggity.
M-to-the-ASSIVE world to explore? Check. You have no idea. I've barely mapped out ¼ of the first map, and that's not including dungeons, chests I couldn't open, beasts and the locations they guarded that I couldn't tackle yet, etc.
Secrets and treasures and quests in every nook and cranny as far as the eye can see?
Check-checkity-check-check-check.
Brutal, immersive survival elements? Balrum is to Minecraft as Saw is to Teletubbies.
Or maybe I should reverse that?
Teletubbies are pretty scary.
Balrum is to Minecraft as Teletubbies are to Danny Devito.
...
...
I mean Check.
Dying of dehydration? Find a well, eat a watermelon, collect falling rainwater (if it's raining, newb) and fill your cantine, or heck, collect swampy puddle water in a bucket if you're desperate. (Pray it doesn't have maggots in it.)
Dying of starvation? Hunt deer, chop down a tree, build a campfire with the wood, cook the meat on the spot, eat the meat. Or shoot a newborn fawn with a fireball, skip the campfire stage, and eat fire-ball-grilled baby-meat with half the effort. Then find an outhouse. (Outhouse for roleplaying purposes only. Assembly required, pooping optional.)
Oh, and one time I found a bug in my character's backpack eating all the apples I'd just picked. I squashed the little bugger (lol) with my bare hands. Don't touch my apples. ACTUAL THING THAT HAPPENED IN THE GAME SERIOUSLY.
I've not run into any major bugs so far. (Except the one in my backpack.) The game has a classy, retro look that I absolutely dig.
It's a really good CRPG. There's less choices in dialogue than there should be, (at least in the first main area, which I'm still in,) the writing can be a bit too info-dumpy, and I have yet to find any Necromantic skeleton-army-animating spells, but apart from that, it's a real gem.
TL;DR: For the current price of thirteen-ish USD, Balrum is a criminal steal.
