The next thing I noticed was a much more linear progession. The Tatau system from Vanilla FC3 was replaced with a simplistic "Earn XP to get to this level to unlock this ability" system, which I found useless after Level 20 out of 30. This plus the annoying "complete this task to get this Weapon's attachment" made it a bit more of a challenge to become a super-soldier, which took me a lot longer than the game's story.
Moving on to said story, I'm mixed. I detested the arcady/8-bit style cutscenes, skipped them all because I couldn't stand them. Don't know why they chose this over normal cutscenes. Anyway, the story was interesting. You had a guy who acted similarly to Duke Nukem in his quotes etc against your typical bad guy who wants to "fix the world" in his twitsed evil way. While very Hollywood I found the story hilarious as it didn't take itself seriously whatsoever. The last bit of gameplay includes
Admitedly, I probably only enjoyed Blood Dragon because of its Far Cry 3 roots. Had I bought this standalone I would have hated it. This game is what Paranautical Activity should have been, but it was not.
Basically, what you need to know:
-there are lots of magic spells to use AND to unlock
-multiple characters that each have their strenght and weakness
-a lot of monsters, more or less fair(talkin' about those homing shots monsters)
-carrrots. That's a monster... and a thing...
-leveling up is harsh but satisfying, unlocking new abilities as you go trough. Your level is reset to 1 after each death.
-there are bosses you need to fight to progress trough the levels, but each of them need a key that you have to find around the map. This mechanic can be annoying from time to time, but I like it from the usual "Find the boss and fight him"
-and lastly, the game is a roguelike genre! That means you can play as much as you want, and (potentially) not get bored sooner or later.
As a final verdict, the game is fun to mess around with, casting spells left and right, I give it a 9/10, just because of the homing shots monsters. Seriously. They are annoying, especially on the last floor, where the rooms are flooded with them. Why ;-;
So yeah, 9/10, would kill carrots by casting skulls at them again.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided - it's an interesting game. Overall, the gameplay and mechanics have been greatly improved from Human Revolution. The new cover system is a big improvement, stealth mechanics are more realistic and there are more ways than ever to sneak past enemies or to complete a mission. There is a ton of exploring to do - Prague is a massive city hub with tons of optional side missions, and every area has hidden away rooms or hard-to-find items that can change what happens later.
Mankind Divided doesn't finish all of what Human Revolution left behind - it wasn't intended to. Rather, it's more like another chapter in an unfinished book. But although there are several hints, the last mission doesn't quite make it clear that this is the end of the game. Because of this, the game can end pretty abruptly.
As for the ending itself, the game did a decent job of wrapping up everything that happened since it began, and it also answered a few other questions. Mankind Divided also handles multiple endings slightly better than Human Revolution, as you'll have to put in a bit more work to view all the endings.
Despite all that, the game is still decently long, mostly due to the abundance of side missions and the sheer size of Prague. I found it took me 30 hours to finish both Mankind Divided and Human Revolution (Director's Cut).
So overall, this is a good game. The story was a bit lacking but everything else was very good. I'd probably give it an 8/10.

Deus Ex is no longer a complex yarn of grey aliens, super computers, and classic conspiracy stories. Now it's a complex yarn of arms dealers, international terrorism, and the subjugation of minority groups. These are the broad strokes of Human Revolution up close and personal with Adam Jensen's world now entering an era of - in Eidos' own words - "mechanical apartheid"; a new age where augmented individuals are feared and bullied by the "natural" people and their Illuminati puppet masters.
The writers' use of a provocative term like "apartheid" is emblematic of the distance between this sequel and its forbears and is just one of the controversial ingredients that has made this game so divisive. And the hard truth is that for every actual scene of persecution that Mankind Divided depicts, none of it ever really conveys a meaningful message beyond the basic sentiment of 'prejudice is bad'.
If you go into this game looking for an insightful comment about the topic of prejudice then you're going to be massively disappointed. If however, you're more concerned with sneaking about, hacking computer terminals, and using explosive harpoons to pin mobsters to walls, then you're going to have a much better time of things.
In gameplay terms, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a wonderful distillation of all the things that made its prequels so great. Eidos Montreal have put considerable effort into their world building and throughout Prague; where most of the game's events take place, you'll discover many interactive areas that feel alive with possibility.
It's easy to get lost in this sprawling metropolis, though you probably won't mind too much if only because you'll get more time to appreciate the gorgeous in-game graphics. The art style might look a tad plainer when compared to Human Revolution's gaudy orange sheen, but Prague is a more pragmatically realised environment than Detroit ever was and the sheer amount of hi-res clutter that goes with that approach is likewise very impressive.
Mankind Divided plays like a dream too. The array of control schemes are smart, tutorial pop-ups are superbly integrated, and the dependable thrills in both the stealth and action-based slices are just as fun as they've always been. The mission levels are tremendous in their scope and yet they never betray that trademark Deus Ex quality of allowing multiple routes around any given problem.
In one instance I found myself trying to get into a locked apartment. I was sticking to a strict 'no hacking' policy at the time so accessing the front door was a no-go. I hadn't spotted the precarious ledge that might allow me in through the open window so I checked the adjoining apartment and found a ceiling grate that could get me in through an air vent; classic!
Sadly, the damn thing was too high off the ground in order for me to reach and I didn't have enough Praxis points to spring for the enhanced jumping ability that could get me up there. Now granted, my eventual solution of using Adam's strength augmentation to upturn the downstairs fridge as a platform was not very elegant, but it got the job done and once again highlighted why Deus Ex is so revered for its thoughtful mission design.
It's a shame when bugs have to upset this rhythm. I've experienced the odd CTD, a number of flickering textures, disappearing gun turrets, and some badly glitched NPCs. What's also strange is the near terrible waypoint system. The map screen itself is fairly robust and useful, but the crucial waypoints that lead to your next objective are extremely unreliable and often direct you to the wrong place entirely.
I became impossibly stuck in one mission because my HUD marker had sent me into an endless loop starting at the top of a particular elevator shaft. It took an arduous Google fact-finding tour to work out where I'd gone wrong which was a huge shame seeing as how tense and exciting the mission had been up until that point.
The final mission may well be the highlight of the game too and overall the journey as a whole does not feel as short or truncated as was suggested in earlier previews. Deus Ex: Mankind Divided does feel like a complete and worthy chapter in the Deus Ex canon, but I will agree that the awkward ending format - that revolves around a bunch of choices that ultimately make no real difference to anything - creates an abrupt feeling that screws up the catharsis of the game's conclusion and can potentially lead to another infamously flat finish.
Mankind Divided doesn't need much of a hand in the infamy stakes either as Square Enix's rage-inducing inclusion of microtransactions, into what has always been a dedicated single player game, does a better job at spoiling things than any weak ending or off-colour headline could ever do. The main menus and the new alternative gameplay mode called Breach are host to microtransactions of a truly insulting pedigree from the paid-for Praxis Kits and wholly unnecessary credit boosters to Breach Mode's booster packs.
Breach mode is an arcade-style side attraction set in a world that looks like the movie Tron, and aside from a few good ideas, it’s a mostly enjoyment free experience that has you chasing a carrot that you never get a chance to eat.
The microtransactions tailored for Breach, that unlock everything from advanced weaponry to cheat-based power-ups, are almost essential for anyone looking to tackle the mode's hardest missions and there's the rub; why is Square Enix expecting you to pay more money in what is already a full price AAA release? And more to the point, why is this promoted in a mode that is single player only? The publisher here is actually expecting you to pay money to compete with yourself as Breach is nothing more than a single player experience with score attack leanings; that's it.
The screen entry for these exorbitant purchases aren't correctly rendered either with certain packs featuring incorrect labels and even spelling errors. It's a sorry state of affairs to see such a once lauded series being associated with this embarrassing nonsense and to think that valuable programming time was wasted here is just nauseating.
The hangover from Mankind Divided's abandoned 'augment your pre-order' scheme is still present in the "free" DLC mission that's ironically titled Desperate Measures. In this standalone chapter (that's completely walled off from the main game) Jensen goes out looking for a mad bomber and you can clearly see the seams of what used to be a side quest before it was unceremoniously snipped out and offered up as a "separate" piece of exclusive content.
Clearly Square Enix are keen to release another director's cut edition somewhere down the line, but doing so in such an artificial and invasive way is extremely galling and it's a rare player indeed who will find derive enjoyment from side content that cannot yet be integrated with the main campaign mode.
I take no pleasure in bringing down Deus Ex: Mankind Divided because as a moment-to-moment experience it is certainly up there as one of the best entries in the series. There are plenty of little touches I've not yet mentioned; the tweaked XP yields, the moody cutscenes, and the restrained use of the "I never asked for this" meme are just so commendable and overall it's still a joy to walk in Adam Jensen's shoes and think about all the crazy stuff you'll get up to next.
However, Square Enix needs to re-evaluate their approach for the inevitable sequel and if they really are keen on developing this new Deus Ex Universe of theirs then they need to seriously consider the damage they're doing to the brand's image with their anti-consumer practices.

What can I say other than, absolutely brilliant. There are so many things I could talk about when discussing this masterpiece.
The game drops you in a dark area, with no objective, and nothing but a torch and an Automatic Kalashnikov for company. The lack of an objective or any instructions really brings out the survival horror elements of the game, showing the player of the chaotic world they are about to find themselves in.
You can't go too far without noticing the harsh reality you suddenly find yourself in. The world has been overrun with infected humans, and these flesh craving beings will stop at nothing to tear you apart, limb from limb. Your character, dressed in blue and armed and deadly, must protect himself from these hellish things the only way he can, with his Shooting iron and his wits. You can only shoot in the direction you are facing, and the only way to turn is to walk, this is some next level immersion, true survival grit, and a very daring move for the devs. This has payed off, as I found myself completely immersed in the game, and it really brings out its survival horror elements.
The zombies I found to be quite realistic, and their movement patterns, as well as their movement speed, are very reminiscent of games such as Left 4 Dead. The scarcity of ammunition is such an important addition to the games whole survival feeling, and running out of ammunition can really bring out the best survival elements of the game.
At the bottom of the screen, there is a counter for ‘Lazer’, set at 0, which, to me, symbolized the lack of a future for the character, and it was up to the player to destroy as many zombies as possible in order to change the future of the character, and indeed, the world he lives in.
I really love the lack of a menu, as it symbolizes the lack of options humanity has in this post-apocalyptic world. The Resolution is locked at 800x600, the optimal resolution for playing this masterpiece. Pressing Esc does absolutely nothing, symbolizing the inability for your character to escape the situation he is in. At the end of the park you find yourself in, there is a large pink circle with “Evacuation Zone” written on it, showing that your character has no way out, and must fight until the end.
The lack of a soundtrack really draws the player into full immersion, as all you can her is the sound of the darkness.
Graphics: 10
This game just looks fantastic, the zombies are terrifyingly realistic, the ground and tree textures look almost photorealistic.
Sound: 10
The game has no soundtrack, and it doesn’t need one, all of the sounds add to the horror elements, as I felt like I was really there.
Functionality: 10
I encountered absolutely no glitches during this game. I did see a few invisible ZOEDS, but I am sure that was intentional, a completely new enemy type.
Overall, I have to give this game a 10 out of 10, and recommend it to anyone who enjoys survival horror games, horror games, survival games, zombie games, or just games in general, theres something for everyone here. A must buy.

Overall, I liked this game.
The art was absolutely outstanding; the combat, though... meh. Most combat consisted of button mashing to victory, and returning to the last checkpoint when my damage dealers died (which, by the way, does not reset enemy health or numbers). So, the only gripe I had with the game was that there were virtually no consequences to screwing up. As a result, I found myself not nearly as interested in combat toward the end as I was toward the beginning.
The puzzles were unique enough to keep me interested, and not hard enough to have me bash my head against my desk. I loved that there were often multiple ways to solve puzzle (given that the interactable objects are bound to a physics engine). In fact, for one puzzle, I completely bypassed the mechanic I could see the developers wanted me to use, and instead propped open a gate with some boxes I conjured up, then ran under the gate, moving the boxes with me.
I feel it fair to say, though, that given the short game duration (~12 hrs for me), I cannot recommend the game at the $20 pricetag. If, like me, you are not an achievement hunter, this game doesn't have much replay value. Wait for it to go on sale.

Well, this was fun as all heck. Probably the most entertained I've been in a multiplayer game since Torchlight 2.
...Except for that part when we were being attacked by rejects from the Dune setting. That wasn't fun. Should've seen the giant sandworms coming, really.
I played Trine 2 with friends, and can't honestly imagine how anybody manages it on single player, though (I presume it adapts to the number of players present and adjusts the difficulty accordingly) because it required a fair bit of teamwork for us to get through most of the levels. I'm not sure how the game manages that level of interaction in single player mode. Still the story was fun, the game-play was creative and the environments were beautiful to look at. I loved the illusion of depth, considering that we were playing on a 2D screen. Not to mention the amount of gut-wrenching laughs we had playing this together whenever one of us messed up. I've never been so entertained by failing in a game before. (I'm sorry, RR, but dropping boxes on your head because you keep destroying the bubbles we're using to travel will never stop being funny.)
There were moments I considered flawed - some puzzles weren't especially intuitive, but the game provided several ways to solve each individual crisis. There were a couple of minor glitches and boss battles were nothing short of frustrating. But the rest of the game more than made up for it. Definitely a good use of a few hours, though could've done with a couple more hours of play (even considering we had the DLC, it felt very short). I'd definitely suggest getting this with the intent to play with friends rather than alone.

Bloody Walls is a short, fun, and interesting Indi game that grabbed my attention based on the graphics alone. Now this game has got some updates that have changed how the game plays from when I played 1.00, so I will state some of these changes.
The story of Bloody Walls is a terrible accident happened at a bio-weapon research facility, which has caused the whole world to become infected and turn into mutants/zombies. There is an antidote that can block the infection temporary, thus making it very valuable, and becoming the currency. You have to make it to the last floor of the lab to find a large amount of the antidote (and thus win the game.)
Now right off the bat, the game tells you VERY little on controls and how to play. It's not hard and very easy to learn. You can only shoot the mutants by shooting them in the head (or weak spot,) which will also give you a number below them. This number is your (Damage %.) The closer they are, the closer to 100 it is. Getting 100 means you are dealing full damage. Now you have no health, if an enemy touches you, GG you lose and have to start over. When you move in this game, the camera doesn't actually follow you and keep you in the middle of the screen. The camera more or less will "lazily" follow you, and will "reset" onto you when you get to far to the sides, or if you right click. Thankfully in a later patch, the speed of the camera has been increased so it's not as jarring as it originally was. The player moving speed was also increased a bit in the same patch.
Now originally there was only 1 difficulty, but now there is 2, Easy and Hard (the original difficulty.) This decides on how much antidotes you start with. Easy having 45 and Hard having 5. You also have side missions where you will have to collect an item from a lower level, and bring it back to them and they would give you a code to open up the safe/box to get your reward. Originally you had to go BACK to the same floor to open the safe, but in a recent patch, the safe/boxes are all right beside the NPC that gives you the quest.
As I said, the main reason why I played this game was the graphics. It has the old Nintendo GameBoy colour pallet, but with the extra bloody red added to the mix. It's a very simple pixel art, but feels well done and everything fits together. The mutant variety is also great, and all look very different. There isn't much sounds other than firing your weapons, using landmines, and the elevator doors. The music is great! The fighting music is very metal, and would LOVE to get my hands on it so I can listen to it more... But you can't sadly.
In terms of weapons, there isn't a lot. You start out with an Assault rife, and you will end up using pretty much that only. You can purchase an SMG and Shotgun from the shop at the start, but you won't be able to afford them right away. I found the SMG to be completely useless and stuck with the rifle, till I just had enough to get the shotgun at around the 6th floor (on hard).
I will say that I'm glad to see the dev pump out quite a few updates for this game. Since the time I beat it on 1.00, they have added more floors, some fixes, and added more enemies to the game. It's good to see Devs adding more into their games!
Pros:
- Good pixel graphics.

- Good amount of variety of enemies.
- Music is METAL.
- Good amount of updates.

Cons:
- Very short.
- Controls were annoying at first.

Initial impressions:
Ok, so far, severely disappointing. I see a lot of good reception for this game but have absolutely no clue where it comes from. The graphics look more like they are from 2006 rather than 2012 and still the game manages to lag every time a new thing appears on the horizon. The writing has been fairly simple so far and the quests have been about collecting or killing an x number of something.
The controls are actually inferior to standard MMO controls. Whatever happened to clicking on the enemy and your character running up and attacking automatically? Was that too advanced so that we had to go back to manually running to targets and getting smacked in the back because we ran a bit too far and clipped through the enemy, as your character won't attack unless he is facing the enemy? It's not like the old control system is being traded for advanced fighting techniques (like in Elder Scrolls) since the rest of the cotnrols is still just about clicking on enemies and pushing hotkeys.
The game isn't terrible. I did notice that the world seems to be gigantic, which is nice, and everything seems to be functional, but so far LOTRO it's just a standard barebones MMO. If that is what I'm in for then I might as well go back to playing Lineage II from 2003. I keep pushing through to see if it gets more interesting or special later, but so far...no.
CORRECTION: sorry, indeed the game turned out be from much earlier, so I take that part back, but as for the other stuff, I realised that I just don't have the time to wait a while and see if things get better. I really want to like Ziggurat, but I can't. This is hardly a RPG, and it should be stated that this is a permadeath "RPG" FPS.
I can see the replay value for someone who's favorite game type is FPS. I bought this game looking for a RPG, and it fails miserably in that regard.
The maps are "randomized", but they're not randomly generated as far as I can tell. There are a few map layouts to choose from it seems, so that you don't get the same thing every time, however, even on the first level I started to notice repeats within about 30 minutes of playtime.
No inventory at all, just "perks" to choose from when you level up, and when I say choose, it's a choice between two random cards, so you might not get anything you want at all. Essentially what I'm getting at is, you're not building a character, you're choosing random buffs as you level, which is bleh from an RPG standpoint.
Basically you clear one room at a time, and if you die, well, you're dead. Then you get to start the game all the way over at the beginning with nothing. Sure, you can unlock other characters, so that stays with you, but once you unlock them all, no progression from an account standpoint.
So yeah, you start out with only one character class choice, quickly unlock the second and the others come later.
If you want to play a modern Hexen, this is for you.

While not punishingly difficult (at normal difficulty) It does in fact reward players that can master its movement mechanics and be situationally aware. You can and will get blown up if you slack off during an encounter. My only gripe is how you lose speed if you jump while sprinting a  minor issue and I got used to it quickly.

I will preface with this: I enjoy the game, and the singleplayer is excellent. However, the main catalyst for rage on my part and one of the main selling points of this game is the online. My salt will be focused to bolster the claims and cries by other like minded gamers.
When I say rage, I do not mean "REEEE HACKER!" I know I am awful at this (and many other) game(s). The online is a grind, and not a very short one. It is a very arduous as well as tedious journey to the top of the food chain. Now, you could either find a community to guide you there and make it somewhat bearable, however in this eventuality you end up grinding the same heist over and over again, close to five times a day to get anywhere. The alternatives include freeroam activities (which could be fun, more on that later) or doing missions with randoms, which in this game happen to for the most part be awful. I mean straight garbage. Your fourth and quite frankly final option if you hope to have fun after the first 30 hours of online (not incluiding singleplayer), you will purchase shark cards. IRL money to buy IG money. People will say this is optional, so it doesnt affect me. Keep in mind other people play this game, and opt to purchase the aforementioned cards.
I neglected to divulge to you the content of these freeroam missions, so here goes. You can buy and office or biker clubhosue from which to stage your operation as either a luxury vehicle exporter and wholeseller of all manner of illicit merchandise, or a biker gang pushing drugs and running jobs as guns for hire. Either costs literal millions, close to 2mil to actually start earning anything exporting and around 1.5mil (dont take my word for it) for biker gangs. This sounds quite fun, and it is. For an hour apiece. Then it becomes boring, repetitive and easily exploitable. Oh, and might I add, you need to be in a public session, leaving yourself vulnerable to the *friendly* community of GTAV. How lovely. Now, you have established your presence and then begin to recieve numerous unrelenting calls about a new hangar, how this can expand your empire even further. Or, you see that you can purchase a bunker. You opt for either one, and lo and behold, same crap. Grind out boring, repetitive missions while you are being viciously maueld by various aircraft and the like.
What you could do, is decide to cut your connection and quickly reconnect it in order to force yourself to be kicked from an open session into a closed solo session that counts as a public session. Simple exploit #1. You are welcome. Whats so bad about this? Well, it gets even more repetitive, though significantly less frustrating.
Almost forgot, you could run monotonous jobs and missions that earn you meager cash rewards, and are simply difficult if you do not have the money to purchase good vehicles and missions. That and nobody plays anything. Good luck finding people.

This is a shallow and deeply flawed game. But to begin talking about why I've come to this conclusion, we're going to have to go back to what exactly this game is, and lay out the basic formula. I will also only be reviewing the BASE GAME, from my experience completing the game on casual, normal, and veteran difficulties with the outlander, engineer, and embermage classes.
In T2, just like Diablo 2 from which 99% of the gameplay for this game was directly stolen (maybe not the right term, since the original creators of Diablo went on to make this), you control a character from one of a few different classes at an isometric view, clicking around on randomly generated maps and killing massive hordes of enemies with abilities unlocked by leveling up. As you explore, you enter various different dungeons, taking on basic "go there, kill that dude" quests, with the ultimate reward being giant pools of money and randomly generated gear violently spewing out of every chests and boss you fight. It's a satisfying system, and it's the reason that Diablo became such a hit; the addictive quality of the rewards and the chunky, power fantasy combat appealed to both the hardcore rpg enthusiasts, and the more casual players who just wanted to see explosions. In a way, it's the perfect formula for a game, so much so that a lot of the mechanics of Diablo were repurposed and combined with Warcraft lore to create World of Warcraft, which is still one of the most popular mmorpgs ever made and defined the genre for the past decade.
Now with that established, I'm going to start to get into the things that T2 does wrong. I am going to assume a basic familiarity with Diablo or isometric rpgs; if you're 100% unfamiliar with the genre besides my short explanation, I recommend watching a few minutes of a random D2 longplay on youtube to get the idea.
In comparison to slower, more tabletop-rooted isometric rpgs like Arcanum, Diablo's strength is that there's no turn based system, to dodge an attack is not about a percent chance it's about you as the player moving your character out of the way of the attack. This might seem like a dumb thing to bring up, but I think it's an underappreciated aspect of Diablo which was part of its massive success. T2 doesn't understand this at all. Enemies in T2 are not meant to be dodged, there was ZERO consideration in the game for how autoattacks are supposed to be negated by a melee character. If you're playing melee and you're against something that can't be CC'd by the one CC spell you dumped points into (D2/T2 favor highly specialized characters rather than general purpose builds), you're at the mercy of the mob entirely, getting kicked around by nearly-instantaneous attacks; this of course being combined with a heavy level of tracking, where slow♥♥♥♥♥giants will perfectly follow you and spin around like tops to make sure you can never get behind them. Sometimes the harder monsters or bosses will use big wind up attacks, and I think these are the best part of the game as dodging them can get really tense sometimes, but that's totally negated by the fact that the enemies that have these moves ALSO do the tracking autoattack moves anyways in close combat. So what happens is, you take guaranteed damage from bosses, so you chug potions. You chug potions, so now you have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of health regen all the time anyways, trivializing not just the autoattacks, but every attack from the enemy. So, you now stand directly next to the enemy, chug potions, and hold click, with no thought process going into the action at all. There were only a few bosses which challenged this approach on veteran; the Alchemist being one good example, with his laser which pushed you back and did massive damage, but couldn't quite spin around fast enough if you circle strafed. Good use of a unique ability, I just wish that the rest of the game followed this mentality.
For the sake of comparison, let's look at how the embermage has it in this game, in particular. The embermage is widely considered the best class in the game and for good reason. Prismatic bolt, the main attacking move for its most popular build, is an amazing ability, which stacks every possible elemental debuff on your enemies, and can be combined with passive skills for the embermage which causes damage bursts whenever enemies with those debuffs get hit with an attack. The result is that single attacks can proc all the passives at once for HUGE damage burst potential. On top of this, embermage, with a _single_ skill point, can unlock the ability to teleport for nearly no mana cost. This instantaneous teleportation ability alone lets you rather effortlessly kite giant groups of monsters around at no risk of injury to yourself, and also gives you the best possible way to dodge the slower wind up ranged moves from bosses as well. So, to reiterate, the class is a ranged attack class, with the best mobility, cc, and damage in the game. How did anyone think this is fair?
The biggest draw of Diablo and Torchlight is the loot system, and how addictive it can be constantly getting better and better items and finding bigger stacks of gold. But for some reason, in T2 you hardly get any loot at all! Even in the very final dungeon, there's still pickups of 6 gold coins lying around, at a point where a single health potion costs you 400 gold. It's almost insulting, like the developers didn't even consider increasing the gold drops in the later stages, or just forgot. Torchlight 2 often touts during its tooltips that in multiplayer everyone gets their own unique loot drops, which is great. But if you can control drops on that level to give everyone their own, why can I get drops that are exclusive to another class? The class exclusive items were a very obvious place that T2 could've improved over Diablo, but instead it not only has the same problem, it made it even worse. There is no worse feeling than playing singleplayer on an embermage, and getting an outlander-exclusive drop from the boss at the end of an act that's _actually an upgrade for you_, and just vendoring it off. The mechanics and the item stats are all so generalized anyways, all the classes use the same "charge bar" mechanic for example, so it's like they wanted items to be useful for every build, and then they slapped class-specific requirements on for absolutely no reason I can see besides♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the player off. There's even a tooltip that says to "just trade the item to another player of that class!", as if that solves the issue in singleplayer...
Pretty much every track in the game sounds like a variation of the Act 1 theme from D2 with the iconic lute, up until the last boss, and it borders on annoying. Act 3 feels rushed together and isn't anywhere near as exciting as it could've been, mostly being a green forested area like Act 1 again, until suddenly you go through a gate and you're in the hellish awesome steampunk setting of the final dungeon, which is the only memorable locale in the game. The aoe dancing lightning ability some enemies have is bugged and does imbalanced amounts of damage, being able to kill you almost instantaneously. Bosses don't regenerate health if you die to them, so you can just keep respawning, running in, doing an attack, dying, and repeat over and over.
On and on the list goes, but I feel like here I've covered most of the main points. People rate this game highly because at the time of T2's release, D3 was still fresh on people's minds, and that game really was atrocious. So in comparison, T2 seemed like the better game, and it was. But as time has gone on my opinion of this game has very much soured. The complexity just isn't there. The loot isn't fun. The hardest part of the game on veteran was managing my gold so that I could buy potions and have even a chance to survive. If you like D2, chances are, this will be an interesting distraction. But really, the game's disappointing. Not recommended

Deus Ex has come a long way since the original. This latest installment has definitely kept up with the insteresting & mature story full of massive conspiracies, great voice acting, numerous augmentations, various approaches in playstyle and highly variable gameplay the series is known for. What hasn't kept up, in my opinion, is game length, character depth and focus. Just as the story got going it seemed that I was watching the credits roll. The characters were a bit all over the place, it's been two years since Human Revolution yet for the most part the deveolpers act like we've know what's been going on in the life of Adam Jensen. Characters we come in contact with have little to no depth, I didn't feel all too connected to them (Alex being a big one since you find out almost nothing about her). You do find out more about everything else by reading the glass pads scattered all around but there are huge gaps in  truely understanding. The choices between supporting fellow Augs or doing your duty could have been expanded on. The discrimination will definitely get your blood boiling at times but in the end there is no resolution. That being said, what was delivered was a living breathing world for you to explore and you actually feel part of it. The side missions are exceptional, and as per usual there are numerous ways to complete them. The augmentations have been expanded on which is a huge plus, who doesn't love variety. All in all you'll have fun playing an interesting story and customizing you character to suit your play style. But as much as I liked the main storyline it's too short and it doesn't really feel like it moved the overall story forward. Hopefully the next few games will keep the better parts of this game but start developing characters again, and making us feel we're moving forward in finding answers and affecting change.
Bottom line: You'll enjoy the game, it has most of the hallmarks of what Deus Ex should be, including high replayability, but don't expect to be satisfied by the campaign length, ending or character depth.

Okay... look at the preview video, look at the old school original Diablo top down style graphics.  Make sure you are cool with that before considering purchasing this game even for another moment...
Good?  Now imagine you starting off in an all too familiar RPG back story... we've heard this same sort of story many times before and as you start the game and read the dialogue, you'll swear it's deja vu again.  ..You were a kid and your parents died to some horrible death, something so bad that even dear old grandfather can't bear to tell you anything about it.  Something awful happened is all that you know and your grandfather raised you well as other nearby people of the NPC type taught you some basic skills such as basic carpentry, a little bit of alchemy, etc.  Twenty years later, you now wake up with dear old granfather just a little older, but still much superior to you with ten times your starting HP and MP etc and theres rumors of someone with a torch trying to burn your granddfather and your wooden house down and they burned down the house completely of a nearby family.
And that is where you start.  You'll get to wander around exploring the town and visiting all the NPC people, choosing what to say and what tasks you'd like to complete.  The great thing here is that every quest feels like it has a real purpose, none of the "go kill 10 wolves" or "go collect 10 butterfly sacs" garbage that drive so many of us RPG fans bonkers.  It's refreshing to have quests that actually feel like they serve a purpose.. things like chopping down trees in a forest and buying nails from another NPC to repair a burnt down wall of a house or fixing another npcs crop field fence.
Be careful as well in this game.. Don't think you can just walk in people's house and start snooping through their chests and taking whatever you like because doing so in their line of sight will pi.ss them off and have them attacking you until either you or them dies.  I love that.
So let's talk about the UI...  it's a little awkward to get used to for sure and will take time.  For example sending in your pet (yes you can have pets you command and who serve you) ... but sending your pet to attack an enemy require you left clicking the target foe.  But for you to attack, you need to choose your attack and then right click on the same foe.  ..That's just one example of how the UI can be almost overwhelmingly confusing when you begin.  But soon, you'll get the hang of it and feel much more comfy with the game that definitely doesn't hold your hand.
My biggest gripe early on is the hunger and thirst survival mechanics of the game.  I chose the normal difficulty and haven't tried the easy mode yet but...  at this early point into the game (4 hours), the thirst and hunger is almost annoying because it feels like every 30 seconds, you have to drink or eat.  Fail to notice these chat messages or icons in the upper right of your screen, you in no time flat you'll be near death from damage taken from "invisible pain" due to hunger or thirst.  The solution?  Easy once you figure out to stock plenty of food on you and hydrate and eat to 150% of both thirst & hunger each morning when you wake up.
The hybrid turn based mechanic is one I really like.  It means that every NPC (including enemies) move and do their thing and time moves if you stand still or if you are working to complete tasks.. it's a real time game, except once you engage or once an enemy engages you into the games combat.  Once you are in combat, whether your choice or not, it's all a slower, much more strategic life-or-death turn based battle where any wrong move could be the difference between you surviving ot dying and re-loading the game from your last save point.
There's also a rune your grandfather gives you early in the game that you'll want to put in your hot bar immediately.  I didn't even notice it until 4 hours in, and it allows you to click it anytime to be whisked away to a safe facet of your existence where the map looks the same, but no other npcs including enemies exist.  It's your safe haven, and when you first go there, there is a huge empty prarie the size of the small town all your own.. a place you can build your dream home and escape to any time you wish.  There, you are given a nice starting supply of resources to help get you started building whatever home you want, and pressing the B key (for Build) opens up a generous build menu where you can build your dream home, place furniture, trees, shrubs, chests, etc.  This safe zone is an awesome feature that I absolutely love and to me is something that takes this game over-the-top.
While this game has it's steep learning curve and interesting UI to get used to, it offers a depth rarely seen in even the most hyped triple-A RPG games.  This is certainly not a review where I've played the full game and can tell you exactly how much depth it has, but at four hours in, I feel like someone here on earth looking up into the sky at all the stars thinking OMG WOW.  It feels like I haven't even scratched 1% of this games offerings at 4 hours in.  There are tons of ingredients everywhere for crafting and alchemy, more then you can shake a stick at.  There are dozens of dungeons I haven't even begun to explore.  There is a safe zone area I've only started to build my house on.  And there are so many strange creatures I've stayed away from seen peering at me from the thick woods beyond the town.  When I get killed by two spiders near the town or a bear on the edge of town, I can't even begin to think of battling whatever evils exist in the depths of the woods or all of those dungeons yet.  And THAT is a feeling that leaves you in awe as you are learning the ropes and UI of this game and completing all the many tasks and quests available at the start.
There is no doubt in my mind that this game will be up for "RPG of the year" on many peoples lists to choose the best-of-the-best from once 2016 is over.  It's refreshing to see, especially at this games surprisingly lose price point.  Many people will compare this game to Diablo or Diablo 2 looking at the graphics, but I have played both of those games long ago, and from my early game time in Balrum, this game may not be an action RPG like Diablo or throw quite so much crazy loot out, but it looks to have a depth that far surpasses both Diablo and Diablo 2.  It does have a steep learning curve, and a strange UI that takes getting used to, but I think this game is one that any true RPG fan shouldn't miss!
Once I complete this game, I'll come back and give it a proper review, and share how many hours I spent beating it.  Until then, here is my scoring just based on what I've experienced so far...
Value (Worth 40 points max) :  40, no doubt about it, this game delivers crazy over-the-top value and likely hundreds of hours of gameplay for it's small asking price.

It isn't Dwarf-Fortress. But it's the next best thing.
Gnomoria is a city-building/kingdom management game directly influenced by the beloved dorf-fort; You and your small little group of gnomads are plonked into a procedurally generated map with nothing but a few basic supplies, and are expected to carve out a glorious mountainhome in the name of profit, prosperity, and beards.
At it's core, the game is essentially DF boiled down to the basics; it doesn't contain the sheer depth of the older game, lacking world simulation, history, the in-depth tracking of every single personality trait, physical features and relationships of every living entity in the world, or any of the other features that makes DF as amazeballs as it is. In place of these things, however, Gnomoria has one vital feature that many dorflikes lack; Accessibility.  Half the challenge of DF is learning to navigate the convoluted, inconsestent, and ugly interface, with no mouse support. Not to mention learning to read the initially indecipherable code that makes up the world; first-time DF players may as well be seeing into the matrix, and while graphics packs are available, the game will still look fairly ugly and confusing to many people.
Gnomoria, on the other hand, has a clean, simple interface that can be fully navigated via keyboard hotkeys, or using the mouse. All of the commands are in fairly intuitive and logical places, and you probably won't find yourself unable to find anything specific. The visuals are clearer too; Gnomoria plays from an isometric perspective, and while the character/creature sprites could use some work, the game has a nice, clean style that looks decent without making things look cluttered or confusing.
The game also has some nice logistical improvements over DF; namely, the ability to set priorities and stocks on workshops. This allows you to automate production of goods, to an extent; when you select "craft to X", the gnomes with the appropriate skills, or the one assigned to the workship, will keep crafting that particular product until it reaches the desired quantity, then stop. If stocks ever fall below that value, they'll top it up again. Combined with some clever priority management, this allows individual gnomes to have multiple jobs while still maintaining a constant, efficient production line. For example, charcoal can be made from wood in a furnace, and can be used in a smelter with some ore to create bars. Crafting to, say, 10, on the charcoal production job, will insure that there's always enough fuel available to smelt the ore, but will make sure you don't use up all the wood, overfill the stockpiles, and constantly tie up gnomes in hauling/wood burning jobs. This feature also applies to resource gathering, to an extent; in addition to the farms that already exist in DF, Gnomoria features 'Groves', which allows trees to be planted, harvested and/or cut down in an area, without manually ordering mass deforestation whenever you run low. Pastures can also be automated; you can set a certain population threshold in a pasture, and excess animals will be butchered without any manual input from you. This keeps things from getting out of hand or annoying.
The game doesn't quite contain as much Fun as DF; while there are plenty of things that can kill you, and you are almost guaranteed to fall into decline eventually, without the use of cheese tactics like walling in, the game is much more forgiving than DF, and doesn't include the bane of all forts, the tantrum spiral. Catocalpyse, seiges, demonic invasions, attack by megabeast, disease, vampire attacks, murders and magma, flooding and fey moods,  all of these things are missing right now, making the game less Fun, but still fun.
In short, this is definitely worth looking at if you're interested in the genre, but don't have the patience for DF, but hardcore Dwarf-Fort players will probably find the lack of content, smaller scale and general fairness of the game a little unfulfilling.

The description of the game claims that it is quite complicated. But in reality the game is very simple. What’s complicated is figuring out how all these poor game design decisions came together to form this mess of mechanics.
Zombie Zoeds pits you as a nameless thing shooting other things. You can only shoot in the direction you are facing, and moving around feels like you are steering a cart drawn by dead horses. Your character has to forcibly swing himself around like a boat in order to change the direction he is facing. But all of these clunky movements fit perfectly because your bullets actually fire off center. So while you are surrounded by zombies and being mauled from all sides, you will soon discover that the zombie directly in front of you is actually dodging all of your bullets because he is in front of you and your character wields his gun completely to the side of what he is looking at. It gets even better though, because this particular gun you start with (the Patron) is modeled after Haley’s comet because you only shoot one bullet every 75 years or so. You also shoot bullets the size of threading needles. So don’t ever worry about trying to hit an enemy on purpose, because this is mostly a game of waddling around and clicking in hopes of hitting something.
I have no idea where the game goes beyond that. You have some kind of score based on your kills and also how many survivors die. This score doesn’t really go anywhere. There is for the weapons “Lazer” and “Lazer 2” at the bottom of the screen but I don’t think I can commit to ever finding those weapons. Along with the lack of goals, the game is incredibly bland in general. The game’s sound design is brought to you by public domain night sounds, nonstop. The art style has poor color choices and too much repetition in general.
The trees in the game all look the same and, together with the ground, seem to be from a completely different style from the enemies and player. Despite this being a top-down game, the trees all have their trunks visible and don’t follow the perspective. On top of this, these trees are surrounded by an invisible box that is impassable. This means that your game of wildly unintuitive shooting and movement is also interrupted by these clone trees wielding force fields. They are out of place stylistically and I have no idea what they add to the game. There is no need to take cover behind them because that would require quicker movements than your character would allow. These trees also don't provide resources, because this game has no mechanics beyond shooting the same stock enemies for no other goal than to watch a number get bigger.  The trees also fail at being landmarks because they all pretty much look the same, and chances are if you are close enough to see them, you are probably in danger of being caught up in their invisible walls.
You are controlling an old boat disguised as a person, shooting tiny straws slowly around your enemies while treading through treacherous waters of mismatched art, trees, and no sense of purpose.  This game needs landscaping among so many other things.

This is an okay free donation-ware 4-bit arcade based around fetch quests in a zombie-infested building. As other reviewers state, it's an ex-hardcore game turned recently easycore, so anyone can have a little fun. Unfortunately, game is very light on content unless you hunt the achievements, and the "original" mechanic is actually frustrating pixel hunting in an arcade game. The 'original" mechanic is about scoring damage only with headshots, but harder zombies have tinier heads (like crimson turkey heads) and it's about about your ability to be precise pointing on screen while two waves come crashing at you. As expected, if one zombie touches you, you die, swear like a Russian (suka blyad) and try again. There isn't even randomization for the fetch quest locations, so you can easily learn them on the 10th run.

I really enjoyed DLC Quest. It's fun to play, has a charming atmosphere, and is quite humorous in poking fun at lots of cliches and tropes of the video game industry. At its core, it's a simple, comedic sidescroller with an ostensibly generic storyline, yet it never hesitates to point out its own irrational logic, from its cliched characters to the seemingly bizarre aspects that are currently part of today's gaming industry.
The premise behind DLC Quest is that a bad guy captures a princess, so obviously it's your job to stop him and rescue the damsel in distress. Heard this story a million times before? So have the developers at Going Loud Studios, so what they've done is put their own spin on this age-old premise. Your task is to first collect enough coins to buy DLC within the game world itself. A clear commentary on the cash-grubbing nature of the video game industry, these little packs are initially required in order for you to do the most basic actions, such as moving both left AND right and being able to pause the game. As you progress, the game gives you some nice aesthetic features as well as weapons/items.
I was surprised at how good the control is. The jumping mechanic feels like the original Super Mario Bros. (where you can control height and momentum in the air), which I appreciate immensely. You move left and right at a reasonable pace, too. The controls are customizable and the graphics are vibrant and appealing. Aesthetically, the game's design gives it an NES feel. The dialogue is often funny, with characters acknowledging their ridiculous requests or their arbitrary roles in making you run off and do stuff with no justification other than that's how these games work. DLC Quest on a whole is very tongue-in-cheek that way. That being said, there were a couple things that I thought could be improved. To progress through the game, you obviously need to get enough coins to purchase certain DLC items, but a couple of times I couldn't figure out where to go, because I thought I had cleared out all the areas. Turns out there are some secret areas you have to look for where the walls are missing their borders, which are easy to miss. There are also some areas that you might not realize you can get to for similar reasons (boulders or bushes obscured by the foreground, etc.). Otherwise, I found the platforming to be relatively easy, simple enough for an old fogey like me to get through.
Overall, I think DLC Quest is a very creative, imaginative, quirky, charming, humorous game well worth its price point. It pokes fun at itself and other gaming cliches, but even though it admits its own "faults," it still kept me wanting to play. If you're at all into sidescrollers, I'd recommend giving this one a try.

This is a shallow and deeply flawed game. But to begin talking about why I've come to this conclusion, we're going to have to go back to what exactly this game is, and lay out the basic formula. I will also only be reviewing the BASE GAME, from my experience completing the game on casual, normal, and veteran difficulties with the outlander, engineer, and embermage classes.
In T2, just like Diablo 2 from which 99% of the gameplay for this game was directly stolen (maybe not the right term, since the original creators of Diablo went on to make this), you control a character from one of a few different classes at an isometric view, clicking around on randomly generated maps and killing massive hordes of enemies with abilities unlocked by leveling up. As you explore, you enter various different dungeons, taking on basic "go there, kill that dude" quests, with the ultimate reward being giant pools of money and randomly generated gear violently spewing out of every chests and boss you fight. It's a satisfying system, and it's the reason that Diablo became such a hit; the addictive quality of the rewards and the chunky, power fantasy combat appealed to both the hardcore rpg enthusiasts, and the more casual players who just wanted to see explosions. In a way, it's the perfect formula for a game, so much so that a lot of the mechanics of Diablo were repurposed and combined with Warcraft lore to create World of Warcraft, which is still one of the most popular mmorpgs ever made and defined the genre for the past decade.
Now with that established, I'm going to start to get into the things that T2 does wrong. I am going to assume a basic familiarity with Diablo or isometric rpgs; if you're 100% unfamiliar with the genre besides my short explanation, I recommend watching a few minutes of a random D2 longplay on youtube to get the idea.
In comparison to slower, more tabletop-rooted isometric rpgs like Arcanum, Diablo's strength is that there's no turn based system, to dodge an attack is not about a percent chance it's about you as the player moving your character out of the way of the attack. This might seem like a dumb thing to bring up, but I think it's an underappreciated aspect of Diablo which was part of its massive success. T2 doesn't understand this at all. Enemies in T2 are not meant to be dodged, there was ZERO consideration in the game for how autoattacks are supposed to be negated by a melee character. If you're playing melee and you're against something that can't be CC'd by the one CC spell you dumped points into (D2/T2 favor highly specialized characters rather than general purpose builds), you're at the mercy of the mob entirely, getting kicked around by nearly-instantaneous attacks; this of course being combined with a heavy level of tracking, where slow♥♥♥♥♥giants will perfectly follow you and spin around like tops to make sure you can never get behind them. Sometimes the harder monsters or bosses will use big wind up attacks, and I think these are the best part of the game as dodging them can get really tense sometimes, but that's totally negated by the fact that the enemies that have these moves ALSO do the tracking autoattack moves anyways in close combat. So what happens is, you take guaranteed damage from bosses, so you chug potions. You chug potions, so now you have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of health regen all the time anyways, trivializing not just the autoattacks, but every attack from the enemy. So, you now stand directly next to the enemy, chug potions, and hold click, with no thought process going into the action at all. There were only a few bosses which challenged this approach on veteran; the Alchemist being one good example, with his laser which pushed you back and did massive damage, but couldn't quite spin around fast enough if you circle strafed. Good use of a unique ability, I just wish that the rest of the game followed this mentality.
For the sake of comparison, let's look at how the embermage has it in this game, in particular. The embermage is widely considered the best class in the game and for good reason. Prismatic bolt, the main attacking move for its most popular build, is an amazing ability, which stacks every possible elemental debuff on your enemies, and can be combined with passive skills for the embermage which causes damage bursts whenever enemies with those debuffs get hit with an attack. The result is that single attacks can proc all the passives at once for HUGE damage burst potential. On top of this, embermage, with a _single_ skill point, can unlock the ability to teleport for nearly no mana cost. This instantaneous teleportation ability alone lets you rather effortlessly kite giant groups of monsters around at no risk of injury to yourself, and also gives you the best possible way to dodge the slower wind up ranged moves from bosses as well. So, to reiterate, the class is a ranged attack class, with the best mobility, cc, and damage in the game. How did anyone think this is fair?
The biggest draw of Diablo and Torchlight is the loot system, and how addictive it can be constantly getting better and better items and finding bigger stacks of gold. But for some reason, in T2 you hardly get any loot at all! Even in the very final dungeon, there's still pickups of 6 gold coins lying around, at a point where a single health potion costs you 400 gold. It's almost insulting, like the developers didn't even consider increasing the gold drops in the later stages, or just forgot. Torchlight 2 often touts during its tooltips that in multiplayer everyone gets their own unique loot drops, which is great. But if you can control drops on that level to give everyone their own, why can I get drops that are exclusive to another class? The class exclusive items were a very obvious place that T2 could've improved over Diablo, but instead it not only has the same problem, it made it even worse. There is no worse feeling than playing singleplayer on an embermage, and getting an outlander-exclusive drop from the boss at the end of an act that's _actually an upgrade for you_, and just vendoring it off. The mechanics and the item stats are all so generalized anyways, all the classes use the same "charge bar" mechanic for example, so it's like they wanted items to be useful for every build, and then they slapped class-specific requirements on for absolutely no reason I can see besides♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the player off. There's even a tooltip that says to "just trade the item to another player of that class!", as if that solves the issue in singleplayer...
Pretty much every track in the game sounds like a variation of the Act 1 theme from D2 with the iconic lute, up until the last boss, and it borders on annoying. Act 3 feels rushed together and isn't anywhere near as exciting as it could've been, mostly being a green forested area like Act 1 again, until suddenly you go through a gate and you're in the hellish awesome steampunk setting of the final dungeon, which is the only memorable locale in the game. The aoe dancing lightning ability some enemies have is bugged and does imbalanced amounts of damage, being able to kill you almost instantaneously. Bosses don't regenerate health if you die to them, so you can just keep respawning, running in, doing an attack, dying, and repeat over and over.
On and on the list goes, but I feel like here I've covered most of the main points. People rate this game highly because at the time of T2's release, D3 was still fresh on people's minds, and that game really was atrocious. So in comparison, T2 seemed like the better game, and it was. But as time has gone on my opinion of this game has very much soured. The complexity just isn't there. The loot isn't fun. The hardest part of the game on veteran was managing my gold so that I could buy potions and have even a chance to survive. If you like D2, chances are, this will be an interesting distraction. But really, the game's disappointing. Not recommended

Mankind Divided has everything I loved about Human Revolution and yet it doesn't feel like a simple rehash or rebuild. It stays true to the original games in style and story, and exploring the deep world is just so much fun.

As many others have pointed out, the DLC and short length of the game are problems.
But the MUCH bigger issue for me is that A) the game runs very poorly and there are frequent and annoying glitches, that sometimes require a restart of the game, and B) the content that IS in the game is simply not up to what it should be.
The entire experience, from the voice acting to the level design, is not as good as it should be. It feels rushed, and awkward.
The plot is kind of hilariously bad. The setting is supposed to be after Human Revolution but after Deus Ex 1, but it absolutely does not seem that way. Simply bringing back a couple of Deus Ex characters is not enough. The whole setting feels amiss, and the idea of ghettos for people with expensive augmentations is absurd. I found myself laughing out loud at times, both during cutscenes and while listening to the ambient dialogue.
This is a total disgrace to the Deus Ex franchise, from top to bottom. The only single way this is an improvement over Deus Ex, a 16-year-old game, is graphics. Not good enough.
Don't buy this unless it's on sale for $10 or less.

Application 1 (as it calls itself) is a baaaad game.
So I load up Application 1 one day, bored out of my mind, looking for a game to play, and it opens up to a very low-resolution screen that says "Loading." So I assume Application 1 is loading me into the first level, right? I go and clean up my floor, brush my teeth, take a trip to the bathroom, and grab a dried fruit pouch to find it
not "loaded." Of course, I click the "New Game" button on Application 1's loading screen, and unexpectedly, Application 1 then thrusts me into this grassy plain with a bunch of boxes in front of me. Being a fan of free stuff, I lunge at Application 1's boxes and see that nothing happens. "Okay Application 1," I think, "maybe my ammunition or something is full." That is when Application 1's specialties come at me, the zombies. Using the gun that Application 1 has supplied me, I attempt to shoot. One shot. And the sound doesn't even finish. I hold down the left mouse button, telling Application 1 that I'd like to shoot, but of course, it only fires one shot, again (even though what I'm holding seems to be an automatic weapon). Of course, Application 1's zombies murder me, because I am unable to shoot more than one bullet at a time.
Would I recommend Application 1 to a friend? Probably not even an enemy.

I have to say that I was much more happy with this game than the first one, and that is simply because I was able to play online co-op with a friend. The whole premise isn't necessarily original, but the levels you go through are pretty interesting, and it is so enjoyable to plan things out with a friend as you are playing along, accomplishing the puzzles.
Some of them took us a good while to accomplish - some because they were actually hard, and some because we simply missed something and would feel stupid afterwards. But that's why I liked this game so much more than the first, because I had a friend to talk to that gave a different perspective. Playing the first game got sad because things are much more annoying to accomplish on your own in the puzzles, and I simply don't think it's as fun.
So would I recommend the game? Yes. Great graphics, some nice humor to the premise, nice little puzzles and levels. But definitely make sure you have somebody to play it with!

An extremely basic game, Bloody Walls is a 2D action game which combines simple gameplay with Game Boy or NES style pixel graphics.
Bloody Walls is very simplistic – you control a man with a gun. He has some antidotes on him. Each antidote keeps him safe for 60 seconds, and they automatically are used as the last one expires.
You start out on the first of ten floors, where there are five mission-givers and a store – a store at which you can exchange antidotes for guns and mines. There are two guns other than the starting one – a SMG with slightly worse range but much better damage, and a shotgun with vastly worse range but massively more damage (and a slow reload speed). Mines can simply be deployed by clicking on them or pressing 3 or 4 (whichever slot they are loaded into), which causes them to be deployed at your feet. You can’t run over them, but your enemies can.
You have a limited amount of inventory space – 20 weight, and your gun takes up a chunk of that. The mines will generally occupy the rest unless you buy two guns for some crazy reason (you can sell your original one, too).
Each of the quest givers shows you a location in the levels below, though you don’t have to talk to them beforehand to get the relevant items. The quests are fulfilled simply by opening up a container on that level, and then bringing it back to your buddy on the first floor for a reward in a nearby locker.
The actual gamplay itself consists of shooting monsters in the vulnerable parts as they come towards you. There’s a small variety of enemies, but ultimately most of the types are pretty much the same save for hit points and movement speed. If any enemy touches you, you die and have to start the entire game over. But the game is very, very short – only ten floors, and most of the floors can be cleared within a minute each, with a couple exceptions.
The main exceptions to the general rule of “all the enemies are the same” come towards the end, when you encounter enemies which only are vulnerable if you’re far enough away from them, enemies which only open up when you’re right next to them, and enemy spawners which periodically deploy an enemy after you. These three things are the most dangerous kinds of enemies, though the spawners are ultimately easily dispatched after you’ve killed everything else. That said, they are *tedious* to dispatch, sometimes taking several minutes to get through the enemies they send at you before you can kill them all.
While in theory you are in danger of your time running out, in practice, it never happened to me; the real threat was the enemies.
But there really isn’t much variety here; the levels do vary slightly but they are almost identical from playthrough to playthrough, and frankly, there’s very little of interest to note here. Beating the game plays a very short cutscene, and then the game is over.
The whole thing is very minimalist, but ultimately, it is a fairly basic tactical challenge, and not even a very complicated one at that – there’s really a basic strategy which works on every level, and the only thing that the mines are for is so that if you screw up a bit you can avoid losing.  The amount of clicking you have to do is kind of tiresome, and can make your wrist sore after a bit.
I can’t really recommend this game. It isn’t terrible, but ultimately it is a kind of forgettable experience that doesn’t really go anywhere.

TL;DR - Nice game but you can't really progress without paying.
Awesome idea, the game is nice and intuitive but all of this is trashed by the fact that like most free-to-play games it becomes more and more frustrating to play as you progress unless you spend real money to buy the game's virtual currency (diamonds). If you open your physical wallet there's hardly any challenge. If you don't - it's practically impossible. Detailed explanation follows.
You need to level up many skills as well as progress through jobs; each level up takes double the amount of time as the previous level. This means that beyond some level it is impractical to play as it is. There are two multipliers that help speed up - One is buying it with diamonds. The other is by using the "prestige" mechanic, which allows you to convert progress to speed, i.e. you level-up quicker next time but you lose all progress you've made so far. This means that in order to progress beyond a certain point you will have to restart the game again and again and play the first part of it so many times that you go crazy and you have to use diamonds, which you have to buy with real money (actually you do get a few diamonds through gameplay but the total number of diamonds you can ever get that way is finite and not very large).
It's really a shame because this game could have been really fun and I would have spent a few $$s buying it if it were to feature a fair gameplay that does not favor people just by the amount of real money they spend. The way this (and so many other free-to-play games) is built does not present any actual challenge, it just tries to get you to spend money. Real shame indeed.

Ziggurat is possibly the best FPS roguelite I have played thus far. It does a number of things right that were either missing entirely or not fully realized in Heavy Bullets and Fancy Skulls (both of which I think are good, just not quite where I wish they were).
The first thing it does right is weaponry. While I have so far only held a handful of weapons I have seen that I currently have around ten unlocked with more on the way. This keeps the playstyle interesting and makes each run more unique. Being gated to hold only one weapon of each type is in my opinion a plus, as it further pushes the survival and "make use of what you have" mentality of roguelikes in general and of Ziggurat in particular.
They have also successfully added upgrades to the game, and at a pace which keeps you "wanting just one more". Possibly my biggest gripe with other fps roguelikes,  Ziggurat has made it so your upgrade path affects your gameplay and is something that constantly happens. It's not a diamond in the rough that happens once per game for marginal benefit.
While I only have one other character unlocked, the fact that there are a plethora available all with clear unlock goals is wonderful. All my favorite roguelikes- Dungeons of Dredmor, Binding of Isaac, FTL, Dungeon of the Endless- utilize a similar system, where you can actually start the game with compeltely different gear. This furthers replayability and gives the player various challenges and goals to shoot for.
On top of that, so far the enemies are very remiscent of DOOM enemies. By this I mean they are large hulking guys with telegraphed moves. What this means is you learn how to play against each one and feel yourself getting better at handling their individual quirks.
Lastly, the overall aesthetic is pretty stellar. It's somewhat cartoony but in the best way possible, while keeping a serious hexen/doom feeling.
TLDR;  Ziggurat is a stellar entry to the FPS roguelite field. They capitalized on the genre's ability for varying gameplay results by including an array of upgrades, weapons, starting characters, and enemy attack patterns to make the player hone their skill while learning to live with what they have. I am definitely glad I did not pay as much attention to all the critique of this game as it was possible. Though bought with a discount, I am satisfied with the outcome of the game as a huge Deus Ex fan. For the most part. The optimalization for the game is still a mess and the requirement for the 16GB RAM can seem quite hilarious.
If I'll just jump from that topic (which is usually being sh*t on), I can honestly admit that I appreciate all the work that went into the atmosphere, the storyline itself, the expanded options compared to what Human Revolution could offer, many ways to change the story, weapon customization and many other things including the Czech voice acting. It might seem trivial to any other foreigner but as a Czech myself, I was very happy to finally play a game where you don't hear Russian, Arabic or Spanish most of the time (don't get me wrong, I don't necessarilly hate those languages but they are so common in games and especially movies, that it gets sickening as the time goes by), so that's a huge plus for me.
There are few minor glitches that could be tweaked in the future such as Jensen's head bobbing through the collar of his coat during conversations or the odd looking animations of the speakers' bodies. Cutscenes in general look fluent and feel nice. Too bad the lip-sync in the game itself isn't as good as the one in the cutscenes.
What made me play the game more and more to progress through the story was that Mankind Divided was tryng to be a bit different than Human Revolution but still stay on the same tracks. You don't get to fight as many bosses, which is what upset a lot of people, but then again it would be boring if the game cycle was repeating.
Nearly 18 hours and I've just finished the game, looking forward to another run to play a different style for a different story outcome.The game length is very generous. Some might claim otherwise as if other games can do it better. If you can play the side missions as well, the game can offer a lot of fun.
In general, it is a very specific game that can only be enjoyed by a specific group of players but it is still a very decent game that can deliver the atmosphere that it was selling before the release. A bit wobbly here and there but it is something to be expected considering the game developers originally planned to release this back in Feb 2016.
When considering the purchase of the game, you should ask yourself what do you expect from it and if you think the expectations will be met. Way too high arrogant standards of course will never be met.
TL;DR Purchase the game only with a discount and only when knowing what are you going to get from the experience. I definitely recommend it to lovers of stealth games, even to people who haven't played any Deus Ex games before.

I don't undertand the criticism.  I got scared off by the recent bad reviews, but I'm an absolute fanatic about the Deus Ex series, so I took the risk when it went on sale -- glad I did!

As far as gameplay, definitely lives up to the franchise. Rewards stealth play, good number of interesting augmentation builds possible, great action.  Very interesting and immersive environments.
GRAPHICS: Beware.  This game's graphics are insanely good, better than any other game I own, but that means it's demanding.  I read many reviews complaining about the performance, but often when I check their specs (for those that wrote it), it typically has a GTX 960 or other midrange card.  You CANNOT expect to run this game with high settings on a midrange card! Not an optimization issue, the graphics are truly extremely good.  A lot of cool technologies with reflections, volumetric lighting, tesselation, termporal AA, etc.  The game runs amazing with all this crap off, not an engine problem.
Additionally, the developers have improved optimization with many patches, and multi gpu improved substantially with DX12 (about 15% more fps for me, both cards woking 99% changing only the direct x version with no other graphical changes).  Nevertheless, I get about 77 fps average on the built in benchmark @ 1440p and everything max except MSAA.
My Rig:
i7 4790K @ 4.8 GHz with h110i Cooler
16GB DDR3 @ 1600 MHz
2x GTX 980 Ti in SLi @ 1415 MHz
ROG SWIFT 144 Hz 2560x1440
Performance: 77 FPS AVG on game benchmark, 1440p, max settings, no MSAA

Essentially, technical issues aside,
is a stealth action game done right. It has all the ingredients necessary for a successful representation of the genre. There always is a variety of ways to accomplish the same target, there are solutions for any path a player might choose, and oh my! even a boss can be neutralized "peacefully". Well, not by means of talking, of course, but still.
I had a lot of pleasure doing the side quests as well as the main storyline, and I took my time there - decision I never regretted. Some guys I saw on forums and in reviews were complaining that they finished too fast... well, I feel sorry for their girlfriends. I got full 50 hours from the gameplay, and that's a great result for me. There's much fun in going around, exploring, looking into every corner, finding paths and stuff here and there.
The story itself is also interesting even though obvious in certain spots. The world feels less atmospheric than it was in
, but sometimes it becomes strikingly similar to our reality, and it has some heart-piercing sights and moments where you just clench your teeth with silent anger, feeling painfully unable to change anything.
As for fights, the arsenal of both weapons and augmentations is nice and enjoyable to use, but enemy AI is inconsistent. Sometimes it is cunning and sometimes it's just plain stupid. It might have to do with medium difficulty level I chose - it probably disables some decisions and abilities in the AI.
The worst part of the game is obviously its performance. It's not even about the fact that you need a most state-of-the-art PC to enjoy the graphics in its entirety; it's about the fact that the majority of graphical settings do not influence the FPS counter at all. You may reduce the preset to "medium" and still get the performance as bad as if it were "very high".
Overall, it's a very good game, but it takes some pain to enjoy it. If you're new to the universe, I'd recommend to begin with
and then decide if your love to the franchise is strong enough to go through a bit of suffering.
