Brothers – A Tale of Two Sons is an experience, first and foremost.  It's a story told without words through the medium of a well crafted game.  One that you may identify with, or one that at least resonates with the general nature of humanity.   That's all before you even get to the reality of the mechanics having the player control two characters simultaneously with an analog stick dedicated to each.  Which ends up creating some of the most imaginative gameplay of its time.
It's important to identify Brothers for what it is up front for those that may not be compelled to 'experience' game rather than simply play it.  You'll take control of two brothers set out on a journey in the same vein as other adventure games.  You can do little else in the process but guide them to various positions where they can hit triggers to perform other actions, such as climbing, turning a crank, or moving an object.   Each brother has specific traits, such as the older one being taller and stronger and the younger being smaller, which is advantageous for getting in to tight spaces.  These traits will be used in a variety of ways, both separately and together, to solve puzzles that you come up against in your progression through the game.  That is what you're actually going to be doing from start to finish.  It's not particularly difficult in any respect, once you figure out how to control both brothers at the same time effectively, it's more a matter of being able to solve puzzles that, by design, won't leave you struggling.
However, Brothers exists less to be a demo of a neat control scheme and more to tell a story of two siblings set out to find a cure for their father's sickness.  Their journey has them meeting all sorts of friendly, indifferent, and sometimes vicious characters that weave their way in to the story and the expedition.  As you navigate through the town in which you start and move further and further from your home, you find increasingly majestic and mysterious lands that sometimes fill your screen with strange creatures or grand visages.  Each corner you turn could be a whole new realm more spectacular than the last, and each step may lead you in to another puzzle to solve before you can dive in.
You may look at the time I have played this game and the time others have as well and think it's short.  That's not an incorrect perception, but the game isn't designed to be challenging or replayable.  The developers goal seems to be for it to connect with you on an emotional level and tell a great story in a unique universe.  That may only take three or four hours of your time, but when you're finished you will have something to look back on with appreciation for being able to be a part of it.  I don't think that it would have had as much of an impact of the game was significantly longer or more difficult.
Brothers – A Tale of Two Sons is a game I think anyone that finds value in a strong narrative and great environment design should purchase.  It's an old game now, but I played it well after release and still found it to be well worth the time.  Also, as far as the pricing, while it may have a base price of $14.99, it is regularly on sale for as little as $1.49.   For that price, it's worth it just to see if you are one of the many that plays this game and comes away with it making an mark in your life.

The most important is that it favors Intel processors and graphics for hardware acceleration, which will not work if you have AMD graphics or Intel incompatible card and CPU. The track editor lacks some essential tools for managing the video/audio sequences in tracks: for example, moving all the sequences in one track means going through whole track and selection all of them individually, then move and test. If you are unhappy with the results, you have to repeat it again.
The other things are weak support for audio and video files import and complex management of movie export (default settings render average quality movie, technical knowledge is needed for better manual setup).
Not recommended in current state.

Inspired by ‘80s action movies (some involving Arnold), Farcry 3: Blood Dragon is a welcome change in atmosphere. Everything is neon (because hey, future), everything is colour-coded and the entire concept of playing in a VHS dystopian sci-fi action movie from the ‘80s is just nice. From cheesy synth music to even the loading screen looking like you’re scanning through an old VHS-tape, there’s lots of humor throughout and it surprisingly avoids the trap of overusing reference-humor that most of these kinds of things tend to fall into.
The gameplay is the same as Farcry 3, don’t expect any different. Farcry 3’s skill upgrades are given to you quickly to make sure you’re not wasting too much time regaining the skills you’ve already battled for in the base game. Speaking of which, I do have to wonder why this is a standalone expansion and not a DLC. There’s relatively large content for a DLC, but it obviously leans heavily on the player already being familiar with Farcry 3.
Aside from this, there really isn’t much else to say about Blood Dragon. For what it is, it is pretty damn good. It’s a nice little extra for people who want more Farcry 3 in a new, fancy, funny jacket. Get it if you really enjoyed Farcry 3 like I did. If you didn’t like it, don’t expect this to be better. If you didn’t play it at all, play Farcry 3 first.
The Good: Stylish, works just as well as Farcry 3, cheesy ‘80s vibe is worth a few chuckles, relatively large amount of content added, cinematics done in a style reminiscent of old videogames.
The Bad: No flightsuit which makes traveling boring, actual blood dragons more annoying than fun, island itself slightly boring as it is mostly very dark.

I really recommend this game to people who like FPS games, mixed with some RPG elements.
You are a wizard who tries to complete an ancient combat trial by defeating monsters in the Ziggurat. You proceed room by room, floor by floor until you meet your final challenge. When you enter a room you need to clear out all monsters before you may continue (similar to The Binding of Isaac). To aid you in your battle you have magic weapons in 4 different categories: wand, spell, stave and alchemy. All have different properties and for each type there are several variations available. On each floor you will gain one new weapon and you will need to find the portal key to fight the boss of that floor and continue to the next.
In the meanwhile you gather XP in the form of tiny yellow crystals that drop from the corpses of your foes. In addition you will loot mana crystals that serve as ammo. When you level up, you get to choose from 2 perks that upgrade some of your stats. Pretty simple.
Awesome. The basic rules are very simple, but there is enough variation to keep it interesting. The devs achieved this through the variety in weapons, characters, randomly generated floors and perks. Combat is quick and diverse. You are not just backstrafing to dodge enemies (as was often the case in other games where hoardes of enemies try to get your hide, such as Serious Sam), because some attacks will be targeted or create fires or acid pools.
Especially on the higher difficulty levels you need to watch your mana pool and switch to weapons for which mana is dropped. This makes for interesting gameplay since it forces you to rotate between weapons. Furthermore, most weapons are situational: some are better for AoE (mostly the alchemy weapons), some are better for smaller targets because they fire homing missiles, some can only damage ground targets, etc. You can always use your wand as a fallback, since it always recharges over time (but it is a lot weaker than the others). I found only a few weapons that I don't like, but with a bit of luck you can replace them during the game.
You are not being distracted by inventory management, comparing weapons for stats. There is no number crunching to get the optimal build. Which is a good thing, it keeps the action going. Perks give you little stat buffs (hp, mana, regen increase) or risk-reward choices (lose HP for a bigger bonus). Still, these choices are significant enough to build the character the way you want.
Rooms can be pretty big with lots of stairs and obstacles, which you can use to your advantage. Sometimes you need to backtrack through the floor to get to unexplored rooms, but sprinting through the rooms is pretty fast. You can't sprint through the maze mindlessly though, because sometimes the floor is literally lava! Trap rooms add some nice variation to the floors, but on their own they are nothing more than easily traversable obstacle courses.
The best aspect of this game is that it just keeps on going thanks to the variety in its gameplay. We all know the 'one more room, one more floor' feeling and this game has it. The replay value is OK, there are enough characters to play, content to unlock and challenges to complete. The atmosphere in this game is great and the graphics remind me a bit of Torchlight and the combat of Heretic/Hexen. Some monsters are maybe a bit too cartoony and don't really seem to fit in, but it keeps the game light-hearted I guess. There are not that many bosses and the bossfights could be more interesting (no stages or changing targets, just shoot the big guy 'till he drops dead). I really love the RPG elements in this game, they are simple and add a refreshing touch to the FPS gameplay.
One of the best acquisitions this year!

Great game, but was ruined by the devs, salty players, and updates in general. I started playing this game back in 2015, when it first went into open beta, and I used to play it a lot and really enjoyed it, but I pretty much just gave up on it when Ragnir (the dragon legend) came out. This game had a lot of potential and now it's rubbish. I've lost my patience with this game, to be honest. Every legend that came out after Ulgrim has either been broken, over-powered, or both (usually both). The game is very unbalanced at this point. New legends get all the attention while the old legends are neglected and most are completely outshined by the new ones. Most of the old legends, especially the classic ones (from Bodvar to Teros) have simple, extremely basic moves that can't even compare to the signatures of the new legends (e.g. usually just a simple swing of a weapon for old legend signatures). By contrast, newer legends (legends that came out after Ulgrim) have strong, fancy, detailed signatures/movesets that have a lot of range, are fast, and/or do a lot of damage, and so they're much stronger and are much easier to spam. Some of the newer legends even have unique abilities no other legend has, and while that isn't bad in and of itself, it ruins the balance of the game since older legends don't have unique abilities. And yet, the devs just seem to be neglecting older legends and don't revamp them, balance things out, or anything (and no, adjusting a single hitbox or boosting knockback by 1 does not count as "balancing," so don't try to say they aren't neglecting older legends). And we haven't even gotten to weapon balance (swords outclass most other weapons, spears are easy to spam, etc., and this has been a problem for a long time), older weapons versus newer weapons (gauntlets and now scythe, especially), the extremely toxic community (almost as toxic as Rumble Fighter's community), the intense lag (you can literally be attacking your opponent one moment and suiciding the next without knowing what's happening, among other things), etc. Overall, the game could've been so much fun and had a lot of potential, but the devs seem to have just screwed it up and haven't really listened to the community's complaints, mostly because the toxic players outnumber the other members of the community and are louder than they are, and that's because most of the other players have left BECAUSE of the toxic community, so it's just a cycle in that sense, where toxic players come, other players leave because of the toxic players, more toxic players come, and the cycle repeats. The game also isn't very friendly toward rookies. Most people that I knew that used to play this game during its earlier stages ("veteran players," if you will) seem to have just quit playing. I made it to Diamond (the highest rank) and I can't even say I'm proud of that accomplishment, since it really wasn't worth it. I could say more, but I think I've made my point. I can't recommend this game anymore. It's still free to play, but it's definitely no longer fun to play.

Let me start off by saying i'm a massive Deux Ex fan. I've played the first one atleast a dozen times on 3 different systems.  I even enjoyed the sequel Invisible war which pales in comparson to the first one.  2 years ago ago Human Revolution came out and I was blown away by the world and universe. It seemed like the DX series was coming back to form.
And that's really what Manind Divided is- another solid chapter in the DX series. A smart man's FPS-RPG that forces you to make choices. Some directly, some not so direct but never too far away from the formula.
And maybe that's why it is getting so many mixed reviews. It feels more like an expansion to Human Revolution then anything else. The gameplay feels the same more or less some new augs. The graphics are starting to look a bit dated but nothing crazy. The biggest annoyance is the plot. I'm a hardcore DX fan and i struggle to keep up with all of the players and names and characters. Some call backs from HR, and some call 'forwards' to DX1 and mixed recieved DX:IW. Even with the plot a little all over the place, the gameplay is still solid. Sneaking around feels great when you're able to run from start to end never been seen and the combat has been improved for survivablity so if gun fighting is your way, you'll do just fine.
It's a great game and totally worth $60s even with its issues. But if you can pick it up at the next steam sale for 20-30$, you can't miss.

Heard a lot about how short this game is, how small the maps were and my first thoughts when I left my apartment building were that the game must be very short indeed.  I went round the block by accident just having a look around.
well it turns out thats not the case, theres plenty to do, plenty to discover and it is a mighty fine game overall.  The detail put into the environments is mental, the decorative objects that a lot of people will just run past in a furious gun battle were stylish and highly detailed, adding to the believability of the world.
sometimes this goes a bit far however and some of the areas had so much decoration going on the game really chugged and combat felt sluggish at times.  My machine is pretty powerful but this game demands power like it's Crysis all over again and you need to balance out your graphics vs performance.  My very first impression was that the game was too zippy, movement was just way too fast, but then the skins looked broken around the mouths and the lip synch was totally off.  Cranking the optional settings up to the max fixed the lip synch but made gameplay occasionally sludgy and took away from the otherwise great action in sections with a lot on screen.
Also had a gamebreaking bug when meeting the ARC leader, so save before you go into the room and reloading made the section passable the second time round.  Maybe it had to do with the acheivement, who knows.
That aside, the Jensen coolness is still alive and well, and the many ways to approach a Deus Ex game are still alive and kicking.  I cant imagine getting the pacifist acheivement but it's do-able and one of my steam friends just did it so if you are that way inclined, stealth is viable, as much as blasting everything that moves.
Praxis are few and far between though so hack hack hack anything thats hackable and get your augs the old fashioned way. Earn them.
Just finished, and I'm already keen for the next Deus Ex.  Recommended

Overview: I've played all the Deus Ex games and this is a good addition.  It is fun FPS with a good mix of stealth, minor RPG elements and story that gives you multiple ways to solve problems.
If you've never tried this franchise, you could start with Human Revolution and jump right into Mankind Divided for days of good fun and good story.
Good
+ No technical isssues.
+ World is small (see below) BUT very detailed. Lots of hidden areas to discover if you like to explore.
+ Story is good. Some say it ends abruptly with too many open ends. I think it was fine, but I was able to get the 'best' ending.
+ Good side quests. Interesting and fun.
+ Fun stealth. Being sneaky and doing takedowns was very satisfying.
+ A great mix of FPS that blends into 3rd person cover shooting when you want. A great mix of both genres.
+ A good mix of upgrades to play with to personalize your style of play. I only played stealth/no kill so I don't know how the more agressive upgrades played. They seemed a little lacking, but they may be fine.
+ Quick saves. I abuse the Quick Save, Quick Load to get that "perfect" story and I'm glad the game lets me do it.
+ Replayability. There are many ways to tackle the problem. Try a different style of play and it should be a unique experience again.
+ It is possible to finish the game with zero kills. It is a good challenge if you like being sneaky.
Bad
- Small world. The city is two areas with other areas you visit during the story. I love to explore and this world felt cramped very quickly.
- Slow load time. Going back and forth between areas can get tedious.

The Gameplay, design, voice acting, the new ablilties and Adam Jensen himself is the best thing about this Game.
But unfortuneately these silver linings didn't really save the Game for me -
The Game didn't really have alot to offer on it's Story nor it's connection to the initial Games which dissapointed me the most. There's only 7 main missions (but it felt like 4), the AI is still a bit clunky, a Holy amount of Air vents, and the whole Game had only one boss fight which you can literally beat with your eyes closed.
The whole Game itself felt like a filler and even when finishing the Game, nothing's changed and all your efforts didn't matter at all; It all went nowhere - Underwhelming and Unsatisfying.
This Game is very PC Unfriendly, that even high-end systems were choking under this Game's weight. And I know for a fact that people worked really hard on this and tried to make it like Deus Ex, but now I don't really see Mankind Divided ever surpassing the very first predecessor of the whole Franchise :( Despite having an additional year to work on the Game.
My biggest issue, other than the Game's instability with the PC Port, was it's lack of connections to the Original Deus Ex, The year in the Game was 2029 - The Year where JC Denton WAS BORN - Surely that would've meant something, but no.
There aren't many returning characters either. But seeing that some did actually make it in the Game was still a really great thing they did.
But what I was really hoping to see in the Game was:
Young Anna Navarre
Young Gunther Hermann
Young Walton Simons
Paul Denton as a Kid
JC Denton being created in a Test Tube, before going to Area 51 or something (as an Easter Egg this would've been cool)
And so forth
And since that these characters are slightly younger in this, I'm sure voice acting for these guys shouldn't really be that Hard.
I mean look at this Fan-made video of Deus Ex, they hit the head of the nail with Gunther's voice and the video wasn't even made from a AAA Company.
In Retrospect, I don't hate this Game, I'm just really dissapointed with what they made, despite having all the resources and time in doing so. This Game really didn't do the Original Deus Ex Justice, but I really hope they step it up on the Next installment.

An engrossing puzzle platformer that doesn't overstay its welcome.
PROS:
* Single player co-op! – You play as two brothers. The older is controlled by the left control stick and left trigger; the younger by the right control stick and right trigger. With these simple mechanics the designers are able to craft a wide variety of puzzle scenarios.
* Story – The narrative and character development are mostly advanced through the gameplay, rather than through cut-scenes or dialogue, which makes the experience more engaging.
* Visuals – The art design is spectacular. There are several benches in the game where the brothers can sit, and the camera will pan out so you can drink in the visuals. It was worth stopping every time.
CONS:
* Bugs – I encountered two bugs in my playthrough on a Windows 7 machine. One where an important NPC got stuck, causing me to be trapped in an area where there was nothing to interact with. It was confusing because at first I thought there was a puzzle I needed to solve. Restarting from the last checkpoint fixed the situation. In another instance, the same cut-scene played twice in a row, which didn’t make any sense, but it fortunately didn’t hinder my ability to play.
* Tropes – All the prominent female characters in the game are damsels or some other regressive trope. It mars an otherwise creative plot. There is one “plot twist” in particular that is so obvious, because it’s been done in so many decades of video games, that it comes across as cheap and cliché, rather than surprising.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS:
* Short – The game takes about 4-5 hours to play through completely and there’s not really any replay value. Personally I felt the game was engaging the whole time, and I’m glad the creators didn’t try to pad the game with any additional “grind”, but I think it’s important to consider when you’re calibrating your expectations.
* Mature – Since the gameplay mechanics are quite simple, it seems like a great game to gift to or play alongside a child, but keep in mind that there is quite a bit of gore and mature themes like suicide & death explored in the game (the brothers’ mother dies in the opening scene). So be sure to consider the emotional maturity of any child you choose to introduce this game to.

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is an entertaining standalone "DLC" of Far Cry 3. Blood Dragon reuses quite a few assets and animations from Far Cry 3, although you probably would not overly notice this because everything in this game is coated in neon.
You play as SERGEANT REX POWER COLT, a gruff-voiced 1980's action hero who delivers delightfully corny one-liners (*rips out cyber-heart* "I suppose that was the heart of the matter"). The game's story involves saving the world from a generic 1980's action villain and his plans to rule the world. It isn't overly engaging stuff, yet there are some humorous moments in there. Plus, the cutscenes are all rendered in a tiny resolution with deliberately bad animations and SNES-like graphics. It's charming, although do bear in mind that the main story can be completed in three to four hours.
The gameplay is largely similar to Far Cry 3, which may or may not end up being a bad thing, depending on how well you like Far Cry 3. I personally loved it, so I had no issues with the similar gameplay. The biggest difference comes in the form of the titular Blood Dragons. They add an additional strategic element to taking over enemy garrisons (bringing democracy to the commies), as you can lure one of the buggers to the enemy and have it take care of the mooks whilst you lean back and watch the carnage.
Overall, Blood Dragon is a short yet very sweet game. If you are looking for a stylish open world FPS with plenty of references to 1980's pop culture and copious amounts of neon, this is the game for you.

Okay, so... this game is alright. There's some ups and downs, and I'll be specific about them.
Racing is tight, fun, and awesome. It can be competitive, it can be like a Mario Kart race. By far the best thing about this game.
Deathmatches are fun. They too are well balanced and a blast to play.
Riding around doing missions with friends is a hoot, but playing missions alone sucks.

The idle is the real problem with the game. Just walking on the street when you get gunned down by some kid who's killing everyone. So you turn on Passive Mode. Now, not only can you not rob stores or fight back against cops if you hit something, but people can still blow up your car or run you over with theirs. And you can't shoot them back. It was an interesting idea, but it doesn't work too well. If you're not playing in a friend/crew only server, you'll pay for it.
Buying new weapons and vehicles varies, too. Some stuff is really, really cool and working for my Turismo R was a rewarding turnaround. Some stuff sucks to save for, though. Tanks and most air vehicles are crazy expensive and require a crazy amount of grinding - by which time they've probably added another vehicle or gun that would be more worth paying for. I get that the 30s car is supposed to be a Luxury thing, but if it's outperformed by a common street car and other players will just blow it up anyway, what's the point?
The game is one of the best things to play with friends, and crewing up was actually a highlight of a life I would call rich in experience. But if you don't have any friends who own the game, you're going to suffer.

Okay so, after having put in some nearly 600 hours in the game I feel its time to make a review.
Graphics wise on PC, the game is pretty solid if you have the hardware required. You can see it wasn't just a straight port from consoles. The attention to detail in sounds, dialogs and everything is quite astonishing! The singleplayer story is interesting, though some characters mainly Trevor just feel kind of... forced. That is excuseable however since everything is in order and with quite some polishing put into it. There's plenty to do singleplayer wise, altough until now there is no word as to singleplayer DLC's like the episodic DLC's for GTA IV.
The bad thing when it comes to singleplayer is mods. Not too long ago, the developers decided that modding this game is bad, and that you should feel bad if you mod it, pretty much killing the entire modding comunity from day to night. That has generate some huge backlash (take a look at other reviews).
Now let's get to the rotten core of this review, the multiplayer aspect of the game. Now, you have to understand, when the game was just released on PC, the first week of online play was quite nice, barring server issues but even those weren't that much of a problem and most of the issues started to rise later on and most of them are still very much unadressed up until now.
The first big issue is the amount of hackers in game. It was worse, but it's still quite bad. Often times you will find yourself in a lobby where you get exploded out of nowhere. Or have an UFO and other things spawned on top of your head pretty much preventing you from doing anything. You may also find that the streets and roads have turned to quick sand meaning you'll end up driving a few feet and your car will get dragged back to the starting point over and over and over again. That won't happen if you're on foot though. Shortly after you will get sniped by someone on the other side of the map as they also simultaneously snipe everyone else. You will also occasionaly  be teleported to other places or face people with machine guns that are fed with rocket belts.
Other than the issues mentioned above with hackers, the main issue is hackers dropping tons of money out of the sky on top of you, most of the time also preventing you from avoiding these pickups and turning you into a millionaire by accident. On any other world this would be a good thing but it is not in GTA Online, as Rockstar has been known to occasionally ban players who receive hacked money. They don't really seem to worry much about you getting hacked XP points though, or so the community has pointed out. As of the latest hacked money wipe a lot of people who earned quite a few bucks legitimately with the double money events also had their legitimate gains wiped out with the Smuggler's run update that added hangars and a variety of helicopters and planes.
Speaking of the online DLC, here's the really crippling issue, that seems to outweight the bugs, hackers and everything else with online. While the online aspect of the game is free to play and you can build your own fortune from the ground up, there are "soft pay walls" that will likely lock you out of the DLC content in online as it is quite frankly, extremely expensive. The most recent DLCs, Smuggler's Run and Gun Running are a very good example of one such thing, with most of the content requiring a few millions for you to purchase a hangar and the vehicles you want. If you happen to want cold war era bomber tough luck because it will cost you over 5 millions to buy it, + a few more depending on the hangar of your choice.
With the gun running DLC, it's the same issue. You will need to buy a bunker in order to research the upgrades for your vehicles. Want an APC with missile launchers? You'll have to buy the bunker then research it. But here's the thing, you CANNOT choose the type of research to perform so if you're unlucky, it'll be the last thing on your list. Of course you can boost these research projects at a cost of about 220,000 each, and if you boost them all it'll cost you a whopping 11 millions in online currency. Then you will also need to buy a mobile command center WITH a vehicle workshop and then buy the APC, and then spend the money to add the missile turret to it. Oh, and it doesn't lock on aircraft.
Now you may be thinking that making a few millions in this game isn't so bad... Well... it is. It really is. When you think about a tough grind, you might think of World of Tanks and it is quite a grind indeed, but it's not as bad as GTA Online's. The regular jobs you get from contacts... Sure, do them so you can get a good amount of RP, but don't trust them to net you any significant amount of money. Heists can be interesting if you're the leader, where you'll take most of the payday after the heist finale. But they're much harder and it is very difficult to find a team that will not troll you, will not act as idiots and will not generally just give you a VERY bad time.
There are other options such as exporting cars once you buy the car garage, but don't exepct it to be as easy since you have to source the car, pay for the repair on it if it gets damaged, then pay for the mods if you want to sell it at a high value and then whatever damage it sustains from your warehouse to the delivery point, comes out of your commission. Oh, and expect plenty of military helicopters and jets to try and succesfully bomb your while you're delivering the car, causing you to lose money on it.
You can get around this grind if you can shell out money for the shark cards. The ones that give you any real amount of money that you'd be able to actually spend on things you might like are more expensive than the game itself. And with each online DLC, odds are you'd need AT LEAST 2 or maybe 3 of that one specific card. One DLC comes to mind where the total amount of vehicles and other assets you could purchase totals in the 33,000,000 for all the content, so unless you plan on making GTA Online your full time job, you will likely not see most of the online content. The exception being if you were lucky enough to be playing it when it was released on the PS3 and Xbox 360 and where around when the "moneypocalypse" happened and you're pretty much an in game billionaire.
And by the way, the online DLC content that comes from time to time, does not get put in the singleplayer portion of the game and you'd only be able to access with mods, which are not okay according to GTA V developers.
Edit - 25/10/2017: As of recently, rockstar has announced there will be no singleplayer DLC for GTA V. Also, corrected some bad spelling and non-sensical sentences in this review.
TL;DR The singleplayer portion of the game isn't bad, but don't expect any singleplayer DLC soon. The online portion is riddled with connection problems, hackers, trolls and is somewhat toxic. The DLC content for online does not get put on singleplayer and is safely tucked away behind a soft paywall (which is actually a VERY thick paywall). The only real way to get significant online currency is buying shark cards that are pretty expensive and you'd need several with each DLC to be able to access all the content.

Owned it and asked for a refund. The foremost reason I asked for a refund was because the game won't work in fullscreen on Linux Mint (known bug in an obsolete version of Unity) and that after waiting for 1.5 week, asking for a fix in three different ways (forum, email, in-game contact) the answer was to wait which would disable my ability to ask for a refund.
But I don't really regret the decision, because the game isn't worth the asking price. It's way too simple and I could code it on my own if I were a better graphical designer. The concept is simple, too simple, and might be fun for a board game for what-will-we-do-that-is-not-too-hard evenings with friends. But as a PC game, the simplicity makes it a bit boring.
I read that the AI is very good. That is actually true, but with these simple game mechanics, creating such an AI isn't too much of a challenge either. The approach of just looping through all possible actions and selecting the best one is sufficient because within the limits of the game, this will never take more than a couple of milliseconds to calculate.
Also, the DLC is just some extra maps and I believe one DLC adds some extra rules. I bought all DLC's when I bought the game and it gave me 3 extra gameplay options that didn't seem to give that much extra spice to the game. I must admit though that only playing the game for about an hour may not have been enough to fully understand the implications of these extra's but my feeling tells me that it wasn't worth the big extra bucks charged for it.
For these reasons, I can't recommend the game for the asking price.
Maybe, a big maybe, if the game is on sale some day for say 5.99 for the whole package, AND if the bug is fixed (it's as 'simple' as upgrading to a newer version of Unity which should not be a hard task if you are a good developer), then maybe I will buy it again and I would recommend buying it, because the game isn't bad.
No, the game isn't bad at all, it has been worked out quite good (except for the bug of course, I hate playing games in windowed mode), but it's way too simple and too boring for the asking price.
You might ask which games are cheaper and much more challenging (but less eye-candy)? Go check out Solar Settlers and Axes and Acres (and his other games).

What looks like a simpleton cousin of Dwarf Fortress is actually a fantastic game of it's own, full of personality. Not as complex as the Bay 12 classic, at least not for now, but is certainly worthy hundreds of hours of fun, building your kingdom, training your troops, conducting crazy and useless super-constructions, mining greedly and dying miserably :)
Gnomoria feels and plays like an alpha - because that's what it currently is. However it can only go straight up to the pantheon of divine sandbox games, since even as early as it is, the game is already brilliant. RoboBob, the mind behind Gnomoria, works to evolve the game weekly. Literally. Patches are out every tuesday and they're usually very tasty, tasty enough to make me start another kingdom every now and then.
As the game fleshs out, there will probably be a lot more to do, more enemies, more resources and more FUN! - if you know what I mean - and that's exactly where Gnomoria beats me. I absolutely love sandboxes, playing with destiny and creating your own stories and legends. Who never heard the tale about the Fall of the Diamond Halls before the mighty Mant army? Well, probably no one because that happened to me and I never told anyone about it - but I certainly could. Gnomoria is that perfect kind of game where you create a story and every story is different, every story is your own and you have to live it until you get to the inevitable end.
Sweet pixel graphics and a really enjoyable soundtrack (Seriously, the siege music is amazing.) completes this great game promising future.

Now, this is what I call a worthy successor: louder and longer, but at the same time not too different!
When I started the game I thought it would have been a mediocre sequel, but this wasn't the case here, as I was pleasantly surprised with Dead Space 2's quality.
Graphics and music were pretty much similar to the first game's, but in this case that was a good thing, since the original was an excellent space horror.
Gameplay was also very similar to the first, but with some, well received, improvements. Most of all I appreciated the new Zero Gravity controls, in which you had full freedom to move and levitate in open space, whereas in the first one you could only jump from one surface to another.
Of course, new weapons and suits were also added, which was nice, though I ended up mostly sticking with the weapons I had gotten accustomed with in the first game... and I wore a suit that was a lot reminiscent of the first one's also. Old habits die hard, I guess.
The enemies were, too, a lot similar to the original Dead Space's, but some new ones made an appearance as well, most notably a big necromorph called The Tormentor, which chases you for a good part of the game.
The story is good,  set 3 years after the events of the original game and manages to bring the atmosphere to life in a very similar tone as the latter. The game, as a true sequel would demand, is also 3 chapters longer than its predecessor and, while at times it felt a bid dragged, does what it does very well.
What maybe could be described as my only complaint would be the fact that it sacrificed the first's scary and tense atmosphere for more flashy effects and action sequences, filling it with plenty QTE-like battles, probably influenced from the trend created by modern action games, such as the God of War or Assassin's Creed series, which, in itself, isn't necessarily a bad thing, if it wasn't for the horror factor that suffered a bit from this.
In a few words the game became, as I wrote in the first sentence, "louder" than the previous one, as most sequels tend to be.
However, that said, the game still remains a lot scary and is a worthy successor of the Dead Space name, needless to say that there is even a level in which you enter the "playground" of the first, the planet-cracker spaceship Ishimura and re-visit some areas you explored the first time around and see how it changed over the years.
Last but not least, I remember one of the hardest and most stressing parts of the first game was fighting off a miniboss-like necromorph, called the Hunter, which had infinite regeneration and, as such, could not be killed by normal means and you had to run for your life, while fighting other necromorphs as well... as you might have guessed, this pricky son of a gun makes an appearance in the final levels of the second game as well, this time called the Ubermorph, lowering a lot your survival rate!
Such a pity that the third game doesn't exist on Steam and that, as such, this is my final review here for the franchise, but, for what it's worth, Dead Space 2 was really a blast and a good horror ride, recommended for all of you, fans of chills and thrills!

The game is absolutely beautiful, with the most amazing graphics. While the graphics are simple, they work for game and they look amazing for what they are. I couldn't ask for any better from the game. The environments in this game are beyond breath-taking and I could spend ages telling you about all the little details.
The actual gameplay is quick and fun, but easy to pick up and a little hard to master. While you master one character, you have a chance to go back and play the same class but level up different skills, allowing yourself to have a new skillset to master. While the small class selection is definitely a con, I wouldn't say I hate it. I like the four classes presented. However it won't stop me wishing there was some more. Perhaps what disappoints me more is the character customization. It's minimal to say the least and although it's not an important aspect of the game, I feel like it could be a little more.
One thing I noticed while playing was my abnormal experience gain. Each area has recommended levels but every single time I'm above the recommended levels purely because I'm exploring everything. Although this is part of the bonus of exploring everything, I would prefer my reward be in the direction of loot, rather than levels, so the game can still be challenging.
This also leads me to multiplayer. When you play solo and you go on easy, it goes to one difficulty. When you play with others, you can set it to easy, but this is the exact same easy as solo, meaning that the game becomes incredibly easy. Some kind of implement that increased the enemy strength according to the number of players would be nice.
While I have issues with the game though, I would strongly recommend it to any fan of games like this.

It's a very atmospheric and intense shooter. It has the same kind of feel as Killing Floor does to me. I love to space out with music and this game. That aside, though.
The sound effects are good, but nothing to boast about.
Gameplay is incredibly fun, different rooms offer different challenges or benefits, you never know what you're going to get until you enter a room. It can be an extremely challenging game that demands all your focus or you'll be slaughtered.
The content for this game is infinite. No dungeon playthrough is the same, so stakes are very much raised, however, after a number of playthroughs you'll have seen all the enemies and the kinds of rooms, things are just scrambled up every time. That doesn't take away any kind of fun though, just because you may have seen every enemy doesn't mean they can't still wipe the floor with you if you aren't paying attention.
The music is crisp, atmosperic, and mood setting. It fits in perfectly with the game and immerses you into your role.
The graphics are beautiful and mood inspiring. The kinds of colors the game uses are very saturated, which works well for this game. This game makes me feel happy to have a high end graphics card. Keep in mind that it is an indie game, so graphics were at the very bottom of my expectations list. This company went above and beyond and it clearly shows.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a style of game like Killing Floor, for them it's right up their alley. I also recommend it to any other fps fans. It's a very well done, no brainer, stress relieving game.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a great game with a lot of problems. Some of the game's design decisions left me scratching my head, and I ran across a couple of irritating glitches, but I still had a lot of fun exploring the dark cyberpunk fantasy created by Eidos Montreal
Mankind Divided ran fairly well for me on my decent but not top-end rig (i5 4690k @ 4.2 GHz, GTX 970 FTW, 16 GB RAM) on a mixture of high and very high settings. I typically got 60 FPS, but there were definitely a lot of noticeable dips in certain areas and during certain sequences. It wasn't uncommon for me to see drops into the 40s. Some of these dips were obviously because of something happening on screen, but a great many others didn't have any readily apparent causes. Fortunately, the dips were neither common nor severe enough in most cases to bother me much, and I tend to be pretty sensitive to framerate changes.
Mankind Divided is expectedly fantastic when it comes to sound design. The soundtrack is moody and conspiratorial, and it perfectly captures and conveys the feeling of the game. Sound effects tend to be pretty convicing, too, though I noticed a few times when a sound either didn't fit what I expected when completing an action or was unusually loud. The game's voice acting is probably the weak(er) part of its sound design, and there are a few conversations where the actors fail to deliver their lines convincingly. But the acting is decent overall, especially during the conversation "boss fights" you encounter during your march through Prague. Just try not to pay attention to the lip syncing or the strange body-language animations that often make Jensen look like he’s going to punch the other person in the face for no apparent reason.
Prague is gorgeous. Eidos Montreal has done a fantastic job of taking a relatively small area and making it feel dense and populated enough to stay interesting throughout the game. The feeling of living in a discriminatory police state pervades the game, and Prague does a good job of setting the stage and carrying the narrative. Citizens mutter anti-aug slurs at you as you pass them, police constantly stop you to "check your papers," and checkpoints, robots, and criminals abound. The city pulls together its different districts into a cohesive whole that has its own feel, its own character. Admittedly, this is not Rapture or Black Mesa or Velen. But Prague still did a good job of feeling flavorful enough to keep me interested throughout. In a lot of ways, it evoked memories of Half Life 2's City 17. That's a very good thing.
On top of all the normal exploration stuff, Prague houses a number of really, really good side quests. Many of these quests begin simply, then spiral into some surprisingly deep, interesting stuff. In fact, at least a few of them--most notably one about a serial killer targeting augmented people--were arguably more compelling than the game's main story. Add to all this the interesting evolution of the city as the aug-natural division deepens, and you have all the makings of a great setting.
There are a few other places you visit during your time in Mankind Divided, including a mountain research facility and a London hotel. But with the exception of a brilliant excursion into Golem City, a ghetto/virtual concentration camp for Augs that is arguably the high point of the game, these diversions feel tacked on and unnecessary. It’s almost as if the developers threw them in just to mitigate player complaints about the fact that Human Revolution covered a lot more (and more diverse) territory than Mankind Divided. Fair enough, I guess, but I found myself yawning through most of these excursions.
As you probably already know, Mankind Divided follows the events of Human Revolution. More specifically, it takes place in a world that has turned against augmented people following the Aug Incident at the end of the last game--an incident in which augmented folks were sent a signal forcing them to fly into an uncontrollable rage that killed millions of people. Cheerful stuff, right? Anyway, that incident has left the "naturals" feeling very distrustful of Augs, and that distrust has led to a situation that looks a lot like segregation. As I already mentioned, the game does a very good job of conveying the discriminatory nature of this new world order, especially as Prague descends deeper and deeper into the realm of police state over the course of the game.
The game makes some very salient points about discrimination and prejudice, but it also muddles a few of the issues rather badly. Referring to anti-aug discrimination as "racism," for instance, is silly. Worse, however, is the fact that Mankind Divided never quite trusts itself enough to let the world and the events on screen speak for themselves. There were numerous times that the game did a perfectly fine job of conveying a moral, political, or philosophical point all on its own before a character hopped in with a line explicitly stating the point. Thanks, Captain Obvious. The feeling that Mankind Divided never quite trusts the player to be smart enough to pick up on its messages does a great disservice to an otherwise strong examination of prejudice and discrimination.
Just don’t expect a satisfying ending. It never comes.
The game suffers immensely from some serious pacing problems. Early in the game, every new street is full of enough interesting stuff to mask the fact that you will be spending an awful lot of your time walking back and forth between locations, sometimes with a train ride (and accompanying cutscene) thrown in for good measure. As the game goes on, though, the sense of discovery begins to fade. The story starts getting interesting, and you will want to find out what happens next. To do that, though, you’ll need to trek all the way across the map to talk to someone. Then you’ll need to trek all the way back to where you started. And then… well, you get the picture.
This design flaw becomes a major problem in the last third of the game, when Prague is locked down so tightly that you have to sneak between waypoints.  I nearly gave up the fifteenth time Mankind Divided asked me to sneak through the same courtyard to ride the same train to the same spot  just so I could turn around and do it all again. It’s very, very tedious, and it makes what should be exciting moments in the game slow to a crawl. It’s a big issue.
Fortunately, the gameplay is generally good enough to overcome these problems. Sneaking around is immensely satisfying, there are always multiple ways to approach an objective (some of which are not at all obvious), and I found Jensen’s arsenal of augs to be fun to use. I’m told you can also shoot your way through the entire game, but it’s hard for me to imagine that being an enjoyable experience.
Sadly, there’s little in the way of really meaningful choice when it comes to player development. Sure, you could opt to grab armor augs instead of, say, invisibility augs early on. And yeah, there are some side areas and alternate paths that are gated behind certain abilities and “experimental” augs require you to deactivate another aug to use them until later in the game. Overall, though, the game never punishes you for choosing one upgrade path over another, and the choices don't feel very meaningful as a result.
All told, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a strong stealth game that scratches the cyberpunk itch in a way few others can manage. It’s got some significant issues, but it’s still worth a shot.

I have played the Tomb Raider games since I was a kid, and Tomb Raider: Anniversary might be the best Tomb Raider experience for me. The old games are difficult to get into, with their outdated graphics, complicated controls, and  less forgiving save system. Tomb Raider: Anniversary takes what was good about the classic games and modernizes it (in the best way), resulting in a game that is still surprisingly faithful to the original while being accessible to new fans.
As someone who played the original game, one of my favorite things about this remake is the unlockable content. Each level has a few artifacts and relics (like the secrets in the old games), which unlock outfits (including the original, polygonal Lara from Tomb Raider 1), the ability to rewatch cutscenes and listen to the game's music, as well as various promotional images related to Tomb Raider. Among the most fun of these are the comparison images, which show the game in the same spot in the orignal and the anniversary games side by side.

A Remake done right. Obviously way prettier graphics, enough of the original remains to be recognizable while all expansions are done in a sensible and coherent way. Also longer and more difficult than TR Legends.
Longer simply due to the fact that they stayed pretty faithful to the original in terms of level layout/design. You could spend ages in a single intricate room in TR1, doin puzzles and climbing around, same with this.
More difficult in that puzzlewise theres some actual headscratchers where you gotta stop and figure out what the ♥♥♥♥ youre supposed to be doin and the climbing is more challenging - alot more timed bits. Altho in some way its way easier since reloading checkpoints refills your health and those are somewhat plentyful.
A notable downside of that increased difficulty especially in timed climbing bits is it amplifies some issues which arent usually a big thing. For example when hanging from a wall you can either jump backwards, sideways or just up and the direction to push for each jump type is fixed but becomes sorta context sensitive with changes in camera angle or position. If you can take your sweet time pushing a direction will make Lara sorta wiggle or look backwards to indicate where she will jump. If youre on a timed section where you cant afford to wait for the visual clues i somewhat frequently found there to be...misunderstandings and only after goin splat once i knew which direction i had to push to go where i wanted.
Also spending more time in bigger rooms means you sometimes traverse the same section multiple times, moreso when getting optional stuff. Cant remember if TR1 did this aswell (probably yes) but theyre getting alot more mileage out of a single place compared to Legend where you just breezed thru locations. Your mileage if you like this may vary - the occasional "i gotta climb this again?" popped up for me but i didnt mind generally.

Who'd have thought the sequel to a rather impressive title could hold its own to the original? Well... I did, before Dead Space 3...
"Welcome to Titan Station Isaac Clarke, we've been expecting you."
Some time after the disaster that struck the USG Ishimura, Isaac Clarke again finds himself in another Necromorph outbreak. Having to traverse his way through the entirety of Titan Station, battling his way through Necromorphs, unitologists, and reaching closure for certain events that haunt him from his past, Isaac has far more problems than just rejuvenated corpses trying to kill him.
Right off the bat, this game hooks you like crazy. Yet it is different than the original. The original game used mystery and uncertainty to hook you. This game does definitely do that, b ut if I mention the crucial part this title uses it may spoil some story elements for you, so I will keep that secret.
Immediately, the most notable improvement from the original is the VASTLY improved controls. No input delay, no having to over-aim. This game is crisp as can be.
Secondly, there is much less repetition. With regards to the environment, there is only so much you can do with grey spaceship. Now there is much more color, fire, lighting and more. In terms of enemies, their behavior has been tweaked, there are a few different more types of Necromorph, and the introduction of hardcore mode makes it feel like a true test of abilites.
Thirdly, graphics have been improved in the three year gap between titles. While I mentioned in my review for the first game, it holds up very well for being almost 10 years old, this game looks even better.
Lastly, Isaac can talk! So instantly there is a character you can relate to much easier, since he can communicate with other humans and you can see how he relates to certain people over others.
The only cons I have with the game are mostly plot and motivation based.
Firstly, the central antagonist of the game. Why? Like, I can understand making this character an antagonist definitely will mess with Isaac's head, but its so formulaic when it comes to the ending I almost wasn't surprised by the end result.
Lastly, the ending wasn't quite as emotionally resonant as the original game. That game tugged on your heartstrings and really made you feel for this guy who went through all that to just find out the truth. This game, as previously stated, very formulaic, and almost a bit of getting what they deserved (in terms of the antagonist).
All in all, despite the lacking emotional resonance with the conclusion of the game, Dead Space 2 still has the terror and tension building of the original, with an actual protagonist, and enough firefights to please the hardcore shooter/survival fan.

Like the title says, the game plays quick and as such, makes it fairly simple to learn. Perfect for when you just want to play a full game of something and not have to save and later try to figure out what direction your strategy was going.
Plays a little like Risk in that there are countries and continents to control, but it doesn't utilize dice for battles, instead you have a row of 6 face up cards with actions on them some of which allow you to defeat enemy units. The leftmost card is free and the cost of cards increases as you move to the right. Since you only get 11 coins to start the game, you have to spend those coins wisely as you'll get no more. As a card is bought, the cards shift left to fill the hole and a new card is placed at the end to become the new most expensive card, so the best cards are usually purchased before they can reach the free space. If you spend all your money early in the game, you'll be stuck with selecting the usually less desirable free card for the remainder of the game. Cards are for moving units on land,  moving units across water to conquer new continents, building cities which can produce units, and combat. Points are awarded at the end of the game for resources aquired and lands controlled.
A very easy game to learn, but with great strategic choices to make each turn. UI is clean and easy to use.

Having played other games in this genre, namely Diablo 3 and Path of Exile, this game is quite the gem. I have played as many RPG's in various forms as I've had hot dinners. At present I simply do not have the time to dedicate myself to anyvone game and becoming hardcore(MMO's) or a Pro(First Person Shooters) is something I cannot do right now due to being overly busy. At the same time when I do have free time I like to immerse myself in a game that doesn't bore me.
From what I've research the level cap is 100, with it going as high as 999 then. I can't help but wonder where my adventures wil ltake me, the distance lands, the enemies I'll encounter, the situations I'll find myself cursing the screen and blaming god knows what on my failures.
In short, this game is very enjoyable. I don't have many complaints except for the lack of storage space even though each character has a "Shared storage" and "Personal Storage", both of course are self explanatory.
Having experimented with 3 out of the 4 Classes, I settled on "Outlander", a gun/Bow/Crossbow single and dual wielding ranged class. All classes have pets but this class particluarly allows you to spawn shadow minions when you kill an enemy and speccing mroe into them gives you a greater chance. Most of the weapons also come with knockback which simply amazing for survivability. Most times enemies rarely get near me and when they do I have a Rapid Fire abilitiy that blows them to hell. It also offers snaring and other Crowd control abilities making, at least for me, the most viable class to play long term.
I feel I also have to be in honest in that I'm only half paying attention to the lore simply because the way the Devs have gone about it, doesn't seem overly immersive which is a bit of a bumemr as the gameplay and mechanics are quite enjoyable. That being said, I have not played the first one so that is most likely a major factor in my lack of perception in regard to the story.
If you're looking for a game you can play 'Offline' and 'Online' as well as casually and still enjoying both this and real life. This is the game for you.

Mankind Divided is a worthy successor to Deus Ex: Human Revolution. The stealth and immersive simulation nature of many missions is top-notch and makes for a very enjoyable playing experience. Unfortunately, the plot, pacing, and dialog sometimes hurt the overall narrative.
Two major complaints I'm seeing a lot are the game's length and performance.
With regards to the length of the campaign, I was pleased overall despite the previously-mentioned narrative issues. If you complete side-quests and explore the streets of Prague, you'll definitely see the core game was crafted with love and respect for the series' roots. It would have been nice to have multiple hubs as in HR, but Prague is definitely atmospheric and very memorable.
In terms of performance, I didn't run into game-breaking bugs or crashes. There were a few weird issues where dialog sound bytes didn't load and the people I was talking to just sort of stood there for a few seconds. AI can be kind of dumb - for every time the AI reacted in an interesting way, there was a time I'd be scratching my head over why enemies did something. I ran this game on my fairly modest rig and thought the overall performance was fine - I can easily tell this isn't as well-optimized as, say, Doom 2016... but I imagine it's still very playable on most reasonable machines.
My biggest gripe with performance would be the load times. While this was never detrimental to my overall completion of the campaign, it did hinder my desire to pick up and play this game for short sessions. I know this is an immersive sim with tons of data to keep track of, but the load times somehow seem unacceptable to me - especially given that even people with speedy SSDs are having similar issues.
All in all, this is worth your time. I didn't find it quite as good as Human Revolution, but it's definitely enjoyable and faithful to the Deus Ex formula.

DLC Quest is a game that teaches you about the dangers of buying DLC. It also teaches you about the dangers of buying DLC Quest.
First of all, the "mechanics" of DLC Quest have already been seen in games like Upgrade Complete. Upgrade Complete is a Flash game that has better art design than this and it's actually FREE.
So DLC Quest has mechanics already seen before. So the gameplay is good then, right? Nope! In the actual game there is no way to die, and in the DLC (yes, this game did have DLC when it was on Xbox, which is by far the most counter-productive thing imaginable) you can die, but there's no penalty to it. In fact, there really isn't any difficulty at all. Just collect coins until you win.
The story is going to get a free pass here because obviously it's not important in a satire-based game, but the main issue here is that the satire is so tremendously weak. In the DLC, there's a character that makes nothing but bad game references. This would be funny, if the game ITSELF made nothing but bad game references. Seriously, the game spares no expense to include all the "hilarious" memes such as Oblivion's horse armor, THE CAKE IS A LIE!!!11!, and Minecraft.
So the message of the game is defeated as soon as you buy it, it's not fun, and it's not funny either. DLC Quest is as much of joke as the DLC it tries to mock.

Graphics:
The people that are saying this game is dated or doesn't look good are playing on medium. Especially if you are able to take advantage of DSR or other similar technologies and run on high to ultra-high, this game still looks AMAZING! Just be patient and tinker with it.
Gameplay:
Combat mechanics won't blow you away, but that's not what traditional MMO's are for anyway. HOWEVER, the way each class plays is VERY unique and interesting if you take the time to learn them, thus making the combat feel less clunky than it probably is.
Leveling:
Questing is similar to the snatch and grab MMO model; however, a good bit of story and random traveling is incorporated as well (in a good way) to allow you to explore a bit and familiarize you with what is happening around you, story-wise. You are eligible for instanced content at level 10 but don't expect to jump right into a group instance because it won't happen, the low levels are populated but you level so quickly most people don't even think about instances until they are eligible for skirmishes (skirmishes are so♥♥♥♥♥♥
End-game Content:
There is plenty to do at end-game; however, like any other MMO, it will take you some time to coordinate and find a group for any serious content completion, BUT the potential to do so is definitely there.
Community:
Best of any MMO I've ever seen, players are constantly offering up items for free to newer players, quick to hand out advice, and most of them, excited to help you on your journey throughout middle earth.
TL;DR -- DO NOT let the bad reviews prevent you from downloading this game. If you are TRULY a fan of traditional-style MMO's (think WoW) you will most definitely enjoy yourself. The players complaining about things being "slow", "dated" or "clunky" merely do not know how to configure their settings for the game to run properly on their system.

I rate the side-scrolling platformer puzzle-adventure game Trine 2 5/5. Excellent.
+Outstanding graphics. This is positively the best-looking, more beautiful side-scrolling game I have ever played. I think it easily ties Skyrim for being the most beautiful game I have ever played.
+Excellent controls.
+Excellent but not frustrating puzzles and most have multiple solutions.
+The puzzles are not totally identical to the puzzles in the first Trine game and many make use of entirely new puzzle elements (like making water flow to a particular spot to make a plant grow which you can then climb up).
+The multiplayer looks like it may be lot of fun but I haven't gotten to actually try that.
+No bugs and runs smoothly.
+Good upgrade/level-up system.
+Useful sound effects of good sound quality.
+\- The story is classic but, given that its fairly classic, it is also fairly boring and predictable.
+/- Dialogue is merely adequate.
-The only major problem with this game is that it is a little too short (and that can be remedied by getting ahold of an excellent, but very difficult, DLC add-on called Goblin Menace).
-Oh, and the music, like the music in the first Trine game, is fairly sedate and boring.

Dead space 2 takes what was good in the first game, pretty much everything and then fixes most of what was bad in the first game, which was the controls and fov and makes a much better sequel that is dark, fun, and you get to shoot up ugly monsters all over the place! What can be better!
Just like the first game, the visuals are amazing, even better in DS2. Like mentioned before the controls have been fixed to actually have a fun playable experience that is smooth and fun, very unlike DS1. You go through an amazing set up experiences, great cutscenes and launches into different areas such as anti-gravity, space, vents and tunnels and much much more.
Now saying that, yes there are still problems with DS2. You are limited on weapons and armor due to your small inventory space so you normally have to focus on 1 weapon, maybe 2 max instead of enjoying the variety of weapons that the game introduces you to. You have the ability to upgrade your weapons and armor and unlike other games, you don't find "better" items later usually, so your fully upgraded weapon is going to be your main weapon for most of the game, because if you find something else it isn't upgraded with 20-30 nodes and is vastly weaker, so why even use it.
There is also still the horrible problem with the sound. The sound is great in the game except when it comes to talking and understanding what people are saying. Normal speech is fine but lots of scenes, cutscenes, they try and do "monster" voices and such, and they are 100% not able to be understood, which ruins the reason for actually trying to say something in the first place. Way to much "scary" modulation which makes the speeches just babble.
Still very good game, finally good controls, just wished for better inventory management so you could enjoy all the weapons equally instead of having to wait until new game+'s to use them.

I got 3, Pets, Generations, and Seasons for around £19 total. That's probably what it's worth.
On new hardware you will need to do a bit of work to get it running properly and even then the performance will progressively lag as the in-game world accumulates clutter, needing further modding to get optimal functionality.
On top of that the game is still by default priced stupidly high, likely to put people off of buying it in favour of the similarly priced Sims 4?? I don't know.
The gameplay, as the Sim's careers progress and they go from broke to stinking filthy rich is probably the best the series has produced, although The Sims 4's ability to have Sims multi-task is something I already find a glaring set-back.
The building construction is the series' best, and has had its functionality stripped back considerably for 4. Although if you've tried 4, and then move on to 3, it will look old.
4's isolated lots replacing the open world also results in a much more stable game that is able to handle many more sims in the same space at a time without performance issues.
The Sims 3 is the series' high point, but no one should ever pay the price they're currently charging. Given its overall performance and the constantly increasing content via its many updates, I'd probably recommend 4 at this point unless you can get 3 for cheap. Then again, The Sims 4 is also grossly over-priced, so maybe go and spend the money on an indie game and save EA Maxis their smug satisfaction.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is an atmospheric adventure that I would classify more as an "experience" than a "game". It's a short but highly story-driven singleplayer co-op title. That's right, the main highlight/gimmick of Brothers is its control scheme, where the player uses both analog sticks and triggers to maneuver two separate characters at the same time. In other words, you're probably going to want a controller to play this one. This allows for some very interesting puzzles and game mechanics that definitely lead to a unique playthrough.
Brothers is one of those titles that has been highly recommended to me by tons of people, and for what it's worth, it deserves a lot of the praise it receives. I definitely found it a unique experience, and I can see why the story resonates with many players. However, I personally just did not find this title all that compelling. The controls and gameplay felt clunky and progressed slowly. The story, while powerful, wasn't anything earth-shattering or brilliant. The game, while featuring some beautiful scenery, is definitely dated in terms of graphics and animation (which usually isn't a big deal, but this game relies on these aspects for its storytelling). Ive played this game for a considerable amount of time and here is my legit review of the game.
Brawhalla is a 2D fast-paced fighter that can rival super smash bros brawl in a game style sense. The community is a toxic bunch of blokes who will say "f**king easy" after a 1v1 win, this game is also one of the most rage inducing, wall punching game that is comparitive to league of Legend, Dota, CSGO and more. the game is quite balanced but in other senses is completely unbalanced, this can be realised when you go into the loading screen and say "F**k why (insert character)".
Spam, although those who climb into the higher ranks always detest that there is spam in the game, is actually a big part of the game, examples of this is: Rocket Lance S-light and S-signature, Katar air D-light, and N-light (and all moves in general, they are basically built for speed and spam).
Additionally the game struggles with matchmaking at a level that players can smoothly climb and instead, chucks you right into a new ELO, this can be seen in the main struggle for players to climb from high silver to gold, as you rise into 2280-2300 range, players experience a dramatic change in skill level and will inevetably drop back down multiple times and yo-yo until they gain the skill to climb up into gold 0.
I know you guys are probably bored of reading a wall of text so here is a list of pros and cons to help you figure out if the game is for you
Pros:
- fast-paced gameplay that can be extremely rewarding
-wide range of characters all unique in weapons and signiture moves
-simplistic style most pc's can run
nice animations and the artstyle makes everything look a little more "extra"
-find match finding times
-enter a bot match during a queue search
-two player ranked to climb with friends
-variety of weapons
-combos galore
-alright comeback potential
Cons:
-bad matchmaking
-spammers are common
-games can be lost very easily from virtually one small mistake
-lose about 1.5-2 games worth of wins per lose
-rage inducing when you lose
-easy tilt from being mad at game
-weapons can be unbalanced (depending on who and what weapon)
-you can get completely combo stunned
-no time to flame opponent after lose (just a joke jeez)
-I dont know if this is just me but the mouse stays onscreen ingame (minor)
Things that they should add:
-more weapons
-a kind of combo blocker, so you can turn around a fight mid attack
-more maps
-more gadgets
Additional reason for me to downvote is this is one of those toxic addicting games that you rage in (League of Legends)

This is a fun game, i've been hoping for a smash bros like game for pc and ive found it. Also I've gotten the impression that the devs actually care a fair bit about this game which is always nice. Tl:dr fun game with good buisness model, definetly should give it a try

Most of the hit boxes in this game are inaccurate in a numerous variety of ways. Knuckles, hammers, lances, and scythes have awkward hitboxes that aren't hard to master, but ARE hard to defend against since they are very, VERY, deceiving.
With the minor delays and lag in the game, it doesn't seem like a problem, but the more you play and better yourself. The more you see these flaws becomes prevalent to gameplay.
Spear in-air specials (Up and down) have especially tricky hitboxes that are plain hard to defend against as they also seem to extend above the spear. Normally this is ok, but the game has very precise hitboxes for everything, it seems unfair to give that special such a "generous" hitbox. Combo this with those minor hiccups in networking and you get some wacky deaths that shouldn't have happened even with the game's super precise and tight hitboxes.
THIS GAME IS REALLY NOT GOOD

The way the game handles lag is honestly terrible... Rather than having the game freeze like a normal fighting game would, or any game that requires accurate reactions to play, the game has your characters rubber banding all over the place, making you think you hit the person you're playing against, until their health regenerates a few seconds later.
Doesn't help that the lag comes frequently, even when it's not necessarily visible. You'll assume things happens only to realize they're mirages of what could've been. Really hurts a fighting game when you see this particular type of lag.
Community is also garbage in my opinion.... Don't ever try to spark a conversation in chat. The skill gap is also really tiny. You could probably learn every single combo for a character in one day. It'd be useless, though, since the game uses character rotation, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, just a quirk of mine, and I'm not about to spend $20.00 you fix that.
I will say the devs are pretty generous with the coins, which is a positive. A few hours and you'll have half the roster unlocked. I wouldn't recommend unlocking half the roster, though, since they all use the same weapons, with practically no variation. The only different is their specials, which you won't be using unless you've got someone at near death. They add a bunch of usable weapon meisters simply to distract you from the fact that there's only a few weapons.
Another problem is that you can choose not to get hit at all or just keep hitting as fast as you can. This goes back to the skill gap. You won't often be punishing people, you'll just be spamming X, A, and the right trigger as many times as you can until your opponent dies.
The game does have a relatively small download, though, and is worth putting time into, it's one of those games you won't stop playing. Ranked isn't fun at all in my opinion, since the meta is legitimately just running around and air dodging, continuously grabbing and throwing weapons, or pure button spam. You could probably get to a point where people actually start doing cool techniques, but I haven't reached that slope, and I don't feel like trying to get that far. This game is fun to play against your friends, and maybe tournaments could be fun too, but I couldn't see it becoming too popular of a game in its future. Doesn't help that a lot of people consider this a meme.

Torchlight II is a dungeon crawler RPG, created by an indie developer Runic Games. In this review, I decided not to talk about the story of the game because I was not paying attention to the story (pretty much killing mobs to obtain legendary loot or leveling up) and it is really difficult to remember what happened so let's get on the review. The game's theme is robotic, magic wizardry and witchcraft. Once the player progresses the story (Acts) of the game, it will take you to different lands and it's completely random generated dungeons as well. There are 4 classes to choose from; Engineer, Outlander, Berserker and Embermage. The game's mechanic is obviously similar to Diablo's gameplay. The loot system, weapon add-ons, pet system are great. You can do the item micromanagement without going home by sending your pet to the home portal and sell the inventories you have been hoarding for you, so you can keep grinding on the fly. The skill system on each classes have unique skill trees. Including Active and Passive Skills. They have 7 Active skills each trees and 3 Passive skills (About 21 Active skills including Ultimate and 9 Passive skills). It's very accessible skill trees, you can build whatever you like. There is an end game content, like purchasing any random generated scroll map to level up and your fame level (to earn fame level, you kill any legendary monsters to earn EXP or XP and gain skill points.) You can do another play through or New Game Plus which is great additional, whatever floats your boat.
For the final review of the game, the gameplay mechanics are strongly familiar to Diablo III. The classes are great but I wish they have sub-classes. The content is limitless because of the mods, RNG dungeons on end game content. But no one cares about the storyline of the game and I found it shallow and snooze fest. The looting system of the game and all RPG aspects that make me want to grind more. The final score for this game is an 8 out of 10, a strong recommendation. I would recommend you Grim Dawn or Path of Exile (Free to Play game) if not.
