The way the game handles lag is honestly terrible... Rather than having the game freeze like a normal fighting game would, or any game that requires accurate reactions to play, the game has your characters rubber banding all over the place, making you think you hit the person you're playing against, until their health regenerates a few seconds later.
Doesn't help that the lag comes frequently, even when it's not necessarily visible. You'll assume things happens only to realize they're mirages of what could've been. Really hurts a fighting game when you see this particular type of lag.
Community is also garbage in my opinion.... Don't ever try to spark a conversation in chat. The skill gap is also really tiny. You could probably learn every single combo for a character in one day. It'd be useless, though, since the game uses character rotation, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, just a quirk of mine, and I'm not about to spend $20.00 you fix that.
I will say the devs are pretty generous with the coins, which is a positive. A few hours and you'll have half the roster unlocked. I wouldn't recommend unlocking half the roster, though, since they all use the same weapons, with practically no variation. The only different is their specials, which you won't be using unless you've got someone at near death. They add a bunch of usable weapon meisters simply to distract you from the fact that there's only a few weapons.
Another problem is that you can choose not to get hit at all or just keep hitting as fast as you can. This goes back to the skill gap. You won't often be punishing people, you'll just be spamming X, A, and the right trigger as many times as you can until your opponent dies.
The game does have a relatively small download, though, and is worth putting time into, it's one of those games you won't stop playing. Ranked isn't fun at all in my opinion, since the meta is legitimately just running around and air dodging, continuously grabbing and throwing weapons, or pure button spam. You could probably get to a point where people actually start doing cool techniques, but I haven't reached that slope, and I don't feel like trying to get that far. This game is fun to play against your friends, and maybe tournaments could be fun too, but I couldn't see it becoming too popular of a game in its future. Doesn't help that a lot of people consider this a meme.

I know I'm going against the grain here, as I did enjoy this game but felt compelled to leave it a negative review after much thought. To begin with - Mind boggling puzzles, a fantastic narration and beautiful graphics to top it off. Whilst confusing at first, the story eventually sucks you in, and it kept me saying "...one more level before bed". I have played all 3 Trine games, and this is by far the best of the bunch - and is the standard that Trine 3 should of built on, not tried to 'improve' (more on that later).
Unfortunately as good as Trine 2 is - it does suffer in some places. Whilst not a graphically demanding game, it can sometimes suffer from poor optimisation causing graphical stutters on intense levels. After much research, I've found that there is a bug that can sometimes stop unused textures being removed from RAM, causing the game to fill up your entire memory until eventually it crashes to the desktop.
Another gripe I have is to do with the way the story is told in some levels. As an example, the Archer (universally, everyone's favorite character) ends up being the baddie all along and kills the other two characters in the final cut scene. It completely obliterates the story as it was great up to that point. and leaves you scratching your head as to why the devs would implement such a cliché in an otherwise great fairytale (non playable by the way, it's a cutscene no less!)
To sum it off, I would say it's a great game but no without its faults. Due to the predictable ending however, I can't recommend it.

Extremely funny pun at the DLC-habits
This is a very funny, small, but well-made and well thought-off game. It's essentially a sidescrolling platformer, with some jumping action and minor skills required (a gamepad comes in handy). Graphics and sound are minimalistic, even quite retro (I was reminded of the games of the 80's). But this serves a purpose: to make fun of the ever-growing DLC-habits (and sometimes misuse) in the games of, let's say, the last five years.
So you start the game literally without anything. You can hardly move your character, there is no sound, even no menu. All of these have to be purchased as dlc-packs, to be paid for with in-game found gold. It's a simple but original idea, and it's very well executed, with lots of humour. I found myself laughing out aloud quite often. There is even a totally non-important sequel, so the sequelitis also gets a slap at.
That's all there is to it, really. The game is original, funny, and - despite the tons of dlc's - very short. But for very little money, do try it, and treat yourself on some great moments. It even has Steam-acievements (which are also made fun of!) and Steam trading cards, so for badge-hunters this is a real treat.
Gameplay: 21/30 (the basic idea gets done well, but that's it)
Graphics: 10/20
Sound: 6/10 (I liked the retro sounds)
Replayability &long-lasting appeal: 10/20 (it's very short, but it's cheap too)
Stability/patching: 18/20 (no issues whatsoever)
Final score: 65/100
Worth the dollar I paid for it and not much more.

Dead Space 2 is a great horror game and a brilliant sequel to the another great horror game.
Set, I believe, three years after the events of the first game, Isaac Clarke wakes up in a psych ward in a hospital in a space station, just as the infection that wreaked havoc on the Ishimura (space ship) from the first game breaks out on this space station. Clarke makes his escape while having hallucinations but is also guided by a stranger. This is where the story really kicks off. Because I'm going to avoid giving away any spoilers, I'm just going to say that the person you hallucinate throughout the game is Nicole, Isaac's former love interest from the first game.
The brilliance of the horror elements in this game is that it isn't a jump scare type of game. It's genuinely terrifying because of the extent of damage done to this space station due to a breakout in the disease that transforms the people into these abominations of creatures. The most memorable part is, arguably, when you're in a nursery and you see a woman, still alive, trying to cradle her baby, who has visibly transformed. Well, the baby has a yellow, soft belly and if you've played the first game, you'll remember that the yellow areas are weak points prone to explode. You can probably guess what happens to the woman.
The soundtrack is nice but the game really shines when there isn't any music at all. Just the vast void of sound is so profound and the slightest creak will catch you off guard. The sound mixing in this game is done expertly. The graphics are stellar. I mean, I can tell it came out in 2011, but the lighting is so great and the textures on the walls and characters are generally fantastic. All around splendid job on graphics. The level design is done well enough where each chapter has a varied design. I especially loved the zero gravity flying around in space. The vastness of it, and being able to see Saturn in the distance (I'm pretty sure it's Saturn) is just so unique.
Anyway, I feel like I've said enough. Really, fantastic game. Highly recommend.

This game makes me think of Hexen/Heretic in many ways while still carving out it's own unique take.
Essentially, you play as one of a selection of characters with their own initial strengths/weaknesses and navigate through a randomly generated dungeon, proceeding further when you have defeated the boss of that level.  The weapons you begin with (outside of the basic wand) are random as well.  Through numerous playthroughs you will unlock a variety of different weapons, amulets and character abilities (of which you choose from a selection of at least 2 upon each level up) making sure that no two games will play the same.
For some, the luck-based nature of the randomly generated layouts, abilities and weapons may be a turn off, but I consider it to be one of this game's strengths.  While you only get one life to navigate the Ziggurat, the randomness keeps a constant freshness to the game.
The basic game is only 5 levels, which makes my approach to this as an old-school arcade game with one life and enough variety in each playthrough to make it worthwhile to revisit.
If you wish to play a longer version, there is a setting among the difficulties to play it up until your character finally perishes, which I have not yet tried, but I imagine is like a survivial mode.
Most of the randomized skills you earn are at least not harmful, and a few are rather helpful.  You may run across a shrine wih punishes you and some monster combinations are brutally efficient, but I do find that the longer you are able to survive, the easier more things are to deal with.
The variety of characters to choose from is nice since you can play to their strengths if you are given the right choices at a level up...or at the least, you can minimize their weaknesses to a degree.
Overall the game is challenging and addicting.  If you approach it with the mentality of a randomly generated arcade style game rather than an RPG or other longer game, you should be very pleased with it.
Graphically, I'm fine with the art direction.  There are times that enemies may have attacks that obscure your view with the special effects, but I consider that a part of the natural hazard the game is built on.  In a larger room, you can at least maneuver around it.  Getting trapped in a smaller room with enemies that attack with lots of special-effect laden attacks can be tough.
The music is just the right amount of background atmosphere needed to fill the game.  The distinctive sounds of various enemies is very helpful in identification of what you are up against.
The controls are responsive (I'm using a 360 controller to play this) and I have not personally had any difficulty in gettnig my character to perform actions, nor dealt with any slow response time, except insofar as it is built into the character itself, such as a slow firing rate with a particular weapon. So I am very satisfied with the tight and intuitive control of the game.
Milkstone Studios has done a fantastic job on this and I recommend it to anyone looking for a game that is simple enough to pick up and play, but challenging enough to keep them engaged.  Another nice touch is the ability to create a save point between stages in case you only have a little bit of time to play and want to get back to your game later.

The fact that weapons and perks are randomized might rub you the wrong way if you take this game too seriously or if you want it to be more of an action RPG than a rogue-lite. For everyone else though this just means that you'll have to adapt to what the game is giving you in order to succeed.

If you want a difficult challenging game, this is the wrong game. If you are a rogue like fan, who thinks, randomness = difficulty, this is the right game for you.
We wont talk about the story, because the story is irrelevant. This is a game like binding of isaac or paranautical activity (or what paranautical wanted to be).
You have a random set of:
- weapons
- dungeon rooms
- bosses
- abilitys
- boosts
- negative boosts
Short: In story mode you get dropped into a dungeon challenge with 5 stages. Each stage has a set of randomized rooms (not random generated, after your first few games, you know every room), with a random set of enemys, that sometimes have special abilitys.
With each room, you get levelups which you can spend in perks. Each time you can choose between two random perks.
Also you have, beside your main weapons, three types of weapons. Staffs, Spells and Alchemy. For each stage, you get a new random weapon. If you are unlucky, you can get the same weapon on every stage. Each weapon type has its own mana bar, so you have to switch between them, sometimes saving your best one for the boss fight.
While playing the game, you will unlock new characters (each with unique playstyle), new perks, weapons and amulets.
The amulets are a little bit unsatisfying. It is very hard to get one and then you should be lucky enough to get a good one. (sometimes you have good combos like playing a staff guy with a amulet with a + staff attack speed, which felt like an boss insta kill)
Created from feedback from the community, the developers released a endless mode, which is also nice to play, but getting really imbalanced on the higher stages (I got around floor 30).
The whole gameplay is a little bit like oldschool shooters similar to Serious Sam, where you are in a small room with hundreds of enemys. In Ziggurat every enemy, beside 3 types, have a ranged attack, which can end in a endless storm of attacks in the higher stages of endless mode.
The big con of this game is the great amount of randomness:
You can have a great round, rushing through all waves, getting + attack and + defence and good spells.
You can have a bad round, loosing weapons, getting negative buffs, bad weapons and the hardest boss.
And the game has a lot of randomized parts:
- enemy encounters
- rooms
- loot
- levelups
- boosts and debuffs from shrines
- weapons
- amulets
- aditional loot rooms and secret rooms

Milkstone have really outdone themselves. After being a middling shovelware developer for the Xbox 360 for several years, they have created a very tight, very well crafted roguelike FPS with some genuine challenge and enough unlockable material to keep most players occupied for quite a while. On top of that, at the time of writing, MIlkstone is still consistently adding content to the game including weapons, bosses, and new character perks.
My only real criticisms are that the game is a bit short--the titular ZIggurat can be completed fairly easily so long as you have the controls down and pick appropriate perks--and some of the various magical weapons are demonstrably better than others--the balance isn't quite perfect.
Other than that, highly recommended. Definitely worth the price.

Cantina Deluxe has nothing on Cafe.
The good old Shufflepuck Cafe, when I played it back in another age on a Mac Classic in my school's computer room, was immensely challenging, with each character taking serious skill to beat. Each had their distinct play style, each responded perfectly to some moves and were susceptible to others, each served in semi-predictable or totally unpredictable ways, and all the opponents were ranked from easiest to impossibly hard, and rightfully so. Maybe there was nothing else to the game, it was pretty simple after all, but the gameplay made up for the simplicity.
Shufflepuck Cantina Deluxe introduced 3-D graphics, in VR for those so equipped, and added tons of extras - a multitude of mallets and pucks and "embodiments" to choose from, quests, missions, collectibles, and let's not forget special attacks... Too bad that the core gameplay fell far, far short behind the original's. All the opponents have exactly the same core difficulty level - even the newbies can successfully defend against fast cross-courts and rebounds, and even the boss occasionaly fails to catch a slow shot. They differ only with their serve technique (perfectly predictable after 2 or 3 rounds), special moves (also perfectly predictable, except for Phan-Le's "cannonball", but those turn matches against him into mindless smashfests along one side, until he finally misses). Also the concept of mastering special moves is completely useless, as opponents randomly either defend against lightning fast specials, or hopelessly fail to hit a technique executed by accident and slow as a snail.
Then there's the progression, represented by collecting points, credz and completing quests. Again, however, they're ridiculous in design: "boss" missions, completed to collect spaceship quests, are simple "reach 15 points" matches, of which I have not lost even one as a whole; characters' quests, in turn, often involve winning over a dozen points in "survival" mode against an opponent, which is far more time-consuming (considering opponents being as predictable as described above). And while the easy spaceship missions award game-finishing items, the hard survival matches yield points and rewards ten times smaller than a single match against any high-level opponent. Oh, and the final boss of bosses? He's just as hopeless, his only power is that he switches between styles of all the other characters with each ball played.
But an experienced player should easily complete the game by beating all the opponents, right? Nope. The spaceship parts take credz (cash) to obtain, and those are collected by grinding, that is playing hundreds, thousands even, of boring, repetitive matches against inept opponents.
Bottom line? Avoid this, if you expect a challenge similar to the old Shufflepuck Cafe. This remake is a shameful disgrace, just wrapped in pretty graphics.

The Lord of the Rings lore is translated fairly well from the movies to the game. It's the standard MMO fair of hacky, slashy, grindy, and skip all the dialogue quest completion but with a little twist. You can also grow crops, harvest furs, tan hides, make armor, prepare arrows, and a whole host of other things. It's still grindy but it attempts to own the grind in a match I haven't seen since Runescape. But eventually you'll get bored of your profession and want to do something else, and that's when Lord of the Rings Online starts grinding down my patience.
Most of the interesting quests are locked behind paywalls. I don't mind developers locking additional content and adventures behind a pay barrier, but at least don't lock all quests within a certain level range behind a pay wall. If you want to be a subscription based game, just be a subscription based game. If you want to be freemium with a subscription model after a certain level, do that. This is just poor business practices.
Finally I guess I have to talk about the PvP. It's a neat little idea where you have playable monsters and heroes fighting one another, but it turns into a mess when you realize that most of the monster races are locked behind further paywalls and the heroes are all more qualified to kick your♥♥♥♥♥than you are to do anything against them. Then you'll run into the other problem where there aren't any heroes online to fight because to access the hero side of Lord of the Rings Online you have to reach 95 and pay a fee.
The funny part of all of this is that they introduced a balance patch in the game in Update 13 and it took just a couple new patches to break it into pieces.
If you're a die-hard Lord of the Rings fan who doesn't mind the grind, go right ahead. Otherwise I wouldn't waste your time.

The Lord of the Rings Online is by far the Best MMORPG I've kind of played.  I was a late to the game, but I subbed for a few months with some friends (and even more since f2p).  The fellowship quests and group content is as solid as it gets for old school MMORPGs.  A time came when new and shiny things came and Lotro was left behind for me and my pals, But I still go back every now and then.  I love the rich lore/story, the fantastic graphics (even today they look good), and the truley epic settings.
LOTRO at first glance when playing is odd.  I totally understand when someone says they just didn't like it.  Yet at it's core, this game is as good if not better than any MMORPG made during it's time.  It just does things a little differently.  For instance it tries really hard to stick to the books (the I.P it draws from-not the movies) so there are no mages or wizard classes bc the only Wizards are the famous ones - (Gandorf, Radhadgas, Sarapmon). There are however classes who play like mages using knowledge of powders (Lore Master), ancient runes (Rune Keeper), and...music (Minstrel).  There are no "hit points" or health.  The green bar is morale, and when it reaches zero you die..so yeah its health, but not really, and some abilities are just silly like the crowd control Burglar ability "riddle" (in the heat of combat you tell a riddle and the enemy thinks about it for like 20 secs).  Thats what Lotro does.  It holds true to the lore of the book and the world it created.  Each class is very fun and there are quite a few 'one of a kind' classes in Lotro. So often mmos copy paste classes.  At the start of the game, the music is not great, your gear looks like barf, and you're screaming at enemies to do damage. It's different and these can push ppl away, but the music is optional, lotro has an amazing (before it's time) outfit/wardrobe system that is fully customizable with dyes and overlays, and screaming at enemies lowers their morale so get over it.
The main reason I don't play it very much is the lack of friends who will play it.  Like many MMORPGs back then, playing with friends is a tricky and often demanding experience.  Need to be on the same server, and need to be near the same levels. Servers have merged, players are a bit low, but It's still good and the Free to play model isn't horrible.  You can do anything by grinding Deeds.  The f2p model locks out questing zones and trait slots, and sometimes the paygates get annoying, but if you don't care to grind deeds it's really not that big of a deal.  Especially if you make alts bc their deeds count towards the in game currency too.  If you are a fan of Lord of the Rings in any form, nothing beats exploring and visiting all of the awesome iconic places you've only read about or seen in movies.  Give it a try! I know I will as long as it's still alive.

Dead Space 2 is a great horror game and a brilliant sequel to the another great horror game.
Set, I believe, three years after the events of the first game, Isaac Clarke wakes up in a psych ward in a hospital in a space station, just as the infection that wreaked havoc on the Ishimura (space ship) from the first game breaks out on this space station. Clarke makes his escape while having hallucinations but is also guided by a stranger. This is where the story really kicks off. Because I'm going to avoid giving away any spoilers, I'm just going to say that the person you hallucinate throughout the game is Nicole, Isaac's former love interest from the first game.
The brilliance of the horror elements in this game is that it isn't a jump scare type of game. It's genuinely terrifying because of the extent of damage done to this space station due to a breakout in the disease that transforms the people into these abominations of creatures. The most memorable part is, arguably, when you're in a nursery and you see a woman, still alive, trying to cradle her baby, who has visibly transformed. Well, the baby has a yellow, soft belly and if you've played the first game, you'll remember that the yellow areas are weak points prone to explode. You can probably guess what happens to the woman.
The soundtrack is nice but the game really shines when there isn't any music at all. Just the vast void of sound is so profound and the slightest creak will catch you off guard. The sound mixing in this game is done expertly. The graphics are stellar. I mean, I can tell it came out in 2011, but the lighting is so great and the textures on the walls and characters are generally fantastic. All around splendid job on graphics. The level design is done well enough where each chapter has a varied design. I especially loved the zero gravity flying around in space. The vastness of it, and being able to see Saturn in the distance (I'm pretty sure it's Saturn) is just so unique.
Anyway, I feel like I've said enough. Really, fantastic game. Highly recommend.

A mechanical masterpiece, this game utilizes the controller in great effect to create such an immersive experience. Every other game that I've played has used the contoller or keyboard as a means by a story. Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons creates its story through its controls alone. Albeit short and not too difficult, it's a very well paced and well written game that I can definitely recommend.

TL:DR
Immersion breaking controls
RAMBLY THOUGHTS
I wanted to like this game. Everyone else seems to. But frustration with the controls totally took me out of the game early on. Apparently every rope ladder in the land is broken 2 feet from the top in this land as well. "Oh look another broken half ladder I have to toss the younder brother up to" I kept thinking to myself.
A spot early on involves weight and constant movement. Despite the big brother straining to pick some things up, they were not used all together to weigh an object down. Instead these mostly stationary things needed to be used in a way that they suddenly decided to move. It was not intuitive.
A section a little further on tasks you with dragging an object into place to halt some machinery. The younger brother refused to grab one end, so I figured that the older brother had to move it by himself while the other was going to do something else. I was able to drag it alone, so got it to the vicinity where it was obviously needed. I couldn't pull it onto the place it seemed it should go, nor could I poke it into a hole that seemed like another possibility. Finally I gave the younger brother another go and he decided to help this time. After 10+ minutes of wasting my time, I still don't know why the younger had previously refused to help.
Eventually you'll encounter a section with some flip flop swinging that people will recognize from Baron Von Munchausen. IMHO it drags on far too long and there is a bit in the middle where they brothers are walking on either side of a gap still tied together that necessitates some back and forth zig zagging. It was a minor thing, but why wouldn't they untie for that?
Many sections require you to hold the triggers fo rextended periods of time. Perhaps it didn't help that I played the game straight through, but more than once I felt a little cramped and accidentally let a brother fall to his death. At another point the game had taken control from me for a cutscene and had the brothers running away from a monster. It them stopped moving them without warning and I died and had to repeat the section. It was only a 5 second section, but it still added to my annoyance.
I was completely taken out of the game by the time I had the issue with the dragged object due to the controls and interaction issues. I didn't care about the brothers, their dead mother, or their sick father anymore, this was simply a game I was fighting with. I only kept playng because I knew it was short. It didn't win me back. When the event near the end hit, I was mostly just annoyed that I had to wait for extended cutscenes and perform certain actions myself. The story was rather meh other than sad motivations and we didn't learn much about the characters other than the younger brother being a twerp with a fear of water who will spit in wells and annoy townsfolk.
I have played through this tonight after having played completely through Limbo, Inside, and Corpse of Discovery in the past 4 days. So I've definitely been in the mood for Puzzle/Platform/Walking Simulator games. Limbo had some tricky puzzles. Inside was fairly easy but was a very intriguing world and was careful to not reuse gimmicks. Corpse of Discovery had some jankiness and a little less polish being a very small production, but had interesting writing. I'm rather disappointed to have played Brothers last of the lot as I caught up on backlog since I enjoyed it the least.

A touching story about 2 brothers on a quest to save their dying father. The game implements a unique singleplayer co-op system where you control both brothers at once (Using the left side of the controller to control the older brother and the right side to control the younger brother) to work your way through obstacles and solve varies puzzles in each chapter. This can sometimes make gameplay a bit jarring and I recommend trying to keep the older brother on the left side of the screen and the younger on the right when you can to help orient yourself.
Pros:
+  Strong Story and Relateable Characters: The story is mostly conveyed through body language and is used very well to characterize each brother and keep the player engaged. Facing hardship with your family is a universal theme I think many can relate to and the emotional moments in this game are powerful. There are also side activities you can find while exploring each level that also adds some extra depth to the story and its world.
Cons
- Jarring Controls: While the control system is unique and works with the theme of the game, trying to control 2 characters simultaneously led to moments of confusion that took me out of the game. I feel like having a 2 player local co-op option would've been good for this game, but unfortunately that is not the case. It is by no means a deal breaker, but I feel it is worth noting.
- Short and without much Replayablity value: The game will take you no more than a few hours to complete and there is not much incentive to play the game more than once. This my deter some players who are looking for a game with more longevity. But with that being said, I see this game as quality over quantity and believe it is well worth a playthrough.
This game is a favorite of mine and I highly recommend it for players who want a well written story-driven game.

Brawlhalla in a nutshell:
Pros:
Free to play and not pay to win
Smash Bros. esque fighting style, a familiar but still fun type of fighting game
Cons:
Well, unfortunately these outweigh anything else that the Pros have to offer.
The game has a weapons system-each character has a different combination of weapons to make them unique, but weapons are shared between characters. This causes the cast to be less diverse than it looks, as weapons have basically the same moveset for each character.
This problem doesn't get better in higher level play; the strong characters are all the same and there's just no diversity. Some characters can be completely countered by a single weapon, rendering them almost useless.
The unbalancedness and lack of diversity combine to force a player to lose to the same thing all the time, lest they play the same thing all the time.
I'd play this game casually with friends for an hour, but nothing more.

ZIGGURAT is like a Zen like experiance where level design, art and soothing audio come together to deliever a gaming experiance harking back to games of old such as Raven Software's HERECTIC and HEXEN while feeling current yet timeless.
You play in the first person leveling up and opening up the choice to use different characters with their own skill sets once you progress far enough. As you level up you will recieve what seems like an infinite amount of perks in the form of cards randomly offered by the game world. Most of the time you will have the option of selecting one of two cards granting you different powers. Other times you can choose cards which allow you more then two choices.
There are also statues of ancient gods who will bless you in trade for some of your health,mana etc. Some times though gods being gods you will get nothing or even something negative for your troubles. Along with this is a huge selection of powerful mystical looking weapons. From staffs, bombs and even guns ZIGGURAT like everything else it does knows the meaning of variety with joyful abandon.
The world of ZIGGURAT exists in randomly created dungeons which are beautifully designed with plenty of colour and ambient lighting alive with many a lethal trap making combat a fantasy thrill seekers delight while bringing a amazing soothing surreal meditative calm between battles as one gazes upon the suddenly very peaceful gorgeous setting as haunting ageless music plays in the background. Its like listening to a spiritual harp touching the soul making one reflect on the positive setting the player up for some fun battles at any moment. There are many secret areas to be discovered in the environment which is very destructible with collapsing walls hiding hidden locations. Candles can be snuffed out by running past them, books destroyed and scattered to the winds, huge Atlas like statues shattered etc.
The monsters are quite bizzare looking as if made for a childrens game yet once i fought against them i learned to fear them as if they were creations of some demented mushroom garden or psychotic Dr. Seus story. They really fit in and compliment the labyrinthian and maze like dungeons of ZIGGURAT adding a sense oddness and of being off kilter with the normal like a HP Lovecraft story.
Milkstone Studios are unstoppable with their genius creativity and inspiring work ethic as they keep working on their beautiful child ZIGGURAT with each new almost daily update transforming it to an even more of a action packed fun filled stunner making me think to myself, "Wow i would have never thought of that" :)
Buy ZIGGURAT and enjoy a mix of explosive action and meditative tranquility rarely scene in this fps fantasy rogue mixture that delivers like the finest alchemical potions the most senses awakening brew of morning coffee!
Thank you Milkstone Studios for the excellence.

Do not believe the naysayers.  PC gamers seem determined to prove that we're a bunch of immature whiners.  Microtransactions are not all over the place in this game.  I played for 10 hours before I even noticed they were there.  They are by no means necessary, nor thrown in your face.  Basically, you can pay a couple of bucks to level your character faster or give yourself money, which is hardly required to play the game properly.  I received plenty of "praxis" (skill points) by just playing the game well.  It's also very much a complete game, full stop.  Sure, it's definitely set up for another sequel, but it's hardly "unfinished".
OK, as far as the game itself goes now that we're done addressing the whining and gnashing of teeth, it's fantastic.  Take everything you loved about Human Revolution and make it better and you've got this game.  Want to play as a pacifist?  Very doable, even moreso than previously.  Want to go in guns blazing and play like a shooter?  It requires investing in the right augs, but it can be done also.  There's more combat-oriented offense/defense augs than in the past.  The conversation system is much improved, and when you need to persuade someone, I feel less like I'm guessing and more like I'm actually feeling them out than in HR.  The story is excellent and the dialogue well-written, with engaging characters.  I've experienced zero bugs other than some minor graphics corruption that's barely noticable (I'm pretty sure it's AMD's drivers and not the game), it also runs very smoothly at a near-locked 1080p60 on my againg i5-3570 and RX480 8Gb combo with everything maxed out.  Again, I'd say the "it's not optimized" whiners don't realize the grunt that modern lighting and effects engines require of a PC.  Anyway, I haven't quite finished it yet, but I love it so far.

I easily sunk 80 hours into a single playthrouh, on normal difficulty, exploring heavily but still even getting 100% of the game content. Hell yes I will be playing again sometime. Just because you rarely leave Prague didn't make the game feel small to me. Sure, HR took you on a more globe-spanning quest, but I really don't feel like that point in and of itself added much value. This game instead focuses you on a smaller geographic area, but one that felt like every inch was packed with content. I've gotten pretty deep into HR and I don't remember ever feeling like there was this much content.
So yeah, if you blitz through the game and ignore the staggering level of "side" content, massively upgraded mechanics and feel, amazing graphics (even on my 3+ year old midline GTX 760), and the immersion that made me feel like Prague was my city somehow, then sure, you might think this game wasn't that great. But I think you're being dense and a snob.

Shufflepuck Cantina is a modern recreation of the classic "Shufflepuck Cafe" which I originally played on the Amiga.
It's an air hockey simulation where like the original, you have crash landed on a strange planet, and the only way to get the parts you need to repair your ship, is to compete in air hockey (shufflepuck) and beat the various alien players in a nearby cantina.
The game builds on the classic 2 paddles/1 puck by adding special moves you can earn through wins, and there are also paddle and puck upgrades you can buy. There's a gambling machine on the ground floor for a mini-game, there are various challenge modes (game types) for the air hockey, and in order to earn the parts for your ship, you need to complete a encyclopedia on each alien/player. There are many encyclopedia parts, and each part needs to be purchased with credits earned from playing that alien ..... and that's about the point I lost interest.
I wish there was "meh" option for steam .. because this game takes a classic and improves on it. The graphics and sound effects are very good, you do feel as if you are in an alien cantina, the aliens have the same Star Wars vibe as the original, but no matter how many bells and whistles they've added, the game is still simply air hockey, which is fine if you like air hockey and have good reflexes, but from just an hour of play, I could already see what a grind this is. Having to play the same opponent over and over and over to earn credits, so you can use those credits to learn more about them, purchase upgrades, and eventually buy a ship part so that you can move onto the next alien ...
If you like air hockey, and the market isn't exactly overflowing for choice, this is a good one .... but you should "really" like air hockey, or like me, the grinding will turn you off. Try to pick it up in a bundle or a sale.

Its a really nice puzzle game, that is easy to get into and encourages you to stick with it. Its a 2.5d platformer, in which a character has to navigate a bunch of platforms, collecting 3 orbs on the way to escape on a final teleporting like platform. Puzzles / maps get progressively more difficult and interesting. The nice thing about this game is the rotation of the environment, and the way you do it. Tomb Raider: Anniversary is a solid re-imagining of the original game which makes use of the Tomb Raider: Legend engine, meaning a game that's much more user-friendly and playable control-wise, and of course packs quite the graphical upgrade.
Controlling Lara is a breeze with her acrobatics and various feats of parkour coming out smoothly and naturally whether using a gamepad or keyboard and mouse. This makes the fact that a good 70-80% of the game is straight platforming and puzzle solving all the more enjoyable. A keen eye and critical thinking are required to leap, grab, and grappling hook your way out of each scenario, and the game has a fairly generous system in place to help guide Lara to platforms, but most of the work is still up to the player.
The only real downsides of this remake are the combat and sometimes dodgy camera control and how that can interfere with some late-game platforming segments. Combat in general feels very mushy. Gunplay never really felt satisfying, though the lock-on and shoot mechanic does help smooth things out a bit. Issues arise however when enemies are able to get close, and especially if they're enemies capable of flight. The camera really loses track of what to do and can often cause a lot of seemingly unfair damage to be taken because of the obstruction.
The camera particularly fails in one of the final areas of the game (The Great Pyramid), where a long series of timed jumps are required to proceed. The camera gets positioned in ways that obstruct the path and you may find yourself making blind leaps and grappling hook attempts in vain. Even worse is that movement can end up completely fudged in this sequence since the controls are relative to what the camera is doing and leaps and grabs you were capable of earlier in the game suddenly have to be performed with different or nonsensical button combinations because the camera hasn't decided what forward and backward are or hasn't communicated it properly.
Even with its faults though, this is a fantastic puzzle platformer with a silly as all hell story and some great locations to parkour around in.

Otherwise, you'll probably prefer more recent entries in the franchise and other similar franchises like Uncharted. That said, the puzzles are good and can be real head scratchers and the movement mechanics are still pretty good. The combat is the game's biggest weakness.

A very nice, refreshing remake of a classic game that does not feel like it actually came out 10 years ago. The game's strongest suits are definitely the beautiful visuals and the tasteful approach in remaking a classic, timeless piece. Crystal Dynamics really did a great job with their trilogy.
What I didn't enjoy at all were the wobbly controls, especially during platforming (I fell to my death because of the controls at least 50 times), and the shoddy aiming mechanics. Honestly, the automatic aiming is broken, and seldom gives you an advantage - I'd rather aim manually than rely on this. The most frustrating part of the game was The Great Pyramid, all thanks to the aiming mechanics. Good luck shooting the winged demons while Lara automatically aims at the switch you're supposed to shoot after you kill the demons. Oh yeah, to add to the fun, you're also standing on a tiny platform and the demons are shooting fireballs at you. Enjoy falling to your death a million times and screaming at Lara to finally point the guns at the demons and not at the switch.
The game is far from perfect, and it's disappointing that such a beautiful, great game is burdened with controls and automatic mechanics failures. Nevertheless, it's not very often that you'll rage at these issues, and most of the time you'll be having fun - especially if you're a lifelong fan of the original like yours truly.
All in all, the remake is a worthy installment of its own, and a nice example of a remake done (mostly) right. I can honestly recommend it to both classic TR veterans and newcomers unfamiliar with TR games. Now let's try Underworld!

Mandagon is an interesting little game. It throws you straight into a beautiful and cryptic world to explore and unravel the story of the game.

A touching story about 2 brothers on a quest to save their dying father. The game implements a unique singleplayer co-op system where you control both brothers at once (Using the left side of the controller to control the older brother and the right side to control the younger brother) to work your way through obstacles and solve varies puzzles in each chapter. This can sometimes make gameplay a bit jarring and I recommend trying to keep the older brother on the left side of the screen and the younger on the right when you can to help orient yourself.
Pros:
+  Strong Story and Relateable Characters: The story is mostly conveyed through body language and is used very well to characterize each brother and keep the player engaged. Facing hardship with your family is a universal theme I think many can relate to and the emotional moments in this game are powerful. There are also side activities you can find while exploring each level that also adds some extra depth to the story and its world.
Cons
- Jarring Controls: While the control system is unique and works with the theme of the game, trying to control 2 characters simultaneously led to moments of confusion that took me out of the game. I feel like having a 2 player local co-op option would've been good for this game, but unfortunately that is not the case. It is by no means a deal breaker, but I feel it is worth noting.
- Short and without much Replayablity value: The game will take you no more than a few hours to complete and there is not much incentive to play the game more than once. This my deter some players who are looking for a game with more longevity. But with that being said, I see this game as quality over quantity and believe it is well worth a playthrough.
This game is a favorite of mine and I highly recommend it for players who want a well written story-driven game.

DLC Quest is a short platformer whose message is crystal clear the second you start it up. It has some quirky humor, a few 4th wall breaking moments here and there, and, of course, "DLC" to purchase with the currency you find in the game.
In order to advance, you have to buy all of the DLC offered by merchants, which is the blessing and bane of the game. In the first few minutes, you have to buy DLC to pause and jump, which is a little funny. However, by the 2nd area, the gimmick loses its charm, and the game quickly devolves into a game of exploration of finding all the coins so you can buy all the DLC and advance the story. In a weird twist, it seems that DLC Quest is bogged down by having to buy all the DLC to see the end. Maybe this was intentional, but it went on just a little too long.
Despite this, the retro graphics and music, the quirky humor, and the shortness (there's an achievement to speedrun it in 2 minutes, so it's a short game), it's worth checking out if you like self-aware jokes and a quick run through a game with a clear, if overbearing, message about the current state of modern games.

Note: Unlike other early access games, Gnomoria is totally playable and has been even before it came out on Steam (I bought it from Desura first). The bugs are minor and the updates add or change content. If you are wondering if you should wait to buy it, don't.
Gnomoria is easily in my top 5 games on my Steam library. It may not have the scale of Dwarf Fortress, but it certainly retains the enjoyment, mechanics and most fun features, while instead being more accessible, user friendly and beautiful. It is also brutally hard (for a noob like me), but you can make it peaceful or easier if you wish (or much harder). One of the best parts is that it is an incredibly polished Beta that recieves fortnightly updates in the form of content from the awesome one man developer. It's also like the best replayability to price ratio on Steam, so holy crap just buy this.

It is Dwarf Fortress. Whether that's a bad thing or a good thing, is up to you. Where Towns takes some liberties on the formula, Gnomoria is a much more straight remake. They take ease of use pretty seriously, though, and the game is infinitely more playable than DF. The game gets patched on a weekly basis and the creator is continuously adding lots of new convenience features and more content. Compared to DF, it has much easier menu navigation (with full mouse support, obviously), greatly reduced micro management (issue an order to build a workshop, and orders to build the necessary components for it will automatically get sent to your other workshops!), much easier resident management, and so forth. It also has much less detail (no randomly generated descriptions based on your fortress's history for statues, for example), but they're adding more and more of that all the time. It's still not an easy game, mind you, and there's no tutorial so you will need either a wiki or a lot of patience to learn the general flow of things.
Thing I like the most about it: General ease of play, it's super easy and relaxing to just lean back in your chair and watch the fortress go about its business as you just casually issue some orders every now and again. Thing I like the least: It's still pretty complex from a mechanics standpoint with a horrible lack of tooltips and no tutorial, making it not a simple task to learn. Thing I want patched in the most: Emotions. It's actually the one thing from DF I miss the most. Your Gnomes have no mood and always behave the same way no matter what.
Overall, really fun game and is easily worth the price if you're willing to jump in early knowing that it's still an alpha/beta/whatever they're calling it.

Ziggurat is an interesting take on the Rogue-lite genre. It takes the problem that many games like this had with the dull combat and attempted to fix it. It's combat mechanics are first person, which is new and interesting, and the variety of weapons that can go in any of your four weapon slots are varied, yet maintain a certain theme.

The level design leaves something to be desired. They are very square, or rectangle, and the aethstetic is very similar almost all the way throughout.
At times it can feel like the game is just hurling enemies at you for the sake of a challenge, but the random nature of the game makes it so that it adds a layer of replayability, instead of an annoyance.
The choice to use a progression system for your character is interesting. Instead of relying soley on random item drops, like many games in this genre, you level up based on experience orbs. This mechanic allows you too choose a perk from a random set that the game chooses for you. However, the choices the game chooses are often influenced by the previous choices you made, so you can make a certain build for your character.
They are still coming out with content for the game, so what you see now may not be all you get. At the moment you may be able to get 20-30 hours out of it before all character and items are unlocked. However, if the combat system is not too your liking, then this game is not for you, as that is the only real aspect in which this game shines. Everythign else is competent, but the combat system is the real meat of this game.
Buy it! Buy it! It's worth every penny! Seriously though, it is.

This is a fantastic game.  The gameplay is extremely tight and responsive, which is good because it is also very challenging.  Skillful play is rewarded.  In this respect it feels similar to the old style FPS like DOOM where you would find yourself with little health, no ammo and a roomful of baddies, hoping that one of the vanquished will drop you 10 hp to keep you going for another room.
There are also roguelike elements.  The ziggurat is different on every playthrough, and the weapons you find are randomised.  Sometimes you will find a grenade weapon and then encounter a room with hordes of little enemies.  You will have an easy time.  Other times you will find a crowd control staff and a few massive bulletsponge enemies.  Tough luck.  When you level up, you can choose one of two randomly drawn perks.  Some will be very useful, some will replenish your health in a one-time deal, some will make you stronger over the long term.  There are also treasure rooms and shrine rooms, where you can sacrifice health and ammo to the gods, who might reward you or if you are Superjunk punish you every time.
I definitely recommend this game.  It's good old-fashioned FPS goodness with a healthy serving of roguelike on the side.  But if you are skillful, the roguelike elements can't doom you from the start like in other titles, where you might keep restarting the game until you get a good starting item.  There are also evil carrots in this game that try to bite you.  I hate carrots in real life, they are an awful vegetable.  So it is good to shoot them with my stick.

Warning: In this review I will be comparing this game to Scribblenauts Unlimited, just for convience and ease of explanation! You have been warned!
Scribblenauts Unmasked: A DC Comic Adventure is very different from Scribblenauts Unlimited. Different in their freedom, different in their objects, different in achievements, different in level desgin, and different in their challeneges.
In Scribblenauts Unlimited there was unlimited freedom, as it says on the tin. But in Scribblenauts Unmasked there is a big limit, and this limit can inspire even more creativity than Scribblenauts Unlimited. The limit in question is that in each level in each session, you can only use a certain adjective or noun once, and if you continue to use it, points will be deducted. (These points are merely a type of coin system you can use in-game to perchase in-game costumes for your character.) This will force you to come up with a different object to use instead of the one you were going to use, or it will force you to come up with a way to do the same thing you were doing, but without that adjective or noun.
Scribblenauts Unmasked is obviously a DC Comics game, and thus you can spawn DC Comic related things, which means that the objects you can spawn are very different from Scribblenauts Unlimited, in that they are actual copyrighted things that are allowed in game. This doesn't just serve as a theme, or as a nice little detail to fanboy about, but also it can serve as another way to challenge you or to give you new ideas. As well as it being DC Comics, you are also allowed to make your character some description of a superhero, or supervillian, when you desgin your own character you can give him/her super powers and a swanky costume that you designed yourself. Of course the super powers are a bit limiting, I will warn you, as they only really involve attacking and nothing like flying or invisibilty, but those can be added after character creation with adjectives or even nouns, such as a flying ring.
There are almost double the achievements (Scribblenauts Unlimited 25, Scribblenauts Unmasked 40), as well as adding random (showing up at random) challeneges when you enter a level, which will challenge you to not use adjectives, or only use DC characters, which can be interesting and a lot of fun. Because there is so much to unlock with the points you collect, when you finish everything in the game then you can gather heaps of points and try and buy all the costumes and super powers.
The level designs are much different in Scribblenauts Unmasked, as they are a lot darker and grittier. There is also a level path for certain parts of DC comics, such as a Batman path, where at the end you can 'learn' about his backstory, just in case you were so isolated that you don't know.
If you are going to buy this game, keep in mind that although it has many positives that Scribblenauts Unlimited didn't have, you will most likely get more playtime out of Scribblenauts Unlimited then this game. But this game has a lot more potential play time then Scribblenauts Unlimited had. And in some ways it is better than Scribblenauts Unlimited,

Grand Theft Auto V evolves nearly every mechanic that was in the previous Grand Theft Auto games. As far as driving goes, the vehicles have been greatly improved, with Rockstar running more complex physics on them. The cars can even hold to the ground slightly better. The driving mechanics feel more like a racing game, particularly the Midnight Club series, compared to Grand Theft Auto IV's rocky, boat-like handling system. The shooting mechanics are better in terms of the feel of the mechanics and larger compared to the melee mechanics in the game, but that doesn't mean that the melee combat won't be fun, as it as been improved over the previous titles as well. Weapon selection has now also been changed. Instead of the old way of selecting through all the weapons, there is now a Weapon Wheel, which is similar to the one featured in Red Dead Redemption, another game made by Rockstar Games. Grand Theft Auto V draws inspirations from many different Rockstar titles in the past, including Max Payne 3, Midnight Club, Manhunt, and Red Dead Redemption.
There are many unique features in the game, one of those features is that when the players are playing as one of three protagonists in the game, the other two are out living their independent daily lives, and you will be surprised by what you find the characters doing when you switch back into them. Another unique feature is that the character swapping feature is executed in a Google Earth-styled manner and was displayed during a Game Informer demo, which was showed to have ran smoothly and without lag. The PC, PS4 and Xbox One versions present an exclusive feature, the first-person mode The whole game can be played through the eyes of the protagonist. This gameplay mode presents a whole new way to play the game. Cars have detailed interiors different from one another, shooting is like that of an FPS game.
New activities have been added, such as yoga, triathlons, jet skiing, parachuting, tennis, golf, and scuba diving. Random events have also been added to the game and can appear any time, while the player is exploring the map. The mobile phone has returned from Grand Theft Auto IV but is now only used for calling the player's contacts, surfing the web, and quick saving. Giving people the middle finger is another new feature the player can use while in a vehicle (which Rockstar recommended you do in various locations around Los Santos to see the outcome of this effect, depending on where the player is at, they will get different reactions from pedestrians).
Rockstar has also made changes to the pedestrian mechanics; some pedestrians can be seen at the bus stops in East Los Santos, and the same people can reappear in Rockford Hills working in the gardens of the opulent mansions. Some minor mechanics that help convey the environment and appearance of Los Santos occur at certain times of day, such as a sprinkler system being turned on in the morning in wealthy areas like Morningwood.
The map is larger than Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, Grand Theft Auto IV, and Red Dead Redemption combined. After some calculations by members of
, that would equal to around 27.5 square miles/71.2 km2 when land and sea are combined.

I used to really like Tomb Raider: Anniversary as a kid, but it really hasn't aged well. The story is dull, combat is a joke, which consists mostly of just shooting animals, the climbing is terrible, as Lara will very often miss ledges, or the game won't be clear about where you should jump. The game is also very inconsistent when it comes to checkpoints. Sometimes, it will give you way too many, while other times, it'll give you way too few. It can be very annoying. Graphics still look pretty good, but that's about the only positive I can think of. Puzzles feel pretty copy/paste after a while, too.
It might be interesting to go back and see where Tomb Raider started (this is a remake of the original), but other than that, I think you should stay away from this one. It really hasn't aged well, sadly.
Edit: Looks like some people blinded by nostalgia downvoted my review. Let's be objective about this. How is the story good? There barely is a story, and it's incredibly cliché. How is the combat good? It's the same easy, repetitive fights over and over again, where you just shoot animals or monsters, with a few boring QTE boss battles. The combat definitely is bland. What does that leave us with? Puzzles. Puzzles are annoying because Lara often won't grab ledges, and a lot of puzzles are just copy/paste puzzles, where the real challenge is whether Lara will grab the ledges or not. Take of the nostalgia glasses; the game hasn't aged well, sadly.

I am putting this one down as "recommend" on its own merits. It was a good game, is a good game still, in a way.... but did you know there is a newer Sims? It's not on Steam, reviews are not stellar (but not terrible), and it is already 3 years old at this point. No, I haven't played it.

I have over 150 hours in this game. I love it, and I would keep playing it for another 700+. So, why don't I reccommend it? Because EA broke it. For the first two years I had it, I would play it nonstop and it ran like a charm. Butter smooth, a great example of how a heavy game should run. No lagging, no crashin, no freezing...until the last time I was able to play it. Same system, same specs, same everything. I was playing on a world I had been playing on for weeks, and everything had been running smoothly. I didn't think anything of the update. Why would I? Nothing had broken before, I thought, so why would I pay any mind to this one.
And then everything changed. It wasn't long before the launch of Sims 4. I opened the game, loaded my save, and noticed something odd. The trees looked horrid, like everything had been changed to low res. I had to zoom in almost until I was inside of them before they returned to their normal, beautiful selves. Then, as my sim watered her garden, I tried to move the camera, and I noticed a jarring lag, turning the game into a slideshow. I zoomed out, and the trees returned to their horribly rendered state. I thought maybe the update hadn't installed properly. No big deal, it happens.
I verified the cache. Everything was...normal. Nothing was wrong, as far as the integrity of the files was concerned. So why, I wondered, was the game behaving so oddly? I ran a virus scan, malware scan, everything. The whole nine yards. At that point, I even uninstalled and reinstalled the game. Nothing worked. Every time I opened the game, I would get a maximum of 30 minutes before it crashed. Everything would appear to be working, and them it would die.
I never wanted to believe that a company would stoop so low as to ruin their own game, but that's the only conclusion I could reasonably come to. I scoured the web, hoping someone else would have a solution. All this time later, and even running it through Origin results in the same ending: runs for a maximum of half an hour, then it crashes. I loved the sims 3, and I would have happily bought Sims 4. However, any company that ruins their own game to force you into the next installment is a giant back of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that doesn't deserve my money. Who's to say they won't do the same with sims 4 when the next game comes out?
TL;DR: EA is a shady, garbage company with garbage policies regarding their golden egg. Don't support them. Don't give them your money. Buy from a company with some decency.

Have you wanted to try Dwarf Fortress but got scared by the ASCII graphics, a crafting tree so complex your eyes glaze over just trying to figure out how to make soap, and game mechanics so complex that you actually need that soap to keep your post-surgery dwarves from dying to infection?
Fear not, Gnomoria might be just what you're looking for. Gnomoria takes many of the mechanics of Dwarf Fortress, tones them back to a moderate complexity level, and gives you an improved GUI and charming graphics to work with.
In Gnomoria you'll command your gnomish settlers to dig out a fortress and work in 3 main job categories: agriculture, crafting, and defence. Like Dwarf Fortress, many of the jobs in these fields are interrelated, with one supply chain feeding into another.
Combat is both one of the fun and weak points of the game. You'll enjoy kitting your gnomes out and watching them chop goblins limb from limb, but you'll need to work fast and train hard to prepare for your first Mantis invasion. Inevitably, your first (and second, and likely fifth) run-through will leave your fortress a slaughter house, if it doesn't end with your dwarves starving and dying of thirst.
That's ok, though. Gnomoria, like DF, is a rogue-like. And, like DF, "losing is fun".
If you liked Minecraft and Terraria, you may very well like this! Build the castle of your dreams, fight monsters, and dig dig dig!

This game is a wonderful dungeon crawler that ditches the sword and shield in favor of a wand and robe. Here I will go over the five main features of the game, its story, gameplay, controls, mechanics and graphics.
STORY: Like most Roguelikes, the game does not have much of a story to follow. Instead it uses most of its features to provide simple fun gameplay. However, that being said, the concept is a unique idea with a rather in-depth backstory... which makes it unique from most games of this genre.
GAMEPLAY: Yeesh is it fast paced. Most of the game involves you frantically running around rooms that span from claustrophobic to immense size. Most rooms will come with about 10 enemies, however in my two playthroughs I saw rooms with up to 20 and as few as four enemies depending on the size. It's extremely fast paced and really gets your adrenaline flowing when you have low health and no ammo, as the permadeath system is in place.
CONTROLS: Jesus christ is this game fast! I would suggest turning the mouse sensitivity down immediately; turn it to four if you want it to move at a reasonable pace, any lower and you might just be stabbing yourself in the back on more intense battles. Anything above 5.5-6 is headache-inducing. I also turned off motion blur, because it sort of messed with my head, too. However, with everything else in place, the game is a delight to control, just a little speedy with the default settings.
MECHANICS: The whole concept of the game is that you own four different weapons, a wand with infinite ammo, and a spellbook, a staff and a bomb with limited ammo. However, you /can/ pick up more ammo if you find a crystal. You're exploring a large dungeon (can be made endless) called the Ziggurat to keep the evil spirits at bay. The weapons are extremely varied and a bunch of fun to mess around with. My favorite is the bomb, reminds me of a magic grenade. The ammo does get a little sparse around the boss fights to a point where you'll be using the trusty wand to keep the big man at bay. Your health, too, does not recover but rather must be refilled with a special card (you get this at level-up) or potions which the enemies drop. This adds to the tense experience overall and keeps the roguelike feel.
Graphics: Most roguelike games are 2-D, and 8-16bit. Some games are 3-D, but still follow the chunky pixel concept (from experience, Delver [good game, by the way]). However, Ziggurat has a really up-to-date graphics engine. If just a tad cartoony (almost reminds me of an improved TF2 graphics engine) it is appealing to the eye and adds to the overall experience.
SUMMARY: Ziggurat is a fun gaming experience that is a great addition to the roguelike genre. I would have a hard time scouting something out that looked as good as this does, considering the audience it caters to. It can run on just about any low-to-mid end PC (I have a midend laptop and this game runs like a charm on the Normal graphics setting. It can run on High, too) which tells me the engine is highly prioritized. Overall, a must-reccomend to a fan of the roguelike genre.

Ziggurat is a "rogue-like" fps, which means the levels are randomly generated.  You are never going to have the same level twice.  Some reviews have stated it's like Heretic or Hexen.  This game is not Heretic or Hexen.  But in a world where Triple A developers are advertising their games as "Like Skyrim but with Guns and Vehicles" could you really blame anyone for comparing this to Heretic or Hexen?  Sure it plays similar to an old school FPS.  Secret Areas (1 per level).  Able to carry more than 2 weapons.  Just because you play as a wizard doesn't make it like Heretic.
I think any fan of old school FPS will enjoy this game, it doesn't have the same strafing speed that we had in the 90's but it's definitely a fresh breath of air in a genre that has been decimated by the likes of modern military FPS.  For $15 dollars you'll get more than your money's worth.  This game could be replayed over and over again.  I think even fans of Minecraft or other Roguelike games where the world is randomly generated will enjoy Ziggurat.
Overall this is one of the best indie FPS I've played all year.  (2014)  I wouldn't let it pass you by.  If you can get it on sale then great, but if not like I said, this is definitely worth the full price.

I have been playing this game for a few months now and I have to say that this is how Free to Play show be done. So far I've not felt the need to purchase anything and have enjoyed every aspect of the game. I can also see someone who wouldn't want to invest the time paying for the unlockable items which are mostly cosmetic and additional characters.
I'm not much of a vs. player, specially in online games. Mostly because I always feel outclassed by players that have mastered the game. But the mechanics of the game make it really easy to pick up and play. I've noticed that even though I'm not a great player I never feel like I am being destroyed by other players. I think this is mostly due to the game relying on learning the timing and range of attacks rather than a long list of special techniques, combos and counters.
Another positive for the game is that they cycle through the locked characters, I think weekly, so even if you haven't unlocked all the characters you get to try them out.  Lastly there are several game modes and ways you can customize each mode giving the game a lot of playability.
I cannot recommend this game enough, it's free, it's good, and even though it's early access it feels very much ready for launch.

AAA titles need to be held to a higher standard, and Deus Ex: Mankind Divided doesn't measure up.
It's the definition of a shoddy console port.  Apparently most of the major optimization issues and bugs have been ironed out, but it still suffers from massive load times and frequent crashing.  I had to repeat the end of the intro mission three times because the game couldn't get through the subsequent extended opening credits and cutscenes without crashing, and there is apparently no autosave after the first mission or during any of the cutscenes.  That doesn't bode well.  Much of the cutscenes is not skippable, either because it is a veiled loading screen or scripted gameplay and not an actual video.
Past that, and past the gross microtransactions and anti-piracy measures that everyone knows about, the game is riddled with small, strange errors in judgment that just make it not fun to play.  Sniper rifles have no reticle outside the scope, so every time you pull the scope up you spend five seconds recentering it on what you thought you were looking at.  Melee takedowns require augment energy, but it's not clear from the HUD whether you have enough left to make one, so you don't find out until you're right behind your target and he's about to turn around that you can't /hit him with your fist/.
I'm interested in playing in the Deus Ex universe, but judging from the criticisms of this game's length and story, I doubt putting up with DXMD's instability and bizarre design choices will be worth my time.  I wasn't happy with the ham-fisted end of Human Revolution, and this looks to be a whole game about dealing with the aftermath of that conclusion.  There are so many interesting ways in which cybernetic enhancement will cause societal chaos -- the new Deus Ex games treat the subject matter with the subtlety of a sledgehammer.
Judging by the number of people who have played this game through and enjoyed it, I'm sure there's a game worth playing buried in here somewhere, and if you can get it for under $20, like I did, it might be worth seeing if you want to tough it out.  I still haven't decided if I'm going to bother.

You’re shown this isn't a game about story: it’s about wholesale, gleeful slaughter. You burn and poison and slash at hostile beasts with sharp weapons until they die and spill gold and gear all over the ground. You scoop it all up, scan stats to see if any discovered treasure can serve as an upgrade, then move on to the next monster pack and repeat. You do this for roughly 30 hours until the final boss falls over, then you start up new game plus and repeat the whole thing.  It may sound like a wearying grind of a dungeon crawl but it’s immensely rewarding.
Like with Diablo, item drops from monster are randomized, so you’re never sure what will fall from the dead. Sometimes it’s a basic pistol you’ll never use, sometimes it’s a rare two-handed sword with high damage and the perfect statistical attachments to complement your play style. Playing is a constant tease, where each magic blast or arrow flurry might reward you with the ideal upgrade, which when equipped inspires confidence, a feeling of ever-growing personal power as you descend into the next dungeon and battle whatever unknown dangers await. It’s an expertly paced cycle of upgrading that never leaves room for rest, as more menacing challenges are never far away, and the promise of greater reward never fades.
After the first playthrough is completed there’s still plenty to do, too. A map room unlocks at the very end of the game, where more dungeon runs can be purchased with in-game gold, you can try out additional difficulty settings, roll a hardcore character where death is permanent, and can start up a new game+ mode where you restart the adventure with all character progress intact, letting you level to the cap against more challenging monsters and really get a sense of how powerful your class can become. Who knows what’ll wind up coming out of the modding community that builds up around Torchlight II, but even without community-created content, Runic’s already included plenty of reasons to continue playing for many, many hours. Considering this all costs $20 on Steam, it's a pretty incredible deal.
So torchlight II doesn’t do anything radically new, but does everything incredibly well. It fits all the pieces of varied monster behavior, interesting items, excellent skill design and random surprises together into a near-perfect formula, where the action never stops and rewards are never far away. Every level up, skill boost and item replacement flirts with a sense of invulnerability in a world obsessed with killing you, demanding continued play by teasing eventual omnipotence. The story and characters aren’t particularly memorable, but that hardly hurts the strength of Runic’s focused design in what’s one of the finest loot-driven action-RPGs available.
