Torchlight II is one of those wildly popular Steam games which hardly requires any introduction for fans of isometric-style action RPG's. Developed by Runic Games in 2012 as a more polished and refined version of its previous incarnation (Torchlight), it is widely hailed and beloved by scores of fanatical gamers (well over 3 million+) for its many favorable similarities to the equally popular Diablo series.
The true hallmark of this title however, is that the sprawling world it offers to you on a very reasonably priced silver platter is a gorgeously inviting one awaiting to be explored to its fullest....tempting you with countless secrets to uncover & treasures to collect. In fact there is more loot to be found hidden within its myriad of locations than you could possibly wrap your mind around. It's easily one of those gems with which you can sink hundreds of hours into, since it offers level randomization for enhanced replayability inside of its open world system...one which includes weather as well as day/night cycles incidentally.
Featuring a very tight local + online co-op mode (in addition to solo offline play), you'll soon notice that you will be introduced to a diverse bounty of seemingly never-ending quests & side-quests given to you by those who require your assistance in one way or another. And fortunately, you'll have a ferocious pet by your side to help out in battle as needed, one who even possesses its own inventory!
In addition to the exploration and loot collecting, your primary objective will be to battle against a wide assortment of variously menacing monsters as you gradually level up your character with more skills, gold, and gear during this compelling campaign. Action is very fluid, brisk, and energetic...with a satisfying number of both weapon upgrades and weapon types (including melee & guns) to keep you more than entertained.
Both your mana (ie. energy) and health bars will be depleted during combat, and must be replenished as necessary with collected vials which can be used up at any time.
Character customization is present, although somewhat limited and basic in scope I felt. It's probably the most glaring aspect of the game which could have been improved further still. Nonetheless, it is still present at least, and you'll have your choice of either male/female characters spread across 4 distinct classes: Embermage, Outlander, Berserker, Engineer.
Level design was quite impressive & varied in an overall sense, with some specific areas like the dungeons being especially atmospheric. It was quite a joy for me to explore every single nook & cranny of each individual section traversed as I hunted around for items to collect between waves of enemies....who themselves were sufficiently unique enough throughout the campaign so as to not feel repetitious in any way.
There is just so very much to do in the game, and even after investing a few quality hours into it, there was an undeniable feeling that I've still only barely scratched the surface as to what awaits me further into its story.
What I especially appreciated about the presentation, is that this world is surprisingly vibrant in color as opposed to being dreary & muted looking in appearance as some other such similar games are. Which is then reinforced furthermore by the distinctly cartoon-style graphics found here. This in turn is all neatly tied together by a very well-done lighting system which somehow breathes a sense of intriguing realism into this magical place. All in all, it is quite pleasant on the eyes and sports a unique charm to it. And best of all, there are an ample number of graphics options available for fine-tuning your display preferences.
Voice acting was definitely above par, and sounded quite slick for the many varied characters present. (Although at times I felt that your character's obsession with his depleted mana levels was a bit overly-repetitive!). Whereas music itself was mellow & symphonic in nature...wonderfully balancing out the mood of each particular scene in an appropriate manner. And finally, sound effects were more than adequate in accomplishing their task of enhancing immersion...especially so with delightful effects such as thunder reverberating through the rainy night, for example.
It fully is, and includes both trading cards and a whopping 119 achievements to be unlocked.
None available.
The vast collection of available mods via the Steam Workshop is where this game truly shines like no other. There are literally hundreds of them to choose from in every possible category imaginable, and quite honestly you could find pretty much anything your little heart desires here.
Torchlight II has to be one of the best values out there in ARPG's...because while it only costs a fraction of what its pricier triple-A competitors do, it nonetheless very much competes as one, and more importantly, feels like one with its overhauled & redesigned user-interface which was a breeze to use. Accessibility is fantastic here as well, showcasing a streamlined and mostly straight-forward character leveling system which I greatly appreciated. Because being hopelessly confused inside of skill trees is not my personal idea of a fun time, and here, they most certainly get it right in steering the focus onto actual gameplay instead.
And along with its multiple difficulty settings, just about anyone can enjoy what it has to offer...from the very casual side of the spectrum for those who simply wish to explore its scenery, all the way up to the no-nonsense hardcore setting for those veterans out there who wish to master its more subtle nuances.
All in all, Torchlight II has underwent quite a lot of refinement to date, and runs at fantastic framerates even on less than cutting-edge hardware.
But most of all, this is an exciting world to step inside of and one which you can very much have a great time with since there is always something interesting to do along with an accompanying sense of accomplishment felt as each goal is successfully completed...and that is why...

I have played both Tomb Raider: Legend and Underworld twice, and have played through both the Tomb Raider reboot and it's sequel Rise of the Tomb Raider on console, getting a hundred percent completion rating in those games and all the story-based DLCs, even playing the first game twice.  In essence, I love games like Tomb Raider and Uncharted.
But I do not love, or even like, Tomb Raider: Anniversary.
While it has the modern sensibilities that Uncharted introduced, but comes nowhere close to that quality.  The reason comes down to the simple fact that Anniversary epitomizes jank.  The way the camera moves will make you nauesous, and the many times that Lara will jump the wrong way or simply not grab on to something, plummeting to her death, will drive you insane.  In one instance in the game, there is long segment of finding cogs to make platforms move, so you can reach higher places.  To get to one of these, you grab on to a swinging pole, then jump to another, and then to a ladder that is fairly long, but when I leapt for it, even though Lara's jump reached the apex of the ladder, she somehow managed to forget to grab on and plummeted to her death.  And this was with Manual Grab off.  Putting it on just makes the game more frustrating.
The combat is always hit or miss, depending on if the enemies stupid that round or not, running into invisible walls and not knowing of the concept of turning around, even though their eyes are on you while you strafe around them or flank them, unloading bullets into them.  During these encounters I was reminded of one time I wet to my local zoo, where I watched puffins in a glass cage, and one of them continually swam and swam...straight into the wall.  It didn't turn and swim in any other direction, and I watched it do this for about five minutes, totally transfixed at how stupid it was.  The enemeis in this game can constantly be just as dumb, if not more so.  Other times, if they are acting smart, other janky issues can pop up where you shouldn't get hurt or killed, but you just do.
Death should always be the fault of the player.  A game should never feel like a death or game over is the games fault.  But the vast majority of the times your death will unmistakenly be the game's fault.  One of the major sins of this game is that the ORIGINAL plays better, even after all these years and with new modern sensibilites in this game.  While the old games may have had the tanky controls of old, the kind that are awful to play with now, if you go back and get used the original's controls and movements, death becomes the player's fault, and that says a lot, regarding this game.
As for the graphics it's nice to see Lara and the environments get the full remake treatment from the original.  It's just not worth the expense of the inferior gameplay, however.  Especially when there are many times when animations can be downright horrible at times, or the many other issues that were more apparent years ago, but all over the place in this game.  One time, I kept running around in circles, moving the camera along with it, simlpy because of an hilarious glitch, where Lara's braid would get caught on either the camera or some other unseen force, and her hair would stretch to where you had moved to, to impossible lengths.  Other times the graphics can effect gameplay, where you might be hanging on a ledge that goes around the corner to the otherside, but when you move around, for a brief second Lara is holding onto nothing, hanging in the air, because of horrible animations.  I'm fairly certain a lot of these animation issues, and clipping issues, are the cause of so many platforming deaths.
Then their is the story, which hasn't gotten any better with age.  Which simply means it's that much worse now.  I won't say any more on the story, because it's completely forgettable and not the reason you'll be playing this game in the first place.
The one thing the game has going for it is the developers have added things to unlock, for if you do enjoy the game it might give you more incentive to play the game again.  But that depends on the very rare chance that you like the game enough to want to.  There is also the ability to explore Croft Manor, but that and the other features don't improve the broken issues, so they probably won't make the game any more enjoyable.
In the end, the developers first attempt into the modern era was a complete failure.  Fortunately, however, the next two games, Legend and Underworld, though still quite janky at times, lost much of those issues, and became fun to play, even having a much more compelling story.  It's just too bad they had to learn how to make those games by making a game that falls short in every way possible.

It plays a lot like Heretic/Hexen would if they had Roguelike elements. Map layouts are far more arena-like and not as complex as they were in the classics, though. You must pick from a number of characters (you start with one, but can unlock others) and reach the 5th floor to win, and every floor is randomly generated from a number of pre-built rooms that are then strung together. A floor ends when you beat its boss, and you will need a Portal Key to summon the boss. The game has permadeath and you can only save between floors.
There is a good variety of weapons (the pool grows bigger as you unlock more of them) spread across 4 categories. The first is the basic wand, whose mana (ammunition) replenishes quickly and automatically for all characters. Different characters will have different properties for this starting weapon, such as faster or slower ROF, a differently-styled secondary attack, less or more accuracy. The second class of weapons are books, whose attacks are typically shotgun-like and  don't consume too much mana. The third type are staves that function as rapid-fire crowd control weapons, and mostly have a primary attack with good accuracy and a secondary that excels at close quarters, burning through your mana rapidly while firing a barrage of projectiles inaccurately. The fourth and last type are weapons that deal area damage. These are usually firearms or throwable explosives, and often have a steep mana cost per use. Some weapons deal self-explanatory status effects, such as poison, stun, or freezing.
You can find usable amulets that must be recharged (by killing monsters), lore scrolls (these give a large EXP boost) and occasionally perks. You also get to choose between two (or three with the Bookworm perk) random perks on level up. In roguelike fashion, you can find statues in certain rooms that allow you to trade your health or mana (or offer nothing, for a lower chance of success I presume) for a possible bonus. You can get a random effect (Divine Indifference) or even a punitive malus from these statues.

As someone who can't play rogue lights / roguelike games because I don't have enough skill to do so, I think this game doesn't suffer from the roguelike genre. The roguelike elements of this game actually make it better. I guess some games are designed around the ideas of randomness, but this game just seems like a really good game that happens to be somewhat random. It helps that it is technically a FPS game and I do like my FPS, but it offers more. The gameplay isn't just shoot shoot shoot, get behind cover, shoot shoot. Its more like if I shoot too much I'll run out of mana so I'll run around the enemies and dodge the incoming projectiles like Neo, shooting them as I run buy. It is also really fun in the sense that you start with a different secondary each time you play. This makes the game really replayable because you can get different items that can help you in different situations. It is also really gratifying when you unlock new perks and weapons making the gameplay experience different and more fun everytime. All the unlocks in the game are really good and you start to build up preferences for certain items and perks. For instance, I really like the first character you unlock and starting with a poison staff. Then when you level up you are given a decision between two perks. Some of the perks are situational, for example get 50% of your life back, but some change the entire game. This can range from more mob drops, to more health when you get a health potion, to a permanent sprint boost. The amazing gameplay plus the more ways that you can play as you play is really nice. Plus IT HAS AN ENDING, granted an endless mode has been put it, but IT HAS AN ENDING. The game isn't about how far you can get, its about how much skill do you have to beat it.

Ziggurat, is a very nice and also very difficult game.  I love the fact that almost every time you play the game you feel yourself physically improving even if it's over a short ammount of time. No run is like the other with it's constantly generating dungion. Fight through 5 floors of various monsters, each unique in it's own way. Many monsters are color changed and size swapped to show that they have special attributes to them.
The game has 4 weapon types as well as a large array of starter characters for you to choose from, rivaling that character roster from binding of issac. The 5 floors you adventure through grow more and more difficult, switching themes the farther you go down. The Ziggurat,(The tower you are challenging to become a Master mage) Is a very difficult task indeed. You can hold up to 4 weapons, of various kinds of magics. Starting with the Wand(Starter weapon for each mage, can't be swapped out) Staves, Spellbooks and Alchemy. Each of the magics all have their own ups and downs. There is a secret room on each level you adventure through, depicted as a crack in the wall. Each room contains a perk, and a little tidbit of information about the portrait hanging on the back wall, which depicts another game that Milkstone has developed.
Some Cons, I would point out that some of the bosses look like the minions they spawn during boss encounters, especailly the lost spirit boss. Her attacks are exactly the same as her minion's attacks and they also sound very much the same to boot.

So, I've been playing this game off and on for the last four and a half years, so I would say I've seen enough of it to write an hoenst review. What I love most about the game are the story and the immersion you feel when you're playing. You really feel like you're a part of the Middle Earth World, which to me means a lot (I'm obssessed with Lord of the Rings). The regions are varied enough that you feel like every place is different. Also, each class has its own unique characteristics that set it apart from the other classes; most people have multiple characters on multiple servors because they want to capitalize on all the different class options and play styles.
The main problems I have with LOTRO are that the combat is getting clunky, certain classes are way overpowered compared to others, and the questing in certain regions is getting a bit monotonous. The combat is generally the same the whole game, so it's important that you pick the class that goes with what you want in the game. It can just be very repetitive at times. Likewise, certain classes are way stronger than other classes. My hunter is so frail at level 89 compared to most other classes. So frail that it becomes difficult to get through basic solo quests. Finally, the quest are around the same thing over and over again. I know there can only be a finite number of quest ideas, but I would appreciate more diversity in questing.
Overall, I find myself coming back to this game every couple of months, getting bored, and then coming back again in a cycle. I've done this for four years now, and I expect to d othe same for at least a couple more years. 8.5/10

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided - Base Game = HIGHLY RECOMMENDED.
Desperate Measures DLC & System Rift DLC = RECOMMENDED.
A Criminal Past DLC = VERY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED.
The Deus Ex Franchise returns in grand fashion with Mankind Divided, thanks to Eidos Montreal absolutely putting out a fantastic game & follow-up to the excellent Deus Ex: Human Revolution. With a lot of choices in how to approach your tasks with different lethal & non-lethal tactics + some actual choices in the outcome of missions & quests in this action-packed FPS/RPG/stealth game hybrid, this seems like a recipe for actual greatness. For the most part, it is just that.
But, this game fails to reach complete greatness. While this game for me was not short by any means after spending around 47 hours with it - where all of these hours were loaded with me doing lots of experimenting; saving + reloading; & whatnot, by the way - I just still can't help but feel that something is...missing.
:
As great as the game itself is & that is the major reason to recommend it, the story + character development seems to be going great here and building into something awesome - until the game finishes up abruptly & lands into "anti-climatic" territory, suddenly rolls credits, shows a few clips to set something up & feels like a major set-up for either DLC's and/or a sequel.
It feels like either a whole Complete Act (or a few even, maybe) or Entire Game here is completely left-out, as threads from the main quest + some side quests either reach dead ends, get dropped entirely, and/or get hit with cliffhangers by the time the game abruptly ends, rolls credits, & they have some clips to show how things shaped-up from your decisions. But even your decisions, they seem to be just be really set-ups for something grander later - likely in DLC's, Expansions, and/or an inevitable Full Blown Sequel to Mankind Divided.
Also some things here don't feel fully developed or rushed, as well - completely leaving a foul taste in one's mouth. Worst of all here, this is a series that is very well known + regarded for its great story, character, narrative & plot development. You will likely be asking the question of "Wait, that's it?!"
In this game, you play the hero from Human Revolution, Adam Jensen. A few years after HR's events and the major incident, Jensen returns & bombings began to happen. Prague becomes the center of attention here, as a bombing takes place there + the country is torn b/t racism. The Augmented  (those who have cyber body parts implanted into them for any reason) + Naturals (those humans who have no Aug's) have tensions that continue to rise to new heights b/t the two groups, after the Incident (from Human Revolution) shook the world. You're to find out who is at the heart of these attacks + bombings, which turns out to be a matter of different factions, groups, & politics might actually be involved.
The game seems to be building to something intriguing & special, until it abruptly ends too quickly. This game has a huge story arc +  labryrinth of a plot going on, until it all just suddently & abruptly ends + we get clips mostly setting-up where the next piece of this story (whether DLC's, Expansions, or a Full-Blown Sequel). They feel more like a trailer for the next installment than an actual game-ending, TBH.
In typical Deus Ex fashion, you have at your disposal all kinds of skills, lethal weapons, non-lethal weapons, and items in the game-world. You can approach most quests, main or side, with numerous different approaches. You can go in, guns blazing. You can use stun-guns and do non-lethal melees attacks, knocking out foes. You can hack security systems and turn them on your enemies. You can go all stealthy, lethally. You can mix & match these styles, however you see fit. You can upgrade your skills + Augments, turning yourself into an even more awesome Adam Jensen. This approach to gameplay here always has been Deus Ex's greatest strength, across just about every main Deus Ex title.
With the huge open-world of Prague at your disaposal - which is absolutely fantastic, BTW - the game is loaded with tons of in-game Lore + Atmopshere., to help the player easily get involved + immersed into this excellent game-world. While load times can be all over the place (depending on the size of the hub), this sci-fi, futuristic, & cyberpunk style of Prague that is going on here is an interesting & wonderful setting for this game.
At 1440p w/ High Textures, Shadows on Medium & V-Sync Off - the game looked + ran quite well at those settings, in most instances. Most of the time, performance was in the 50-60FPS ballpark. Occassionally, when a ton was going on, the framerate would get pushed down even further even towards the 30-40FPS mark - but it wasn't much of anything that the engine just couldn't have that many issues bouncing back from.
What it boils down to, is that Deus Ex: Mankind Divided delivers a fantastic actual game itself, which shouldn't be missed by gamers. Fans of the Deus Ex (original) & Deus Ex: Human Revolution will feel right at home here, as this game doesn't disappoint in the gameplay department. Despite issues of the game's story, plot, narrative & character development not feeling entirely finished here, that shouldn't stop those looking for the great gameplay they'd normally expect from a Deus Ex title.
It's a shame that the game's story arc + scope is so big, that even after a lot of hours (around 40+ hours), that this game's development of its story + characters doesn't always execute to its best ability, namely only b/c it does feel like it's actually incompl--
Story-wise, Desperate Measures takes place after the events in Golem City, filling in some blanks for the player. This is accessed from the "Jensen's Stories" (DLC section) of the Main, so this is designed as its own section. This is one big place to infiltrate, more or less, so you won't have access to Prague's hub, Golem City, or anything of that sort.
The player has a completely reset character & is given enough Praxis points to upgrade their skills to likely where they would've been after Golem City incidents - as Jensen goes to infiltrate a Security Building to find out abotu certain important footage and who might be behind the bombing.
Like most of Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, the player can approach this however they see fit - guns blazing, stealthy, or a mix of both. The level is well-designed & this short campaign is well-done, filling in some blanks and a few more little important details to MD's story - but the player might want more Deus Ex content after this. It only took me around 2.2 hours to complete, according to Steam - but it was a fine 2.2 hours. Despite its brevity, since this DLC is basically free & is quite well-done - how can I not go ahead & recommend this?
With a new small hub to explore & some side-quests, System Rift delivers more Deus Ex: MD. The story is good & feels self-contained, but who knows how & if it'll tie into the base-game's Illuminati story. Feeling more ike a small hub section & one big huge mission in a Bank, you pull of a heist in Deus Ex fashion to get info on this Shady Bank. As usual, you can approach it how you see fit & make decisions, which will impact the story. And yes, it's a good DLC, taking me around 5 hours or so to complete, feeling meatier than the Desperate Measures DLC.

I'm a huge fan of this series, and Mankind Divided brought back pretty much everything I loved about Human Revolution except better. There's a pretty common complaint that the world is small (we had 2 cities in the last game, but only a single one, save for a few missions, in this one), but I really disagree. The world may be a tad smaller, but it feels like there's a lot more packed into each square inch of the world in Mankind Divided. Each district of the city feels different enough to make snooping around fun, though I can admit that the variety within a single city only goes so far...some of the areas feel really different, while others feel like more of the same.
The gameplay feels tighter in this game. There's more ways to sneak around each level, as well as an enhanced suite of augments to pick from to really make the game your own. One of my favorite additions is an augment that allows you to read social cues of people when you're talking to them, giving you access to previously unavailable methods of finishing out the conversation...sometimes changing how the mission plays out entirely. The gameplay is probably the highlight of Mankind Divided - it's everything I loved about Human Revolution, but more polished.
The game also looks gorgeous, though I had some weird texture issues through out the game where my screen would be almost entirely black because random textures would stretch all the way across the screen. Pretty annoying, but quick saving and reloading usually solved the problem. It wasn't annoying enough for me to put down the game, but it did cause a fair bit of frustration before I figured out a workaround.
The part of Mankind Divided where things didn't improve (but didn't necessarily get too much worse) is the story. As many have stated, the story kind of just ends...and you're left feeling like there's so much more to this plotline they have going that you just didn't get to. It's abrupt to the point where it actually lessens the Mankind Divided experience, regardless of how much fun the gameplay is. The story feels like it's so obviously setting up for a third (and I guess final) entry into the Adam Jensen story...it makes total sense where they stopped it because it perfectly sets up the last "act" of the series, but I think a little more effort could have been put into making the game feel more complete when looked at separate from the series.
With all that said, the story is great up until it just ends. Like it's solid and enjoyable all the way to the end, the end just leaves a bad taste in your mouth because it's such a huge cliffhanger. The characters are just as good as Human Revolution, as is the voice acting work. The game is also serious fun to play, so despite the negatives I've listed, I have to recommend this game.

Brothers has a very unique control scheme where you use a gamepad controller's 2 analog sticks to control each brother indivdually and each the 2 triggers for them to interact, jump, etc. It is a a little difficult to pick up at first with you losing hand eye co-ordination at some moments, but nevertheless it is interesting and gives the game it's own standout feature.
With the game's story I see others applauding how touching and sad it is. i can agree to some extent, but i could not find myself drawn to these charcters or their predictiment, i think i only played to get to the end late in the game because it was so mediocre. I know the ending wasn't exactly cliche or anything, but I kept asking myself why the devs would make a plot decision such as that. What kept me interested through the most of the story however, was the unique fantasy world that had been created.
the soundtrack for the game is quite spectacular and well done.
besides the story which disinterested me, overall this game is a good game to sit through and play for fun and achievement hunting. I would strongly recommend playing with 2 people on the one controller for some extra fun.
Overall I give Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons a 6.5/10

I decided to buy this after playing Pro Basketball 2014, the only other available one on Steam.
I'm in love with simulation games, and this one fits the bill for a decent basketball simulation. There are very cool options to tinker with, such as simming seasons that date back to 1978. So you can create a very interesting team during the process, though I don't like how the coaches do not reflect the actual coaches of the time, they're randomly generated. Despite some of these setbacks, I very much enjoy other options, like the draft, trades, and free agency. It can be tedious, but also very fun.
The biggest problem with this game is it's instability. I've had to restart plenty of simulations because of crashing that happens on my saved seasons. Even keeping as many as 8 save files I use during that simulation, they can all be destroyed a game-breaking crash. Unfortuntely, this happens more than I'd like.
If I had to give this game a score, it'd be about 7.5/10. It's gotten me up to 100 hours of entertainment at this point, and for the price tag, I feel that it's worth it. This score would be moved much higher if the developers were able to fix the stability issues with the game. All in all, a very enjoyable game!

When I first set eyes on this game ‘Recycle – Garbage Truck Simulator’, I had absolutely no idea what I’m going up against. Yes, it’s a garbage truck simulator however what the heck do you do besides hauling garbage? So, I played the guessing game and my conclusion is not much – that is there’s no real replay value. However, it turns out that there’s plenty of things to do like hauling garbage with different types of garbage trucks (small / large / crane), manage your landfill with three vehicles being the crawler, truck and bulldozer and, of course playing the role of a garbage manager. So, to my surprise, it’s a decent game however the user-inference and a game crippling bug can make you toss this game into the tip (excuse the pun).
Because there’s no real ending to this, you can literally go on forever however I cannot think any good reason why you want to do that. I used the achievements as a baseline so once completed, I deemed the game as ‘conquered’. That said, the game’s pacing is extremely slow with a bucket load of micro-management. I think what the developers was trying to aim is there’s a lot more to it than just collecting / dumping rubbish – there’s a whole network of systems to be concerned about.
Whatever the case maybe, this game certainly tailored to the very niche market and granted, there’s plenty of busy work to do (especially when you need to manage a number of trucks). Plenty of lost opportunity here however it’s not a game to be totally written off as there’s a lot of evidence of love poured into this game. However, because the game is now regarded as ‘abandoned’, meaning there won’t be any more patches, it’s a game that you need to take huge precautions to play it, especially that game breaking bug where the AI truck never returns to the depot.

The Good: Tons of great loot dished out often, tough boss fights, varied dungeon and enemies, the pet system is revolutionary for the genre, strong classes, a lot of abilities to acquire, $15
The Bad: Forgettable story, gets boring after so long (that's just the genre though), can be down right hard later on requiring a partner, underwhelming graphics
With fans being so upset with Diablo III, I have to first say turn here. Torchlight II builds upon the already excellent engine and adds more content, a lengthy campaign, and tons of great loot. The dungeon crawler genre is all about the great loot, leveling your character, and fighting tough bosses. Once you get to the last couple of dungeons you will be guzzling potions like crazy. The game is non-stop action with no breaks. While Diablo III may have larger budget in the millions, a better story, and better graphics, Torchlight II delivers on what the fans want; loot, dungeons, and bosses.
You can pretty much forget the story. It is told in three pieces and isn't very interesting. Something about Nephilim invading the world and you trying to stop it? I honestly don't know. I lost track because the story is broken up too much and told in between three large acts so you forget what happens. What does matter is the action. You can choose between 4 strong classes that are typical for the genre. Mage, duelist, warrior, and a middle ground guy. Each class has a slew of great abilities that you actually won't completely acquire in one play through. I chose the duelist and stuck with akimbo pistols. There was even a perk called Akimbo! There's something here for every type of player.
The loot feels nearly endless and it is actually good. There are boss chests, large chests, and just regular ones spread throughout. You don't have to worry about getting good loot. Of course most of it ends up being junk, but when you beat a boss you will get something good. You can equip rings, belts, shields, leg and body armor, helmets, you name it. You can enchant items that add random stat increases, add jewels, even disenchant items to regain money. There was even an option to use junk loot to create new items like potions. I'm glad there are a lot of options for the main part of the game; the damn loot.
I found the dungeons and enemies to be plentiful and varied. I never really got bored. Each area has small, large, and champion enemies that get tougher to fight. Some times you will be swarmed by over a dozen, but that is the whole point. Every step led to an enemy and I felt the urge to uncover every part of every map. I always found a secret somewhere or a new champion to beat. Doing this helps you level up faster to make the game easier. There are side quests that are fun, and some down right tough bosses. A couple at the very end had to be beaten 2-3 times over which is a challenge all on its own.
When you die Torchlight punishes you with gold instead of lame armor damage. Resurrecting at the entrance is the cheapest option, but doing so in town is free, just inconvenient. The best one is resurrecting on the spot but costs 3 times as much as at the entrance. This really makes you think if it is worth it or not. Usually I only resurrected on the spot in the middle of a large overworld area where backtracking would take forever.
You still get a pet this time around, you can equip armor and other items on it. You can have your pet take your loot back for you, sell it, and now you can give it a list of items like potions and scrolls to bring back for you. You lose your pet for 2 minutes, but this is a life saver. Let your pet do the tedious work while you continue fighting. I found this almost revolutionary for the genre which is already one of the least updated in the gaming world.  If you want one reason to play this, the loot is what kept me going. I wanted to acquire new abilities, and get the best weapons and armor. There is also great balancing in multiplayer which is what most people are going to play.
Overall, Torchlight II is a lot of fun and has all the genre staples that people want, lots of great loot that is dished out often, tough boss fights, and a lot of strong varied enemies. Sure, the game isn't a technical hound, but who needs that for this type of game? The story kind of sucks, but in the end we just want to click away and kill stuff. Diablo III and TL2 are always being compared for a reason. TL2 did everything everyone expected D3 to do and it didn't. For even a fraction of the cost of D3 this game is a steal.
~Score: 8.5/10

Overall it was a fun hack and slash, Diablo style game. Like the borderlands games, I would recommend that you play this game cooperatively with friends. If you played the first Torchlight game, the second is much more polished and fun to play. If it goes on sale, order some pizza and drinks, grab some friends, and pool some money together for the 4-pack and have a good time.
Pros:
-Good color color pallet choices for the cartoony art style
-All classes felt unique and fun, all were very viable in single player and multiplayer (a huge improvement from Torchlight 1) [seriously, this felt like one of the best class balances I've had in a long time]
-Compared to Torchlight 1, there was improved UI customizations, runspeed/navigation tweaks, etc. (generally more user friendly and comfortable to do various things)
-The music choices were generally decent (though I haven't played in a while and may not remember this aspect the best)
Cons:
-Storyline was sparse, but was functional/adequate. There weren't nearly as many cutscenes as I thought there would be or would have liked there to be. The written dialogue wasn't very engrossing, but it set the premise for the character actions in the game.
-If you liked the darker/grittier visual styles of Diablo, Path of Exile, or The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing, the cartoony artstyle may be offputting to you

Long story short - this game gets a lot right but it also gets way too much wrong. And Rockstar is the Devil.
Short story long - GTA V is rather hard to review because what the game does well it does really well but what it does bad is an abomination and an insult which makes reviewing this game an incredibly conflicting experience. Parts of this game really shine such as the voice acting never fails to disappoint and adds to the immersion and cinematic effect of the game. Cinematic effect is also one of the games strongest points as it has Hollywood level story telling atmosphere, really making you believe that you are living out your craziest criminal fantasies as a drug dealer, CEO, Arms dealer or (as of late) smuggler. The games graphics help to achieve this as while they are slightly dated they still feel remarkably modern and are certainly satisfactory.  Incredibly wide customisation that range from your player themselves, to their car and aircraft also allow you to build your criminal empire in the image you want. Given this a GTA game it also offers an acceptable amount of exploration on a considerably large map however the map lacks some of the depth and detail of previous Rockstar titles, whilst this may be nostalgia talking, even the original  San Andreas way back in 2004 felt like the map had more thought put into it.
Lack of depth is a common trend in GTA unfortunately but it is hidden under a mirage of pay walls and a pretty and colourful surface layer. The best example of this is the vehicles especially the cars, on the surface cars seem incredibly diverse especially with the customisation and impressive visuals, but after you’ve spent millions on purchasing and upgrading them they all feel and handle incredibly familiar with minor differences. This theme is the same with the weapons, all apart from the top level and most expensive are just mind numbingly similar with bland audio and handling. By far the most aggravating example of this lethargic attitude to content is the businesses. On the surface these businesses such as being a drug dealer seem fun and entertaining first and a way to gain money and XP second however after a few hours of owning a business, its function for being fun plummets and its priority for making money skyrockets. This occurs because you realise there are so few missions for each business that it just becomes an endless loop of you repeating the same missions over an over so you can grind your way to buying an overpriced car that turns out to be as identically disappointing as the last one you bought.  The only reason you continue to use the business is because it is the fastest and most reliable method of making money, but this is relative to the other methods, in absolute terms it is still incredibly slow and unreliable exposing GTA Vs lack of depth and adding to the grind.
The term ‘grind’ is important here as when playing GTA online you get the sense that the game is engineered to force the player to grind, GTA has so much grinding in it might as well be that homosexual dating app. The reason for this is that it is in Rockstar’s interest to make acquiring money through in game means as tedious as possible yet just fun enough to not make their marketing strategy so obvious. This marketing strategy is the Shark Card.  The Shark Cards are essentially a cash converter that converts your hard earned real world money into in game money, this gives you a way out of the tedium of grinding and after you’ve been driven insane by this tedium the Shark cards seem even more attractive. The evil of this marketing strategy can be explained using Rockstars fish analogy, the dlcs are the bait and you are meant to be the dumb fish that can only eat it by becoming a Shark.  This strategy is so deceptive and evil because on the surface it appears like Rockstar is a cool developer that releases free content but the game is engineered to push you as hard as it can to make you pay for it in the end, but crucially this method is less likely to alienate Rockstars customers.
The Shark Cards may be more forgivable if Rockstar didn’t still charge nearly £40.00 for an almost three year old game (PC version) this however is not the worst element of the Shark Card. Shark Cards are the hammer that drove the final nail into GTA V’s coffin, (pause for dramatic effect) Hackers! Given Shark cards encourage spending on a game that had already been paid for illegitimate and frankly illegal companies’ piggybacked Rockstars marketing strategy to offer people a cheaper and quicker alternative to Shark Cards or grinding. Programing companies such as A i m w a r   e and Force Hax quickly discovered they could get rich by selling hacking software to players cheaper than Shark Cards, now GTA is riddled with mentally destroyed grinders, people with no real life money and hackers who ruin it for genuine players still clinging onto the shattered remains of GTA online. The way Rockstar deals with hacking makes them look like the Gestapo as anybody who has even been in the same server as a hacker has their account drained and any friendly mods are caught in a blanket ban intended to take out the hackers. This is obviously because anyone who has obtained money the free legitimate way or illegitimately is unacceptable in Rockstars eyes because it means they won’t make their intended profit margins.
Notice how this review neglects the single player this is both because of Rockstars neglect of the single player and to provide a methaphor to show how little Rockstar cares about single player.
Ultimately it boils down to the simple question, is GTA V fun? The answer to that is overall no; however GTA masks this fact with addiction. GTA V is an addicting game it has you working hard and grinding for a measurably satisfying conclusion but this addition could be described as like being addicted to Heroin (I assume). At first its great and you do it over and over but then it becomes about preventing withdrawal and eventually it destroys you and leaves you penniless.  If you have no life ambitions or you are a millionaire thus you have no need of employment then this game is for you as it is great for replicating all the positives and negatives of a full time job but instead of giving you an income it sucks it dry faster than drying your p e n i  s  by sticking it in a Dyson. (I assume).
I don't support poor business practices, put your money into worthwhile indie devs, not these big companies that don't give a rat's♥♥♥♥♥about you, only your money

I bought this based on TotalBiscuit's top games under $5 recommendations. He said that the game had stuck with him for years and now, after I have completed the game, I can fully appreciate why.
The game at first seems like just another puzzle game with a twist in the controller mechanics due to one stick per one brother. But then it goes and throws real damned feels at you. I will not go into details as it would definitely lessen the emotional impact of the scenes that play before you as this unravels from a "hey let's play this with our kids" into "oh what -- can they do that in a game?!".

Controlling two chracters with a single controller is a great and rare concept. It's a workout for your brain. I felt mine twisted and rewired, like when you try to draw a triangle with your left hand and a circle with your right. I want more of this kind of gameplay. I just don't want it to be like Brothers.
The gameplay is so novel and mind-bending, that having a serious tone piece and theme feels disjointed. Puzzle games and realism do not mix. The best example of story in a puzzle game is portal. Portal's concept is absurdly awesome, so it's story has the absurdity to match. It never takes itself seriously and sprinkles humour throughout. The reward you get for completing a puzzle is funny dialogue and immedietely more puzzles. The reward for completing a puzzle in Brothers? Grim unskipable cutscenes, some world building walking around, and sight seeing locations, but it doesn't do dark themes, world building, and visuals better than the myriad of other games, movies, or books can do. I will talk about my opinion on the ending last, in the spoiler section. I have my reasons for disliking it, though lots of peopled seemed to disagree. The non-spoiler version is that the ending has pacing issues and like the good puzzle or good story telling struggle, the game tries to have it both ways.
So onto the puzzles. I have some minor gripes. Early in the game you have to wait for a troll to help you pass about 4 obstacles which could've been shortened. And everyone has put sheeps on the bridge (see Dunkey's video "Brother Bear") when the solution is something else. It sucks to think of a logical solution in a puzzle game and have it not be it. The rest of the game is genuinely creative so I won't spoil them here. I am excited for further exploration of this concept by future developers.
I hope that someday there will be a pure gameplay focused dual-controllables game, then I would recommend that one over Brothers. For now enjoy the game, read my spoiler section, and let me know in the comments if you disagree.
Spoilers -------------------------------
The pacing issue comes from the fact that right after someone dies, and it's this big distraught moment, we get on a bird and fly through an awesome landscape with a full blooming orchestra. Either put his death later in the game or have this section be sombre and silent. You can't have both.
The death itself feels cheap. And mechanically does not make sense. For all of the game I control both characters. It doesn't feel like my big brother has died because I was controlling him. You care less about the playable character in a video game. As gamers we see them die again and again, and more importantly you don't feel an emotional bond when you help yourself. On top of that it turns out big brother can help little brother the same way dead as he was alive. You can still do everything! The whole helping you from the other side was cool, but doesn't fit the overall theme. If they're truly inseperable and his death was indeed a big deal, then have the little bother reach water and drown, have their father perish without sons by his side. It delivers the grim promise of the world more effectively and makes more sense. Again, the game tries to have it both ways by delivering a bad and good ending. It ends up underdelivering on both.

During the first few minutes of playing the game, I wanted to just close the game and submit a bad review. The reason was simple: the game is almost unplayable on a keyboard, and on my controller both sticks were inversed on the Y axis without any option to modify the controls (which is a big no-no for PC games).
Furthermore, barely two minutes of gameplay had passed and I already encountered a bug: the first crankwheel moved extremely slowly (we're talking at least five full minutes of holding two buttons to finish the segment). By snooping around on the internet I discovered that this is a known issue for keyboard users, since you need to mimic a rotating motion with both sticks at the same time. Too bad that A: my keyboard has N key rollover (it can detect an infinite number of keypresses at the same time) and B: I was using a damn controller and it STILL didn't work.
The issue with the inverted Y axis can be fixed by editing the .ini file, but honestly it shouldn't be something to worry about in such a high profile indie game.
That's a pretty lenghty segment on negative aspects of the game, and they were almost enough to turn me off the game. Luckily, I heard a lot of good things about it so I didn't let it dissuade me and kept going. The graphics are enjoyable and pretty to look at, but the sound and the imagery are the artistic aspects that really help the storytelling here.
I will not dwell too long on the story itself, but you basically need to find a cure for your sick father by finding the Tree of Life. Many of the places you visit are heavily inspired by Norse mythology, and you can just frolick around in the villages and sit on benches, play with dogs, pet cats and play pranks on the locals. This has no effect on gameplay, but it does help immersion a lot.
Speaking of gameplay, when it works it's really organic and fluid, you control both brothers at once with the left and right stick, and there is just one interact button for each brother to avoid complicating things too much.
While uncoordinated people might have a really hard time moving two people at once (especially if the brother that you control with the left stick is on the right of viceversa).
The puzzles you encounter will be creative but simple, even people who are pretty bad at puzzle platformers like me had no issue finishing the game quite quickly.
The last thing I want to say is that the raw emotion of this game is something that is rarely found. It is not forced, it happens on its own (there are no *cry now please* moments, although it might make you cry) and in the end, you feel like life goes on, as it should. This is sometimes tied very well to the gameplay mechanics, but I can't make a specific example without spoiling the end of the game.
At the current price of less than three dollars/euros, I would definitely recommend this game. At full price it is a tough sell, but if you do not mind the technical issues you might have, it still is a very unique game and work of art that you will enjoy and remember for many years.

Guess I should say right out the gate - I never played the original Deus Ex.
I don't mean Human Revolution - I did play that - I mean the OG of the OG Deus Ex. I think when I was a kid, I may have gotten my hands on it for about an hour at MOST on ps2 but I never played it through and thus I cannot compare it to that or really say what it's place is in the series.
I think it's a good game.
-STORY-
The story is the typical techno-future cyber-noir we're used to. Adam Jensen speculates on the killers and motives of the illumaniti in dulcet sultry tones that sound like Nick Nolte ♥♥♥♥ed Tom Waits in a tobbaco closet. He's not that interesting an character, does he need to be? He's just an empty vessel we experience more interesting characters and side stories through. Some really great written side quests here featuring interesting and funny characters, though they feel like they're over before they begun. Which seems to be a huge knock against the game in general. A lot of people feel like the game is too short. I put 10 hours in the first time but was side tracked by IRL stuff, so my actual playthrough is about 26 hours compared to the 43 hours I put into Human Revolution. In my opinion, the length of this campaign is not really my issue. I think the way the story has been paced is an issue. Even 10/15 hours in, I wasn't really sure what was happening. Like i was experiencing an extended prologue. And that's kinda what the whole game feels like - an extended prologue to a trilogy. And here I thought Human Revolution was the soft reboot to the series? /s
Personally, I'm happy with the amount of hours I got from the game. Just not particularly happy with how they chose to pace their story but I had a lot of fun PLAYING the game.
Also, the social commentary is not as heavy as the early trailers would have you believe. It's there but it never takes one side or the other. It really leaves it up to you, as the player, to decide how you feel. So for those of you with an incredible aversion to pandering won't find it here.
-GAMEPLAY-
Mechanically, the game plays probably the best it ever has. It just feels good to play.
I found in DE:HR, that the shooting felt janky as ♥♥♥♥. So despite them giving you the option to play through the game as a Rutger Haur clank from the depths of the 80's shooting people in the face, it just didn't feel good and thus HR was really just a stealth game with RPG elements.The shooting in this game feels really good and exciting. So I can definitely see people doing run and gun runs and stealth runs.
You can upgrade your weapons using a mild crafting system to increase fire rate, ammo capacity, dmg ect some weapons can also be upgraded with a laser targeting system, holosight and a silencer.
However, in some ways like HR, I think the game gives you more options to play it as a stealth action game than a bombastic first person shooter. And I also feel that it's more rewarding to play the game that way. I feel like there are way more unlockable abilities to facilitate a stealth preference. Such as;
Remote hacking = :') I'd like to thank not only god but jesus for having this as an unlockable ability.
There are some interesting offensive abilties like the Typhoon, shooting blades from your wrist, combat focus to almost slow down time during a firefight, armor skin ect and some things that just seem flashy and not at all an essential utility to the gameplay. I can't really talk on how these abilities FEEL as I played stealth and talked my way through most situations.
On top of that, they just give you so many different routes and options to dealing with your objectives. I felt like even when I was scouring every corner, i'd get into the office i was tasked with infiltrating only to discover there's a ♥♥♥♥ing vent, that woulda bypassed all the camera dodging.
-PERFORMANCE-
Rig: i7 4770k, 980ti, 16gb ram, win 7
It seems to run fine... for the most part. There were at times framedrops right down to 45fps. It seems to be rock solid during playing within interior levels. The game looks great but not so amazing that these fps drops in Prague feel warranted. It should be better optimized than this. I also noticed some really bad graphically glitches. Some weird ghosting on the weapon models, graphic tiles flickering and some objects colliding with other objects caused some catastrohpic physics bugs. Not sure what that's all about. There are times when the game seems incredibly polished and then times I feel like i'm walking through an alpha build. It didn't mar my enjoyment of the game THAT much but it's worth noting that this far from release it's still not fixed.
Overall,
I really enjoyed my time with the game. Learning more about the world, the side characters were really appealing and the gameplay had me enthralled and playing into the early hours of the morning with a neat story that's just poorly paced and unfortunately feels like the prologue to a bigger story, and some baffling performance that should be fixed by now.
I won't reccomend it for full price but I think it's worth playing at a later date.

In short : It's a throw away game, entirely skippable. The design and execution is stale, seen a 100 times before, with nothing exciting or innovative to keep your attention. The story has no soul, you are just going through the motions half bored to death. And to top it all, there is little attention to detail and you keep noticing flaws that kill immersion because they remind you it's a video game.
+ Graphics (but who cares about graphics if the game is not great?)
- This is the big one : THIS IS HALF A GAME. You're buying a car without the wheels, sold separately as DLCs. I am ok with DLCs and often buy them, but when the base game FEELS stripped and half there? No thanks. Did you know that you won't even close the ending / story without a DLC?
- Boring! From dialogues to characters to the "story" nothing seems to draw you in. It's just typical color by the numbers BS that we have seen 100s times before.
- No attention to detail, so many flaws that interrupt immersion.
Attention to detail is often what differentiate a great immersive story that draws you into its world and universe from a mediocre excuse of a video game. A couple of examples : First cutscene, 2 NPCS walk THROUGH ME. Have they even tested this? At the appartment, the mirror in the room doesn't reflect you, worse it reflects a different room from the one you are in! Another example, you get to the airport, there are clearly 2 doors, one marked for humans, the other for the enhanced (supposedly showing you the divide in society and opression of the augmented)... BUT everybody just walks through the human door including you, even though there are more security guards surrounding you than people. Why bother creating a world if it doesn't even abide to its own rules? All of these 3 flaws are in the very beginning of the game. Those messed up details keep showing up and it is frankly very distracting and immersion killing.
But worse is the setting and story and the pacing. It is hard to play this game because everything feels so stale, boring, and "seen before a 100 times". Even if it is supposed to be story oriented, in 6 hours it didn't make me care about anything. I don't care about the plot, nor the characters, nor what is going on, nor the outcome.
It's more of the same. Your typical vent climbing simulator, with the typical "I lost all my powers after the intro". The hacking is boring. The loot is boring. The restricted inventory is boring. The locations are boring. The voice acting is not bad but dialogues are boring. It is just more of the same and they failed to make you care about what is going on in the game. There seem to be nothing exciting here that can hold your interest. Playing this game just feels like moving through the motions without any innovation from previous games.
So the motivation to keep playing this is very low, especially considering how everyone is saying that the ending is not in the game (cliffhanger to sell DLCs). So not only nothing really interesting is happening, we don't even get to close the story?
Meh. Should have skipped this until DLCs and the "paid ending" were released. That's what I recommend you do if you like the deus ex series : Wait until all DLCs are out, and buy the whole package in a big sale. The game is nothing great, you're not missing anything by waiting for a sale.
If you haven't played any deus ex or not especially a fan, definitely NOT recommended. This game is entirely mediocre and skippable.

I don't really understand all the hate - it does not deserve mixed reviews in my opinion. The monetization (you can use real $ to buy praxis kits) is philosophically irritating, but you can just ignore it because you can overmax Praxis just in the game. Breach mode is a great concept and generally fun - although the later missions can get harder and more ridiculious, I've been able to complete them so far without any mictrotransctions. Philosophically aggrivating choice for the dev, but they are basically giving you a extra game and dozens of hours of extra game time.
I preordered the game, and I couldn't run it at all at more than 5 fps on my 4+ year old potato laptop originally - new desktop handles it okay. I really hope they make the next game in the series even though this one apparently sold lackluster, because it's great. I'd pay full price again in a heartbeat, which is a rarity for me. If it goes on sale and you like HR or DX1, grab this sucker. If you're a DX die-hard, I'd say just grab this sucker now.

Eidos Montreal's hugely anticipated sequel to Human Revolution was met with mixed reactions. I hate to say it, but a lot of the criticism had a fair basis.
1. The game is short, feels like half the scope of DX:HR.
2. The final mission is underwhelming, and the ending gives you so little closure that you effectively feel like you've only played half a game that promised so much more.
3. Story DLC was announced at release, confirming that Squenix intended to make you pay again - several times - for the other half.
4. Jensen's new augmentations look promising, but you can't use them without a rather clumsy overclocking mechanism for 75% of the campaign, and realise they are anything but critical to completing the other 25%.
Yet.
Yet I'd be dishonest if I claimed I didn't enjoy this new installment in the series. If I said the story wasn't compelling, if I claimed the atmosphere wasn't powerful, if I pretended the themes were not thought-provoking. Sure, the resonance with modern issues such as racism, segregation and terrorism feels naive or simplistic at times. Yet the picture can be strikingly convincing at others.
More importantly, I had a good helping of classic Deus Ex fun while navigating, exploring and infiltrating the multiplee layers of DX:MD's recreation of Prague. My cyberpunk itch was massively triggered by the exploration of Utulek and the subsequent infiltration sequence, which is up there among my best memories in the series. And even though I was ultimately let down by the ending, this only emphasizes how deeply I had been into the game up until that point.
I would still recommend it to DX enthusiasts, although maybe not full price, and certainly not with season pass or any DLC. There isn't even that much extra content released or announced yet, so better take MD for what it is: a very solid half game. Maybe 70% of a game. Episode 1 or something. Episode 2 might suck, be a ripoff or just never materialize, but 1 is solid.

GTA is in itself, especially story-wise, a great game with loads of features and tons of stuff to do.
Multiplayer is an extension of that and what I will be focusing on here.
It brings a bunch of new vehicles, features, missions, characters into the game and allows you to play, with friends or alone, in the city of Los Santos and do as you wish. Fly a bomber plane, get a tank, buy an office and start stealing cars, buy a yacht.
Multiplayer does however also include outragiously priced items such as a 50000 hat or a 100000 Suit. And that is just the clothing - which is optional. Vehicle prices skyrocket from "acceptable, but high" to "insane" very, very quickly. Some "normal" super cars cost upwards of 2 million dollars, with more added rather frequently. Others, so called "special vehicles" cost upwards of 3 million - the APC for example.
There are a bunch of buisnesses for the player to run, you can craft weapons and sell them, smuggle narcotics and other illegal stuff, become a CEO and steal cars/supply crates or get yourself a motorcycle club and produce drugs which you then sell.
Those are some amazing things to do, admittedly. The issue, with all of them consnsitently, is the pricing. 4 million dollars for an office, between 1 and 3 million for a bunker, another 2 to 3 for a hangar - the motorcycle club actually comes in rather cheap at 200000 dollars. Oh, I nearly forgot, to actually make money you again have to invest into your buisness, sometimes going over one million dollars.
Now lets get into the cool stuff, I will just list a few prices here:
With the, at the writing of this review, most recent DLC airplanes were added into the game. Most of these are really rather cool to fly and kill people with - but at the same time the cool ones start 4-5 000 000 $.
With the update before that the developers added a sniper rifle that shoots explosive rounds. It takes just a few of those shots to, without exception, destroy all airplanes. Heck you don't even need to reload to get multiple of them.
Now the prices wouldn't be that bad if it weren't for the fact that you have to grind for ages to get anything done. Hours to get to 500k, and guess what, you need 10 times that. Easily.
Rockstar has also decided to drip-feed content to the users over weeks, even months, which makes it even worse. New content would be great if it would be affordable.
At this stage GTA Online has become such a grind that any attempt at getting into it now, without cheating, is futile and a waste of money.

I have played this series through most of it's incarnations. DDS: Pro Basketball 2017 is by far the best.
If you are interested in a basketball GM sim, in the vein of Baseball Mogul or OOTP Baseball, or are a fan of management games, this game is the best basketball game available. In previous versions it was difficult to build teams using the draft, this version while not perfect offers a realistic team building experience. Occasionally you will find the next LeBron James or Stephen Curry, but more often then not you do not. You have a wide variety of stats to sift through including advanced stats like TS% and +/- stats. Often times a player's rating does not reflect their actual impact on the game and in this case carefully tweaking the roster can result in your team winning more games. Overall it is an accurate simulation of being an NBA basketball GM.
I have put hours into this game and similar versions and overall I highly recommend the game for people who are into this genre. It is a lot better than the previous versions as far as statistical accuracy.
PROS:
Best Basketball Management Game on the Market.
Fairly accurate stats.
Computer generated players have relatively realistic statistics.
Team chemistry matters.
You can make expansion teams
Tons of stats to sift through
Cons
You can exploit CPU AI(To a degree, the CPU GMs are not complete idiots)
Too many players play all 82 games
The D-League Draft takes too much time.
Draft is a little too predictable, no random surprises in the 2nd round.
Overall highly recommended. Much better than previous incarnations.

In the past, I have used the term "cheap 80's action film" as a derogatory term towards games that I felt had lots and lots of explosions, but had a weak or nonsensical plot. But what if the game's very intent is to be like a cheap 80's action film? In that case, I can't really use that term as a negative point, and it is exactly what Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is trying to be. Everything screams 1980's vision of the future: nuclear apocalypse between the US and USSR, lasers, cybernetics, lots of neon, and a plot that fits quite well.
The gameplay itself is basically Far Cry 3, but on a smaller scale and with all the aforementioned style changes. You are still on a tropical island, and it is still filled with animals that will try to kill you. If anything, its even more dangerous this time around because the titular Blood Dragons are extremely tough and are by far the most dangerous enemies in this game. And there are bases to liberate that later give you missions and fast travel opportunities. If you have played Far Cry 3, you know exactly what you are getting into here.
So if you liked the gameplay of Far Cry 3 and would enjoy messing around in another island map, but with a totally different sort of style to it (one that may even be better done than the one in Far Cry 3, actually), then this is worth checking out. It's a bit on the short side with me having taken ~12 hours to 100% the game, but it was a fun little adventure where I got to make alot of things blow up.

These include a DLC that adds the action of moving left and jumping, a DLC that gives your character a useless top hat, a DLC that fixes a bug that could have been fixed before game release, a DLC that adds a useless NPC, a DLC that gives the chance to change your name once, a DLC that shows a health bar...
Besides the idea of buying DLCs, the game itself is well-made. The control feels fluent, and the graphic and soundtrack combine to produce an 8-bit oldschool style. And the final boss battle is creative. I'll not spoil it here, but it also involves DLC, and is fought in a way I've never seen before.
+ a game about games
+ fluent control
+ oldschool graphic and sound
+ humor
- 1st campaign is too short
- would be better if the Map DLC actually gives a map
9 out of 10, marvelous.

Let me get straight to the point: Ford Racing 3 isn't a genre-shattering experience. If anything, it can feel pretty generic at times.
Even though I originally played this game on the PS2 back when it came out 10+ years ago, I can safely say this game is NOT a looker. The graphics aren't awful, it's just that everything looks bland, even for the year it originally released, and yes I downloaded the widescreen patch. The soundtrack is completely forgettable and on default audio levels you almost won't even hear it. The car handling is kinda floaty and small bumps can sometimes send you spinning out of control, which can be mildly annoying the first time and pretty annoying later on. The AI racers are a joke, only mildly rubberbanding to your position every once in a while and failing to pose any sort of challenge unless this is literally your first racing game.
In other words, Ford Racing 3 is kinda meh. On the other hand, it's also kinda consistent in its own low budget arcade racer sort of way.
For starters, Ford Racing 3 has some cool race types. Relay races where you drive a lap with one car, "pass the baton" to a second car which you switch control to, and then pass to a third car for the final lap. Racing Line races where you have boost, but only acquire it by sticking to the ideal racing line of that track. That's only 2 of them, and there's like 12 different race types here, including the expected standard race and elimination of course. Some of these are just solo challenge style modes, like overtaking a certain amount of cars or grabbing green pickups while dodging red ones, but the variety in race types is kinda good regardless.
The other real plus of this game? The cars. There are quite a few different kinds of vehicles here, even if every single one is obviously a Ford. From rally cars and trucks, to classic muscle cars and more modern sports cars, there are some interesting cars on display here. Unreleased concepts? Yep. A NASCAR stock car circa 2004? Check. There's a championship near the end of the championship mode where you have to use classic cars, and by classic I mean Model T sedans. How many racing games let you drive a Ford Model T down a country road at 100+ mph like you equipped it with nitrous? If that single sentence doesn't convey what kind of racer Ford Racing 3 is, I don't know what would.
Is Ford Racing 3 a fantastic game? Absolutely not. Is it fun in a cheap arcade sort of way, like something you would find in a bargain bin at a local game store or in the back corner of an old arcade shop? Yeah, I like to think so, especially considering this game apparently did receive an arcade version. Do I recommend it? Sure, especially if you've exhausted most of the more well-known options in the racing department and are looking for something kinda disposable but not bad. Besides, this game is over a decade old now and I've played way worse racers that cost much more than this does nowadays, like Motorcycle Club...ugh.
That being said, as of me writing this I'm currently playing through the sequel to this game, Ford Street Racing, one I didn't play back when it came out, but I'm playing for the first time. How they went from this kinda fun racer to...well, that half-baked snorefest, is a story for another time.

I played and enjoyed Human Revolution quite a lot. While it didn't hold a candle to the original Deus Ex, the gameplay was sufficiently diverse and interesting, with multiple options to go through each map. Which means my expectations for Mankind Divided were high. I mean, you follow up a successful game with something bigger.
That didn't happen. While the gameplay remains mostly the same, and you can still find a lot to enjoy there, it all feels rushed. There's a sense of unwarranted urgency to the main storyline, which feels like the first two acts of a three act play. In other words, way too short, and quite frankly, uninteresting. Which is also the word I would use for the characters. They feel generic and, if possible, even more underdeveloped compared to HR. There's little else to invest in here, as the conspiracy part, which should be the backbone to any Deus Ex game, is slim and somewhere on the outskirts, intangible. Even HR managed to do a better job of integrating that into a silly story(which is to say each part of the story was more interesting than the sum of them), and HR was laughable at times.
While I do recommend picking this up if you're a fan of the series, I also recommend doing it at a reduced price, otherwise you will not get your money's worth.

* EXTREMELY LOUD SOUND. Seriously, my ears are almost bleeding. With my sound set to 10, I still had to take off my headset. And I could still hear it!

* STUPID RESOLUTION. Because the game has no options or settings, I can't change the resolution to fit my monitor. It's only half the screen that's used, the rest is just white.

Because of Steam taking some of the money you make from selling on the Market, you'll only get around 0,05€ per card. This means that I will be able to make 0,15€ off of a game that I spent 0,15€ on. Which means, that this is basically free 7 XP for your Steam profile. Off course there is the miniature chance of getting a Booster Pack or a Foil Card drop, which will make this more valuable.
Don't buy this game. Not even for the Trading Cards. Unless you're able to get it for free or for less than 0,10€, don't get it. It's not worth it. Trust me.
