TL;DR - Pay-To-Win, grindy/boring/long progression
I love WWII games. I love this game. I also hate this game. I play until I'm sick of it, and come back to months later hoping it's improved at all. It never does.
Progression is a crawl. I've played plenty of multiplayer games in my day that have progression - MMOs, FPSs, you name it. It's not necessarily difficult to progress in this game, but it's so slow, it feels like you aren't progressing at all. On top of that, any upgrades or gear you can purchase in-game cost insanely high for anybody trying to improve their chances. Don't forget that you have to repair your gear every few matches, which sets you back even further.
I refuse to pay for premium or premium currency. That alone makes this game incredibly difficult, grindy, and unrewarding. You're stuck with low-quality weapons in low-res/low-visibility combat situations where you don't have a chance unless you've been grinding for hours and purchased your first SMG. Even then, you hardly stand a chance. Don't even think about optics, as they are very expensive and will take you hours upon hours of grinding to unlock (unless you pay for progression). Don't expect to get a sniper rifle and scope when you transfer your soldier to the Sniper class, either.
There are 10 player levels, each with minor rewards. You can get to player level 9 quickly, and each little boost to your funds is a welcome gift. Once you're at level 9, however, you're stuck there with no other progression or rewards for quite a while until you reach level 10, and unlock the strategy game - if you hadn't already paid cash for a General.
The bottom line is, this game is blatantly Pay-To-Win. While you CAN spend hours upon hours grinding for viable gear, you'd probably be better off dropping $50 to get the good stuff right away so you can at least enjoy the game.

First and foremost, the game has pretty severe lag issues.  When lag strikes, your character basically teleports all over the screen and dies.  You'll find yourself fallen underneath the level when a split second ago you were punching your enemies, and you have no idea how your more recent inputs could have possibly put you there.  It just happens.  At random.  All the time.  And my internet isn't bad.  I don't have bad lag issues with most games.
Second, I came looking for something reminiscent of Smash Bros style fun, and didn't find it.  The only things similar are the control scheme, and the goal being to knock enemies off the screen.
Item chaos is nowhere to be found.  There's only a couple that drop about, and they're incredible uninteresting. I get the feeling that it's because this game tries to he a hyper-competitive "FINAL DESTINATION/FOX ONLY/NO ITEMS" style approach to the game type founded by Smash Bros.
The variety among characters is also pretty subtle.  They have slight variation in 4 stats.  When not holding a weapon, their movesets are all identical.  When holding a weapon, they get basic moves and power attacks.  The basic movesets are identical between different characters.  The only difference is their power attacks.  Each character has access to two different weapons, and there are only a handful in total.
The movesets are not intuitive to learn.  When first picking up the game, you'll often find attacks placed in a completely different direction from what you would expect based on your input.  And they require a decently high level of precision.  For example, many attacks will not hit an enemy right next to you.  They'll hit some space a good distance away from you, at the outer edge of your weapon.  The visual feedback in the animations does not indicate this very well, and early on, you'll find yourself wondering why the hell an attack didn't connect.  Your weapon passed right through them.  And given the unintuitive nature of many attack placements, this can get really frusterating.  Such as a character's forward attack may aim at a spot somewhere up and out from them, that will only ever hit an aerial opponent, and only of you judge the distance exactly right.  When hitting an opponent who is standing on the ground right next to you should be the simplest thing to do in any fighting game, I find this really frusterating.
But what gets me most is how the game disproportionately rewards certain things.  After playing for a couple weeks, I got to a point where I was dealing most damage and often taking the least damage in almost every match I played.  I could hold a small platform with 3 other people fighting for it, and be the one landing by far the most hits, repeatedly clearing space.  But I would lose most games.  And it seems to be because there is a ridiculously heavy focus on edge game.  You get kills by dunking people who are trying to recover off the edge with aerial downward attacks.  You can easily get kills on people who have almost no damage on them this way.  And the more advanced players seem to be able to move their opponents around the screen with ridiculously long combos.  So you can dominate the field for the whole game, dealing tons of damage and knocking people around all dramatically.  You'll feel like you're winning.  But you'll always lose to the guy who spends the whole match unassumingly baiting opponents to the edge, moving them out over it with a combo, and finish it with dunk to the bottom of the screen, with hardly any damage put on their opponent.
Coming from Smash Bros... this just isn't fun to me.  This is aimed at the competitive type of gamer who wants to invest a ton of practice in learning how to adapt to efficient execution of a universal meta, repeating the same gotcha tactic over and over again.  It's not for the type of gamer who likes to pick up a game that behaves intuitively, feel their way through the flow of combat, and aim to win by dynamically performing better at landing more and stronger hits overall than the other guy.
It's early access, but I have no reason to believe the feel of the game is going to improve, unless the developers change their design philosophy.

Grand Theft Auto V, as well as GTA Online, (although one can argue that they are the same game, just different modes), is a pretty good game. My review says that I "recommend" this game; in truth, I only chose that because there is no middle option. The game itself is fun, with many game modes, missions, and fun stuff to do. However, there are many, many problems with the game.
1. Hackers
On GTA Online, hackers are a serious problem. basically when you join a session, you have aa 50/50 chance of having a hacker on the server. Now, I am going to say this; not all hackers are bad, and not all hackers ruin the gaming experience. The problem is with the few that do cause issues. For example, the ones that repeatedly kill everyone on the server, or the ones that turn people into Christmas trees. These are huge problems. R* just makes it worse by lumping both hackers and victims together. My friend once was playing GTA Online, when a hacker dropped about $3,000,000 onto his character. At first he was overjoyed;that is, until he was banned for "hacking in money" a couple days later. All in all, the support for the hacking problem needs to be fixed.
2. Shark Cards
Making money in GTA isn't exactly difficult, but it sure isn't easy. Shark cards are R* way for players to spend real money for ingame currency. This wouldn't be so bad, if only the shark  cards gave more money. In the game, there is a vehicle, a plane to be precise, that costs $10,000,000 of the games currency. The largest shark card you are able to purchase costs $99.99, and gives you $8,500,000 in game dollars. Let me rephrase that; There is an object, a virtual object, in a virtual game, that costs more than $100 real dollars. For that much money, you could buy a couple new games. Shark cards are probably the biggest reason for the hacking problem. If money was easier to obtain, there would be no need to cheat it in. The whole money making system could use a rework.

I wish Steam would allow neutral reviews, because that is how I feel about this game. It's only my second aRPG after Victor Vran and it greatly suffers by comparison. I will examine this game in terms of the Story, Presentation, Gameplay and Loot.
Story in this game is just passable but very forgettable, I only played through the story a few days ago but I have already forgotten most of it. I can remember that it is some generic "save the world from some random but super powerful antagonist" dribble but beyond that I can't remember a single character, plot twist (not even sure if there were any or not) or an event. It's not terrible but you really wouldn't want to play through it multiple times.
Presentation is good in this game, both sound and visuals are quite decent.
Gameplay is a mixed bag, I have only played as the Outlander since I cannot stand the idea of playing through the story more than two times and while it is a serviceable character, most of the abilities seem to be worthless and you end up shoehorned into a build that works. This gets old fairly quickly since you end up approaching every situation the same way. Experimentation is hampered by an extremely mediocre respec system.
I have made this a standalone point because loot and farming is an integral part of games like this for me. I have enjoyed this aspect in all entries of Borderlands and I enjoyed it in Victor Vran. I did not enjoy it in Torchlight 2. Farming and min-maxing gear in Torchlight 2 is just bad, in my 55 hours in the game which included two playthroughs, multiple Mapmaker levels and some dedicated farming I have not picked up a single legendary item. Now you might say that they are legendary and that justifies their rarity but they are worthless to me as a loot horder/min-maxer if I can never get to play with them.
Enchanting is another letdown, it is an RNG plagued affair, both in terms of finding the enchanter you are looking for and the enchanting itself. Say, you are trying to enchant an item of armor with "goldfind" using the "Lucky" enchanter. Well, RNG decides whether you actually enchant with "goldfind" which is only one of 4 of his possible enchantments, it will also decide how great the value of the enchantment is. What's that? You didn't get the enchantment you wanted? Well, that will be 10k gold to disenchant, thank you very much and you can't disenchant a specific enchantment, you have to disenchant all the enchantments at the same time, if one out 3 enchantments was bad and the other two desirable, you will lose all three if you disenchant. Thoroughly disappointing mechanic.
Torchlight 2 is not a bad game but it's not a particularly good one either. The story is just middling, the presentation decent, the gameplay is repetitive and the loot mechanics which is what gives this sort of games their longevity and replayability are thoroughly disappointing.

This little nugget is the product of angst in the gaming community over DLC, freemium games and all things microtransactional. It sets out to entertain you with satire, and to its credit, it doesn't fail in that respect. The protagonist is anything but silent, and I can't help but admire the amount of personality the developer squeezed into him. There were many moments that made me laugh out loud, and it wasn't always the dialogue, as there are many gags in the levels themselves.
While the overall experience is stellar, it's only sub-par as a game. Platforming is functional, albeit a tad slippery, but nothing a veteran can't handle. For most people it will take 4 hours, but if you're savvy in the platforming genre it won't take longer than two hours to beat both campaigns, a little longer to hunt down the achievements you may or may not have missed. Despite the humor being bust-out hilarious, the segments in between, collecting coins, avoiding spikes, jumping gaps, can feel somewhat forced in that they are only there to reinforce the "game" element. I found myself rather bored at one point attempting to find the rest of the coins I needed to open the door to the final boss, only to realize I've been taking the wrong turn to the last depot of coins the whole time. It would help if there were some sort of way to know where you missed coins, but unfortunately, despite all the comical "DLCs" available for purchase, there is no "Coin Radar" or the like. Arguably, though, that would have detracted from the overall message that games that rely on unnecessary DLC (especially DLC that should have been included in the base game) for their business model will ultimately alienate their players. I will recommend this game on the assumption that you will take this more as a narrative, comedic experience than a "game".

First and foremost, the game has pretty severe lag issues.  When lag strikes, your character basically teleports all over the screen and dies.  You'll find yourself fallen underneath the level when a split second ago you were punching your enemies, and you have no idea how your more recent inputs could have possibly put you there.  It just happens.  At random.  All the time.  And my internet isn't bad.  I don't have bad lag issues with most games.
Second, I came looking for something reminiscent of Smash Bros style fun, and didn't find it.  The only things similar are the control scheme, and the goal being to knock enemies off the screen.
Item chaos is nowhere to be found.  There's only a couple that drop about, and they're incredible uninteresting. I get the feeling that it's because this game tries to he a hyper-competitive "FINAL DESTINATION/FOX ONLY/NO ITEMS" style approach to the game type founded by Smash Bros.
The variety among characters is also pretty subtle.  They have slight variation in 4 stats.  When not holding a weapon, their movesets are all identical.  When holding a weapon, they get basic moves and power attacks.  The basic movesets are identical between different characters.  The only difference is their power attacks.  Each character has access to two different weapons, and there are only a handful in total.
The movesets are not intuitive to learn.  When first picking up the game, you'll often find attacks placed in a completely different direction from what you would expect based on your input.  And they require a decently high level of precision.  For example, many attacks will not hit an enemy right next to you.  They'll hit some space a good distance away from you, at the outer edge of your weapon.  The visual feedback in the animations does not indicate this very well, and early on, you'll find yourself wondering why the hell an attack didn't connect.  Your weapon passed right through them.  And given the unintuitive nature of many attack placements, this can get really frusterating.  Such as a character's forward attack may aim at a spot somewhere up and out from them, that will only ever hit an aerial opponent, and only of you judge the distance exactly right.  When hitting an opponent who is standing on the ground right next to you should be the simplest thing to do in any fighting game, I find this really frusterating.
But what gets me most is how the game disproportionately rewards certain things.  After playing for a couple weeks, I got to a point where I was dealing most damage and often taking the least damage in almost every match I played.  I could hold a small platform with 3 other people fighting for it, and be the one landing by far the most hits, repeatedly clearing space.  But I would lose most games.  And it seems to be because there is a ridiculously heavy focus on edge game.  You get kills by dunking people who are trying to recover off the edge with aerial downward attacks.  You can easily get kills on people who have almost no damage on them this way.  And the more advanced players seem to be able to move their opponents around the screen with ridiculously long combos.  So you can dominate the field for the whole game, dealing tons of damage and knocking people around all dramatically.  You'll feel like you're winning.  But you'll always lose to the guy who spends the whole match unassumingly baiting opponents to the edge, moving them out over it with a combo, and finish it with dunk to the bottom of the screen, with hardly any damage put on their opponent.
Coming from Smash Bros... this just isn't fun to me.  This is aimed at the competitive type of gamer who wants to invest a ton of practice in learning how to adapt to efficient execution of a universal meta, repeating the same gotcha tactic over and over again.  It's not for the type of gamer who likes to pick up a game that behaves intuitively, feel their way through the flow of combat, and aim to win by dynamically performing better at landing more and stronger hits overall than the other guy.
It's early access, but I have no reason to believe the feel of the game is going to improve, unless the developers change their design philosophy.

Okay, so where to begin with this game. Overall I've said i would NOT recommend it but i think its more fair to say it depends what you like to play. My recommendation is based on how me and my core friend group like to play games.
So, the single player i have admittedly not completed but it seems like a lot of fun, like any other GTA Game except with the added bonus that the heist setups and heists in game seem to add something, even though theyre basically just missions. In general i do find it a pain that i have to swap between characters to complete missions and i think thats the reason i stopped. If i don't like a player character it tends to put me off the game, this happened with GTA IV and TLAD expansion, i just gave up on it. Otherwise id highly recommend this as a single player game to people who like WYSIWYG games. If you like modding or cheats, like i do once ive completed a game then id be guarded about buying this unless you intend to outright disregard the multiplayer or are a capable hacker as there is the possibility you may get banned.
Which then neatly brings me to GTA Online and the online version of the game. So for the most part its pretty good. Grab a team of 3 friends, train and do the heists and its a lot of fun. Thanks to the continuous addition of expansions you can now own a fair amount of property and a lot of cool stuff (if you can get the money in). I also feel to some extent that its a credit to rockstar that they have actually bothered to continue adding content to this game as long as they have where other developers have offered to do this and then given up after a year of limited additions. Of course, this does come at a price in GTA Online. With the exception of Heists nearly everything expansion wise is disabled in anything other than public matches, probably so you cant farm them with your crew without others being able to challenge you. But as someone who enjoys playing Solo or with a group of friends this is nearly damming, since it only takes one hacker or griefer to ruin a server, yes this is how GTA has always worked, but its also why ive never wanted to get involved in that part of it. If you have no friends youre pretty much limited to the low paying jobs (20k at best) unless youre lucky enough to stick with a team throughout a whole heist that you can get along with. All the other high paying jobs are pretty much locked away in public multiplayer. Items from the latest expansions are often 5 to 20m credits (depending on whether its a new car, boat or core feature of the expansion) but put this into perspective. If you are the average person, you wont know how to cheat, you probably wont have a huge gang of friends to play with and youre probably not going to be top of the leader boards. So, if you want anything remotely quickly they expect you to buy shark cards 3.5m credits are around £30. If you want to play this casually and build up slowly or youre happy to sink money into this then id argue its a great game. Same if youre okay fighting off griefers, swapping server whenever theres a hacker or otherwise generally just want to mess around with people who want to do the same to you.
As for graphics, i honestly would still consider them pretty awesome. When, a year and a half ago i bought 2 980Ti to SLI, i was amazed to see that at upper graphics, you can get building reflections on the inside of your cockpit or star reflections. all things i had never seen with my 780. Now whether theyve further improved it as part of patches for the 1080 i have no idea but this at least impressed me.
My concern with the latest negative reviews at the time of writing this review, is while to be best of my knowledge i havnt had any money taken away from me, if they ARE modifying peoples wallets based on potential hacking, then while some may be saying "well dont cheat" i dont think some people consider just how hackers may decide to grief players. and if theyre offering in game money for real money, then they need to be VERY careful how they apply this rule to players who have paid additional money into the multiplayer.
In conclusion, Detach SP from MP so that cheaters can cheat offline if they want. Mods in single player should never be a problem, no matter the attitude of the developers over IP, most of the developers i know now started life modding games.
Stop forcing me back into public multiplayer if i drop out of a private MP match (it takes longer to load and party find for something im going to quit anyway).
And if you like GTA and havnt at least tried the single player then by all means buy this game, preferably on sale because it feels near criminal that the price has barely dropped since launch yet they have a perfectly good micro transactions system. And the multiplayer is worth at least taking a look at to decide whether or not its for you.

Pressured is a mathematics game in which you have several rows of boxes with numbers in them and you have to click on the boxes to add them up to reach a target number, over and over again.
Then the next level will give you a new target number.
Reaching the target number has to be done within a set time, hence the "pressure" part of the game.
Unfortunately, sometimes the target numbers are not very legible - the developer should have used a better font. If you read the number incorrectly, or if you have to stop to try to read it again, then you're going to get a very low score, because of errors and/or time wasted.
Also, it would have been better if there was a clearer delineation when changing target numbers - when I first played the game, and reached the target number, I was waiting for the next one, unaware that the next target number starts straight away.
You can get over the poor target change delineation, but the font problem really needs to be fixed.
If you're into maths, then it could be an OKish sort of game.
However, I found it rather boring. I guess it just wasn't my style of game.
3/10.

Okay, so where to begin with this game. Overall I've said i would NOT recommend it but i think its more fair to say it depends what you like to play. My recommendation is based on how me and my core friend group like to play games.
So, the single player i have admittedly not completed but it seems like a lot of fun, like any other GTA Game except with the added bonus that the heist setups and heists in game seem to add something, even though theyre basically just missions. In general i do find it a pain that i have to swap between characters to complete missions and i think thats the reason i stopped. If i don't like a player character it tends to put me off the game, this happened with GTA IV and TLAD expansion, i just gave up on it. Otherwise id highly recommend this as a single player game to people who like WYSIWYG games. If you like modding or cheats, like i do once ive completed a game then id be guarded about buying this unless you intend to outright disregard the multiplayer or are a capable hacker as there is the possibility you may get banned.
Which then neatly brings me to GTA Online and the online version of the game. So for the most part its pretty good. Grab a team of 3 friends, train and do the heists and its a lot of fun. Thanks to the continuous addition of expansions you can now own a fair amount of property and a lot of cool stuff (if you can get the money in). I also feel to some extent that its a credit to rockstar that they have actually bothered to continue adding content to this game as long as they have where other developers have offered to do this and then given up after a year of limited additions. Of course, this does come at a price in GTA Online. With the exception of Heists nearly everything expansion wise is disabled in anything other than public matches, probably so you cant farm them with your crew without others being able to challenge you. But as someone who enjoys playing Solo or with a group of friends this is nearly damming, since it only takes one hacker or griefer to ruin a server, yes this is how GTA has always worked, but its also why ive never wanted to get involved in that part of it. If you have no friends youre pretty much limited to the low paying jobs (20k at best) unless youre lucky enough to stick with a team throughout a whole heist that you can get along with. All the other high paying jobs are pretty much locked away in public multiplayer. Items from the latest expansions are often 5 to 20m credits (depending on whether its a new car, boat or core feature of the expansion) but put this into perspective. If you are the average person, you wont know how to cheat, you probably wont have a huge gang of friends to play with and youre probably not going to be top of the leader boards. So, if you want anything remotely quickly they expect you to buy shark cards 3.5m credits are around £30. If you want to play this casually and build up slowly or youre happy to sink money into this then id argue its a great game. Same if youre okay fighting off griefers, swapping server whenever theres a hacker or otherwise generally just want to mess around with people who want to do the same to you.
As for graphics, i honestly would still consider them pretty awesome. When, a year and a half ago i bought 2 980Ti to SLI, i was amazed to see that at upper graphics, you can get building reflections on the inside of your cockpit or star reflections. all things i had never seen with my 780. Now whether theyve further improved it as part of patches for the 1080 i have no idea but this at least impressed me.
My concern with the latest negative reviews at the time of writing this review, is while to be best of my knowledge i havnt had any money taken away from me, if they ARE modifying peoples wallets based on potential hacking, then while some may be saying "well dont cheat" i dont think some people consider just how hackers may decide to grief players. and if theyre offering in game money for real money, then they need to be VERY careful how they apply this rule to players who have paid additional money into the multiplayer.
In conclusion, Detach SP from MP so that cheaters can cheat offline if they want. Mods in single player should never be a problem, no matter the attitude of the developers over IP, most of the developers i know now started life modding games.
Stop forcing me back into public multiplayer if i drop out of a private MP match (it takes longer to load and party find for something im going to quit anyway).
And if you like GTA and havnt at least tried the single player then by all means buy this game, preferably on sale because it feels near criminal that the price has barely dropped since launch yet they have a perfectly good micro transactions system. And the multiplayer is worth at least taking a look at to decide whether or not its for you.

Before we start -- I played the most basic version of the game. I got it months after release, had none of the preorder DLC (which they made free, but I didn't get to use, as they did this 80% of the way through my playthrough) or any of the Season Pass DLC.
Let's get performance issues out of the way. I can't really talk about them much. For the record, I didn't have any (pretty solid 60FPS throughout, on highest graphics) but I'm running a GTX 1080 and an i7 6th gen, so performance issues were never really a concern.
Now, onto the actual review:
This game is a ♥♥♥♥ing blast.
I loved Human Revolution, and came into this with high hopes (though I was cautious about it, due to the lukewarm reviews.) I can say I wasn't let down. The story, in my opinion, is good. It felt pretty compelling through the game, and I was able to follow it a lot better than Human Revolution's, which got pretty convoluted toward the end. As for the gameplay, it feels a lot more polished than HR's. Using Jensen's returning abilities felt more smooth and fun, and using the new Experimental Augs makes for some fun experimentation with the level designs.
As for the length of the game -- it is short. Too short, especially comparing it to HR Director's Cut. I clocked in at a little over 24 hours for my first playthrough, but that's counting me doing every side mission, with a bit of random exploration and some screwing around. I didn't particularly feel robbed, but it really could use some expansion.
I disagree that they went too heavy with DLC stuff for the game. Like I said, I played without any added content or DLC and had a lot of fun. As for the in-game "store" that some reviews are complaining about, the only cash store in the game is in the main menu, at the bottom, in a button labeled "store." At no point during gameplay are you prompted to buy something from Square Enix. And in my playthrough without DLC content, I felt like it was perfectly balanced. I always felt powerful enough to deal with whatever the current situation was.
Overall, game is loads of fun. If you enjoyed Human Revolution, don't let all the negative reviews throw you off of it. It's definitely worth a try.
Side note: Like HR, MD has an amazing soundtrack.

Just completed the game and i have to write this review, because the more i read Steam reviews, the more i believe people are just running crazy.
This game is better than Human Revolution on many levels, except for the story and the optimization.
It´s a lot of fun, and it is crazy complex if you keep in mind that every mission can be completed in so many ways. You can seriously finish the game without killing anybody (even the final boss). I missed the achievement because i killed the very first enemy during the tutorial (i blame myself for that). I decided to kill the final boss because of reasons i don´t want to spoiler you.
There are a lot of critics about the story, but let me say something: the only problem is that is shorter than in Human Revolution. It´s a different story, because in HR it was more epic. The side missions (at least the ones i could find in my playthrough) were pretty nice and the charachters are also interesting and well done.
There is a ton to read, to discover and to find. This game rewards you, if you explore like crazy. At the very end i found it easy, because with the invisibility perk maxed you can walk through enemy lines without big problems.
About the microtransactions: no need to buy them. If you play the game as it should be played, you won´t need to buy anything to boost your Adam.
About the critic "♥♥♥♥, the story is cut and you need to buy the DLC". No. The story has a begin and has an end, period. Most of the people are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of because of the ending (which is connected also to a side quest, in my opinion quite important - it should have been a main quest): you were expecting to know exactly what happened to Adam? I don´t think it will be explained in the DLC, probably will be in the next Deus EX game.
The only thing that disappoints me is the engine optimization. I can run most of the games with super high details at 60 FPS (Battlefield One, Titanfall 2, Gears of War 4), but i cannot run this one with the highest level of details. It´s a pity, because it´s an amazing looking game. Great atmosphere, great music and really nice animation.
So, long story short: is it a good game? Yes.
Should you buy it? If you like stealth games, yes.
Are the DLC and microtransactions ruining the game? No.
Eidos just release a couple of DLC (one is a single player mission) for free. Enjoy.

I got in because of all the comparisons to SPAZ.   I knew SPAZ.  Senator, you're no SPAZ.
My main issue is the combat.  Unlike SPAZ, which is a fast dodge and shoot affair with responsive strafing and real time projectiles, Beyond Sol is basically an MMO.  Tab target, activate your spells (laser guns) then wait for the cooldown.  Even the 'fast' ship is miserably slow and can only stop or go forward, no dodging here.
The city building feels a few 'quality of life' patches behind the curve.  You'll be opening one menu to build a structure, then opening another menu to check your inventory of building material, then manually purchasing any material you're short of on the market, then finally building the structure which costs material and credits.  You initially purchased the material with credits.  Why make that a separate step?
I appreciate Beyond Sol's ambition, but I feel like the team spread themselves too thin.  The city building is shallow, grindy, and not fun.  The combat feels like the mobile game version.  Maybe pick this one up if it's really discounted.

Killing the stuff is so easy that even on the hardest difficulty level I never really died unless I became so bored that I lost focus and then died because I didn't bother to even try.
The main objective in Blood Dragon is to collect stuff, so you can buy more stuff, that allows you to kill more things more efficiently. To be able to get more stuff you need to perform series of tasks, but you just cannot do them without liberating a garrison and unlocking those tasks, these tasks involve usually killing certain things in a certain way, and oh boy, it's annoying as hell. When you're travelling you need to collect random stuff along the way.
This is a game where the main story can be completed within a four hours or less. Collecting the stuff takes probably another four to five hours. After the main story is complete the end game is easy and boring marathon. Especially if you're planning on getting all the achievements like I did.
There are few rare moments when you're playing in a closed hallways and arenas which are used to advance the story. The story is mostly just as meaningless and cliché as most 80's action film plots are but in a wrong way. Result is a boring and meaningless mess of things. The script writers had the right idea but they were the wrong people to do it.
I found it funny that although you cannot reach the kind of speed you can reach in Daikatana or Doom, players can still run faster than the vehicles in this game. Blood Dragon in overall has probably fastest gameplay I've seen in a recently released game. However the gun mechanics don't work like they'd work in an old school shooter. That♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off the most as the game is mostly optimised for gamepads.
I could write more about the gameplay but I doubt anyone would read all that. Let me just sum it all up. This game is boring. Just as boring as the Far Cry 2 and Far Cry 3 are.
Most things in Dragon Blood are suitably 80s. I don't need to pick them up and pull apart one by one.
Visually the game functions mostly OK. Sometimes there are really weird slowdowns but usually just restarting the game it starts to work again. The neon lights and the colour palette in the Blood Dragon can cause huge eye strain and I'd recommend taking 15 minute breaks after every one hour spent playing the game. My eyes were bleeding dragon blood after playing this for a while. Blood Dragon also crashes every now and then without any apparent reason but at least it makes automatic saves after any and every meaningful event so you don't lose progress.
The only thing I can honestly say was really awesome in Blood Dragon was its sound design and especially its soundtrack. It's full of really good FX and music with hints to various films and TV series but it still manages to sound fairly original and suitably 80's. It's just the perfect thing in this game. And I dare to suggest that you rather go to
and order the soundtrack instead of buying this game. The voice acting is suitably bad in a good way that fits the game's mood.
The controls work fairly well in the game but it's just weird how many actions there are which require you to hold a key pressed. Why not just pressing once to do the action? It would have made this game a lot more pleasant to play if instead of stopping, holding E, and then moving again players were able to just tap once when they're nearby something they can loot. I do however understand the need to keep Q pressed down to heal. The healing mechanic worked fairly well but I would have expected to have a separate key for the health packs that instantly give maximum health. I also just loved the fact that there's a dedicated "F*ck you" button in the game bidden to F.
Blood Dragon uses Ubisoft's Uplay which means that you don't get to play the game before you've installed and upgraded that thing and oh boy, it can take time. I probably spent 5 to 6 hours in just trying to get the Uplay to work. It constantly kept disconnecting while it was downloading updates. It was awful. And when I finally had it updated and installed... I swear that every single time I started the game Uplay was updating something. It completely stripped me of any will I still had in me to buy other games made by Ubisoft that use Uplay. As a funny side note the Uplay apparently disables screen capture and pressing PrtSrc does nothing.
That pretty much sums up the game. It's a game about funny 80's stuff without being actually a fun enjoyable game. There are much better games out there but at least to my knowledge this is the only one where you can play as a kind of funny walking parody of a Terminator T-800 that uses Robocop's pistol, has the Rambo's attitude, Cobra's moves, and overall is a generic 80's cartoon action hero with Viatnam War II stories to give the character little backstory, and you fight (and later in the game ride) a f*cking dinosaurs that shoots lasers from its eyes just like in the Dino-Riders.
And yes, it even has a sex scene like the one you can see in 80s and perhaps in some early 90s films. The 80's theme goes up to the point that it even is little bit racist in a funny and politically incorrect way which earns it a lot of points. Oh yeah, this game also has Michael Biehn as the voice of the main character. I'll give more points to for that cleverness. I'd say it's worth checking it out if you can get it cheap.

This is a marvelous game.  You marvel at its scale, you marvel at its possibilities.  This, is a terrible game.  The more you look at it, the more you think about it, and the more you compare it, it is a downgrade within the franchise and a shallow expirience.
Singleplayer:  This suffers due to three things in my mind.  1: a development focus on money making multiplayer which leaves the singleplayer seeming old in concept.  2: multiple protagonists fail to be good individual characters.  yes, they may work together well as character types, but within the storyline there are extreme inconsistencies and a total lack of Franklins reason to exist as a playable character except for the San Andreas callback.  3:  the singleplayer is stuck between being a Ubisoft game and being a story driven title.  GTA 3 and its branching titles were all very much sandbox games with a distictly separate story mission set.  GTA  was all narrative driven and reasoned for within the character and world.  GTA tries to be both these things and just comes off confused and not confident.
Online:  Where to begin.  This has an incredibly toxic community.  This has a series of added content that simply makes griefing more accessible, harder to counter, and encouraged in some scenarios.  I understand the idea R* was going for with this, and it interested me at first, but the more I played it, the more I understood that they were creating a milk machine of investment.  The more you play, the more you compete.  In order to compete, you need to get the good gear.  To get the good gear, you need to research it.  To research its means you need money and a business.  To get a business, you need money.  To get money, you need to do missions.  To do missions you need to invest your time.  How does one invest their time?  Play.  Its a money microtransaction scheme of rage at this point with stupid omissions and a failure to keep prices reasonable.
I will give it that they throw in some excellent lines of dialogue and the voice acting is superb, despite the flaws in the writing.  Also, the graphics are an improvement over 4 and are still goodby modern standards, short a few bad texture here and there.  Also, it has the best shooting system of the franchise.  Its not the best third person cover-available shooter, but its still decent.
If you like sinking time in to an ever rage inducing and increasingly worthless example of the phrase "Familiarity breeds contempt" then you may like this game.  Otherwise, its not worth picking up these days.

Pure freaking classic.
This game has almost twelve years and still doesn't fail to bring unrestrained joy of play. Okay, the physics are a strange combination of arcade high-speed turns and little to no braking and sim generally tough-to-make turns, but it's rewarding in its own way when you perfect every single one of that many cars. The models aren't perfect and as highly-detailed as modern racing fans would expect them to be, but they still are impressively similar to the original things - as the game title suggests, Ford fans won't be disappointed. The variety of cars is a strong pro of the game - ranging from 1923 Ford Model T seen so rarely in games to concept models like Indigo - once you dive into the world of the game, you won't feel the urge to leave it too quickly. The sentimental value is superior - FR3 hasn't aged at all. It was fun, is fun, and will be fun, and that's all that matters here. It's not a game that pretends to be the best racer in history. All it aspires to do is to bring joy to players.
Also, it costs freaking HALF AN EURO on sale. You WON'T get ANYTHING better in that price. I bought it for the sheer power of childhood memories I have with FR series (FR2 in particular) and I don't and won't regret it.

The enemies are fun to fight, especially if you find a randomly generated boss wandering the wilderness. This game also has great economy, with ways to earn large volumes of money at low and high level areas. I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone looking for a good RPG -- I hope you will enjoy it as much as I did.

The Lord of the Rings Online (LOTRO) is an MMORPG mainly viewed from the third person. It is based off the Lord of the Rings (LOTR) books and enables players to create their own character choosing from one of the free peoples (Man, Elf, Dwarf, Hobbit) and then choosing an appropriate class to fit their playstyle. Once a character has been created the player can then explore Middle-Earth at their leisure. However players may wish to level up their character before heading to more dangerous areas of the land.
There are plenty of things to do in this game as it is an MMORPG. However the game only gives so much away for free, and even with the purchase of the main expansions you will still have to purchase certain areas in between the expansions separately. This can be done by using real money to purchase Turbine Points (TP) or by earning them in game, but the rate at which TP can be earned in LOTRO is slow as it involves completing certain challenges that can be very time consuming.
LOTRO offers a fresh perspective on the familiar story of LOTR by making the player an independent character to the story who does not accompany the fellowship but rather completes their own quests and writes their own story at the same time as the events in the books. The character occasionally interacts with characters from LOTR and partakes in certain quests alongside familiar figures such as Strider and Tom Bombadil. This makes the storyline entertaining for fans of the series and also for many newcomers.

how many square rooms must a man bunny hop thru?
this seems to be the dillema with almost every “procedurally generated action game”, that the level design usually boils down to a random arrangement of differently square or rectangular rooms, laid out in a sprawl, connected by short hallways- It’s relatively uninteresting and inorganic- A  far cry from the games that it claims inspiration, Doom, Quake, Heretic, the like, which are renowned largely for their inspired and engaging level design- Spaces in which the enemies can truly shine and provide a challenge, rather than throwing their payload at you from across a relatively flat plane obscured by the occasional obstacle. This isn't nessecarily a con- Just a design choice, I suppose. The gameplay itself is very on par with those games- Bunnyhopping, zig zagging between shots, twitch reflexes, the like.  The relatively simplistic level design helps to set the breakneck pace of the game, which is definitely steeped in "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥wizards" type action. On the whole, this is a very enjoyable and tense game- I like the angle of "Wizards and Monsters" that is used, rather than some variety of sci-fi tripe that is becoming increasingly trite in the FPS genre.

This feels a lot like an oldschool FPS with its fast walk speed, ridiculous air control and constant dodging, even some of the weapons (one of the staves reminds me of the ion canon from Doom) and enemies (lost souls) seem to fit that description despite the game's fantasy theme. None of the spells feels as impactful as a double-barrel shotgun though, which is to be expected I guess.
Speaking of spells, there are a bunch of different ones but those I've encountered so far have been variations on a theme (or rather about 4 or 5). It would've been nice to have randomly generated variants of those items in the style of, for example, Borderlands but the arsenal that's there ultimately is enough.
Nitpicks aside, the only thing I didn't like so far is the first person platforming that sometimes is necessary to cross an intersection or get to a treasure chest. The jumping is really floaty and twitchy (which is good for dodging!) and you can't see your feet or any other indicator (like a shadow) of where you'll land and missing the sometimes very small platforms can cost you a good amount of  precious health.
That's my only real criticism though. This game is pretty great and if you like how Quake/UT/Doom/... control you'll probably like this as well.
Some technical notes: Make sure you increase your FoV from 60 to something like 90 and bind a key to zoom. You can also (re)bind your mouse buttons if you switch to it in the keys menu, the selection box at the top is not for picking either keyboard and mouse or a gamepad.
Linux-wise it runs just fine, but the framerate noticeably drops in some rooms which I wasn't expecting (i5 3570, GTX 660). Fairly sure that was related to water reflections. I haven't tested it on Windows yet.

*TL;DR*
It´s a good game and if you like Human Revolution, you will love this one. The engine is not well optimized, but it is still really nice to see if you play with the settings (if you have a GTX 970 like me, just let the GeForce Experience Software to optimize it for you, and it will be everything fine)
*Review*
Just completed the game and i have to write this review, because the more i read Steam reviews, the more i believe people are just running crazy.
This game is better than Human Revolution on many levels, except for the story and the optimization.
It´s a lot of fun, and it is crazy complex if you keep in mind that every mission can be completed in so many ways. You can seriously finish the game without killing anybody (even the final boss). I missed the achievement because i killed the very first enemy during the tutorial (i blame myself for that). I decided to kill the final boss because of reasons i don´t want to spoiler you.
There are a lot of critics about the story, but let me say something: the only problem is that is shorter than in Human Revolution. It´s a different story, because in HR it was more epic. The side missions (at least the ones i could find in my playthrough) were pretty nice and the charachters are also interesting and well done.
There is a ton to read, to discover and to find. This game rewards you, if you explore like crazy. At the very end i found it easy, because with the invisibility perk maxed you can walk through enemy lines without big problems.
About the microtransactions: no need to buy them. If you play the game as it should be played, you won´t need to buy anything to boost your Adam.
About the critic "♥♥♥♥, the story is cut and you need to buy the DLC". No. The story has a begin and has an end, period. Most of the people are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of because of the ending (which is connected also to a side quest, in my opinion quite important - it should have been a main quest): you were expecting to know exactly what happened to Adam? I don´t think it will be explained in the DLC, probably will be in the next Deus EX game.
The only thing that disappoints me is the engine optimization. I can run most of the games with super high details at 60 FPS (Battlefield One, Titanfall 2, Gears of War 4), but i cannot run this one with the highest level of details. It´s a pity, because it´s an amazing looking game. Great atmosphere, great music and really nice animation.
So, long story short: is it a good game? Yes.
Should you buy it? If you like stealth games, yes.
Are the DLC and microtransactions ruining the game? No.

Last Inua (Platformer) mini-review
This is a beautiful game with some frustrating controls.  I had to turn the game off a few times due to my frustration, but ended up coming back when I found (via Youtube) that the sequence I was having trouble with was pretty short.
Last Inua is 2 to 2.5 hours long, and although the puzzles aren't really fulfilling, after a while I realized that I couldn't stop playing... I wanted to see where it was going.
There is one collectible per level - a glowing "rune" that is barely-hidden, but still miss-able.  You can replay any level, so you won't have to replay the whole game if you're looking to be a completionist.
There are 17 achievements, but I think that only gluttons for punishment will be able to achieve them all... I died A LOT, and although I think that once you've been playing a while that you will find that it's not as hard as it initially seems, I'm still not going to try to go through the game without dying more than three times :p
I don't really understand the ending, and the controls can be fiddly, but I ended up enjoying myself nonetheless.
I loved the graphics and I actually liked the slow paced platforming part, but the flying stage is just so horribly frustrating I would not recommend this game to anyone.

I have a great deal of admiration for this game and have enjoyed many of the hundreds of hours that I have spent playing it. I wish that I could recommend it but I can't, and for anyone who might be interested here is my experience. There is much to enjoy about the game. I like the fact that it involves interaction with others. The range of activities in game is excellent. The vehicles are great and if like me you enjoy guns and fast cars then you too will love this game. That is the good. What is not good is the ongoing problem of hackers interfering with normal gameplay. They go off radar, blow you up remotely and can use 'godmode' so that they take no damage (among other abilities). I have put up with this and still managed to enjoy the game but ultimately hackers and Rockstar's abysmal lack of support are the reason for this negative review.  Hackers gave me, and many others, ridiculous (tens of millions of dollars) amounts of in game currency earlier this year. Rockstar dealt with this in my case by zeroing my accounts. I was a bit upset. I had dealt with the extra income for the most part by buying things (like Pegasus vehicles and fully upgraded office garages) which I would not otherwise have wanted or been able to afford and carried on playing the game (and earning money). So of the millions which Rockstar took away many of them were legitimately earned. However, I had no real complaints at this time since I was able to sell some of the things I had bought and carry on without too much disruption. Just before the last DLC Rockstar removed money again. I had grinded cash importing and exporting cars for several days and just hit $4 million in savings but when I logged on they had 'corrected' my bank balance by $3,600,000. Which is a lot of money. All of which was legitimately earned. I don't recommend it (rather boring!) but all of this is documented in the screenshots which I upload to Stream. So this time I complained. I got a standard reply which was no help at all and just said they were correcting my balance. So I put in another support ticket and heard nothing back for weeks. When I checked it had been closed. No response at all. So I put in a third support ticket - polite but indignant that a legitimate complaint should be ignored in this way. A few hours after I checked back - closed again - with no response at all. So I would like to warn any potential buyers of this game that Rockstar support is no support at all and that they will take money that you have earned legitimately and then ignore you. As a previously very happy customer who bought two copies of the game and a shark card I am really sad that this situation should occur. I read forum posts (Reddit  mostly) about GTA and know that many players had legitimate money removed recently. I read of one (and only one) player who had it returned.  I have never modded and never asked for money. While initially items in the game seem expensive there are many different ways to earn money effectively after the initial struggle and investment pays off. So, I hope some of you find this informative - if you decide to buy this game you will find a lot to enjoy. But....you have been warned!

A decent take on a 4x style game, rather than intensely micromanaging each ship in your fleet, you are responsible really only for the one in the center of the screen, ship controls play much like MOBA style games.
Economic managment is easy to grasp, control sectors, place radar towers in them and generate revenue with from trade, protect freighters and recieve a buff on trade tarrifs.
Salvage or mine for raw materials to upgrade your ships and stations.
Your ships loadout is fully customizeable and can be suited entirely to your playstyle, from self-repairing hull to faster sector-space movement or even a faster charging weapons loadout.
all in all, if youre looking for a game that you can pick and drop without having to relearn specific mechanics, then i would totally recommend this to you.
Pros;
- Easy to stop and start playing at any time.
- mostly balanced gameplay with features still being added.
- wide veriety of loadout options, both active and passive to suit each playstyle
- easily grasped economics system with city building aspect built in and an indipendent market system for each city.
- nearly everything is upgradeable, ships, structures, player's own cruiser, defense turrets.
Cons;
- no pause function, although reloading a game is quick, it would still be nice to hit the pause-break key and come back 5 mins later without needing to reload my session.
- pirates are a joke in late game, and far too powerful early on - despite balance patching, pirates usually win against lower ranking starbase garrisons, regardless of the tech level of ships. (military base for its cost, needs a huge buff imo)
- fleet ship ai for vessels with short-medium range weapons is a little derpy, ships fly around in circles and dont shoot at the enemy.
- faction personalities are out of whack, with diplomatic ai's becoming more interested in war than military ai's in late game.
the tldr, for me i feel this was worth the price and i would recommend simply for the "ease of access" as like i stated before, you can pick this game up and drop it anytime you like, without having to wait half an hour for the world to load up.

I'm giving this game a qualified thumbs up. As it stands game is 6/10, and by release it will obviously be at least a little better. Some people will like Beyond Sol some will not. If there were a few easy fixes, then the game would be palatable to a wider audience.
This game has you build a city in space, mine resources, establish outposts, and fight pirates and ultimately, other factions, in an attempt to dominate the solar system. You build a fleet of ships, each which have different roles, strengths and abilities.
The game is in early access but runs smooth and there are only a few minor bugs. You can stll tell it's early access, however, because there are still missing features, such as ship systems.
The plus for this game is RTS ship fleet battles within a single solar system are not very common. Yes there are 4x games, but this takes place in a single system and you really only command one fleet, although you can set up other defensive fleets in starbases. So it's much more tactical than a traditional 4x strategy or even 4x RTS, although it does have 4x elements to be sure. So not only has the game found a niche that is uncommon, it also requires strategic thinking and advance planning. You can only build one city, so initial planning while thinking 10 steps ahead is more important here than in a game like Sins of a Solar Emprie or the Galactic Civilizations series (and really this game feels a lot different than those.)
The upgrade paths (to the extent they've been implemented) are well done and the best fleets will include a balance of ships. The game is a grind but most of the time the grind is ok as events that pop up are interesting initially, although they do get repetitive after a while.
I have four gripes about the game. The first one is you can't pause the game in singleplayer, you can only exit and re-enter the game. Simple enough to do, but when you re-enter, your ships start over at home base. This is both an annoyance and an exploit - you can just exit the game and re-start to get out of a losing battle.
My 2nd gripe is zoom in/out is not documented (you use the + and - key) and zoom itself is very very limited. You can zoom in far enough, but this game really needs the ability to zoom out more. It is not uncommon for the range of your ship weapons to extend beyond the borders of the screen on maximum zoom out. This in and of itself is unacceptable.
My 3rd gripe is you can only manage your home city when your fleet is in the city. This makes no sense. Why must I dock my fleet in the city to buy and sell city commodities? Or upgrade the city. I should be able to do that independently of what my fleet does. I think it would be nice to have more than one city and more than one fleet, but I understand the intentional limitation here as the one city/one fleet rule keeps the game more tactical and intimate, instead of going the route of the more generic, 'epic' feeling 4x space RTS with multiple bases, fleets, etc.
My 4th gripe is the game is a little light on content right now. However, this will likely be solved upon the game's full release. It remains to be seen whether all the features, once added in, will be enough to flesh out the game adequately.
Really, if these guys could could fix the first 3 limitations (I imagine the 4th will be fixed upon release) then the game would be solid and good. It really wouldn't be hard to fix the first 3 issues, not hard at all. If you can put up with these annoyances the game is worth it. If you can't then it isn't. I like the game overall so I'm giving it a thumbs up.
